text: earth defense force 4.1 / 5 / 6 — technical knowledge wiki this is a game-centered, searchable reference to the three edf generations: the native formats, mission scripting, enemy and ally ai, rendering, physics, multiplayer, save data and known differences. open a chapter below, browse by topic on the left, or use the search box for a class, filename, mission id, byte offset or other identifier. public beta candidate r192 (17 november 2026). this is an unofficial, community-maintained technical reference, not a claim of exhaustive coverage or verified retail-game behavior. source observations, interpretations and modified-runtime tests are distinguished throughout. the project owner reported permission to incorporate edf knowledge hub and japanese workbook research on 15 november 2026; that does not imply unrestricted reuse of every third-party passage or game asset. the public-site package excludes the original research archives and game assets. open technical questions remain labelled; edf 4.1 → edf 5 → edf 6 — conversion and compatibility cross-generation compatibility is a matter of matching runtime semantics, not just rewriting headers. an old resource may parse correctly while having different collision, shader, animation, script or asset-ownership behavior in the target engine. start with the boundaries three-generation format/version matrix and what actually changes between edf5 and edf6. format contracts and non-rules, mdb native conversion evidence, and cas/canm animation differences. edf5 bvm → edf6 angelscript translation and full 141-mission static value-flow audit. native world and gameplay are separate tests source edf4.1 navigation versus target edf6; edfroom collision solid wall versus npc targeting. edf4.1 mission objects and mapped target classes, edf4.1 vehicle role/asset differences and edf4.1 earth eater layered bodies. ed5/6 dlc1/dlc2 29-mission compatibility matrix and edf5 source bvm versus edf6-side legacy bvm identity. evidence strength game runtime, same exact context: strongest evidence for actual behavior. exact source-file/binary comparison: strongest evidence for retained bytes, structures, names and parameters; not a gameplay pass. static source compiler or offline tests: can prove a reproducible representation and build but not that the target game accepts its intended behavior. community technical notes: useful references with original author/source attribution, requiring build/context boundaries. where evidence stops, retain the uncertainty instead of inventing translation rules. the unresolved game questions are listed in open_questions.md in the archive. further specialist references for source-specific mechanics not on this introductory page, use the complete extended topic index. the zip preserves the older, longer guide without alteration in reference/r147-exact-reader-guides/.

shaders overview a shader is only one part of an edf material. the model's vertex declaration, shader family, ordered parameter records and ordered sampler bindings must agree. an mdb material reconstructed from a shader's reflected variable list is not necessarily a valid native material: the serialized order can differ. material and shader reference question where to look essential rule which shader family applies? mdb shader families interpret parameters within their family, not as universal pbr controls how are parameters saved? mdb parameter and sampler records use native mdb order and typed typebyte / sizebyte values how are metallic/roughness/normal values used? mdb material parameters — roughness, metallic and normals described common/brdf path; other families can differ how does cutout alpha work? bc1/dxt1 alpha-cutout study native foliage demonstrates one-bit-alpha bc1, not a rule for all textures is terrain another mdb material? fmep / fieldrender no: field rendering and its resource schema are distinct do distant objects require an lod-specific shader? lod / farmap shader census not universally; reuse and slot contracts are family-dependent example: snd_brdf_map_common the audited ordinary edf6 mdb profile serializes parameters in the order diffuse, metallic, normal_amount, roughness, specular_color, specular_diffuse_blend. this is not a promise that the shader's reflection returns the same order. preserve sampler order and storage types, including exceptions where a numeric-looking field is stored as raw integer bits. version notes edf 4.1: use source shader family and asset-specific evidence; do not assume edf6 common/brdf storage. edf 5: conversion must map known source material semantics and target sampler bindings; a copied shader name is insufficient. edf 6: detailed native material and parameter examples exist for ordinary mdb resources; fieldrender terrain follows a different path. implementation checklist validate vertex semantics and strides; select the shader family; write parameters in native order with validated types; bind textures in the correct sampler order; inspect blend/alpha/cutout rules; then test in the target renderer. an offline parser pass does not prove that the material looks right. community research (14 november 2026) the community research / knowledge hub provides topic-oriented guidance and audited source facts about camera/input, rendering, gameplay, netcode, ui, physics and format differences. source grades and exact game builds are preserved. native common clip and illumination profiles common clip / common light mdb material contracts related native-game reference pages global and local reflection grids across edf edf5 forward water and deferred windows legacy mech base-color differences edf5 dxbc creation and lighting dispatch native terrain dds versus object-material packing edf6 fieldrender dds arrays and fmb leaf materials documents native terrain-mip and slice-array evidence, including a corrected dxgi 71 vs 72 distinction. this is a different resource path from the static mdb r/m/o-vs-reflect/spec bindings and must not be treated as a model shader sampler profile. captured static mdb pixel-shader lanes on island4 the island4 renderdoc material audit distinguishes shader resource names param_reflect_*_spec_hspec from the artist's packed r/m/o family, including four distinct pixel-shader hashes and r5b/r5c/r6a/r6b negative/diagnostic tests. those are ordinary static mdb observations; they do not establish the separate fmep texture-array abi or a finished artist-faithful shader translation. static shader evidence versus the final image the retained edf6 shader oracle reports 485 native dx11 archive entries and 3,449 compiled dxbc programs, but source and bytecode counts alone cannot certify frame rendering. the five bounded analysis groups are common, common clip, common light, water and fieldrender. see the five-family static/runtime evidence matrix, which distinguishes material serialization, shader writes, bound render state and final compositor output. for implementation, treat these as separate questions: is the mdb/fmb data valid; does the correct pixel shader read it; are slots/constants and targets correctly bound; and does the final native frame match? a pass in an earlier stage does not imply a pass in the next. in particular, water and fieldrender cannot safely inherit ordinary snd_brdf_map_common texture conventions.

models overview mdb carries model geometry and a hierarchy of objects, bones and material references. the vertex declaration tells the engine how to interpret each mesh stream; a plausible-looking vertex array is not enough without matching indices, weights and material slots. reference topics component documentation mdb mesh/header layout mdb model format shader and material schema mdb parameters and samplers bind poses, bones and physics proxies mdb/shkt retargeting canm/cas attachment and animation animation records renderer selection and invalid mdb loads resource dispatch and cmpl failure case compatibility rules preserve vertex declarations and bone hierarchy. when a skeleton is changed, re-evaluate animation bind pose, shkt physics anchors, sockets and script/object references together. the documented retargeting workflow moves joints at both ends and rest-pose definitions rather than translating one bone in isolation. successful mdb parsing does not prove correct rendering, physics or navigation. typed loader mismatch documents an example in which a valid mdb was handed to the wrong consumer. additional native edf6 mechanics references ragdoll bones and weak-point bodies native accessory rig physics related game mechanics (native-source references) edf6 weapon-model mab muzzle attachments further edf game documentation edf5 unused erginus king model further edf game documentation edf6 shkt ragdoll scene graph

textures overview edf textures commonly use dds-family payloads, but format, channel meaning, alpha behavior and sampler binding must all be inspected. a dds file with valid dimensions can still be incompatible with a shader or a specific resource slot. reference subject relevant detail packed material masks dds and packed-channel observations native foliage cutouts bc1/dxt1 cutout and mip evidence mdb sampler order native mdb shader families: practical parameter and sampler reference mission thumbnails mission list → dds identity practical constraints for bc1/dxt1 cutouts, maintain alpha coverage across mip levels when the source asset depends on a binary transparency edge. do not globally convert all alpha assets to bc1. for mission previews, a valid dds has to be stored under the named entry derived from list field 2 in the base offline/online image.rab archives for the studied target profile.

cross-version caveats the documented mab offset-base flag changes across studied generations: edf4.1/edf5 0x03 denotes block-relative offsets, while edf6 0x83 uses record-relative offsets. this does edf6 kill counters and trophy.dat: why variable order matters from an enemy's sgo to battle statistics the examined edf6 kill-counter path reads a name such as game_object_kill_counter from the dying object's sgo and increments the matching variable in the in-memory achievement map. this is name-based at runtime: a missing name does not automatically create a new persistent category, so an imported edf4.1 enemy can die normally while not affecting the intended battle-record row. the variables originate in app:/etc/achievement.sgo under achievementvariable, represented in the retained source as rows of the form: ["variablename", "int", 0] the ui labels are resolved separately from text keys constructed as statusinfo_ plus the achievement variable name. adding an sgo variable without its corresponding localized text and battle-record ui row is only a partial implementation. the compatibility trap: save slots are ordered, not namespaced the source re describes trophy.dat as retaining 200 integer variable slots, with the values written by position in the achievement map's utf-16 name ordering. consequently, merely appending a new name to an editable achievementvariable list is not necessarily safe: a name that sorts before an existing stock variable may shift the existing variable's saved index and make old values appear under the wrong category. the edf4.1 compatibility mapping explicitly uses names beginning with lowercase edf41_ because those names sort after the known stock uppercase-key domain in the studied build. it also rejects the extension if the current achievement table already contains a different name sorting after the first new edf41_ key. this conservative failure is necessary: in the presence of another mod's later-sorting variable, assuming the new rows cannot change saved positions would be unjustified. the rule is about the actual game's comparator and target build. it is not a universal guarantee that adding any lowercase string will preserve arbitrary modified saves. battle-record table capacity and localization the retained re identifies the battle-record constructor as using a fixed 90-row stock table. its row-count comparison is a signed 8-bit limit; therefore a compatible extension must not assume more than 127 rows without an additional engine patch. the save's 200 variable slots and the ui's 127-row bound are two independent capacity constraints: the smaller bound may win even when the save format still has room. the studied edf4.1 port adds 18 categories of its own. for example: mothership401killcount is treated as the source's earth eater/brain category, with one counter rather than inventing two separate saved tallies. nestkillcount accepts the source's anthillkillcount alias while keeping its own 4.1 category; it must not collapse into edf6's unrelated anthill category. categories for hector, deiroi, nephila and the two flying drones retain distinct keys. labels were provided separately for sc, cn, en, ja and kr. a marker (4.1) in each language differentiates these ported rows from similarly named edf6 rows; this marker is a presentation policy rather than part of the actual counter identity. implementing a safe extension determine the native counter name supplied by each imported object's sgo. resolve that name to a stable, collision-free new variable name. keep explicit aliases where old and new class labels differ. inspect the existing achievementvariable table, including other mods' additions, and verify the proposed names preserve every preexisting name's ordinal position. check both 200 persistent variables and the battle record's row capacity in the specific build. add the corresponding statusinfo_… strings in each supported locale; verify actual character encoding and ui display separately. test with an existing saved profile and compare all prior counts before and after installation, removal and reinstallation. the retained source-only mapping does not constitute that runtime/save-migration test. evidence and limits: r9 components/objects/pylib/edf41kills.py includes these names, ordering guards, exact-build edf.dll offsets and map/save assumptions. the current article is a code-level reconciliation of that source, not a new disassembly or confirmation that every game build uses the same save format. related: mission-list states versus saved progress, sgo and dsgo typed-tree records.

edf4.1 objects on edf6 multiplayer: native identity and a custom per-object event channel separate the native object network from the mod's messages in the analyzed target edf6 build, a script-spawned object receives a native networkobject identity. all participating machines execute the mission script, so all can construct the object; the host/owner is then authoritative for the state that needs correction. the retained r9 source describes per-object position/target/damage/kill replication and generation of child identities from a parent's identity. for a boss made of spawned panels or child turrets, a child is not safely identified merely by its pointer or its name. the native child identity registration consumes a uint16 index, uint16 sub pair under a particular parent hash. the custom adapter tracks these pairs per parent control block to reject duplicates; newly created children can be held with weak references until the parent itself has a registered native identity. this preserves the difference between constructing a local child object and making it recognizable to remote peers. the same source also defines a mod-provided small-event channel that reuses the object's existing network transport but is not part of the original edf6 protocol. the custom tag is 12. stock base gameobjectbase event types are described as 0–3; vehicle events can use 4–5, and other mod features may use 13/14/15. tag 12 is a choice scoped to the reviewed environment, not guaranteed free in all installed mod combinations. wire format: 24-byte header the custom payload begins with this little-endian header, followed by a variable-length event body: offset type field +0x00 u32 magic 0x4e313445 (e41n in little-endian byte order) +0x04 u16 version, currently 1 +0x06 u8 event kind; 0 is invalid +0x07 u8 payload byte count +0x08 u64 random process/sender identity; 0 invalid +0x10 u32 sender's sequence; 0 invalid +0x14 u32 reserved; required to be 0 the maximum body is 192 bytes (total message maximum 216 bytes). the decoder rejects invalid magic, version, kind, zero sender/sequence, nonzero reserved field and any mismatch between actual bytes and 24 + size. a zero-length body is permitted when the kind is nonzero. this is not reliable retransmission by itself: the format is a validated, bounded event envelope written through the existing game's stream. the source uses the game's stream small-int/tag writer, block writer and per-object networkobject send slot 16; it intercepts receive slot 17 only on copied vtables for selected classes. it peeks using the reader's mark/rewind operations and forwards other tags to the preceding receiver. it does not overwrite every instance of the original native vtable. reject repeats, stale messages and wrong owners a per-object gate retains up to eight sender watermarks (sender id and newest sequence). a sequence is accepted for a known sender only when unsigned new - previous lies strictly between 0 and 0x80000000 — allowing legitimate 32-bit sequence wrap while rejecting repeats and old packets. if the eight sender slots are full, a ninth sender is refused rather than evicting an existing watermark. the receive path queues events only for guest copies of a registered object. it binds stored state to the object's control block as well as its memory address, so destroying an object and allocating another at the same pointer does not inherit old sequence gates. the per-object queue is limited to 64 events; overflow drops the oldest. events are drained at the object's normal update; the queue is not evidence that remote gameplay has been applied immediately. for child objects, a peer that is not yet registered may wait. registration is retried from the parent update, using weak references; duplicate (index,sub) values under the same parent's control block fail closed. the retained source reserves ranges such as 1 for parts, 0x0100 for spawned children, 0x4000 for batteries, and 0x8000 for earth eater-specific spawn identities. those ranges are conventions of this compatibility layer, not a universal edf6 name-to-id schema. qualification and practical use native network ownership and virtual-slot addresses in the retained source are exact-build observations, not portable binary signatures. the 24-byte format, gate, float bound checking (finite, absolute coordinate at most 1e7) and id-range constraints are custom code, not stock edf6 wire messages. a source regression test executes 36 checks of envelope encoding/decoding, reject cases, sequence wrapping, sender capacity and id-space guards; that proves pure logic only. the r71 audit independently compiled and ran that pure test in linux. this is not a two-peer windows/edf6 multiplayer pass. network message delivery, ownership and cross-mod collisions still require live game testing. before reusing this pattern, ensure tag ownership is negotiated with other modules; preserve the underlying stock receive path and validate object lifetime, authority and child identity. sources: retained r9 components/compatibility/src/edf41net.h, edf41net.cpp and components/compatibility/tests/edf41net_test.cpp. related: native per-object online authority, controlled object-tree restoration, and edf6 transport lanes.

edf4.1 small dragons in edf6: partial-ragdoll body names and hit-reaction crash why importing the model and ragdoll is not sufficient the edf4.1 dlc small dragons (dragonsmall401_hs, redsmalldragon_hs and yerrowsmalldragon_hs) may load their own model, cas, mab and havok ragdoll into the edf6 dragonsmall class yet still crash when hit. the failure comes from a class-side partial-ragdoll selection by name; it is not evidence that the ragdoll file cannot be parsed. on the examined edf6 binary, the hit-reaction state in edf.dll+0x339550 builds the pair {koshi, mune} and sends it to the partial-body consumer at edf.dll+0x4a8570. the target game's existing dragonsmall class expects those bones, as they occur in the target donor's frog-dragon ragdoll. the edf4.1 small-dragon ragdolls instead include koshi, spine1, spine2 and have no mune. a lookup miss is subsequently dereferenced, reaching a null/sentinel case at edf.dll+0x6e42eb. the retained source associates that path with the historical m805 hit crash. the corresponding edf4.1 code constructs {koshi, spine1, spine2} for this hit reaction. it is a semantic mismatch in the consumer's required body subset, not just a name mismatch in the authoring ui. exact, narrow repair pattern in the source-reviewed compatibility patch, a ported object is explicitly marked with the sgo key edf41_ragdoll_bodies, a one-dimensional array of strings. the adapter substitutes those names only for the partial-ragdoll call associated with the hit reaction. unmarked edf6 objects retain the target class's original names. the strict key guard requires an sgo array (type=0) of 1–8 entries, each a string node (type=3) with a nonempty name of no more than 31 utf-16 code units. its exact default for an absent or malformed key is to pass the original class list. the object conversion path is responsible for validating every supplied body name against the actual exported ragdoll; merely accepting a syntactically valid string is insufficient. the class's other ragdoll path (edf.dll+0x339dd6 → +0x4a8620) operates on all bodies and is deliberately left untouched. do not globally rewrite body names or substitute the source list for every call in the class. diagnostic checklist check whether the failure occurs on damage/hit reaction, rather than immediately on model load. extract the source ragdoll's named bodies and compare them with the specific native method's selection list. if the target class selects bodies absent in the port, resolve per-class hit-reaction semantics before attempting geometry or physics changes. validate the exact target binary signature and names. the rvas above describe the retained binary, not a cross-version aob signature. test the actual hit transition in game; source-level guards and regression code do not independently establish runtime parity. evidence: retained r9 components/compatibility/src/edf41smalldragon.cpp, including explicit target and source addresses, key parsing and fail-closed call guard. this article does not claim a newly executed game test. related: dragon ragdoll wake mechanics and cross-generation cas controllers.

spatial audio in edf6 mods: listener matrix, equal-power panning and doppler the retained placement model an exact-source compatibility helper documents the audio-listener representation used by a group of edf6 mod sound paths (jet/vehicle sounds and cinematic recordings). its listener record contains 20 float32 values: listener position cam[0:3], padding, and four rows of the inverse world transform beginning at cam+4. the helper converts world position to listener space using those inverse-matrix rows, including translation. under the documented convention camera-local +x points left. for the given helper, distance is the length of the local position vector. the lateral fraction is right = -localx / distance when distance exceeds 1 metre; within 1 m it is zero. the normalized equal-power gain pair is: spread = 0.75 left = sqrt(0.5 * (1 - spread * right)) right = sqrt(0.5 * (1 + spread * right)) these are the helper's concrete panning equations, not a claim that every stock edf6 sound system must use exactly the same mixer. doppler and optional velocity pointers the unit vector u points from source to listener. for source and listener velocities, the helper takes each velocity's dot product with u, clamps each closing component to ±0.8 × 340 m/s, and forms: c = 340 m/s v_source = clamp(dot(sourcevel, u), -0.8*c, +0.8*c) v_listener = clamp(dot(listenervel, u), -0.8*c, +0.8*c) doppler = (c - v_listener) / (c - v_source) when source distance is at most 1 m, the ratio stays 1.0 and the direction vector remains zero. crucially, either velocity pointer may legitimately be nullptr. a null source velocity means a stationary emitter, and a null listener velocity means a stationary listener. it must not be blindly dereferenced. the retained source records a historical exception c0000005 in a cinematic recording path where no velocity was supplied. the lesson is to validate the pointer contract independently of the audio formulas. when reviewing a mod audio hook, verify the incoming listener and source position pointers, the optional velocity pointers, inverse matrix layout, and source/listener coordinate conventions before attributing noise to the audio bank. scope all constants and equations above are directly present in source components/compatibility/src/sound_place.h in the r9 archive. they are a useful, reproducible helper abi and an account of a historical failure; not a newly verified universal edf6 runtime audio specification. mixing, occlusion, attenuation curves and routing to acb/awb banks are outside this helper. related: audio containers and voice/cue separation and edf4.1 sound-bank lookup/lifetime.

edf6 mission selection and weapon ownership: row-state and save-record boundaries mission-select rows and one exact-build ui behaviour the retained ported-content code documents the mission-selection list as an array of 0x14-byte rows in one target edf6 binary. its source model (listrow) is: offset size meaning in retained source +0x00 4 list-row index +0x04 4 displayed mission number (field 4) +0x08 4 row state +0x0c 4 branch value (field 5) +0x10 1 + 3 padding flag byte the documented states are 0 = cleared; 1 = open; 2 = open branch (field5 == 1); 3 = locked but visible; 4 = locked and hidden. this distinction matters: hidden is not equivalent to completed or merely locked. the source's narrow openall path recognizes a freshly constructed list only when row zero has index 0/state 1 and every subsequent row has the corresponding index/state 4. it then changes those hidden rows to state 1 or 2 according to the branch field, before the engine's normal scan. the documented native scan opens the successor of a completed row. no save data is written in this ui-only operation, and already-cleared progress is not altered. if the initial list does not match the expected shape, the helper fails closed rather than blindly patching memory. the source points to list construction around edf.dll+0x8a2160..0x8a241a, with its stored row list at +0x8a1530; these addresses are build-specific. weapon possession records are not mission-row states the retained game-status weapon row is 12 bytes: a little-endian uint32 flags word followed by eight star bytes. within that flags word, bit 0 = owned and bit 2 = newly obtained. the source's ownership helper preserves all other bits. on first acquisition it sets owned/new and zeros the eight star bytes; on subsequent acquisition it leaves existing stars intact. a separate max-star path sets each to ten (after which the stock game applies actual weapon-specific caps). a disown operation clears owned and new flags while preserving stars. this distinction matters when a weapon or support action moves from the ordinary loadout to another interface or becomes ineligible: erasing star bytes would mutate progress rather than only availability. the mod's content-name gate recognizes edf6vc_e5_ and edf6vc_e41_; it excludes edf6vc_retired_ and call-weapon names. these prefix rules are mod-defined, not universal properties of edf6's inventory format. limits and implementation hygiene this is a source-reviewed exact-build contract from components/compatibility/src/unlock_ported.h. it explains what was patched and why, not a blanket recommendation to unlock all stock missions. verify the native addresses and row semantics for the target build. separate mission-list visibility from saved progression, and inventory possession from star upgrades; the same memory operation should not silently implement both. related: mission identity, list and thumbnails and weapon progression/armor limits. for a different persistent-progress hazard, see achievement.sgo / trophy.dat counter ordering.

edf6 native teammanager — seven stock teams, relation matrix and custom-faction limits a team number is not just a colour or hud label the investigated edf6 teammanager stores both per-object team identity and a directional relation matrix describing how team a sees team b. the native manager in the cited binary uses seven rows, ids 0–6, rather than dynamically discovering unlimited teams. its constructor reserves each row, its relation vector and its all-teams iteration with fixed numeric assumptions. the source research labels the seven native roles in the examined profile: team studied engine role 0 basic faction / unspecified player-facing side in the stock matrix 1 enemy 2 edf/friendly 3 neutral 4 enemy-of-1-only role 5 empty vehicles / boarding availability 6 mission environment these numeric categories are specific native-team semantics from the studied game build. in particular, teams 5 and 6 are not spare numbers for arbitrary pvp factions: empty vehicles and environmental hazards/interaction paths rely on their stock relations. the relation values a native relation is encoded as one byte in a row, with values: 0 = neutral 1 = friendly 2 = enemy the relation table has a team-to-itself friendly diagonal. in the examined stock matrix, enemy pairings include 0↔1, 1↔2, 1↔4; 0↔2 is friendly; other unequal rows not expressly configured stay neutral. a runtime mod should not assume relation symmetry as a universal law merely because the recorded stock relationships were largely symmetric: the implementation stores relation[a][b] and relation[b][a] separately. an object's current team field and its saved “last team” field have separate lifecycles. in the studied object abi, +0x314 holds current team, and +0x318 retains last team. closing an actor with setteam(-1) preserves the last-team information. the value -1 is therefore a closing-state sentinel in the source research, not an available ninth or sixteenth faction id. why extending teams needs more than one constant the examined custom pvp adaptation expands capacity from 7 to 16, allocating additional faction ids 7–15. that is a custom patch, not a native edf6 capability. a legitimate extension must update every fixed-capacity consumer: row reserve, row creation/fill, nested relation-vector limits, and the all-teams enumeration bound. the source lists 15 separate exact-build patch sites for those allocations and loops. merely changing one capacity field leaves native iteration and relation arrays inconsistent and can cause memory errors. the game's mission-start and reload paths also restore stock relation matrices. the custom overlay is therefore re-applied after those resets, not just once at startup. the demonstrated policy keeps the stock rows/columns for teams 5 and 6, including their relationships with any new factions, and validates the diagonal and every relation byte. portability and risk the table, row stride (0x38) and fixed-capacity sites were reverse engineered for a single documented edf6.dll build. do not patch another executable at those offsets, assume the game supports 16 factions natively, or claim host/client pvp correctness based on a source patch. a robust implementation must retain exact-build signature checks, preserve original gameplay relations, and qualify damage, ai targeting, vehicle entry and network team synchronization in the actual game. source: components/compatibility/src/team_native_logic.h from edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9 source research, with documented source-side native-teammanager analysis. no new executable/runtime test was performed while writing this article.

controlled edf6 pvp actors — propagate teams through actual emitters and restore every native baseline one actor is not one team field a custom-controlled enemy or multipart boss is usually a gameobject tree, not a single root object. weapon controllers, gun batteries, child parts, live owner-team lookups and cached damage emitters can each read team data. changing only the root object's current team can give a friendly-looking actor whose rockets still target its old faction, or whose newly created child remains permanently flagged as a pvp faction after control ends. the retained controlled-pvp implementation is an explicitly designed extension, not proof that stock edf6 includes a player possession system. its reusable reverse-engineering lesson is that actual native emitter ownership and lifetime must be part of a team-switch transaction. enumerate typed objects and real emission points the source requires a read-only enumeration of the entire supported native child tree and all emission paths. it distinguishes typed emitters such as weapon bases, indirect-fire controllers, gun batteries, owner-team mirrors and cached fields. the example bounds are up to 256 gameobject members and 512 emitter records per controlled root; these are adapter safety limits, not game-engine universal maxima. a real emitter is not necessarily a gameobject; blindly casting its address to one and writing an object-team offset is unsafe. the adapter validates the emitter's actual typed container, owning member and current lifetime before modifying or reading it. some emission paths derive team live from their owner and need no cache write at all. some cached fields survive the parent object and need independent storage identity. full identity and rollback the controller cannot key only on a raw pointer: native addresses may be recycled. it associates each member with its exact object/control-block identity, tracks emitter incarnation and may preserve a separate live storage identity. a temporary team change is accompanied by an owned restoration lease: probe, read-only, validates the tree and whether every firing path can be represented. acquire captures the real native current and last team plus typed emitter baselines before making team changes. frame maintains the temporary faction only while authenticated control remains stable; a pending/unknown owner fails closed. restore writes back all surviving original values and retains a pending lease if any restoration step fails. a failure during acquisition, object deletion, mode exit or network disconnect must not release the lease prematurely. the ability to restore the exact native team depends on keeping original baseline identity, including the setteam(-1) closing state. -1 must not be rewritten to an arbitrary active faction just because a controlled actor has died. spawns must be reserved before publication multipart bosses may spawn children during a controlled wave. a newly created part can inherit the temporary pvp team, so saving its current value as a “native baseline” would permanently contaminate it. the source uses a bounded prepare → construct/initialize → adopt → publish → finish protocol: reserve the anticipated children, prove each source's real baseline and exact parent identity, adopt the child before network publication, then release unused reservations. unexpected children, overlapping ownership or an unknown baseline fail closed. a mother/boss adapter uses this protocol through spawnwave and the motherspawnownership hooks. that is a custom transaction model for safe modding, not a claim about native edf6's default spawn implementation. network identity is a separate surface the controller accepts a source player identity only after an external authenticated core/coop decision. it never manufactures, rewrites or trusts a requested user identity from arbitrary sgo resource strings. even a valid local ownership transaction does not itself guarantee the correct host/client damage attribution; the actual native network authority of root, child and projectile remains a separate requirement. what the source establishes: a rigorous, testable bounded design for team propagation and rollback, based on real native object/emitter lifetimes and team fields. what it does not establish: 16 native edf6 teams by default, universal support for every enemy class, or newly verified multiplayer runtime behaviour. sources: components/compatibility/src/pvp_controlled.h, enemy_control_legacy_mother.h, team_native_logic.h and online_authority.h in edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9.

edf4.1 bvm command 3025 — multiply current object hp without changing maximum hp source command and target gap the edf4.1 native bvm command id 3025 represents multiplyobjecthealth(object,float). in the examined source semantics it scales the object's current durability, not its maximum health. replacing it with setobjectdurability or a global max-hp modifier changes difficulty, future damage and possibly mission completion. the studied target angelscript api had no directly equivalent public helper. rather than changing bvm bytecode arbitrarily, the compatibility implementation introduces a scoped global script command named: void edf41_multiplyobjecthealth(const ::object& in, float percent) for a resolved object, the source's arithmetic is approximately: new_current_hp = min(current_hp * (percent / 100.0), max_hp) max_hp stays unchanged the lower bound is not shown as a generic zero clamp in the examined native implementation. percent must be interpreted as a percentage, not an ordinary multiplier. an exporter that replaces this with current * percent or updates max_hp is not source faithful. source code intentionally preserves the target's sse minss behaviour, whose nan/special-value details should not be reimplemented by casual arithmetic without tests. why a global function still depends on native abi the registration takes place when the game builds an angelscript engine, after the normal bulk registration of stock functions. the inherited implementation wraps the outer call site rather than rewriting the bulk registration routine. that allows another module which independently extends that routine to keep its existing registrations. the exact-build native bridge has a non-obvious c++/angelscript calling contract: the first script const ::object& in is carried as a wrapper argument in rdx, while the float uses xmm2; rcx is not the object parameter. it resolves the wrapper into an engine object/control-block pair and updates only the current-durability field. the resolved wrapper's strong/weak ownership is then released using the expected native shared-control-block semantics. blindly changing a c++ function signature, treating the wrapper as a raw object pointer, neglecting the control-block release or calling the registrar before stock commands exist can crash the game even if the printed angelscript declaration appears correct. what is and is not portable the command's meaning — percentage of current hp, capped by max hp, without altering max hp — is the useful cross-game semantic finding. the engine registration vtable slots, wrapper layout and function addresses belong only to the studied edf6 dll build, and this release did not rerun windows/msvc/gameplay qualification. treat them as exact-build research, not a general-purpose extension sdk. source: edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9 components/compatibility/src/edf41missioncmd.cpp; the broader mission-pipeline contract discusses where command 3025 appears in source bvm.

edf4.1 before.bvm scenes in edf6 — why the dialogue plays behind a black screen the failure can be ui lifecycle, not missing scene data edf4.1 has source pre-mission before.bvm cutscenes. the examined edf6 mission flow can load such a file using its native before() function and correctly pause the main mission script until the scene finishes. but because ordinary edf5/edf6 missions in the investigated corpus did not ship before.bvm, the game's normal ui lifetime was never exercised along that branch. edf6's main script leaves the headquarters menu and its black fade ui active when it enters playmission_offline. the function calls before() before playmission_common, and it is playmission_common that eventually calls deleteallmenuui(). when a source edf4.1 before.bvm exists, the cutscene can play entirely beneath the black menu fade. the user hears the voices and sees subtitles or radio indicators drawn above the fade, but cannot see the scene. this is not evidence that the bvm script, rmpa, camera tracks or model resources failed to load. the original source lifetime was different edf4.1's own main-script path closed hq ui and deleted the fade before returning to the offline mission loader, so its pre-mission scene ran with no menu covering it. the semantic repair in the studied edf6 build performs the relevant native _deleteallmenuui operation only on the control path where before() has successfully found a scene and is about to load its bvm. that is more precise than moving all menu deletion earlier globally: the game checks whether the mission has a before.bvm and whether save state permits playing it. only on the actual scene-loading path does the compatibility code close menu ui groups and the black fade. the native bvm executor loads the scene as before and suspends the main script while it plays. the ordinary playmission_common menu cleanup later runs safely against already-closed ui. missions without a before scene never enter the correction path. in the studied native implementation, _deleteallmenuui closes ui groups 2, 4 and 3. the hook is guarded by exact instruction bytes and the expected edf.dll build timestamp. copying its numeric offsets to another executable would not be sound. how to diagnose a black before scene confirm the file is really before.bvm and the native before() branch runs. check if voice/subtitles continue while geometry stays black; that is compatible with a still-active ui fade. inspect ui teardown ordering, not solely bvm parser and camera tracks. verify the normal no-before mission path remains unchanged. qualify with save-state logic, because before() can intentionally skip a scene already marked seen. evidence boundary: this is a source-backed exact-build cause and implementation, with a native code-signature audit. this wiki pass did not replay the full edf4.1 before-scene set or run a fresh edf6 game test. source: edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9 components/compatibility/src/edf41before.cpp plus source/main-script analysis cited in its comments.

edf6 area damage versus direct hits — why identical collision bodies can ignore explosions the two damage paths do not necessarily see the same body a preserved edf4.1→edf6 experiment showed imported ufomother301 panels were vulnerable to normal direct bullets but ignored rockets or explosions. the panel's durability was valid, the scene objects existed, and their weak-body damage condition had already been satisfied. the root cause instead lay in collision filter layers used by the area-damage broadphase query. the exact-build target analysis found: explosion-capable bullets deliver damage through applyareadamage, not just the ordinary direct-hit queue. the examined projectile path clears its direct-hit queue for the area-damage operation. the area query uses a collision-filter configuration centered on layer 13. eventanimationobject constructor placed the panel ragdoll bodies on layer 0x11 (17). native edf6 damageable enemy objects in the examined target, including the ufocarrier508 donor and insects, used a body layer of 7. the broadphase only visits bodies whose filter pair is allowed; a body excluded from its query never receives a damage message. an object can therefore be destructible by direct hits yet remain unscathed by rockets without any invulnerability switch in its health code. the historical 2026-10-17 m130 control reported zero explosion damage across 125 enabled panels despite hundreds of blast shots, while an earlier plain-bullet control destroyed 122 of 125 panels. these numbers describe those two reported runs, not universal damage rates. filter-info layout and safe policy the studied havok group-filter number packs several concepts into a 32-bit value: bits 0..4 : collision layer (0..31) bits 5..9 : subsystem bits 10..14 : don't-collide-with subsystem bits 15..30 : system group the active layer table consists of 32 words, with a bit for whether a query on layer a may see a body on layer b. the source hitlayer helper checks the actual filter table when available: keep the current part layer if the area query sees it; otherwise select the native hull/enemy layer only if that layer is accepted. when the table cannot be read in the studied build, the target hull layer is a bounded fallback, not a claimed universal rule for every edf6 object. do not globally move every object to layer 7, and do not modify collision shape or damage invulnerability to paper over a layer mismatch. collision grouping affects physical contacts and other subsystems, so changes must be class-scoped and validated against direct bullets, explosions, melee and player collision separately. practical debugging order confirm the object and its weak collision body are instantiated, and direct-hit damage works. identify whether the bullet applies direct damage or transitions to area damage. inspect the broadphase query layer and the body's filter-info layer, not just the object's hp. verify the relevant filter-table pair is enabled. test both native and ported targets, plus physics contacts, before deciding a new body layer is safe. scope: retained exact-build edf.dll analysis, source-level patch policy and historical m130 runtime observations. no new game test was run while authoring this wiki guide. this issue is separate from shield shkt damage gating and from map/mad collision mesh geometry. source: edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9 components/compatibility/src/edf41_hitlayer.h, with original m130 and edf.dll evidence documented in source comments. further native-game references direct-hit queue and hit record

edf4.1 ufomother301 in edf6 — a composite boss, not one spaceship object why a model swap cannot preserve this encounter edf4.1's original ufomother301 is a composite boss with one hull controller and several different part classes. the examined edf6 compatibility path uses an edf6 ufocarrier508-based hull and separately created eventanimationobject parts, but the visible model/animation is not the entire state machine. script commands, generators, targetability, projectiles, effects and death timing belong to different objects. the examined native source lists these original components: part measured source organization / purpose main hull movement, slow spin, phases, weak-point exposure and destruction sequence hatchlow four generator hatches with independent open/close behaviour hatchmiddle four covers; not ordinary damage targets cannon ten subsidiary cannons with delayed activation and fire cycles bigcannon one main charging/sweeping laser panel four rotating rings with 22 / 40 / 40 / 23 elements the part instances are created on the hull's first update, attached through their own transforms and locator names, and driven through edf4.1's original state timing. a model that displays all of them can still be wrong if the expected parts are absent as actual damageable objects or if their mission actions never reach their owners. script and generator ownership the original boss exposes objectaction(0..17), getpartsobject and generator commands. the retained target bridge recognizes source objectaction (0x1000000d) and part lookup (0x10000017) as legacy semantics. in that studied mapping, part-group 0 is the main cannon and part-group 1 is the indexed smaller cannons; drops are forwarded to an appropriate hatch under a message of class 0x20100. hatches do not spawn enemies merely because the model is “open.” the source state machine opens them before the wave, uses the locator named in the actual generator component, and closes them 240 frames after the final spawn. an exporter must preserve the explicit generator-to-hatch relationship and its script-visible group/index; otherwise the mission can advance without ever creating the correct enemies. firing sequences are class state, not just projectile stats historical exact-build analysis in the retained source captures, among others: the main cannon's long charge window (about 1200 frames) followed by a 61-shot laserbullet02 sweep, with separate open and destruction states. a secondary cannon's preparation about 600 frames, with a cycle restarting after a delay in the 1800–3599 frame range; its beam logic fires through four hatch muzzles in sequence, approximately every four frames. ring panel weapons with distinct laser/plasma rates, including a laser interval bounded below by 30 frames, versus a 300-frame plasma interval in the examined source. porting only fire rate and damage in sgo would lose charge phase, muzzle order, animation gating and script activation. damage gate and the weak body the hull's hit filter accepts damage according to the named weak-point body and the main cannon's destruction state. several covers/hatches remain deliberately invulnerable; parts with an “enabled” flag may otherwise be unregistered or non-targetable. a false positive generic hit or damage applied to the wrong scene object can break the encounter even though the correct boss health is displayed. the source hull phases include open/close exposure, slow spin, disabled vulnerable point while covered, short bursts after hits, and a multi-phase death that differs from the target carrier's native deletion routine. the preserved class-specific adapter uses a separate source state machine rather than claiming stock ufocarrier508 exactly matches ufomother301. source scope and caveats these are inherited exact-build reverse-engineering notes embodied in edf41mother.cpp and the source object's component contracts. numbers are 60-fps source-frame state windows, not a promise of identical gameplay timing at arbitrary simulation rates. full m603 encounter and multiplayer parity must still be tested on the exact installed target; no such test was newly performed for this wiki edition. source: edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9 components/compatibility/src/edf41mother.cpp plus its source edf41classes and original part configuration. read together with the separate cas rest-pose guide and earth eater guide; they do not share one universal boss script.

edf4.1 earth eater (ufomother401) on edf6 — hex-grid parts and multiplayer identity the “mothership” is really a controller for many panel objects in the studied edf4.1 ufomother401 encounter, the hull is a logic controller, not a giant render/collision/hp body. its source 19 × 19 staggered hex-layout rules instantiate panels as real scene objects. the placement formula identified from the source for row i, column j is: x = 172.5 * j + (i odd ? 86.25 : 0) z = 150 * i coordinates are then centered within the map/layout, and newly spawned panels begin about 1000 units above their intended cells, awaiting fly-in or immediate-placement actions. do not assume all 361 cells necessarily produce the same part type or that a 19 × 19 controller is one huge model. the original hull sgo's action_list contains a small instruction language. the examined eight action kinds cover: constructing a layout, flying waiting panels down in batches, placing them immediately, vanishing panels, starting a slow rotation, enabling/disabling attacks, and flying the core away. a mission objectaction(n) selects an entry in that table. a direct pass-through of n into a different edf6 native actor action table is not semantically valid. different panel roles and lifecycle the reconstructed native contracts distinguish at least these roles: panel01: armour panel with mounted gun batteries at named locators. weakpanel: damage triggers a local destruction cascade within approximately 200 m in xz, including nearby panels / core under the source rules. core: the hull's apparent hp reflects core status; its destruction drives a long boss-death sequence (about 50 s in the described source). bigcannon01: opens, charges about 5 s, and fires a downward beam for about 10 s. generator / finalgenerator: forward setenemygenerator and setinstantenemygenerator calls through the hull to the correct indexed child. finalcannon01: has a genocide-beam or five aimed lightning-bolt attack path. smalllaser / sniper / plasma / rapid batteries: independent range-limited targeting behaviour attached to panel locators. the common panelbase manages flying in/out, destruction, burn/fall phases and weak-body damage filtering. only hits on the sgo-defined weakpoint body count for the relevant target, and objects without such a body are not universal damage recipients. conflating panel visibility with panel hp/damage ownership is a common failure mode. how edf6 parts can represent the source object tree the studied compatibility code makes each visible panel an actual target-side eventanimationobject, with a model, cas main player, ragdoll and durability, then attaches class-specific state via a controlled runtime record. the invisible hull uses a very small drawn donor rather than gaining new collision/durability behaviour. part locator transforms for mounts, muzzles and spawns originate from source mab locator data, preserved in named sgo fields. the original sound cue names are resolved from corresponding available audio-bank resources instead of inventing new identities. this representation can be structurally valid while still failing if scripts act on a single parent only, weak bodies aren't attached to their panel objects, or a generator drops from a panel with the wrong identity. network copies and ownership the retained implementation has each peer run the layout controller and its local panel tree. corresponding parts and spawned enemies receive game-native child identity so that durability, damage and target state can be synchronized. randomized attack starts are driven by the host, rather than each peer picking different times. it does not replay edf4.1's wire-level sync records unchanged; it reconstructs target-native identity and authority at the object boundary. this is a concrete example of why “spawn it on every peer” and “network it correctly” are not the same requirement. for the general authority distinction, see registered objects and local copies. evidence: source-side exact-build reverse engineering and design in edf41mother401.cpp (edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9). no fresh two-peer game runtime or full encounter parity test was carried out for this documentation. the hex spacing and state durations belong to the examined source encounter, not a universal edf6 map scale. source ragdoll filter is not identical to the target eao default the recovered edf4.1 panelbase uses two source ragdoll layer states: ordinary panels retain shkt-authored layer 0; only corepanel is keyframed and receives layer 7. layer 13 applies to a separate panel component, not the ragdoll. the studied edf6 eventanimationobject instead initially assigns its ragdoll layer 17. this is a distinct collision-model issue from the panel grid's online identity and from its trigger/delay lifecycle. see full earth eater panel layer comparison. direct edf6 gameplay validation of the source-aligned candidate remains pending.

animation constructor traps — edf4.1 bind pose versus edf6 auto-started cas clips a valid animation file can start the wrong encounter phase a source object may rely on its model bind pose at spawn and start its first cas animation only after a mission command. an edf6 donor class may instead start its default cas player automatically in the constructor. both files can parse, both clips can play, and the model can still begin in a phase that is completely wrong for the original fight. the preserved ufomother301 case demonstrates this precisely: edf4.1 hull begins with its main cas player at rest and does not automatically start a clip; its open/close logic is triggered later by the original state machine. the studied edf6 ufocarrier508 constructor starts close_state at playback rate 1.0. in the imported setup, that target name aliases the source close animation, around 987 frames from open to closed. edf4.1 subsidiary cannons also start at their bind pose. the studied edf6 eventanimationobject constructor starts the clip named default, which the source bridge aliased to appear (about 558 frames). without intervention the mothership can appear with its belly open and close over roughly 16 s, and ten cannons can unfold for roughly 9 s before the source scripts expect them to wake. this is not evidence that the model or the clip was corrupt; the constructor consumed a different initial animation contract. correcting only the initial state the source bind poses were compared with the imported clips: part source required startup bounded target action hull closed model bind pose hold the last pose of close while still in its first source state subsidiary cannon folded/rest bind pose set appear time to zero and playback speed zero until activation hatch, cover, main cannon, panels already matching source bind or static state in the examined setup no blanket override the rule applies once, on the object's first frame, only if the original class's own state machine has not already started its action. on an activation command, a cannon explicitly restarts appear at time zero with speed one. rewinding an already-active clip every frame would freeze the encounter. the rest-state policy is therefore not a global “disable default animation” operation. wider lesson for class adapters a successful cas/canm import must validate the native class's constructor, name lookup and initial player state, not only channel decoding, bone references and visual playback. alias correctness is not enough: an alias can point a built-in constructor to a clip that is only supposed to run later. the illustrated clip/frame counts and donor class behaviour are exact-source observations. they do not prove that another donor class or edf6 build starts the same clips or has identical bind poses. source: components/compatibility/src/edf41mother_pose.h and companion edf41mother.cpp, edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9 source archive. the retained pure logic had unit tests but no new gameplay run in this wiki pass.

edf4.1 giant dragon in edf6 — ragdoll settling, knockdown resets and the 60-second wake cap why a dragon may lie motionless while its ai is otherwise alive the examined edf6 dragonsmall class can enter a knockdown state from a hit with a nonzero knock value, from a hit while already down or from active ragdoll state. every subsequent qualifying hit while down can restart the knockdown state clock. a source edf4.1 dragonbig401 mapped to this target class may therefore appear unable to recover even while target logic continues updating. in the studied edf6 path, entering the state plays fly_damage_large, enables selected ragdoll bodies and later transitions to the down clip. recovery depends on both elapsed time and an aggregate measure of ragdoll motion: settle = σ over ragdoll bodies [mass × (|linear velocity| + |angular velocity|)] the engine's recovery condition in the investigated build is: elapsed > 1.5 seconds and (settle < 2000 or elapsed > 60 seconds) the original edf4.1 dragonbig had the same 1.5 s / 2000 settling condition in the examined path but no 60-second hard cap. this means “wakes up at sixty seconds” is not universal source parity; it is a target-native safety behaviour. conversely, repeated knockdown hits may continually reset the clock, so observing several sixty-second episodes does not necessarily mean that the recovery test itself is disabled. why diagnosis must measure the state variables for a dragon lying still, inspect: whether the hit really carries knock value and whether new hits re-enter the state. whether its ragdoll is active and which bodies contribute to the velocity sum. the actual state clock (not the wall-clock elapsed since the first hit). whether the target's s_down → wakeup transition runs with settle < 2000 or exceeds its cap. whether a source-vs-target mismatch in the ragdoll body mass/speed makes settle stay too high even when the visible dragon looks stationary. do not fix this by replacing the enemy with a permanently upright model, deleting collision or globally disabling ragdoll. the problem is a state transition and physical settling contract, which has to be qualified with the exact actor model and mission. historical 2026-10-17 m166 observations reported the giant dragon staying down for about 60 seconds at a time. the corresponding source includes pure unit-tested gating logic, but this article does not report a newly rerun runtime or multiplayer test. source: edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9 components/compatibility/src/edf41dragon_wake.h and its source-linked exact edf41.exe / edf6.dll state analysis.

edf4.1 queen bee and nephila in edf6 — when identical class names have different attack semantics a class name is not a weapon contract the retained edf4.1 dlc insect compatibility code identifies two distinct differences that are invisible if a modder merely sees a matching edf6 enemy class or a visually correct projectile. its source compares native edf41.exe routines against a particular edf6 edf.dll build and guards affected actors with explicit metadata keys. unmarked native edf6 insects are not meant to change. queen bee — projectile speed depends on a small constant in the examined edf6 giantbee needle setup, projectile speed is proportional to speed6(l) = (l / 400 + 0.5) × 3 where l is the level value passed to that setup. the queen bee path multiplies the result by 1.5. the corresponding edf4.1 class used +0.4, not +0.5, in the common term. when porting a dlc queen bee at comparable levels, preserving the same enemy model and projectile base type therefore changes how quickly and how far the needle travels. the narrowly scoped fix scales the already computed native target speed by factor = (l / 400 + source_base) / (l / 400 + 0.5) with source_base=0.4 for the examined edf4.1 queen. the source report describes observed differences around 15–23% in the dlc levels under study; this range must not be applied blindly at another level. count, projectile life, damage and base spread were not changed in the same source comparison. diagnostic: if a converted queen bee seems to attack at the right intervals but its needles have unusual travel time/range, inspect the level-to-speed equation, not just the object or bullet sgo. nephila — positional and named parameters are not interchangeable the studied nephila02l and nephila03l fire spiderstringbullet01 threads. its constructor seeds ten thread nodes with randomized velocities scaled by random_speed. edf4.1 read that number positionally from bullet_custom_param[0], and a dlc value of 0.01 yielded a tight, nearly straight thread. in the examined edf6 path the constructor looks up random_speed by name in a variant supplied to the bullet. the studied nephila passes a classic sgo node with a different tag; the lookup misses and uses the native default 0.5. the resulting thread spreads dramatically, despite keeping the old source numeric field in the enemy object. the bridge carries the per-nephila source value into the construction call for that one bullet type. it avoids replacing the default globally, because spiderstringbullet02/03 also use the shared constructor but are not consumers of the same source parameter path in the inspected case. this is an example of a deeper migration hazard: preserving the value is not sufficient when the consumer changes from an indexed lookup to a typed, named lookup. integration safeguards and evidence scope the source uses exact-build guarded call sites. it applies the needle multiplier only to marked queen bees and the thread override only while a marked nephila's bullet is being constructed; unrelated insects and thread types retain their native values. these are not universal patch addresses or proof of runtime compatibility on an updated game build. sources: edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9 components/compatibility/src/edf41insects.cpp, with code comments citing the examined edf41.exe and edf6.dll routines. findings are inherited source-backed re, not newly executed game tests.

edf4.1 deiroi landing in edf6 — null-world raycasts and state transitions the symptom depends on how the mission spawns the enemy the studied edf4.1 mission m412 creates deiroi units in the air using generators on the ufomother401 carrier. when those source actors are passed to the examined edf6 deiroi class, they can reach an airborne/falling state that native edf6 missions in this study did not exercise. the retained exact-build analysis identified a crash in that state even without the edf4.1 compatibility plugin. the crashing call constructs a ray from the unit's previous position to its current position, then invokes an older havok-world raycast routine with a null world pointer (xor ecx, ecx at the studied call site). the callee assumes the world exists and dereferences world + 0xc0; the program faults before the enemy can transition to standing. what the caller actually expects back the falling-state caller examines a ray result structure. the important fields in this studied abi are: field meaning for the falling-state caller result + 0x10 float hit fraction along previous→current ray result + 0x50 non-null hit marker / hit object, checked before landing transition the source-only bridge checks whether a valid old-world object was actually supplied. when present, it preserves the original raycast. only when the world pointer is null does it call the edf6 map-ground ray routine with the same endpoints. if a hit is found, it computes a fraction clamped to [0,1], writes the expected fields and permits the native caller to enter its landing state. if no hit is found, it leaves the caller's initialized “no hit” state alone. this is not a general havok raycast replacement, and it is not a new collision mesh or navigation repair. it is an exact call-site compatibility adaptation for a state that older mission scripts expose in a newer engine. the code refuses to patch when exact instruction bytes differ from those expected for the studied dll. lessons for porting enemy state machines a native-class update may contain a broken or unexercised substate; matching the class is not proof that an imported spawn path is safe. reproduce the state transition (airborne→falling→grounded), not merely the enemy's initial position. use the same ray endpoints and reproduce the exact result contract expected by the caller; a boolean hit alone may not suffice. verify the target object's pointer/abi and keep the replacement scoped to the failing state and build. distinguish historical observed game crash, exact-build code analysis, a source-level corrective implementation, and a subsequent in-game confirmation. the last is not supplied by this wiki release. sources: edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9 components/compatibility/src/edf41deiroi.cpp and its referenced m412/ufomother401 investigation. the cited addresses belong only to the investigated edf6.dll build.

edf4.1 four-legged fortress on edf6 movingfortress — startup, core generator and objectaction abi three mismatches with one borrowed class edf4.1's alien4legtank301 maps to the examined edf6 movingfortress class, but both classes disagree about startup state, hatch/core generator identity and the meaning of mission objectaction messages. a valid model and collision rig alone cannot resolve any of these mismatches. the studied compatibility path only runs for actors with edf41_fortress metadata. the native edf6 e510 fortress path is intentionally left unchanged. startup — lying-down target state can prevent any ai edf6's movingfortress constructor begins at mode 0, a ground/lying state without active ai. native target scripts wake it through a specific command or controller. edf4.1's source fortress is already standing and its missions do not send the target wakeup command. the bounded bridge sets the desired target mode to 1 before its native update for a marked edf4.1 fortress, allowing the existing target transition/animation path to run. this is a state-machine mismatch, not a damaged cas. a modder seeing a motionless fortress should inspect its class initialization and mission command vocabulary before retuning actor navigation. two edf6 generators versus one edf4.1 core hatch edf4.1's fortress has one objectgenerator associated with its core hatch. edf6's movingfortress has two and selects one from a message field. the studied target class only opens the critical core hatch for generator [1], which also gates whether the core can take damage. accidentally routing the old drop through [0] can leave the fortress's vulnerable phase permanently shut. the bridge rewrites the generator selection to 1 only while the relevant message is being handled, then restores the sender-owned argument field. the studied dispatch contracts are: 0x20100: configure a drop; selection is carried in an integer at offset +0x48 in the message body. 0x20103: retrieve a generator; selection is the body integer at +0x00. never make a blanket “generator zero is equivalent” assumption across classes. the class can parse both indices and still pick the wrong physical hatch. objectaction — identical id, different operations the edf4.1 mission objectaction message (0x1000000d) uses six part-group switch commands and a destroy action. edf6 movingfortress assigns different meanings to its own action table. in the historical m117 case, a source mission sends objectaction(1) after an earlier wave; forwarding that as a target-native action tried to spawn rubble at a locator absent from the edf4.1 model, crashing at the target function. the correct compatibility boundary interprets the edf4.1 action number first. source actions 0–5 enable or disable the intended part group through the class's existing part-control function; action 6 uses the native destroy/death state rather than a guessed hp-only rewrite. the original message is not passed through to the incompatible target action table. optional walking decisions the source fortress chooses each discrete step with a 3/5 straight, 1/5 turn left, 1/5 turn right draw, unless its edge-avoidance policy intervenes. the borrowed target class has its own step-choice field; in the examined offline path that field is mostly filled by network synchronization, not by the source's locally random roaming. an optional source-fidelity adaptation updates the next choice on clip transitions. the startup and action-message fixes do not depend on enabling that optional gait policy. scope: this article reports a specific actor-class source/target mismatch, exact-build static re and a historical m117 crash report. it does not establish all fortress mission parity or a fresh game-runtime pass. source: components/compatibility/src/edf41fortress.cpp and edf41fortress_action.h in edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9.

edf4.1 uforobo in edf6 — why an attacking boss can remain stationary the important timer runs only in the correct ai state a reported edf4.1→edf6 uforobo port continuously attacked but hardly moved. inspection of the original edf4.1 state machine and the retained bridge located the issue in the interaction of ai states a3/a4/a5 with body states s7/s8/s9, not simply a missing animation clip or bad terrain path. s7: standing/choosing the next action. s8: a step or turn animation, including root motion. s9: an attacking animation. a3: normal movement and countdown toward the next attack. a4: wait until the body is ready to choose/start an attack. a5: hold while the attack animation is playing. in the old incorrect port, ai returned to a3 as soon as s9 started. its attack timer could count down and queue another attack while the body still played the original long s9 clip. at the next s7, a4 immediately started another s9. movement intervals were consumed inside the long attacking phase, yielding a stationary attacker rather than a walking enemy. the preserved edf4.1 logic stays in a5 while the body remains in s9 and goes back to a3 only after the body returns to s7. this keeps the attack timer from consuming walking time during a shot. historical traces identified s9 clips lasting roughly 28–37 seconds and attacks repeating in a way that kept the body in s9 across many 600-frame trace samples. these are historical test observations of that port; they are not a new measurement here. the legs use multiple phases, not one walk target the source legs state stores phase-1 and phase-2 durations, target radius, optional sideways interval/duration, cruise direction and gentle turn rate. a studied randomization uses approximately: phase1 = 1200 + rand(600) frames phase2 = 600 + rand(300) frames cruisespeed = ±speed (backward probability depends on approach state) turnduration = rand(300) frames turnrate in roughly [-0.0075, +0.0075] during approach, the actor moves forward or back according to horizontal distance versus its chosen radius; outside approach it may rotate toward its target before cruising. sideways movement is a separate overlay. the body consumes discrete foot phases and clip root motion, not a continuous “walk forward” request. at s7 the animation chooser depends on current foot position, whether a backward sequence is chained, target turn magnitude and pending attack. a foot already ahead must be returned or continued before an unrelated side-step can safely begin. root motion is sampled from the source clip's x/z/yaw keys and reconciled with the body's current transform. death is a monotonic state machine the same bridge includes a separate fix for a remote copy that has already died. death should be terminal, except for the progression: living s0..s9 -> dying s10 -> wreck s11 -> deleted once dead, a host/network body event must not drag the guest copy back to s7, s8 or s9. once in s10, only s11 is allowed; s11 may not transition back to a living state. without this gate, the old failure could leave a destroyed robot as a lingering non-deleting “ghost.” these findings are about native ai clock and body-state ownership, not a universal fix for remote state replication, pathfinding or source/target collision. the source has pure state tests; no new two-peer runtime tests were performed for this article. sources: components/compatibility/src/edf41robo_ai.h, edf41robo_body.h and source counterpart edf41robo.cpp from edf4.1 r10 hf4 r9; original research comments cite edf41.exe state logic and historical runs.

edf4.1 sk heightfields — converting shfb terrain into edf6 fmb and mad what actually differs between these map generations seven examined edf4.1 map families — sk_heigen02, sk_valley01, sk_kaigan01, sk_sangaku01, sk_sangaku02, sk_stepmountain01 and sk_crater01 — use a terrain asset named <model>_fld2mgrid.shfb. the examined edf6 engine uses mesh-based fmb terrain, an associated fieldrender texture-array contract and hknp compressed-mesh collision. in that target build, rewrapping the edf4.1 shfb header or relying on havok's old heightfield migration does not supply equivalent terrain. the studied source-only converter reconstructs both rendered and collided terrain from shfb. its successful real-source offline tests are not a gameplay/runtime pass. the later edf4.1 sk collision lineage also has its own conservative mesh-shape policies; this article describes the earlier source heightfield generation and its constraints, not a replacement for those later policies. shfb sample, coordinate and layer layout the reverse-engineered shfb reader identified these header fields in the seven sampled maps: offset interpretation in the examined profile 0x08, 0x0c sample width and height: 1001 × 1001 0x18, 0x1c horizontal cell dimensions: 2.0 m × 2.0 m 0x20 block structure: 33 blocks of 32 cells 0x30, 0x34 stated lowest and highest elevation 0x38 per-block tables 0x3c, 0x40 layer metadata / references 0x44, 0x48 material-name index and related table 0x50 packed height/material field 0x54, 0x58 per-vertex blend-weight runs 0x5c, 0x60 utf-16 name storage each height sample occupies two unsigned 16-bit words. the low word is the bit representation of an ieee-754 half-float height in metres. the high word identifies its strongest material layer. this is a decoded shader and source-data observation, not an integer-centimetre height. the observed sk_heigen02 decoded height range was about −10.2266 to 47.25 m. the map's placed shfb object supplies the world origin. a sample (row, col) becomes approximately: world.x = origin.x + col * 2 metres world.z = origin.z + row * 2 metres world.y = decoded_half_float_height rows follow z and columns follow x. a transpose produces misplaced ground and vegetation. as a cross-check, several maps' pre-existing objects were compared against the decoded field; median vertical differences ranged from 0.000 m to 0.29 m depending on map. this corroborates placement, not collision or navigation equivalence. the field also carries layer names, per-layer colour/multiplier tiling and runs of half-float blending weights. an important special case: a source layer with one colour texture has no multiplier; it does not mean “sample index −1” in edf6's unconditional multiplier path. fmb rendering reconstruction for this particular converter the source 1001 × 1001 at 2 m was sampled at every second source point: 501 × 501 render vertices spaced 4 m. render and collision use the same lattice to reduce visible ground/physics divergence. this is a chosen conversion resolution, not an inherent edf6 limit. the resulting field fmb uses 625 leaves of 20 × 20 cells: 21×21 vertices and 800 triangles per leaf. it builds the stock-style spatial aabb tree, mesh records, layer lists and four-corner splat grids. a 0x50 splat-grid record per 4 m cell stores the four corners' weights, normalized to 255 per corner. in examined edf6 fieldrender assets the shader tables cover 1–15 layers and passes 0–2; source leaves needing more than 15 are rejected rather than silently dropping a painted layer. a critical native-profile correction concerns the fmb mesh-record field at +0x28: it is an index into that fmb's shader-record table, not the texture-slice count. across 46 inspected stock edf6 fmb files and 9753 meshes, the index selected a row matching (layer_count, mode=1, pass=0, flag=0). an older writer treated it as a slice count and selected rows with flag=6 or the wrong layer count; this produced the historical black terrain blocks. a renderer seeing black blocks should inspect this relation before assuming missing dds or shader code. the source colour dds array is mapped to edf6's <map>_color.dds;
