ai targeting through walls — collision versus navigation a monster firing at an npc through a solid wall does not, by itself, prove that the wall's collision mesh is missing. edfroom/dm019 gave a useful real-game demonstration of why edf's physical collision, navigation data, target selection, line-of-sight checks and projectile collision must be examined as separate systems. the observed behavior the edf5-derived edfroom mission was brought to a state where the wall physically existed in edf6: actors could not pass through it, and spider web projectiles collided with it. however, in a particular roomb area some spiders still aimed and fired toward allied npcs on the other side. the observed effect was localized, especially evident for spider-to-npc interactions, and should not be generalized to every enemy or map. that observation establishes a narrow fact: layer what the observation supports what it cannot prove collision (mad / havok) the wall blocks actors and tested projectiles all collision shapes/material flags are native-exact projectile physics the tested webs hit/stop at the wall enemy ai checked the wall before selecting a target ai perception/targeting spiders attempted attacks toward occluded npcs which specific perception/los/agent query returned the wrong result navmesh hkt/nvmd potential route and graph inputs worth investigating a missing walkable face or edge is necessarily the cause the map's lighting and wall-mounted enemy-spawner orientation were separate mission-script issues, not explanations for a physically missing wall. the 2001 → createenemy2 mapping was runtime-confirmed for the spawner context. correct structure is not the same as correct gameplay several seemingly promising file-format fixes were real structural corrections but did not fix the ai symptom: the correspondence between hkt face data and nvmd section c was corrected, yet the targeted runtime check was negative. source-derived static aabb trees were checked across 10 low and 10 high tiles. leaves covered their intended faces, nodes were reachable and no missing/duplicate face-tree relationships explained the symptom. incorrect research decoding of narrow integers and hkhalf16 values caused earlier absurd graph/clearance interpretations. correcting the decoder repaired the analysis, not the game. an early hypothesis of a simple missing ~1.75 m roomb boundary was superseded after separating physical overlap, internal seams and streaming geometry. this is a reproducible lesson for any map converter: a parser invariant may be valuable even when the behavior under investigation remains unchanged. a real streaming connection passed through solid geometry the audited high navmesh had a connection between section uids 2 and 3, joining (face 24, edge 74) to (face 195, edge 735) near roomb. the shortest bridge between the relevant edges measured about 1.114206 m, of which approximately 1.108306 m lay inside the closed convex wall collider — 99.47% penetration. a conservative, source-derived detector identified a bridge only if: solid penetration length >= 0.05 m and penetration length / bridge length >= 0.90 and source collision binding is a supported closed convex shape it uses source hkt + source mad/mac spatial context and rejects ambiguous cases. it must not treat every intersection with a surface mesh/mopp as a valid inside/outside test: a mesh surface does not necessarily represent a closed solid volume. the detector selected three analogous source relations in its audited scope (dm019 high, ig_edfroom01 low, ig_edfroom02 high) and none in the listed cave503, heigen507, nw_europe01, kaigan502, sangaku506 and desert508 controls. this is offline consistency evidence, not a general algorithm for generating edf6 streaming links. the decisive negative runtime experiment a narrowly scoped diagnostic removed exactly that one high-hkt connection and its two aabb records. the serialized difference was 80 bytes: one 16-byte connection plus two 32-byte aabbs. the low hkt, ordinary navmesh faces/edges, graph, static tree, clearance and nvmd were kept unchanged. the later in-game observation was negative: spiders still aimed/fired at allied npcs through/toward the wall, while their web projectiles struck the barrier. therefore the crossed-solid connection was a genuine structural anomaly but not a demonstrated root cause of that ai symptom. it should not be silently removed from every map as a proposed gameplay fix. what is still unknown the responsible ai query/target-visibility or los rule was not resolved. it may depend on the target type, agent class, route query or state inside the engine. none of these possibilities has yet been uniquely demonstrated. the low/high hkt variants are not proven to map one-to-one to spider-versus-other-enemy navigation; their observed erosionradius values do not justify that claim. how to debug similar issues verify physical blocking separately: actors, projectiles and the relevant wall surfaces. observe who targets whom (enemy→player versus enemy→npc), not only where projectiles stop. test mission creation/spawner orientation independently from map geometry. validate hkt/nvmd face identity, graph, streaming, static trees and clearance with corrected decoders. use one-variable runtime tests to decide whether a structural repair changes actual ai behavior. only then investigate ai perception, los, navigation query and target selection in the exact engine build. edfroom's ig_edfroom01/02 map family did not have fmb; collision/navigation investigation used hkt/nvmd/mad/mac, with models in other resource containers. don't invent an fmb dependency for these maps. evidence boundary: collision/projectile observations and the negative runtime experiment are gameplay evidence; the crossing detector and byte/geometry measurements are offline/source evidence. the cause of ai-versus-npc wall targeting remains unresolved. see hkt/nvmd compatibility versus native rebake, mad collision contracts and map formats. measured physical geometry and graph controls the converted edfroom collision corpus preserved 297,951 logical triangles after a documented degeneracy filter, and its 101 compressed meshes passed a bounded shape-key/broadphase check (166,084 expected and reachable unique keys). more importantly, 20 examined wall/corridor records retained zero shared-section seams despite source-to-target coordinate quantization. the measured candidate still showed correct projectile/actor blocking in the user's runtime observation. these facts reinforce the distinction between physically present walls and ai targeting, but do not demonstrate global collision exactness. see edfroom mad physical collision case. the dm019 coarse inter-cluster graph contained exactly 84 low and 374 high edges derived from current face adjacency, without extra/missing edges. a source hkhalf16 decoding error had previously made narrow costs appear inconsistent; correcting the decoder repaired analysis only, not the actual ai behavior. see hkt graph/cache decoding. r176 — observed enemy-to-ally asymmetry, without claiming a new ai rule the original user observation for the edfroom/dm019 spider room supplies more context than a generic "can attack through walls" statement: when spiders were targeting the player, they were not reported to shoot the player through the wall. the anomaly was specifically noticed when they aimed/fired webs toward allied npcs behind it. spiders could move toward the obstruction and accumulate by a room corner; one spider then turned toward the player after noticing them, switching from its previous apparent allied-npc target. during the later r2o high-only shortcut-removal runtime test, several spiders still aimed and fired toward the obstructed allied npcs. the observer did not notice allies firing back in that particular observation. this is not a universal statement that friendly ai never targets spiders across walls. the webs still hit the physical wall. neither these observations nor the negative r2o experiment demonstrates a missing mad wall, projectile pass-through, broken ai collision for every target, or a specific defective line-of-sight function. this narrows the diagnostic evidence to target-type-dependent ai perception/selection and possibly agent-specific path/los queries. it does not establish which function or native query returned an inappropriate result. evidence: edfroom_ai_wall_runtime_observation_2026-08-25.json (original gameplay observation) and edfroom_r2o_runtime_negative_2026-08-26.json (subsequent negative one-variable gameplay experiment). the test took place in a modified edf5-derived mission running in edf6, not as a verified defect in a clean retail mission.

mad/havok wire layout: data alignment, primitive indexing and physical state a collision archive can carry geometrically correct meshes and still be rejected by edf6 because its serialized havok object graph is physically inconsistent. the original edf5 representation and the target edf6/havok-2020 hknp representation differ in shape classes, data alignment, pool records and per-body flags. the following rules are derived from paired native objects and independent wire audits, not from copying an sdk serializer. semantic structure versus physical data layout the havok-2020-style serialization includes a type description, an item graph and physical data. it is not enough for a deserialized graph to report the expected class and mesh counts; byte offsets must also satisfy the target's physical alignment and reference semantics. a known source-only desert conversion preserved collision content but had 36 physical data alignment violations. these were chiefly simd/hkvector4 fields represented by zero-local-size aliases that inherited their actual size/alignment from a parent type. a serializer that blindly treats the alias as physically zero-sized can place subsequent data at invalid addresses. independently audited native edf6 controls from cave503, heigen507 and nw_europe01 had zero such alignment violations. rule: resolve physical alignment through the reflected parent type chain. a stronger requested alignment may be applied, but must not override a stronger inherited requirement with a weaker one. the maintained experimental writer also requires at least 16-byte object alignment for pointer/object allocations in its qualified path; this is a writer contract, not a universal theorem for all havok file kinds. hknpmotionproperties and free pool slots the compared edf6 target record for hknpmotionproperties is 104 bytes. a free slot in the target's thread-safe pool is not 104 zero bytes. the independent paired-file audit established the following construction for the examined free-slot class: start from the native target's deterministic default 104-byte motion-properties record. overwrite the first dword with the next free-list index. write the measured free/deactivation marker byte as 0xff. the pool-head serial is (numallocated - 1) & 0xff, producing 0xff for an empty pool. an early desert candidate incorrectly nearly zero-filled 14 free records. that was a physical abi defect even though the corresponding slots were not active bodies. static body mass is not universally zero for the measured static/no-drag hknpbodycinfo class, paired edf6 source uses: field value in this particular class motiontype static dragproperties null motionpropertiesid 0xffff massdistribution null mass -1.0 sentinel in a source-only desert candidate 137 such records had mistakenly been written with mass=0.0. they needed the target-class sentinel. do not convert all static bodies to mass=-1.0: native static bodies with drag properties form a separate class. this is why matching by relevant fields is preferable to guessing one global default. primitive keys, triangles and mesh-section indexing in the examined compressed-mesh primitive representation, c == d means one triangle/primitive key; c != d represents a quad/two primitive keys. mesh-section metadata includes a firstprimitiveindex whose meaning is a mesh-global prefix sum of primitives in earlier sections, not a constant or local reset for every section. the examined triangleisinterior representation is keyed by sparse shape-key space: the required bitfield span follows maxshapekey + 1, not simply the number of source triangles. the accepted desert profile was checked over 11,873 sections in 387 section arrays, with zero firstprimitiveindex mismatches in the independent structural audit. the source-only conservative approach should preserve the section boundaries, ordering and primitive counts. passing this audit does not by itself certify collision gameplay or correct raycasts. the triangleisinterior bitfield is a separate behavioral question this bitfield describes internal versus exposed triangle semantics. its available geometry heuristics include adjacency, exposed boundaries, polygon flatness and local convexity. however, the runtime comparison did not establish a universal interior-bit classifier. changing both mesh topology and interior bits led to failures, and a zero-interior control with the wrong bidirectional flat/split topology also crashed. therefore, interior bits alone were not the proven cause. the stable profile preserved source-backed topology and used zero interior bits. consequently, the accepted desert compatibility rule uses the zero triangleisinterior policy and permits geometry-justified flat→split transitions but not a blind split→flat rewrite. the research classifier and higher-fidelity inference remain separate from the runtime-qualified baseline; no generic exact rule for every shape is established. native cave/heigen/europe data contains large numbers of nonzero interior bits; the desert zero policy is therefore a known compatibility compromise, not a universal native equivalent. see native bit-count and edge-adjacency evidence. do not promote an offline count/byte match into proof of collision parity. validation checklist a robust writer/validator should independently inspect: type-parent-derived physical alignment and data ranges (including zero-local-size aliases). item and pointer/reference kinds, overlapping spans and root graph reachability. motion-property free-list links, default payloads and pool-head serials. body class invariants, including the scoped mass sentinel. primitive-key counts and mesh-global firstprimitiveindex for all sections. triangle interior bits separately from primitive ordering and geometry conservation. in-game collision, raycasts, ai traversability and destructible behavior when claiming runtime parity. evidence levels: paired native file/independent wire audit for alignment/pool/mass; source-only and runtime-profile audits for the desert mesh/index policy. the investigated early wire-fixed source candidate itself was not runtime-tested at the time of its report. for higher-level context see mad/shkt collision contracts and collision versus navigation. decoder-side section-key bounds matter independently of serialization the measured hkcdstaticmeshtree::section record is 0x60 bytes with firstpackedvertexindex at +0x48, firstsharedvertexindex at +0x4c and firstprimitiveindex at +0x50. in one exact-build crash a sentinel compressed-mesh key 0xffffffff became a section index 0xffffff; indexing the section array with that value caused the engine's out-of-bounds read. the invalid inactive-simd-lane defect in a source-built candidate was separately real, but the exact causal path from those lanes to the sentinel remained unproven. for the complete field table and the distinction between shape-type values, dispatch-type values and motion-type mapping, see compressed-mesh shape keys and section records. material response and evidence classification the old materials audit requested fixtures in which two materials share friction and restitution but differ in response/trigger type. this is a necessary test design, not evidence that friction and restitution fully identify a target material. the corresponding target trigger/flag bytes and half-float conversion (including out-of-range values) must be checked against the exact native profile before merging material identities. similarly, a native edf6 serializer round-trip demonstrates that a target file can be decoded and re-emitted under one schema. it does not establish edf5→edf6 conversion parity, nor does an earlier 16.9 mb experimental mad candidate supersede the later independently measured source-only desert/r10c acceptance profile. treat body counts, source geometry and final compressed-mesh topology as separate gates. the historical 16,132-triangle direct-mesh view is only one part of the complete desert terrain collision census. width computation is not the sparse interior-bitfield span for the bounded mad r12 compressed-mesh writer, numshapekeybits = (maxshapekey + 1).bit_length() reserves the all-ones invalid-key pattern. a previous max-key-only width created 61 conflicts; the source audit repaired 122 mirrored fields and reduced the collisions to zero. this field must not be conflated with the triangleisinterior bitfield length, which also depends on sparse encoded key space but is a distinct representation. see shape-key sentinel and r12 width evidence.

edf 4.1 navigation and collision: what the data reveals r19 correction on the 4,971-footprint study historical r19 only: a then-latest natural geometry/ranking path produced 5,026 active footprints (55 above the 4,971 historical oracle), and 4,948 belonged to a different intermediate trial. subsequent r32 source-semantic reconstruction supersedes this count: group-union xz ranking, raw cached-aabb max_xz >= 5.75, 4,994 pre-deduplication instances and 23 source-scoped fixb removals reproduce the required 4,971 population. the exact historical carve/hkt bytes remain unrecovered. the old r1/r1b harness did not preserve that threshold and is not current classifier authority. see how the body-eligibility/groupgeometry distinction works. the 7,872,840-byte figure occasionally cited in old research is a whole-mac size; it was never mapo size. the inner mapo record-family relayout is described here. navigation across edf generations is not just a set of waypoints that can be copied. the studied edf4.1→edf6 research combines map-object placements, collision-body identity, havok-derived geometry, raster/triangle selection and game-specific navigation output. its most valuable community finding is which parts can be reproduced exactly and which remain unknown. map object references must resolve to the right collision bodies the studied mapo/source-mad collision-reference population contains 40,920 non-empty references. a reconstructed identity resolver accounts for: resolution route references recovered strict base + collision identity 27,018 .hkt / base-only recovery 420 unique stationwindow fallback 12 structural fix a: list-shape body groups 1,945 structural fix b: dual base/collision-source identity 3,988 resolved total 33,383 not safely resolved 7,537 the residual cannot be filled by approximate name matching without making unsupported claims about the collision data. fix b's natural selection identifies 16 groups and 26 source bodies; other mopp/storageextendedmesh alias candidates were deliberately rejected rather than count-fitted. reconstructing navigable geometry an exact reference from the studied four-tile map has 1,562 vertices and 2,928 triangles. a later historical target uses the same vertex count but 2,651 triangles, meaning 277 triangles were removed. recovering the correct removal geometry is not the same as simply producing any triangulation with the right count. the source geometry/placement analysis has recovered a 65-group selection with 1,405 placements, consisting of 251 zero-rotation, 1,153 yaw-only and one mixed-xz placement. the 4,971 active footprint population has since been reproduced naturally under a source-semantic r32 candidate. the remaining blocker is the complete historical body eligibility/carve identity and the exact hkt bytes. a retained natural 277-face candidate is 381,544 bytes (+32) against the historical 381,512-byte low oracle; the historical +16 byte comparison came from a non-natural rank-swap control, not the best natural current candidate. neither a matching face count nor nvmd identity qualifies an edf6 runtime nav. what an implementer should take from this preserve native map-object-to-collision-body identity; not every geometric candidate is a valid binding. treat hkt/shkt/mad geometry, map rmpa and native nav/nvmd as separate but interacting sources. distinguish measured source geometry from byte-exact target output and runtime pathfinding behavior. never “fix” a mismatch by arbitrarily deleting 277 triangles, adding/removing 16 bytes or selecting collision bodies to fit known totals. loading donor nav from a later edf can be a compatibility compromise rather than faithful reconstruction. for exact structures and further details see native edf4.1 navigation, mapo and collision study, mad/shkt and map consumers explained. evidence boundary: exact source/target binary observations and offline reproductions are available for defined cases; the unresolved target-specific selection rules and full edf6 gameplay/runtime equivalence must not be claimed solved. why later solid/capsule contact studies still do not finish the nav conversion on original sk_heigen02 source mesh data, a 265-instance mad/mapb survey distinguishes 166 closed 2-manifold candidates from 99 open source surfaces. a radius-0.45 m, height-1.8 m illustrative capsule finds 243 closed-solid candidate 4 m cells plus 495 open-surface hint cells. the 158 source point-in-solid positive cells are a subset of the 243, but none of the candidate cells may be assumed impassable without collision-layer, agent-profile and game-runtime evidence. a tiny four-tile test changes 512 source terrain triangles to 504 by excluding four example cells while retaining three open-only hints; hkt structurally passes, gameplay does not. keep three separate questions: r1d hillycity original-byte oracle, r31–r33 4 m original shfb terrain tile-bake feasibility, and r34–r35 source-mad 3d obstacle/contact hints on one sk map. none individually proves that the edf6 ranger/fencer/hector correctly navigates an edf4.1 map. the latest source studies used a later-game hkt/nvmd backend; this is an output-format compatibility experiment, not proof of sandlot's original edf4.1 agent-size or navmesh-generation algorithm.

map resource architecture an earth defense force map is not one mesh file. the studied edf5/edf6 map packages contain multiple resources with different consumers: registrations and resource identities, placed objects, field/terrain rendering, physical collision and navigation. a map can render while its collision is wrong; a table can parse while the game's object references still point to the wrong resource. the relevant formats format or subsystem known role / practical question mac map container/identity and related map resource structure mapb map registration and references to resource roles, including model, object and field resources mapo object/placement tables and relationships to map/collision content ordinary mdb model individually referenced props, buildings, objects and their model materials fmb / fmep / fieldrender terrain/field and its specialized rendering/material transport mad / shkt / hkt distinct physical/collision and havok-related data paths, depending on profile nvmd, nav and map rmpa navigation/road/area/portal/related map semantics; not mission-owned route/spawn rmpa these are roles observed in the studied assets, not a promise that every map contains every file or that one rule works across all generations. map registration and object placement: mapb / mapo observed paired edf5 → edf6 mapb conversion includes structural record changes: record family edf5 stride edf6 stride specific observed edit t1 56 bytes 60 bytes insert zero dword at entry +0x20; old +0x20 moves to +0x24 t2 68 bytes 72 bytes add four zero bytes at the end; rebase relative references mapb registration suffixes such as .mdx, .trb, .mosb and .fmep identify different resource roles. globally changing suffixes is not a conversion strategy. the corrected mapo object-table element at the studied +0x08 table has a 0x1c (28-byte) stride, not eight bytes. placement/object identity and associated collision bindings remain separate validation tasks. terrain is not an ordinary mdb material fmb/fmep field content uses fieldrender; it should not be treated as a large ordinary mdb model. in a recovered fieldrender material bridge: a cell has 12 local material slots. three rgba8 id textures carry four slot ids each; three rgba8 weight textures carry matching corner weights. 0xff (255) is the invalid material-slot sentinel. material colors come from texture arrays, not the simple ordinary-mdb sampler layout. the sampled terrain normal decoder differs from the common/water mdb r×a convention. see fieldrender local slots and texture arrays for the exact division dimensions, record strides and normalization behavior. collision and navigation are independent proof obligations a successful fieldrender initialization does not demonstrate correct floor collision. likewise, correct-looking static geometry does not prove havok shapes or navigation route/portal semantics. edf4.1 → edf6 work illustrates why donor navigation can load and still be a fidelity compromise, and why unknown road/portal reconstruction details must remain unresolved. for collision structures read mad/shkt contracts; for nav geometry and mapo binding see edf4.1 navigation research. for mission-owned rmpa, see the separate mission scripting and rmpa guide. if you are writing an importer or converter follow the relationships instead of rewriting one file type in isolation: map identity / mac → mapb resource registrations → mapo placements and references → ordinary-model or field-render payloads → collision and navigation consumers keep file-local/profile-specific rules explicit. a version bump or a parse-only pass cannot establish identical in-game map behavior. why file suffixes can crash an otherwise valid map a real edf5→edf6 port showed a mapb/t1 reference to an ordinary model under a .trb resource role. the target game chose the tree/trb header parser, but the decompressed payload was actually a 53,806-byte mdb; the in-memory mdb buffer itself was correct. reading the mdb's +0x28 field as a trb entry count produced 0x300000, leading to invalid tree-table traversal. for a converter, this means resource identity, suffix/type registration and payload abi must agree. the fix is not a global .trb→.mdx replacement: some .trb entries are genuinely typed trb resources. see typed dispatch and cmpl failures. a visual object and its physical body need not share a registry source visual objects are discoverable through rab/mdb and mapb/maco-style resource references, whereas physical collision can be represented by separately named bodies in mad and the map's collision ownership graph. missing a model name in one resource list does not establish that the physical shape is absent. this is important for destructible props, gates and map-specific foliage. see map prop sgo, crashtype and resource ownership. collapse connectivity is authored map data, not inferred at load edf6 mapo contains t50 connectivity and p58 piece/support tables. static engine analysis shows the map loader parses these already-authored tables and passes t50 entries through mapobject_crashmodel to a body-relationship builder. merely copying visual building meshes, collision bodies or mapb placement rows does not preserve their collapse graph. the complete bounded observations are in t50 / crashmodel. when multiple placements are cloned, matching mapb/mapo counts, fresh guids, rebased pointers and parent-child closure are independent from physical mad/hkt update. see mapb/mapo placement duplication.

edf missions: bvm, events, angelscript and mission rmpa the game-specific mission logic and its referenced spatial data are related but not the same format. we have reconstructed important behavior from edf5/edf6 mission bytecode and edf4.1 sources, including event registration, script calls, route/shape/spawn references, and differences exposed when converting them. this page is an entry point; the linked articles contain exact instructions and caveats. what is a bvm mission script? mission.bvm is a compiled mission-logic representation in the studied edf source games. it describes events, factors/conditions, actions and calls into the game's mission api. conversion research decompiled original bvm and reconstructed edf6-compatible angelscript (.ac) logic. this is more complicated than replacing function names. a faithful converter has to preserve control flow, argument types and value flow, event-target identity, loops and re-arm conditions, counts and ordering. a syntactically compiling script can still behave incorrectly in game. event registration and event state the studied source event model uses registerevent registrations and edf6-side internal_createevent constructs. a single target handler can have several registrations with different factors. that does not necessarily mean several independent persistent event states. in one exact native comparison subset, 2,214 reachable registrations mapped to 2,106 unique reachable targets. those targets determine persistent handler/event-state identity; compiler-generated function numbering alone is not the event id. reachability analysis must start at main and follow relevant helper, wrapper and event-target edges rather than count every decompiled branch as live. event multi semantics also matter: source multi == 1 has a specific multi-ready registration behavior in the studied schedulers. preserving that requires more than translating event names. for examples and exact constraints see event-state and reachability findings, opcode and api catalog and direct bvm → ac comparison. what mission rmpa contains mission rmpa is not map rmpa. mission rmpa contains mission-owned routes, waypoints, shapes, cameras and spawn records. its source/target conversion is a specialized structural task, not a generic byte-copy or header-version patch. in the studied edf5 → edf6 mission-rmpa source/target dataset: fact observed value target signature / version \0pmr, version 1 route type-header size 0x30 bytes waypoint record size 0x50 bytes, with 0x30-byte waypoint body header string pointer +0x18 (not +0x1c) route-local numbering rebased to global target indexes while retaining ids and links next-link region variable size, followed by 16-byte alignment a paired source-only 141-mission audit covered 5,103 waypoints, 1,355 shapes and 3,387 spawn records, with 6,665 script-to-rmpa literal references resolved. that is strong static/semantic closure, not a claim of 141/141 gameplay-runtime parity. setaipath(obj, "navigationmap") refers to native navigation semantics; it should not be misinterpreted as a mission-rmpa route reference. for conversion details see mission rmpa source-only profile. missions, maps and shared resources a mission references a map and other resource identities; it is not intrinsically the same thing as that map. in the studied authoring contract, one map can be reused by multiple missions, while a bundle can contain multiple maps and missions. resource references and namespace ownership must remain coherent when packing a mission for edf6. for current modeled relationships see workspace, map references and mission bundles; for earlier-game differences see edf4.1 missionbundle and gameplay research. for the practical multi scheduler rule, shared event target state, once/repeat/nth policies and factor ownership, see mission event registration and scheduling. for resource ownership, see maps, missions and bundles. important unknowns and pitfalls the presence of a bytecode instruction or exported event function is not proof that it is reachable from actual mission entry points. compile success does not establish event timing, runtime api behavior, ai parity or multiplayer correctness. mission rmpa and map rmpa must not share a converter merely because the extensions are identical. edf4.1 differs from edf5/edf6 in behaviors, object lifecycle, friendly npcs and navigation; reusing the intermediate game's data is not a universal translation. third-party mods can be useful comparisons, but cannot by themselves establish what original sandlot game binaries do. mission command ids do not have universal actor semantics even when a message id and argument list exist in both games, a borrowed target class may assign different meaning. in the examined edf4.1 four-legged fortress, the exact objectaction and generator contract distinguishes legacy group switches from edf6's unrelated target commands. a correct command translator must know the recipient class and source-era semantic contract.

bvm bytecode and custom calls a custom-call number is an operand, not a new bytecode instruction. that distinction is important when reading edf mission scripts. the edf5/edf6 mission.bvm frontend uses compact vm instructions and encoded operands, while the actual engine action is selected by a custom-call identifier. the target angelscript api may express the same action as a method, a global function, or—occasionally—have no exposed binding at all. source-identity caution: the inspected clean edf5 shipping bvm corpus is not byte-identical to the edf5_old_script files stored on the edf6 side (0/141 exact pairs in the audited set). see the source-identity comparison. this matters when attributing an opcode or custom call to original edf5 behavior. reading an instruction correctly in the researched bvm stream, byte 0xac represents the cuscall0 opcode. if the following argument bytes are d0 07, their little-endian value is 0x07d0 = 2000, which identifies an engine custom call. neither d0 nor 07 should be interpreted as a second bvm opcode. ac d0 07 │ └─┬─┘ │ └── u16 le custom-call id = 2000 (0x07d0) └────── cuscall0 opcode the example establishes the operand/dispatch distinction; a full decoder must still honor each instruction's actual arity, stack convention and length. the observed invalid/crashing bvm instruction opcode range is 0x39–0x3f, not merely 0x3a–0x3f. this bytecode range is unrelated to custom-call identifiers such as 2000 or 3450. engine-call identity and port mappings the following mappings are drawn from paired edf5 scripts, native edf6 angelscript material and binary-backed translation work. they apply to the inspected call signatures and contexts; they do not imply that arbitrary object types support every method. source custom call studied effect target-side expression / constraint 2000 create enemy createenemy semantics; not a misread opcode 2001 alternate enemy creation createenemy2, independently distinguished from 2000 2008 area enemy-group creation createenemygroup_area; not inherently flying-only. separate spawn steps may be required 3100 ai route/movement speed setaimovespeed(...); an older setairoutespeed name is superseded 3101 assign ai route setairoute(...) in the paired context 3102 assign ai path setaipath(...), independently distinguished from route assignment 4004 / 4005 random ai conversation enableairandomtalk() / disableairandomtalk() rather than a forced constant 3450 search/encounter radius runtime effect known, but no exposed angelscript binding established for the audited build these are examples of semantic translation, not literal replacement of numeric ids with arbitrary text. a translator must preserve source argument order and types, ownership of the target object, execution timing and preconditions. the retained ascommon.h reference defines radiobegin and radioend as provided helpers; earlier notes inferring they must be engine built-ins from a native script's direct radiovoice() usage were superseded. their definition does not imply every source mission calls them: preserve direct voice calls, higher-level radio wrappers and their distinct source control flow rather than swapping them by name. why call 3450 cannot simply be renamed exact-binary analysis identifies 3450 as an object + float operation. the edf5 bvm handler stores the value at object + 0x2e0; the edf6 bvm equivalent stores it at object + 0x470. a separate edf6 native helper performs that target write, but the reviewed angelscript interface did not expose a matching binding. it is not safe to substitute the similarly named setencountreportradius (3024) or setaiformationradius (3150): they access different object fields and have different effects. in the examined shipping set, 3450 occurred six times in dlc/dm006_2. the later user-accepted compatibility policy deliberately omitted these specific writes after a 3450-off runtime test loaded, spawned the frogs and reached mission completion. emit an explicit accepted-fidelity-loss warning, not a silent drop. exact semantic parity remains unproven, but this is no longer a blocker for documentation or the playable port. six independently reconstructed object/vehicle stack contracts beyond the enemy/ai table above, the paired source bvm stack and edf6 target signatures were independently checked for cuscall0 52 (setenablepause(bool)), cuscall0 910 (deletemob()), cuscall3 1000 (setmovearea(string)), cuscall0 1024 (ridevehicle(object)), cuscall0 1027 (setupvehicle(object)), and cuscall0 1028 (object.vehicle_setrideenable(bool)). in the last case the bvm stack contains object receiver below boolean, while the angelscript method takes only the boolean explicit parameter. this is why decoding a method call as a global function, or flattening all call banks into one numeric namespace, can change game behavior even when the visible api name looks appropriate. the complete small table is in bvm custom-call reference. the reconstructed source/api mapping is statically verified, not a fresh edf6 in-game test. registering and scheduling events event registration is a separate layer from the vm custom-call opcode grammar. in the audited bvm scheduler, multi == 1 processes all ready registrations; otherwise it selects the highest-delay ready registration. the target edf6 angelscript event types are equivalent in scheduling behavior: bvm multi == 1 → event_type_async (1) bvm multi != 1 → event_type_sync (0) this is based on the compared edf5 and edf6 native schedulers, not just names. in the measured 141-mission corpus, 5,193 raw registrations reduced to 5,112 reachable registrations (4,540 with multi=0, 572 with multi=1). the other 81 were unreachable scaffolding; do not publish them as active mission events. the source multi and target eventtype are different physical fields: equivalent behavior does not mean identical abi layout. what an implementer should do decode the vm stream and operand widths before interpreting call ids. reconstruct the stack values, object identity and actual argument order at the call site. compare source effects against paired native target scripts or binary consumers. keep mission registration/factor/handler topology separate from the textual order of decompiled methods. preserve unknown calls and fail explicitly; don't invent a convenient replacement. verify the output through source/compile and, when claiming gameplay parity, actual runtime evidence. evidence: exact edf5/edf6 bvm scheduler and 3450 binary contract (studied 2026 builds); paired mission scripts and the r37 transpiler research. no general claim of runtime parity for every edf5 mission api. for related information see event registration and re-arming, accepted 3450 fidelity waiver and mission rmpa. vm stack and side effects: avoid silent event changes not all target angelscript helpers return the same kind of value that the source vm expects. a particularly important group of source bvm calls is side-effect-only: 2002 2003 2004 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009 2010 2020 2021 2022 902 (createmob_path) in the studied 145-mission source set, the group transaction family above had no immediate result consumer (store, storeabs, storerel, cvtstore, pop) and had to be emitted immediately as statements. retaining a target helper's return expression on the simulated vm stack caused later calls to consume or reorder it, which had caused missing ufo group creation in m020/m080. for opcode 902, delayed emission also moved createmob_path calls after sendteamencount in m008, changing gameplay order. the same exact-pair analysis establishes that direct cuscall0 4000 with a voice string is voice(string), not playse. it must also be distinguished from higher-level radiovoice wrappers whose implementation might contain the same low-level custom call. the general rule is: reconstruct source stack effect and source side-effect ordering, then map the target api; do not infer source return semantics from the target function's signature. these are exact-corpus findings, not a declaration that every custom-call id has been reverse engineered. source-to-target call reference a custom-call and factor reference now lists the inspected 2000–2009 enemy/group family, 3100–3173 ai operations, team/vehicle behavior, 3500–3502 group operations, lighting, animations and event factors. it separates static exact-pair mapping evidence from runtime-positive cases and preserves the 3450 missing-angelscript-binding boundary. edf4.1 native ids are not edf5 custom-call ids see the edf4.1 bvm→edf5 exact recompile guide. it distinguishes edf4.1 table-1 native 3000 setencountreportradius (requiring a custom plugin table-1 3003 in the studied compatibility path) from edf5 cuscall0 3450 setaisearchradius (a separate, consciously omitted six-call effect). native ids must be interpreted with their table and generation, not mapped by similar human names. related native edf game references edf5 void calls, switches and voice abi edf4.1 example: createenemy2 is observable as distinct call sites the original edf4.1 m014 decompiled bvm uses 20 calls to cuscall0 2001: eleven source nephila and nine spidernet20/40/80 resources, some referencing the same named map spawnpoint. by contrast, original edf4.1 m002 uses ten cuscall0 2000 sites for single enemies, and m001/m003 use the 2002 group-creation form. this is a bounded six-mission illustration of different custom-call operands, argument lists and resource classes, not evidence that 2000/2001/2002 can be substituted at runtime. the two createmob_path (902) calls and seven createfriend (1010) calls in original edf4.1 m014 likewise show that crowd/path, allied and hostile creations share a mission graph without sharing one interchangeable api. do not conflate this edf4.1 m014 city-script example with edf5 m014 “secret of the cave” and its three-source-call reinforcement fix. see the edf4.1 six-mission native bvm comparison; this edition inspected the decompiled source statically and ran no gameplay parity test. r173 registration graph caution: a callback body is not itself an event a static function list can overstate the events a mission has actually wired. in the original edf4.1 bvm subset m001–m004, m012, m014, r173 followed func1709960674); another procedure may contain a registration that never enters the main-rooted closure (edf4.1 m012's func1974397686 registering func801877805). for m012, immediate factor calls such maps, missions and mission bundles relate a map describes a reusable world, a mission describes gameplay that runs on one map, and a mission bundle groups and packages missions plus their required resources. this distinction is useful when inspecting native mission resources or designing an authoring pipeline. the detailed ownership below is a reconciled authoring model, not a claim that every edf release exposes a public mission bundle file with exactly these editor-side fields. the key relationships map a ← mission 1 ← bundle x ← mission 2 ← bundle x ← mission 3 ← bundle y map b ← mission 4 ← bundle x in the reconciled authoring contract: each mission has exactly one canonical map; a map may be referenced by many missions; a mission may be reused by more than one bundle without silently changing its map; maps remain independently authored and are not permanently owned by the bundle; for a complete bundle with y enabled missions using x unique maps, y >= x; an unused map can exist in the workspace, but an enabled bundle should not publish an unreferenced map as part of its used-map set. there is no bundle-global same-map rule. an authoring tool must allow different missions in one bundle to select different maps. map editor versus mission editor map-authoritative data: terrain/topology, geometry, material and texture resources, object placements, foliage, water, collision, navigation, destruction and map builds. mission-authoritative data: mission ordering/membership, scripts/events, actors and objectives, per-mission map choice, dialogue/audio usage, resource registration and bundle packaging. a mission editor should consume a published map build rather than becoming another writer of map binary formats. likewise a map editor should not silently rewrite a mission's game-script semantics just because a map object changed. identity and freshness a custom map in the studied workspace v1 authoring model is identified by: project_id + map_family a build revision is distinguished by the workspace manifest sha-256. the representation uses metres and y-up coordinates. older workspace data without canonical identity can be previewed read-only, but should not be silently accepted as an authoritative mission map binding. a map can change while the mission still references its previous revision. this should produce an explicit freshness/rebind decision, not an automatic rewrite of every mission-local object or transform. resource paths and packaging verified map build resources are projected to bundle asset references with the runtime path: map/<resource.path> the authoring model distinguishes external/global dependencies, bundle overrides and bundle-owned resources. these are packaging/ownership semantics; they should not be confused with the game's normal resource lookup or native container structure. the mission scene owns its references to placed objects and its gameplay. a map refresh does not justify deleting mission-local authored entities or regenerating gameplay placements without review. native game-format boundary mission bvm/angelscript, mission rmpa, map rmpa, mapo, mad and native navigation are distinct layers. for example, a mission call such as setaipath(obj, "navigationmap") should not be treated as a mission-rmpa path reference without evidence: navigationmap refers to the native navigation/pathing semantics in the investigated sources. practical questions answered question answer under the recovered authoring contract can two missions share one map? yes can one bundle contain multiple maps? yes does copying a mission into another bundle change its map? no, not implicitly may a mission rebind to a new map revision? yes, explicitly, with checks should mission build tools write mad/fmep themselves? no; consume authoritative map publication is mission rmpa interchangeable with map rmpa? no read mission scripting and mission rmpa, map format responsibilities and workspace v1 details. evidence status: recovered authoring/integration contracts, reconciled map and mission ownership semantics, and sampled native file research. the editor architecture is a tool design boundary, not a native internal game-object layout specification.

mission events: registration, scheduling, state and re-arming mission control flow is a graph of registrations and handlers, not merely a list of functions in a decompiled bvm. this distinction matters when translating edf5 mission behaviour into edf6 angelscript (mission.ac), and it is useful when reading a mission's native event machinery. registration versus handler a registration supplies an incoming trigger/factor set, delay and check policy. a handler is the target event body and owns the event state and counter. several registrations can point at one target handler without creating several independent target event states. the relevant research distinguishes: element owns does not imply registration (edge) trigger factors, delay, check mode a separate copy of the target's state event target (node) handler, persistent state, counter, invocation policy that every incoming factor is one giant combined and scheduler selection/append of ready registrations a naive textual function-call order this model comes from native source/target observations and later source/target event reconciliation. an older description with target-owned factors was superseded by the more precise registration-owned factors model. multi is an exact comparison, not generic truthiness in the observed edf5/edf6 bvm scheduler, multi == 1 means that all ready registrations are appended for processing. other values select one ready registration according to the scheduler's delay rule. edf6 angelscript event types map to: source multi == 1 → event_type_async (1) source multi != 1 → event_type_sync (0) using multi != 0 is not equivalent to the observed comparison. the async wrapper must also avoid the sync voice/game-thread handshake (waitvoice, gettalkers) when that handshake is not part of the actual source path. reachable registrations matter a decompiler can expose dead compiler-generated registration branches. in the studied exact44 paired set, 2,233 textual registerevent occurrences reduced to 2,214 reachable registrations and 2,106 unique reachable target handlers. ids are assigned to unique targets in first-registration order, not based on sparse compiler func_n labels. these figures describe the studied fixture. they are not fixed counts for all edf missions. repeated and counter-based events the reconciled authoring model distinguishes three invocation policies: once: run only once; repeat: re-arm after invocation and permit subsequent triggers; nth: share a target counter and invoke only at the specified count. multiple once registrations are source-backed or fan-in: any one qualifying incoming registration may trigger the same target. for a single registration, factors may form and/or conditions inside that registration. an arbitrary logical and spanning unrelated registrations is not established and should not be invented by an importer. a cycle such as start → a → b → a may be represented using explicit re-arm policies. direct self-registration and start/main re-entry need separate evidence; they are not automatically safe simply because a cyclic graph can be drawn. exact factor distinctions some numeric factor codes are easily conflated. the retained mapping includes: code observed factor meaning 9201 factor_objectdestroy 9202 factor_objectencount 9300 factor_aimoveend 9301 factor_aimoveendordie 9116 factor_groupobjectcount 9117 factor_groupobjectencount 9205 factor_ridevehicle do not collapse 9201 and 9202 into the same event merely because their names and use cases are adjacent. how to interpret an unknown handler first reconstruct reachability, registration ownership, event identity, factor conditions, and side effects. only then infer what the handler will do in-game. a source-to-source compiler can preserve these graph properties without asserting that every unobserved engine api has exact target semantics. bytecode versus engine call identifiers a bvm cuscall0 instruction is a bytecode operation with a separate numeric engine-call id operand. for example, ac d0 07 means opcode 0xac followed by little-endian id 2000; it does not introduce opcodes d0 or 07. the shipping invalid/crashing bvm instruction opcode range is 0x39–0x3f in the examined build. read bvm bytecode and custom-call translation for api mappings, argument/stack semantics, and cases where an engine operation has no demonstrated angelscript binding. related discoveries mission scripting and rmpa overview event control-flow and dataflow mappings native mission rmpa profile evidence status: native scheduler comparison for the multi rule, source/corpus reconciliation for reachability and target identity, later mission studio semantics for registration-owned factors and re-arm/counter policies. not a claim that every mission api has been runtime-qualified. event state allocation, reachability and delay: exact-pair findings a handler may be armed more than once. the examined 44 exact edf5 source/official edf6 pairs contained 2,233 textual registerevent calls, but only 2,214 reachable from main through direct calls and event-target edges. those reachable registrations referenced 2,106 unique handler targets. the paired edf6 max_event_id totals also equal 2,106, supporting the following implementation model: one handler body (node) -> one persistent event id / state many incoming registrations (edges) -> potentially the same handler id allocate event ids for unique target handlers in first-registration order, not from sparse decompiler labels (func_27, func_42, etc.) or once per registration. unreachable func_n registrations produced by compiler flattening must not become active mission events. do not remove ordinary named utility functions solely because they are not called from main: some target-facing helpers are preserved for external/reference use. for the inspected registerevent end-event pattern, source delay 100.0f maps to target 100000000.0f only when is_end && source_delay == 100.0f. this is a narrow sentinel rule, not evidence for global scaling of all mission timings. one examined m029 high-level official port normalizes an empty relay chain; that difference does not imply that the source bvm lost its downstream triggers. sync/async scheduling in engine terms the bvm runtime checks the registration's multi field by equality with 1. if it equals 1, all ready registrations are appended. otherwise one ready registration with the greatest delay wins. the edf6 angelscript event scheduler sorts by descending delay, then uses event_type_async=1 to append ready events or event_type_sync=0 to select the first. that is why multi == 1 — not generic nonzero truthiness — is the valid translation for the examined builds. in the 141-shipping-mission corpus, 5,193 raw registrations reduced to 5,112 reachable registrations: 4,540 with multi=0 and 572 with multi=1. differences in manually authored official eventtype choices for m015/m016/m024/m035 do not rewrite independently measured source scheduler semantics. why this matters: if a converter creates duplicate target nodes or guesses event ids from function names, it can change counters, re-arm behavior, voice ordering and mission completion even when the generated angelscript compiles successfully. source-reachable registration topology is therefore a stronger parity check than raw counts of decompiled instructions. related native edf game references edf5 source graph/counter census edf5 native scheduler flags original edf5 source examples: shared counters and relay cases (consolidated) in the exact44 source-paired audit, 2,233 textual registerevent statements reduce to 2,214 reachable registrations, 2,106 distinct target handlers and 2,147 factor sites. the 19 discarded statements reside in unreachable compiler-generated regions. targets, not sparse compiler func_n names, identify persistent handler state. m018 illustrates why shared counters matter: func_3 is armed twice, and the second execution releases 60 red ants. m029 is a bounded special case where the original bvm arms two empty relay handlers from main, but the official target port chains them. m041 has a pre-registration call 9000 denoting a body wait, not a factor on the child registration. none is permission to rewrite arbitrary graph topology. source: edf5 edf5/mission-vm.md, bvm-event-reachability, bvm-event-slot-per-handler, bvm-handler-counter-guard, bvm-m029-relay, bvm-m041-wait-idiom (source/official static pairing). event-body domains: voice and gameplay are not interchangeable a separate source-matched 44-mission reference event-domain census aligned 1,387 cue-bearing edf5 func_n handler bodies by ordered cue signatures: 1,176 aligned to voice_script, 211 to game_script; 6 cue signatures were ambiguous in matching but retained the same resulting domain, and 0 source cue-bearing bodies remained unmatched in the measured reference. this is evidence that collapsing every edf5 source event into the edf6 *_game_event_usercode path may discard important game/voice execution-domain separation. it does not establish that the loss causes any specific reported subtitle-scroll symptom. a conservative proposed classifier that accepted only obviously radio/speech-only or pure talk transactions assigned 1,121/1,387 bodies. it was correct for 1,035, wrong for 86, and abstained for 266 — 92.33% precision among classified cases, inadequate for automatic source-to-target rewrites. the high correlations of radiobegin (64/64) and radioend (65/65) with the game domain are a warning that radio* is not a voice-domain guarantee. talkbegin and waitvoice likewise occur in both measured domains. multiple calls in a handler, not api name alone, determine the supported classification. the 44-entry evidence is a reference corpus; the retained domain census itself warns against claiming it proves every native/sandlot convention, even though separately verified official 44-mission archives exist. multi-registration targets have one shared threshold, not duplicated guards in the examined m020_5 event graph, two registrations both target source func_6 and share a counter threshold of 2. in the failing conversion, an outer target wrapper rejected the second invocation (m_counter != 1), while a second counter in the handler body itself rejected the first (func_6___counter != 2); together these guards prevented the body on both invocations. the blocked continuation would ordinarily activate the two carrier generators. the source-matched high-level reference instead uses one target-owned guard m_counter != 2 and no second guard inside the event body. the same bounded reference comparison identified 14 counter-threshold handlers across 11 mission scripts with n > 1. known examples include m015_3 thresholds 2/3/4/5, m016 threshold 3, and m020_5 threshold 2. these are counter-event semantics: the registration factors remain edge-owned while counter state belongs to the shared target. there is no license to promote a broad counter-pattern rewrite without verifying the source bytecode and effective target branch. evidence: edf5_edf6_exact44_event_domain_census_2026-09-05.json (44 reference missions, not a gameplay test); edf5_edf6_m020_5_r75_event_counter_offline_audit_2026-09-05.md and r75_official_multi_counter_census_2026-09-05.json (source bvm/asm comparison and failing modified-runtime progression symptom). edf4.1 source counterexample: a handler body does not prove event registration a six-mission original edf4.1 bvm decompilation sample provides a narrow independent illustration of the registration-versus-handler distinction: m002 contains the shared func1709960674 clear-handler body but zero textual registerevent and allenemydestroy call sites, whereas m001, m003 and m004 each contain one of each. therefore a decompiler inventory that merely counts named func... handlers overstates what is demonstrably registered in the source. this finding is edf4.1 source evidence, separate from the preceding edf5/edf6 exact44 scheduler numbers; it is not proof object-destruction and ai-move factors. in particular, func455038071 is registered after generator configuration with a 9201 object-destroy factor for the first carrier. later registrations depend on other factors and mother-object action sequences. these facts establish a staged source event graph, not whether every branch succeeds in a target edf6 runtime. exact ids, source hashes and call-site cue-bearing edf5 func_n handler bodies in 44 source-matched missions, with 1,176 matched to voice_script and 211 matched to game_script. the new per-mission crosswalk makes the source cases m091_4 60 44 16 mixed domain; 14 naive errors m021 54 47 7 radiobegin, talkbegin and radioend coexist in game-domain handlers m020_5 46 44 2 two fr_ae065b* cue-bearing handlers each have two reference animation formats — canm, cas and mab overview edf animation has three different data roles: canm stores keyed motion, cas coordinates named players/controllers, and mab contains timed events. those systems must agree with the target mdb skeleton. format directory format role version constraint canm bone/object keyframes, typed and quantized channels edf4.1, edf5 and edf6 channel layouts must be checked individually cas animation players, controller variables and state missing controller variables are not safe no-ops mab events, timing and resource bindings pointer base mode 0x03 vs 0x83 varies by generation start at animation for a version-aware guide, then use the detailed findings below for exact layouts and limits. mab pointer-base differences the prior brief mab note had an incorrect blanket rule. mab v15 internal pointers are not always absolute: edf4.1/edf5 use mode 0x03 (block-relative), while examined edf6 uses mode 0x83 (owning-struct-relative); the four top-level directory offsets remain block-relative. the bounded source research validated 1,153 edf4.1, 1,652 edf5 and 2,487 edf6 mabs. read the full measured mab layout and conversion rule rather than assuming a version-word swap. for event names, sgo parameters and sound ownership, read mab event clocks. exact canm key kinds and cas controller abi the measured cross-generation cas/canm format and conversion gives the real record layouts and field counts: 0x30-byte cas header, 0x20/0x30 canm channels, 28-byte clips, 8-byte tracks, four target channel kinds and float32 euler-to-quaternion behavior. it also records the bounded 836-file cas round-trip and 230 paired edf5/edf6 corpus, including why animated quaternion bits are often not exactly reconstructible from already quantized edf5 data. named cas player groups and vcontrols explain why importing an old object's clip data without certain named controllers can crash an edf6 target class, and why trackless donor-state placeholders are preferable to donor-bone animation copying. the animation findings concern several distinct containers and behaviors, not one “edf animation version.” a converter that edits only the version number is insufficient when record layouts, rotation representation and cross-references change. canm: animated channel data observed edf5 and edf6 canm are structurally different: property edf5 edf6 canm format version 0x200 / decimal 512 0x300 / decimal 768 approximate channel record size 0x20 0x30 rotation/channel interpretation euler-radian channels in studied profiles absolute xyzw quaternion representation in studied animated-rotation profiles additional channel fields earlier layout added xyzw base/multiplier and encoding type a raw version bump destroys these semantic differences. the observed converter findings require real decoding of older channel values, correct encoding into the target representation and preservation of metadata that the target format expects. cas: wrapper data is not the canm generation cas wraps animation/control/group/state information and can contain forward references into trailing canm/string data. observed cas wrapper version words across the games are: game cas wrapper value edf 4.1 00020000 edf 5 03020000 edf 6 04020000 cas wrapper generation and embedded canm generation must be tracked separately. a file's outer cas version does not tell an importer how to interpret all trailing animation channels. a universal cross-game cas conversion schema has not been established. mab: decoded v15 locators, event tracks and pointer bases (corrected) the earlier short note described boneadjust, animationadjust and floatgroup record types, gave universal absolute offsets, and quoted 0x08 / 0x10 record sizes. that provisional description is not the validated mab\0 v15 layout and must not be used to read or convert the examined edf4.1/5/6 v15 files. its original text is preserved under the r150 prior-article snapshots of r151 for provenance. the validated 0x24-byte header at version 0x0f has four block-relative directory offsets at +0x14…+0x20. header +0x08 specifies the format of internal offsets: 0x03 in the observed edf4.1/5 sources means block-relative, while 0x83 in examined edf6 files means owning-struct-relative. the actual decoded record families are 8-byte locator-list headers, 0x20-byte locator records, 0x10-byte event-track headers and 0x10-byte event keys, followed by vectors, optional embedded sgo parameters and strings. sentinels and ordinary integer fields must not be rewritten as pointers. the source parser validated 1,153 edf4.1, 1,652 edf5 and 2,487 edf6 mabs in its bounded corpus. mab stores important animation event timing, locator/muzzle attachments and audio-related event data; it is not a universal static-collision dependency. pointer-base migration is demonstrably solvable for this v15 family, but a valid converted file may still reference missing target skeleton bones, wrong locations, or target-class event consumers. see the complete measured layout, pointer rule and conversion boundary and event clock/audio ownership. the 111-root cas/mrab reference graph counts .cas and .mrab logical paths from an edf4.1 mission-object compatibility manifest. it contains no explicit .mab or .canm paths, which must not be interpreted as evidence those containers do not exist or are not loaded elsewhere. for a hit-reaction failure caused by a class selecting absent ragdoll bodies, see edf4.1 small-dragon partial-ragdoll names.

audio, dialogue and subtitles: what the edf research establishes edf4.1 → edf6 bank collisions, cri loading and shutdown the source-backed audio-bank and cue-resolution guide explains why 1,087 of 1,469 source se cue names collide with native edf6 names, why acb and awb can take different physical file-opening paths, and how an otherwise functioning imported sound bank can crash when released after the audio system is destroyed. timed mab cues and channel ownership are a separate layer; correct cue lookup alone does not preserve event timing. audio in edf is not one interchangeable archive or one string table. voice/audio banks, cue names, localized text, mission-level playback commands and subtitle rendering are separate parts of the pipeline. our research covers pieces of that system; it does not establish a complete edf5→edf6 audio-format conversion. awe, awb and acb the retained criware investigation supports inspection and extraction of the studied awe/awb data, including awbe identity handling and endian-tolerant parsing in the observed tooling. these findings are enough to inspect voice-name/list data and pair metadata with bank contents in the supported research path. they do not by themselves prove: that a bank can be copied unchanged between games; that cue indexes and language routing remain identical; that an unknown acb revision can be rebuilt losslessly; that codec, bank or sequence playback semantics match edf5 and edf6. efarc is tracked separately as an edf6 file/effect-archive research target. the retained work does not establish a universal efarc parser or a rule equating it with rab/marc/criware audio containers. mission dialogue is not just a filename the mission-scripting corpus distinguishes calls and data for voice, dialogue, background music and sound effects. a correct mission translation must preserve the relationship between: the script event that requests playback; the voice/cue/text reference it uses; the language-specific text/metadata; the assets actually included in the deployment; any event/thread sequencing affecting presentation. a structurally valid script can still play the wrong speech, omit text or wait for a voice handshake on an event path that should not use it. the recovered event model treats sync and async wrappers differently for relevant voice-thread handling. localization merges must be conservative a mission/localization merge must not erase unknown keys or a language variant simply because a source text table did not use it. the retained localization work treats key identity and per-language ownership as separate from the current language visible on screen. do not infer equivalence from english text alone. a shared identifier may refer to different localized content or gameplay ownership in another resource. subtitle display is another layer the edf6 subtitle-scroll investigation concerns the presentation/lifetime of subtitles, not a universal change to bank or codec formats. fixing whether long captions scroll or stay visible does not prove that missing dialogue records, wrong cue references or packaging dependencies have been repaired. what to do with an unfamiliar audio resource identify its container/metadata role before writing a converter. preserve original cue and language references, inspect whether it is mission-local or game-global, and mark cross-version playback claims as pending unless the exact candidate has been tested in-game. related articles: awe/awb/acb and efarc boundaries, dialogue, voice, bgm and se usage catalogs and localization ownership. evidence status: source/tool inspection and mission-specific reconciliation. cross-game audio-bank rebuilding and universal efarc semantics remain unresolved. further native edf references edf4.1 music and radio line selection edf5 cri atom bank and talk tables edf6 voice caption table and semanager

edf network behavior: shot state, packet ownership and reconnect engine packet transport versus per-object plugin authority packet delivery correctness does not by itself determine which machine is allowed to simulate an extra npc driver or count one new projectile hit. per-object multiplayer authority and local copies explains the 0x01/0x02 identity word, seat-0 owner fallback, registered versus unregistered copies and why a player's gunner input may be owned by a different machine from the vehicle. some of the most useful recovered engine facts concern which object owns a state, how much information is replicated, and what happens when a network link is replaced. those rules are more informative than treating every multiplayer desync as a generic packet-loss problem. weapon fire direction and replicated projectile state observed code paths distinguish a per-shot fire transform from the ordinary actor orientation. projectile direction cannot always be reconstructed from where a player avatar is facing. the game transports or reconstructs a subset of bullet creation and state properties according to subtype/selector-specific policies. the retained native weapon/bullet findings separate direct-fire modes, star-dependent evaluation and networkbullet selector/contact cases. the amount and meaning of replicated information are profile-specific; a generic “send actor transform and replay” algorithm is not faithful across all weapons. for exact selector/weapon family boundaries see weapon-fire direction, shipped weapon sync policy and networkbullet contact semantics. reliable state survives a transient physical-link replacement the studied sandlot rudp/reconnect path separates the replaceable physical p2p link from longer-lived packet controller/usersession/reliablemgr state. a transient remoteconnectionclosed can replace a physical link while pending reliable records, deduplication and sequence state survive on the logical peer/session layer. a true logical peer removal instead clears the usersession and eventually destroys the retained state. this explains why changing physical transport objects is not necessarily a full clean-session reset. exact fault/retry timing and sticky error behavior must be interpreted from the appropriate engine and peer lifecycle, rather than assuming tcp-like semantics. see rudp and reconnect analysis. third-party multiplayer patches can illustrate failure modes but are not proof of what original game binaries do. what has not been proven recovered ownership and serializer shapes do not establish perfect eight-player multiplayer, desync-free behavior, or all runtime combinations. network correctness depends on exact patch/version/peer behavior and gameplay-state constraints; offline inspection is evidence about implementation, not complete gameplay qualification. for exact protocol identities and a diagnosis that separates what the native code proves from previously rejected theories, see eventcontroller event ids and cross-version desync investigation.

edf6 high frame rates: why new presents may still show old motion in edf6, a displayed frame, a character pose, a camera state and one authoritative gameplay update are different events. raising one frequency does not automatically raise the others. what measurements can tell us an original edf6 moving-camera experiment recorded approximately 90.306 unique camera states per second, 89.728 presents per second and a 59.922 hz fixed cadence. the result shows that a camera can update more often than gameplay without requiring enemy ai or physics to advance at 90 hz. it does not establish a complete 90 hz presentation of every game subsystem. a useful measure of higher-rate visual presentation is the number of new world/camera states per present, not just an fps counter. if a hypothetical 120-hz display stream includes mostly repeated animation poses, its raw present number overstates the actual visible motion cadence. native subsystems have different clocks character animation and skinning, vegetation, shader time, particle effects, ribbons/trails, camera transforms, visibility and collision do not necessarily share one update path. fixed-step network/simulation code may intentionally advance at about 60 hz even if the renderer can run faster. a game can appear smoother in one domain but remain coarse in another. a visibility throttling experiment produced black-surface flicker and delayed shadows, illustrating why fewer occlusion passes are not automatically free performance. likewise, asynchronously scheduled rendering must use state from the correct owned job, rather than assuming a global tick describes every concurrent task. confidence and limits these are local measurements and static findings from selected pc builds and research runs. they should not be generalized into promises about all pc configurations, nor described as proof that edf6 natively offers a fully smooth 120-hz mode with unchanged gameplay. no new game-runtime test was conducted for this article. for the original numeric findings see fixed cadence and umbra visibility.

edf4.1 / edf5 / edf6 — technical quick reference this reference explains what is known about the games, where to read the underlying research and why conclusions from one version cannot automatically be used for another. it is not a history of tool development. first decide which data layer you are reading layer typical native resources main question game archives cpk, rab, cmpl, marc how is an asset stored, compressed and found? models mdb, mdx, mab, cas, canm what are geometry, materials, bones and animations? maps mac, mapb, mapo, fmb, fmep what objects, terrain and visual features are placed? physics and navigation mad, shkt, hkt, nvmd what is solid, what moves, and where can ai travel? missions bvm, ac, mission rmpa, sgo/dsgo what events, spawns and script operations occur? multiplayer and progress gamestatus, missionmgr, mode list, mst, protocol data which state belongs to a player, session or game mode? a file that parses does not necessarily behave correctly in the game. similarly, correctly rendered geometry does not establish collision, and a valid collision mesh does not establish ai navigation. where to begin native archive and resource formats, models and mdb and material/shader systems. map containers and world placement, collision and navigation. missions, scripting and mission rmpa. native gameplay and enemy ai, weapon parameters and weapon upgrades. network architecture and native progress/modelist identity. high-value differences across generations mdb and canm: familiar names do not imply a byte-identical on-disk abi; vertex declarations, channels, materials and sampling differ. havok and nav: geometry, collision and route graphs are separate. edf4.1 navigation cannot safely be inferred from an edf6 donor mesh. bvm and angelscript: event registration, api types, branch semantics and rmpa route names must be interpreted, not text-substituted. missionpack: selecting a mode, resolving its resource request, loading list/txt and updating its save namespace occur at different stages. gameplay rules: hp factors, kill merit, equipment ownership and vehicle/object action ids differ between titles; use the exact game's sources. rendering: shader names alone cannot reconstruct sampler order, packed texture channels or the special fieldrender path. evidence and confidence contributor verified means the cited researcher reported a runtime test; it does not mean this wiki ran the test. native binary/static refers to files or disassembly for a specified build; an address is not a universal constant. open/unverified means a proposed interpretation still needs proof. source-conversion or binary-serialization success is not equivalent to gameplay parity. for difficult discrepancies see the cross-source reconciliation, the negative findings, and the original attributed knowledge hub appendices. some established examples enemy hp and the edf4.1 shield bearer exception. team merit and edf5/6 support-credit compression. edf4.1 uforobo state machine. edf5/edf6 weapon-table row identity. edf6 clear bits and difficulty-level interpolation. edf6 shader and visibility performance. the wiki retains original sources and their limitations. it is an evolving reference, not a guarantee that every build or source collection has been examined.
