m062 / cave503: all three e506 rows were in large chambers with substantial ceiling clearance; m072_1 and m072_3 / base502 already had direct runtime pass; m029 / cave504 and m072_2 / edfroom02 were retained as focused-smoke candidates, not preemptive-repair targets. the important policy survived later work: do not relocate additional humanoid_basic spawns solely because a static clearance heuristic looks suspicious. m014 h1f already demonstrated that a point can look acceptable statically and still fail at runtime, while other statically constrained-looking points can work. build a relocation candidate only after an actual eject/stuck symptom is observed and isolated. the audit initially noted that both known problem cases involved constrained geometry plus immediate locomotion/route context. later dm001 work showed delayed route assignment did not explain the first-frame eject, so this correlation must not be promoted into a universal causal rule. use it only as test-priority context. source: missionpack03_04_05_humanoid_spawn_risk_audit_2026-09-09.md.

edf5 bvm stack semantics: source-void calls, cvtstore and event order evidence: source bvm/angelscript exact-pair analysis of the inspected edf5 shipping mission corpus, reconciled with the native api inventory. these rules concern how the game's vm executes and orders operations. a correct-looking angelscript call is not sufficient if it changes when a side effect occurs. side-effect-only group calls do not leave a result on the vm stack source custom calls 2002, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2020, 2021 and 2022 form a source-void group-transaction family in the audited bvm source set. across 145 source missions, none was immediately followed by a result-consuming store, storeabs, storerel, cvtstore or pop for that operation. the native source stack contract is thus statement/side effect, even if a corresponding target angelscript factory might return an object. 902 createmob_path is another statement-like effect. delaying it past a subsequent team-encounter notification changes the mission's event order. historical exact-pair failures included a missing second ufo group in m020, a lost goldufo group in m080, and reordered createmob_path/sendteamencount in m008. this is a source-vm execution distinction, not a general rule that target api calls never return objects. cvtstore: stored lvalue remains available the recovered vm semantics of cvtstore retain the stored lvalue on the operand stack. an expression with side effects must be evaluated once, not recomputed when the returned/stored value is used later. the same rule must be observed when interpreting compiler-generated switch/dispatch lowering, not only ordinary straight-line bvm. in the 141-mission source-only parity audit, an earlier flawed translation produced 43 duplicate calls of the dm012 op2001 family because of this value-flow mistake. correcting cvtstore removed those duplicates. this is an exact historical source-vs-output mismatch; it is not evidence that the original edf5 game performs the actions twice. source transaction conservation the full reconciled audit counted 3,471 source spawn-related transactions and zero source-order failures after the final source-value-flow corrections. the six source/target literal differences at dm006_2 were from deliberate object-sgo specialization for custom call 3450, not extra enemy spawns or an alternate order. later game testing rejected that specialization and accepted a narrower mission-specific 3450 omission; it must not be promoted as a generally correct runtime implementation of search-radius semantics. for the exact r44 source reconstruction, 141/141 mission.ac outputs matched the historical reference bytes, with 722/722 createenemy2 occurrences. these are offline exact-parity findings. the entire gameplay campaign was not freshly runtime-qualified by that result. provenance markers versus source semantics when an output contains compound helper code, a comment such as edf5_cuscall:bank:id can help an auditor distinguish direct 3152 setaifollow from the distinct compound 1013 follower transaction. the comment is a research provenance mechanism, not itself a feature of edf5's native script format. see bvm bytecode and custom calls, decoded call reference and event registration for the associated vm and runtime contracts. sources: r44_current_research_state_2026-08-27.json, readme_r44.txt, mission_resolved_mapping_reconciliation_2026-08-25.json, and the inspected edf5 shipping bvm/edf6 script corpus. native backward switches and direct voice call (consolidated) the bvm compiler may place switch-case bodies before their dispatch ladder. a ladder can use pushtop, case comparison and jmpne followed by a backward jump to the selected body. the runtime stack must be reconstructed from control-flow predecessors, not physically preceding bytes. m015, m059, m065 provide original source examples where a linear interpretation can select the wrong difficulty branch. in the inspected source corpus, direct one-argument cuscall0 4000 is voice(string), not generic playse. m015_2 has five direct ae... voice calls, with corresponding official voice operations. wrapped radio helpers need separate context. the event-order example in m008 is two friendly squads → three 902 createmob_path operations → encounter notification; moving the path operations changes source semantics. evidence: edf5 edf5/mission-vm.md, bvm-switch-form, cuscall-4000-voice, bvm-902-void, bvm-source-void-group-ops (source static).

systemic flag index parity repair — 21 affected missions patch 1.0.6 identified a converter-wide enum identity defect, not 21 unrelated mission bugs. root cause edf5 source logic can combine numeric flag producers such as: flagon(n) flagoff(n) with symbolic factor consumers such as: factor_flagon(flag_n) factor_flagoff(flag_n) the broken conversion path assigned generated symbolic flag enum ordinals by first-use order instead of preserving the source flag index. a producer could therefore set numeric flag n while a consumer named flag_n actually referred to a different generated ordinal. the required invariant is: flag_n == n for the source flag identity domain. runtime discriminator — m050 / displayed mission 59 m050 exposed the defect as a real softlock. restoring source flag indices while retaining the source allenemydestroy logic produced a user-confirmed runtime pass in rc6. easy/hard correctly skip the high-difficulty wave and still reach final dialogue + mission clear. m050 therefore proves the mechanism at runtime. full affected set the systemic repair applies to exactly these 21 missions in the retained 1.0.6 ledger: m004 m005 m007_5 m009 m014 m020_5 m027 m029 m030 m034 m039 m041 m042_5 m045 m046_3 m047_2 m050 m072_2 m091_4 m098 m099 for the 20 missions other than m050, the rc7 repair is intentionally enum-only: no function/event/gameplay text outside the flag enum is meant to change. qualification boundary m050 mechanism: runtime pass on an earlier rc; remaining 20 repairs: source/static-qualified in the 1.0.6 build lineage; exact finalized 11 october 1.0.6 package: per-mission runtime remains pending unless separately documented. high-value regression targets include m098, m099, m047_2, m004, m005, m041, m045 and m046_3. converter rule do not assign semantic enum identities according to encounter order when the source domain already has stable numeric identities. generated symbolic names must preserve the source numeric identity exactly. this lesson generalizes beyond flags: whenever numeric producers and symbolic consumers meet, prove that the symbolic target domain is identity-preserving before using generated ordinal order.

mission rmpa: binary groups, waypoint ids and serialization pitfalls scope: the edf5 → edf6 source-only mission rmpa profile established from paired mission resources and the retained rmpa_source_only.py writer. mission rmpa is not the same format contract as map rmpa or the rmpa embedded in an mae weather resource. file and group layout the measured edf6 output begins with a 0x30-byte file header. its principal 32-bit fields are big-endian (unlike the little-endian nvmd file). the first four bytes are 00 50 4d 52 (\0pmr), followed by version 1. four top-level group sections are referenced independently: routes, shapes, camera and spawn points. the audited writer places the first route type header at 0x30 and the first waypoint record at 0x50. record measured footprint function file header 0x30 bytes version and group offsets/counts group type header 0x20 bytes group and string-table references waypoint 0x30 bytes global id, position, links, descriptor route group 0x18 bytes membership and group-level references shape 0x24-byte header plus 0x40-byte payload; standard 0x10 metadata shape name/type and geometry spawn point 0x34 bytes global id, two positions and name some small descriptors are stored little-endian even though primary records are big-endian. an implementation must inspect each field rather than treating the whole file as one homogeneous byte order. why route ids change in a conversion edf5 route groups can number waypoints locally. the studied edf6 profile uses one flattened global waypoint sequence. a local outgoing next reference must be translated by the containing route group's starting position. for mission.rmpa specifically, the independently audited mission_rmpa_source_only.py builder flattens waypoint records across source route groups in file order and assigns waypoint.no = 0, 1, …, n−1. each source waypoint.gid remains a separate, preserved identity, and route-local next indices are rebased to global waypoint indices by adding the route group's cumulative start offset. the 141-mission source/target audit confirms this global numbering, gid conservation, next-link rebasing and width conservation for 5,103/5,103 waypoints. do not import a mapb_t2_count + 3 starting-index rule from a map-owned rmpa/placement writer into the mission-owned profile. the inspected mission_rmpa_source_only.py takes only the original mission.rmpa, without mapb placement count input. cross-file identifiers, mapb placement ids and native nav semantics remain separate systems. if another tool uses mapb-based identity construction, that is a distinct format or tool-specific contract requiring its own evidence. alignment and string addressing in the inspected mission writer, per-waypoint next-link arrays are padded to 16-byte alignment when nonempty, and the route-group membership arrays also begin at 16-byte boundaries. the shape and spawn areas have independent 16-byte alignment rules. the shared utf-16be string table begins with the writer's two-byte zero anchor; an alleged eight-byte route-list prefix belongs to a different studied writer/packing context and is not a rule of this mission rmpa implementation. string records are utf-16be in the examined source-only profile, with a two-byte zero prefix. several references are record-relative or field-relative, not absolute file pointers. treat the base of each offset as part of its individual record's specification. one older rmpa description conflated a type-header field with an enumeration-subheader field near 0x1c; the later correction stressed that field offsets are meaningful only relative to the correct structure base. do not paste a context-free 0x18/0x1c pointer rule into all rmpa variants. validation check \0pmr and version, all four group ranges, and internal section counts. confirm the route-local-to-global mapping for every outgoing waypoint link. validate string pointer bases, mixed-endian descriptor fields and alignment. resolve target ids to the intended mapb placements, shapes and scripts. treat structural/byte tests and actual mission gameplay as separate evidence. in the shipping141 source/target research corpus, 5,103 waypoints, 1,355 shapes, 3,387 spawn records and 6,665 literal mission-script-to-rmpa references were accounted for in the offline gate. they are observed test counts, not limits of the binary format. related: mission rmpa source-only profile, mission events and rmpa. evidence: retained mission_rmpa_source_only.py, validate_mission_rmpa.py, source/target audits and portable 141-mission gate. no new windows runtime qualification. source/target proof boundary and one unusual metadata case (r94) the full 141-mission source-only gate reports 5,103 waypoints, 1,355 shapes, 3,387 spawns and 6,665 ac-to-rmpa literal references, with zero missing generated rmpa names. a later portable source recovery matched the historical r1 output sha for 141/141 mission candidates. this confirms a repeatable standalone format profile and source-reference closure, not gameplay-runtime acceptance. the exact target-profile audit found 1,354/1,355 shapes with the standard usage / 通常 metadata and a single reference-port exception in m061, where one camera-named shape omitted it. source semantics did not supply a reliable generic discriminator, so the source-only writer uses the standard descriptor and leaves the exceptional port-specific tuning unresolved, not hardcoded for all shapes. source: mission_rmpa_source_only_shipping141_gate_2026-08-27.json, mission_rmpa_portable_shipping141_gate_2026-09-04.json, mission_rmpa_target_profile_shipping141_audit_2026-08-27.json and mission_rmpa_source_only.py, under /edf5_edf6_research/research/active/mission_rmpa/r1/. shipping141 per-mission evidence see the 141-mission record catalogue and 68-mission reference-tuning casebook for the actual observed record inventories and named differences between paired edf5/edf6 reference resources.

mission list — previews and resource identity reference overview an edf6 mission preview has three separate identities: the mission list.sgo row, its localized title/brief, and the named dds selected from the correct runtime image archive. correcting one does not automatically correct the others. contract studied edf6 target profile mission rows offline/online target order must remain compatible with save/progression identity thumbnail key list field 2; replace / with _, append .dds runtime images base missionlist.offline.image.rab and missionlist.online.image.rab pack-local image.rab not authoritative for the audited runtime loader see missions and mission thumbnails. the historical mismatch below is a case study, not the current desired metadata arrangement. historical offline/online list mismatches the 139-unique-mission offline/online mismatch above is a historical deployment observation, not the corrected target schema. the later maintained missionpack03 resource has 112 rows on both offline and online, with a shared ordinal sequence and matching companion txt/image resources. for the ordinary underground flags=40 behavior and the different special 0x200 condition bit, see underground mission flags and weaponcondition. a custom missionpack may contain a valid list.sgo and still show missing thumbnails or incorrect localized titles. mission ordering, images, text, and gameplay logic are separate resources that must agree. a shared-name image archive can be authoritative in one runtime-traced edf5-content deployment on edf6, the game requested missionlist.offline.image.rab, not each pack's separately named image.rab. correct per-pack image payloads alone did not supply the resource the game requested. the successful historical override used the shared-name path: mods/mission/missionlist.offline.image.rab the tested additive archive retained 147 native entries and added 139 edf5-related entries, with a corresponding online resource. that is one observed loader/configuration; it is not proof that every mod loader or game revision uses the same lookup precedence. three linked tables, three different concerns resource what it provides why archive integrity is not enough list.sgo order, progression and metadata for missions an inserted/reordered row can change display associations localized txt (sgo or dsgo by profile) titles and descriptions txt's serialized form is not universal across deployment roles missionlist.*.image.rab preview-image payloads the loader may request a shared name rather than a pack-local one mission.ac / bvm mission actions and events menu success does not imply the script will execute config / pack registration namespacing and selection an archive can exist yet never be selected later r29 evidence settles the studied edf6 mission-list association: derive the named archive entry from list field2, replacing / with _ and appending .dds. this supersedes the older unresolved name-versus-ordinal hypothesis for that profile. it remains necessary to update field2 when constructing new missions and to audit actual online/offline base image.rab lookup; see the exact format and tested scope. historical 112/111 list ordering is not the later 112/112 save contract an exact r41 audit of an edf5-content converted missionpack03 recorded 112 offline rows (m000 plus the studied online sequence) and 111 online rows (m000 omitted, m082/m083 retained). that describes the audited converted lists, not an independently proven native edf5 offline binary layout. a later edf6-compatible metadata scheme deliberately uses 112/112 shared ordinal rows to keep progress/save identity consistent. see source-vs-converted list contract. online and offline lists are not interchangeable a separate observed deployment had the missionpack03 online list.sgo byte-identical to its offline version. this exposed only 139 unique shipping missions, omitted m082 and m083 from the online list and exposed tutorial m000 online. the mistake was in list generation/deployment, not in what the mission transpiler should support. companion json lists were stale; the loaded binary list was the evidence. how to diagnose a missing or wrong image identify the actual archive filename opened by the running game using file-access evidence where needed. verify the selected archive has the right named entry and decoded image payload. check list order, txt titles/descriptions and thumbnail relationship together. compare online and offline binary lists intentionally rather than assuming they match. check script/mission startup separately from menu display. related: rab/mrab named-entry layout, mission metadata and shared progress. evidence: recorded runtime file-access observation and subsequent mission-list binary comparison in the retained r6 corpus. statements are case-scoped, not general assertions about all installations. for the distinction between mission-list row visibility and saved progress, and between weapon ownership and star bytes, see mission selection and weapon-record states. when two mods change the same mission-image archive, entry-wise ssa merging can retain both named payloads. list-to-image association is cross-file-coupled, but the r29-supported profile now has an explicit field2 name rule; archive-level merging must check that each changed list field2 resolves to the correct named entry. see rab/mrab entry merging.

edf6 mission thumbnail identity: list field2 is the key the september 2026 uncertainty over whether mission preview images were selected by name or a row ordinal was resolved for the studied edf6 mission list/rab format. later r29 source authority and prior runtime file-access evidence establish a named dds entry derived from list field2, rather than an anonymous image_at_row_index relationship. the actual runtime archive path the observed target game requests these base-level archives: mods/mission/missionlist.offline.image.rab mods/mission/missionlist.online.image.rab a custom missionlist_missionpacknn.image.rab can be well-formed and still not be the archive the observed loader requests. this is why earlier custom packs with correct local images showed missing or repeated previews. the base-archive lookup is backed by retained file-access / prior mission-port runtime evidence; the september 18 r29 editor authoring build itself was not yet game-runtime qualified. stable entry identity for the studied mission-list profile, the entry name is derived from the exact field2 display key, using the path-token normalization: entry_name = list_field2.strip().replace('\\','/').replace('/','_') + '.dds' for example, mission/example_a becomes mission_example_a.dds. this is an illustrative synthetic key, not a claim about a shipping mission's literal name. the maintained writer rejects empty keys, absolute paths, path traversal .., an already-suffixed .dds, and trailing separators. it also case-fold-checks duplicate archive entry names. consequences: reordering list rows does not in itself change the key for an unchanged field2. conversely, copying one donor row into every new slot without updating field2 makes distinct missions resolve to the same donor preview identity. a converter must populate field2 consistently with its own thumbnails and verify online and offline references rather than assuming correct images will follow from row ordering. exact archive and payload contract the retained r29 serializer accepts a raw dds, not a png or a filename disguised as dds: bytes dds at offset 0; dds header size 124 at +0x04; validated width and height (source validator bounds 1–16,384); deterministic literal cmpl wrapper and independent decompress-to-original round-trip; ssa image rab version 0x110 with exactly one texture type family; existing named entry replaced in place, otherwise appended; all non-target compressed payload bytes preserved exactly. the source stores per-slot thumbnail dds/hash/dimensions in a portable workspace. it requires an existing legitimate edf6 base image archive; it does not build an empty alternate image namespace and pretend the runtime will load it. the actual evidence hierarchy statement evidence game requests the two base mission image.rab resources prior procmon and mission-port runtime observation retained in r29 authority list field2 derives the named dds entry r29 schema contract, retained packer code and edf4.1 product reconciliation r29 authoring can replace/append without touching stock payloads offline test/build gates; 25/25 tests and synthetic deployment reported new r29 editor build works in the edf6 retail runtime not proven in the r29 checkpoint all future/unknown mission formats use exactly this rule not claimed the reconciling november 2026 investigation additionally ran the retained packer on synthetic data: four valid name conversions, seven unsafe-key rejections, one replacement plus one append, and verified preservation of the one untouched payload. that is tool logic only, not a new game test. see list/txt/thumbnail deployment, ssa rab binary records and rab multi-provider entry merge.

bvm custom-call and factor reference: decoded engine actions the edf5 mission vm stores numeric custom-call identifiers; edf6 mission authoring exposes many of the same effects as named angelscript operations. the tables below are a reverse-engineered reference for the inspected edf5 shipping mission corpus, not a guarantee that every name can be called on every object type or that each conversion has been runtime-certified. an instruction such as ac d0 07 means the cuscall0 instruction with a little-endian custom-call id 0x07d0 (2000). the call id does not change the vm opcode or its operand width. a correct converter must reconstruct stack ownership, arguments, control flow and timing before mapping an api. object, enemy and group operations custom-call id interpreted effect / target form important distinction 1013 create/attach follower group and setaifollow transaction a compound transaction; not the same source event as direct 3152 1024 ridevehicle vehicle setup/ride order matters 1027 setupvehicle initialization is separate from riding 1028 vehicle_setrideenable receiver is an object 2000 createenemy default enemy-creation path 2001 createenemy2 distinct and confirmed for wall-anchored spawners 2004 createenemygroup_spawn group transaction with immediate side effect 2005 createenemygroupug_spawn underground-family variant 2006 createflyingenemygroup_area opcode-defined; no sgo heuristic 2007 createflyingenemygroup_area_route route-bearing flying-area variant 2008 createenemygroup_area also used with a flying sgo in an official sample; not inherently flying-only 2009 createenemygroup_area_spawn dedicated target operation, not .spawn() on createenemygroup_area 2201 setdropboatdrop drop boat behavior 2203 setdropboatautocruise drop boat behavior 3000 delete object source argument/ownership must be retained 3018 setobjectinvincible object-state operation 3020 setobjectdurabilitymin earlier labels may use different names 3021 setignoredamageeventmode separate from invincibility 3022 setencount(object) one object argument in the measured signature 3023 sendteamencount team-id interpretation must be checked 3052 setteamid source team ids: 1 enemy, 2 friend, 3 neutral 3400 leader.follower(index) method form, specific owner 3500 addgroupobjectbegin opens group transaction 3501 addgroupobjectend closes group transaction 3502 getgroupobjectcount reads group state source vm: pause, object removal and vehicle setup these six entries have source-stack arity and target api signature independently checked for the inspected edf5 bvm corpus. call bank and receiver ownership matter, rather than just the numeric id: source bvm call source-stack arguments verified target-side signature important constraint cuscall0 52 1 void setenablepause(bool) use source boolean value, not forced true cuscall0 910 0 void deletemob() no invented object argument cuscall3 1000 1 void setmovearea(string) different call bank; edf6 underground mission flags, air raider support and runtime conditions a red weapon in the mission menu is not equivalent to blocking its use in the mission. the edf5→edf6 underground mission-port research identified separate mechanisms for list metadata, loadout presentation and the weapon-condition state used by the game during actual support/vehicle activation. this article reports native binary and in-game observations. the bit-field meanings below are scoped to the examined edf6 mission-list profile, not an assertion that every possible mission flag is decoded identically in all contexts. two paths from mission flags to no_support in the analyzed missionscriptasimplement metadata application logic (near edf+0x1ddf50 and edf+0x1de770 in the qualified dll), both of these conditions set raw weaponcondition=1: flags & 0x20: ordinary underground-profile route. it also performs additional 0x20-specific side effects. flags & 0x200: an independent route from bit 9 that selects the same no-support condition without that 0x20 side-effect block. the corresponding observed state values are 0 (normal), 1 (no-support) and 2 (force-enable/override family). edf6 exposes the native angelscript api setweaponcondition(::weaponcondition). compatibility checks also consume a weapon's use_underground property, observed at weapon object +0x228 in the examined build. why values 8, 9, 40 and 520 are not interchangeable decimal flags hex menu restriction mask 0x227 raw gameplay weaponcondition in the examined apply path 8 0x008 clear 0 — normal 9 0x009 hit via bit 0 0 — normal 40 0x028 hit via bit 0x20 1 — no support 520 0x208 hit via bit 0x200 1 — no support 552 0x228 hit via both higher bits 1 — no support flags=9 is an especially useful discriminator: it can produce an apparently restricted loadout menu without enforcing the gameplay no-support condition. the ui state alone must not be used as a pass/fail test for an underground port. native edf6 cave missions were observed using flags=40, including the m050 comparison mission. a separate vanilla row rm000 ("today's plans", using edfroom601) uses flags=520 in both offline and online lists. this proves 0x200 is a real game-used condition bit, not a user-created magic constant; its broader symbolic name remains unresolved. what an underground mission should actually do in native edf6, incompatible air raider equipment may still be selected/equipped before starting the mission and displayed in red. the decisive test is whether the incompatible conventional air raid or vehicle/support request functions during gameplay. three custom edf5-content missions were later retested with the ordinary native-like flag value 40: tested custom mission list flags in-mission restriction missionpack03 m000 40 runtime pass in the reported test missionpack03 m001 40 runtime pass in the reported test missionpack04 dm019 40 runtime pass in the reported test these later tests supersede the older interpretation that m000/m001 were inherently broken or that custom missionpacks could not apply 0x20. the original diagnosis confused menu restrictions, temporary deployment mismatches and the actual activation criterion. conversion and authoring rules the audited edf5-derived missionpack corpus classified 15 underground missions: mp03: m000, m001, m014, m027, m028, m029, m056, m057, m062, m072_2, m204; mp04: dm001, dm007, dm019; mp05: dm007_2. the documented production metadata policy uses flags=40 on those 15 rows, with standard surface rows using 8. keep this target list aligned with the correct offline/online mission ordinals and companion txt/image resources; a repair to a stale list can affect save identity and presentation independently of weapon restrictions. do not replace every underground 40 with 520 or 552. bit 0x20 has additional native mission-profile effects absent from 0x200; there is no evidence that such a wholesale replacement is safe or necessary. likewise, adding setweaponcondition(no_support) to every mission script was an experimental diagnostic, not a required production architecture. what remains uncertain the three tested missions establish correctness for those tested runtime cases. they do not certify every underground mission, dlc combination, game build or custom loader. a fresh case should be investigated by comparing the deployed list row, selected mode/mission record, global weaponcondition during mission setup, and the actual support activation result — not by judging the equipment's color alone. for the wider metadata rules see underground-only list repair changed field10 from 8 to 40 for 15 unique missions but only 29 row instances, because the older mp03 online list still omitted m000 (112 offline / 111 online). the mab v15 across edf4.1, edf5 and edf6 — binary structure and the real pointer migration scope and evidence. this is the decoded, bounded mab\0 version 0x0f family in the retained edf4.1/5/6 weapon/object resources. it is based on a tested parser/converter (mab_legacy.py) and recorded paired-file research, not a fresh gameplay test. unlike the earlier short mab reference, the source does establish a concrete generational difference: 0x03 versus 0x83 changes the interpretation of internal offsets. the old rule that mab offsets are always absolute was incorrect. the one crucial compatibility difference header word at +0x08 observed generation where internal pointers are relative to 0x03 edf4.1 and edf5 start of the mab block (absolute within that block) 0x83 edf6 start of the owning 8-, 16- or 32-byte struct (record-relative) the four top-level directory offsets in the header at +0x14 through +0x20 remain relative to the start of the mab block in both variants. the change applies to the offset fields inside list headers, records, tracks and keys. sentinel -1 is not a pointer and must remain -1. for an internal pointer field at address p, with the start of its owning struct base, a previously absolute target t becomes: edf4.1/5: raw_value = t edf6: raw_value = t - base reader: target = raw_value + (base if header_flag == 0x83 else 0) do not globally subtract a base from every 32-bit value. some fields contain literal counts, floats, enum kinds, zero fields or sentinels. the converter must recognize the layout and rewrite only proven offset fields, then validate that their decoded destinations are unchanged. header layout — 0x24 bytes offset width meaning in the examined family 0x00 4 ascii mab\0 0x04 4 version 0x0f 0x08 4 pointer-mode flag 0x03 / 0x83 0x0c 2 number of locator lists 0x0e 2 number of animation-event tracks 0x10 2 number of vec4 values 0x12 2 string-area length in bytes 0x14 4 list-header table offset, normally 0x24 0x18 4 track-table offset (end of locator records) 0x1c 4 aligned vec4 table offset 0x20 4 string table offset; offset + length equals mab size the following region order is enforced by the tested parser: header (0x24) locator-list headers (8 bytes each) locator records (0x20 bytes each) event-track headers (0x10 bytes each) event keys (0x10 bytes each) 0xba padding to the next 16-byte boundary vec4 table (16 bytes per value) embedded sgo argument objects (if present) utf-16le string area an edf5 file may contain nonzero unreferenced bytes in its string area. edf6's exporter zeroes unused string-area bytes, so exact-byte comparisons need to account for this normalization. the actual record layout each locator-list header has uint16 list_kind, uint16 record_count, and an int32 pointer to its first record. in the studied corpus list_kind equals its list index and records are contiguous. each locator record is 0x20 bytes: record offset interpretation +0x00 pointer to locator-name utf-16le string +0x04 pointer to bone/node-name utf-16le string +0x08 locator kind, observed 0 through 4 +0x0c pointer to position vec4 +0x10 pointer to vec4 for kinds 1/2; inline float for 0/3/4 +0x14 pointer to rotation/auxiliary vec4 for kinds 2/3/4; -1 for 0/1 +0x18 reserved zero in validated family +0x1c pointer to an embedded sgo\0 data block the position vector is expressed in the named node's frame. for kinds using a rotational vec4, source observations describe euler radians composed as rz · ry · rx; the locator's local +z is used as the weapon/muzzle firing direction in a known engine path. this is a sampled class convention, not an assertion that every arbitrary mab field follows the same semantic contract. animation events live in mab, not only cas a track header is 0x10 bytes: pointer to first key, pointer to end of keys, pointer to track name, and key count. a key is also 0x10 bytes: utf-16le event-name pointer, float32 time, zero/reserved integer and a pointer to its embedded sgo arguments. event track names match cas clip names. a working parser returns structures such as: fly_attack: 火炎開始, time=t0, args={...} 火炎終了, time=t1, args={...} known examples include uforobo event parameters such as collision, damage, quake and scale, and audio events using se / se_stop with cue or channel metadata. for a new reader, the mab event-track table is a first-class source of gameplay timing; static bone locators alone are not the entire format. see mab event timing and sound ownership and dragonbig401 flame behavior. conversion and source-pair evidence the retained parser recorded full layout validation on 1,153 edf4.1 flag-0x03 mabs, 1,652 edf5 flag-0x03 mabs, and 2,487 edf6 flag-0x83 mabs. the documented conversion accepted every examined source 0x03 block in that bounded corpus. the source converter rewrites only recognized offset fields, sets 0x83, zeroes unreferenced string slack and validates decoded pointers after writing. in 1,318 paired edf5/edf6 resources, the converted source was byte-identical in 592 cases (including 340 that needed unused string-area zeroing). the other 726 paired resources had genuine content changes, not a different unknown pointer codec: 416 changed locator vec4 values (e.g., reauthored ik/muzzle positions); 191 changed locator names or skeleton-node names; 114 changed record/track/key/embedded-sgo counts; 5 changed key times or embedded sgo data. interpretation: the pointer migration is solved for this validated mab family, but semantic model/weapon retargeting is not solved by that migration. a parseable, re-encoded source may still aim a muzzle at the wrong position, refer to a bone that does not exist or omit a required target animation event. exact string-area behavior for exporter authors the studied edf6 weapon mab writer deduplicates strings and orders them by their cp932 (shift-jis) byte encodings while storing their content as utf-16le. each string is padded to a slot of (cp932_bytes + 1) utf-16 code units. the preserved writer reports exact regeneration of 1,676 edf6 weapon mabs with this ordering; utf-16 ordering failed to match 132, and unpadded slots failed 382. this is an exact-byte reproduction property of that writer/corpus, not a unicode collation rule for arbitrary game data. implementation and validation checklist check mab\0, version 0x0f, and one of the recognized pointer-mode flags. bounds-check header counts, 0x24-byte starting directory and string-region length. resolve each recognized pointer with its owning struct base only for 0x83. validate known locator kinds, vector targets, key counts, embedded sgo\0 signatures and utf-16le terminators. preserve raw sgo payloads, key times, unknown values and sentinel -1 while migrating pointer mode. validate that old and new resolved pointers reach the same logical content, then inspect target skeleton semantics independently. claim in-game parity only after a target-class animation and weapon/audio behavior test, not after byte-level round-trip alone. unknowns: compatibility outside the observed 0x0f / 0x03 / 0x83 family, generalized cross-model retargeting and whether all untested mab event consumers have identical behavior across generations. this is not a generic collision-file format. a desert collision crash previously attributed to mab was disproven; the studied map had no mab payloads. source: retained components/objects/pylib/mab_legacy.py from the edf4.1→edf6 r10 hf4 r9 source package (documented measured corpus, mab_layout, mab_from_edf5, mab_events, mab_set_strings). figures and exact outcomes above are recorded in that source, not newly reproduced against installed game archives during r63.

audio containers — awe, awb, acb and efarc awe / awb / acb the retained audio tooling establishes a criware extraction/inspection path, not a cross-game audio conversion law. awe_parser.py is documented as an awe/awb extractor with awbe identity handling and endian-tolerant parsing. the retained cli contract uses -o / --output; an older readme spelling --o is stale. this is enough to: enumerate/inspect awe voice-name/list data; pair awe metadata with awb payload extraction in the supported tool path; preserve archive-relative identity while doing read-only research. it is not evidence that edf5 awe/awb/acb can be copied or rebuilt unchanged for edf6. codec, cue-table, bank, language and game-specific routing semantics still require native/paired evidence. efarc the corpus identifies efarc as an edf6 file/effect-archive research target, but contains no reconciled universal parser or edf5→edf6 conversion contract. its current status is unresolved. do not fill that gap by assuming efarc behaves like rab, marc or criware audio containers merely because all are archives. keep it separate until a source/runtime-backed format contract exists. practical rule use awe/awb tooling for extraction and inspection, preserve original audio-bank relationships, and treat audio replacement/conversion as a resource-specific operation. for efarc, preserve opaque bytes unless a task has format-specific evidence. see also spatial placement, panning and optional velocity pointer abi.

edf 4.1 → edf 6 mission audio: source-only boundary evidence level: offline source-closure pass. the source package intentionally contains no game audio payloads; actual build from user-owned game data and edf6 runtime playback remain separate gates. scope the qualified edf4.1 missionbundle audio checkpoint defines four atomic output groups and ten output files: group output role weapon sound/pc/edf41_weapon_se.acb shared edf4.1 se bank voice.ja edf41_voice.ja.awb + _list.awe voice.en edf41_voice.en.awb + _list.awe table five edf6 voice tables: cn / en / ja / kr / sc known exception: the group name weapon is historical. retaining edf41_weapon_se.acb for mission/object sound fidelity does not add edf4.1 player weapons, models or playable-class data to the missionbundle scope. voice-table behavior observed native behavior: native edf6 rows are preserved. missing edf4.1 cue keys gain caption rows rather than replacing the target table wholesale. the suffix normalizer removes exactly one terminal _e or _s, matching the qualified lookup behavior. embedded _e/_s text is preserved. musenbegin and musenend use the native no-subtitle marker. implementation rule: extend target voice tables minimally; do not regenerate or reorder native edf6 rows from a source-only approximation. build and memory boundary the runner processes one atomic group at a time so the large ja/en voice-bank pair does not need to remain resident simultaneously. it verifies source presence/integrity, validates the exact output set, records sha-256 and fails closed on the first failed group. a user-owned edf4.1 installation or the accepted user-supplied all forces source root may provide source inputs. edf6 target inputs are likewise user-owned. redistribution boundary implementation rule: distributable tooling contains conversion source only, not original acb/awb/awe/voice-table payloads. the audited all forces archive used for project research has no root license file. its availability for private project research is not a public redistribution license. runtime boundary unresolved: the r5 checkpoint proves source/import/suffix contracts only. actual audio conversion using the game payloads, edf6 playback, subtitle timing, multiplayer synchronization and later object-specific cases such as dragonbig401 remain runtime work.

edf6 subtitle scroll fix v1.0.0 project status: released, closed and runtime-confirmed as public v1.0.0. this is a standalone edf6 presentation plugin, distinct from edf5-port voicetable missing-key compatibility. purpose the plugin corrects late long-caption scroll windows. its production logic uses caption audio-duration metadata together with rendered line count to adjust when scrolling advances. final production timing lead: 0.75 s public artifact identity: edf6_subtitle_scroll_fix_v1.0.0_public.zip edf6_subtitle_scroll_fix.dll the retained production architecture is the low-overhead r11 insert-only design. explicit non-goals the release does not modify: talkactor / waitvoice mission semantics; mission timing; subtitle text; voicetable content; audio playback; caption lifetime/fade policy; gameplay; networking. production also omits the old per-frame subtitle update/render diagnostic path and synchronous diagnostic logging. relationship to edf5-port generic-npc captions the two systems solve different defects: lossless voicetable composition supplies missing edf5-derived caption keys/content; subtitle scroll fix adjusts late long-caption presentation windows. do not treat the plugin as a replacement for missing voicetable entries, and do not destabilize the lossless table composer in order to solve presentation timing. qualification boundary the portfolio authority marks runtime verification for release as complete; additional native cross-mission regression is optional only. do not reopen r3-r10 subtitle diagnostics or run old caption-trace dlls alongside the public fix unless investigating a new reproducible regression. further native edf references edf6 base subtitle table and npc cues why a presentation correction can work without retiming dialogue the recovered native edf6 talkactor caption lifetime is an integer counter per actor update rather than direct subtraction of audio elapsed time. talkmanager runs through a framework dispatch with a 59.94 hz nominal gate, and backlog can reduce its actual update cadence relative to wall time. a long caption may therefore scroll too late even when the text lookup and audio cue are both correct. this native path does not prove that every late-scroll symptom has the same cause; the public presentation-only correction has its own runtime evidence. see native voice/caption scheduler details. exact observed caption scheduling defect and bounded correction the original pc control was a long english caption in m011, cue ae115_002: 262 caption characters (264 ui text units including delimiters), laid out as six lines of 32 px, with a four-line / 128 px viewport. the native scroll was scheduled to start at 17.875 s and end at 24.275 s, whereas the observed audio callback cleared with node age 16.800 s and scroll progress 0. the next caption arrived before this node could begin meaningful visible scrolling. this is direct runtime scheduling evidence, not an assumption based on a screenshot. a second measured caption, ae115_003, had nine lines (288 px), the same 128 px window, an audio-duration metric of 23.523001 s, and a native 16-second scroll interval beginning at 18.506945 s. a candidate that merely moved that native 10 px/s motion earlier still lagged spoken content because a full 32 px line needed 3.2 s to reveal, while the average spoken time per nine laid-out lines was about 2.614 s. the subsequently accepted, bounded layout/audio schedule uses the following observed 32 px line-height geometry (do not generalize it to arbitrary font sizes): total_lines = content_height / 32 visible_lines = 4 line_time = aux_audio_duration / total_lines base_start = (visible_lines - 1) * line_time base_end = (total_lines - 1) * line_time lead = min(0.75, base_start) desired_start = base_start - lead desired_end = base_end - lead scroll_start = min(native_start, desired_start) scroll_end = min(native_end, desired_end) the min(native, desired) rule means earlier-only scheduling; it never deliberately defers already-early native scroll. the correction changes only per-caption ui scroll-window fields +0x90 and +0x94 on the examined uidebugmessage node. it does not alter talkactor lifetime, the voice playback callback, caption strings or mission timing. runtime scope: the first hard-scoped layout/audio model made ae115_002, ae115_003, and ae115_004 readable in m011 while the next non-allowlisted long line remained bad. later generalized testing corrected that subsequent line as well. the accepted public configuration used a 0.75 s lead; edf6 native visibility: umbra occlusion and measured frame costs edf6's renderer uses umbra visibility/culling to decide which world geometry should be considered for drawing. a contributor's measured native-d3d11 workload shows that visibility processing can be expensive, but it also shows why simply disabling occlusion is not a general optimization. measured native d3d11 scene the original experiment used an nvidia rtx 3060 laptop, microsoft d3d11/dxgi and 26 stable active observation windows (about 130 seconds). the following numbers are for that machine and scene only: metric observation weighted present frequency 59.318 hz first graphics fence 4.240 ms large visibility callback edf+0x11b5a70 3.169 ms/call other measured callback 0.0562 ms/call umbra::camera::processvisibility share of both callbacks 99.856% wait/getdata inside processvisibility 3.36% of its measured wall time the dominance of processvisibility in these callbacks is not equivalent to an entire frame spending 99.856% in visibility. other frame work was outside this measured pair. why removing the occlusion pass backfired a controlled experiment in the same research disabled the native umbra occlusion path. the result got worse, not better: measurement native-occlusion baseline occlusion disabled present rate 59.318 hz 57.313 hz first graphics fence 4.240 ms 6.584 ms processvisibility 2.387 ms/call 3.288 ms/call with native culling removed, downstream visibility/rendering work and gpu queue depth could grow. it would be incorrect to conclude that the gpu was bottlenecked purely on waiting for an occlusion query. similarly, reducing auxiliary visibility update cadence can produce black-surface flicker and delayed shadows in some scenes. what remains unmeasured a later research instrumentation design distinguished internal work classes, command families, atomic state and query pressure. that design had static/link validation but no retained in-game result establishing a new bottleneck. no supported universal edf6 optimization follows from it. nor do these nvidia measurements independently establish behavior on amd hardware, dxvk or other stages. evidence and scope: originally measured edf6 visibility experiment p1/p2 and source-identified umbra routines. results were captured in a specific modded diagnostic environment; they are not a claim about all stock installations or an endorsed plugin configuration.

edf5 and edf6 mouse input: cursor recentering and downstream aim shaping the native pc game input pipeline uses several distinct stages: windows mouse movement, a game-owned relative-motion sample and downstream class/weapon-specific aim handling. a modern raw-device event is not the same kind of measurement as the stock cursor-centered sample. original relative mouse acquisition the examined edf5/edf6 gameplay path uses the classic cursor position → delta from the window's center → recenter the pointer approach. it reads integer screen coordinates; the relative delta is therefore quantized by desktop-pixel movement and cursor handling. this is different from receiving native windows wm_input relative device counts directly. for the examined edf6 build, source study identified the gameplay relative-motion provider at edf+0x11831f0 and the direct consumer at edf+0x1188479. these are build-specific offsets. the menu's absolute pointer and text-entry/ime routes are separate and should not be described as gameplay-relative input. two action-data families the engine exposes different fields for continuous and subsequently filtered mouse actions: family source-observed fields interpretation continuous mousemovex/y +0xe8 / +0xf0 fresh movement deltas mousex/y/reversex/reversey +0x108 / +0x110 / +0x118 / +0x120 downstream filtered or discrete actions a discrepancy in one family is not proof of an acquisition defect in the other. cursor quantization, game sensitivity scaling, fencer heavy-weapon response and vehicle-turret inertia are separable phenomena. native aiming remains intentional game logic the original downstream route includes scaling, rate limits, saturation/carry behavior and specialized responses for weapons and vehicles. observed code includes a /24 factor and set_limit_rate. bypassing these steps changes native gameplay even if it makes cursor motion feel different. the source does not establish that every disliked aim response is a bug in the mouse sampler. some input and filtering paths are also tied to frame cadence, including wheel consume/reset, action-suppression countdowns and filters normalized to a 1/60 interval. a higher display frame rate therefore does not imply that all input transitions should update at the same frequency. evidence boundary the acquisition/provider mapping is grounded in exact binary/static analysis; the retained modified-input experiment was not a universal runtime confirmation of improved aiming. this article describes the game's input stages, not instructions for implementing an external input hook. see also edf5 keyboard and xinput and input reconciliation.

edf6 rendering cadence versus fixed gameplay updates edf6's simulation and its display output are not conceptually one clock. the source and runtime experiments show that a renderer can present additional visual frames without necessarily advancing enemy ai, weapons or physics more frequently. a real camera observation in an isolated moving-camera trial, the measured rates were: counter rate distinct type-0 camera states 90.306 hz fixed gameplay cadence 59.922 hz presented frames 89.728 hz the test demonstrates genuinely distinct camera states above 60 per second while gameplay remains near the native cadence. it does not demonstrate a complete 120 hz visual update of characters, foliage, particles, shadows or scripted events. visible stutter was still reported. why an fps counter alone is insufficient a present can reuse an earlier world/camera state. the number of presents is therefore not the number of distinct animations. useful independent measurements distinguish fixed simulation updates, actual presents, unique camera transforms and when world render-state submission or character skinning is performed. the 60 hz gameplay step matters to reload timers, weapon cadence, collision integration, ai and networking. increasing those systems' update counts as a side effect of extra presents changes gameplay; it is not purely a graphics upgrade. visibility and asynchronous work an experiment that reduced auxiliary visibility calculations produced black-surface flicker and delayed/coarse shadows. this illustrates a relationship between visible state, occlusion and frame ownership: rendering a new camera position against stale visibility data can create artifacts. a worker that samples a global simulation tick is not necessarily processing the render job for that tick. source observations favor matching local presentation state to the job actually being processed, but a general-purpose synchronized implementation has not been demonstrated by these studies. scope the source contains limited successful camera measurements and separate negative tests. it does not prove full-game smooth 120 fps, correct online behavior at that rate, or stability of every shader/vfx/skin subsystem. native d3d11/dxgi measurements cannot be freely substituted for dxvk or another graphics path. see edf6 visibility cost and high-fps interpretation.

giantant01, reached mission cleared, and restored the test payload. this is a bounded runtime end-to-end proof for that authored mp07 setup, not proof of parity-flipped mp06 acceptance, of mp07/08 two-peer compatibility, or of arbitrary later builds. see alias-free list path and mission startup.

why a custom edf6 missionpack can crash before mission 1 loads a historical september 2026 edf6 build exposed an unusually clean separation between loader timing, missionpack identity/parity, mission-list data, and mission gameplay. the game crashed immediately on selecting a generated mp06 pack; neither the mission's map nor its ac/rmpa had run. later tracing, allocation correction and a source-path fix led to a user-observed, complete offline mission clear for the studied mp07 pack. this is a qualified case study, not a general promise about all custom packs. the observable crash the generated pack existed and had a one-mission packview with mission_001, an offline/online list, local text resources, and correctly hashed mission.ac and mission.rmpa. the loader reported configless loading of slot 6. yet selecting missionpack06 produced windows exception 0xc0000094 (integer divide by zero) at edf.dll+0xdd2a9 in the studied binary. the analyzed game function computes a mission clear/progression ratio and divides by the currently selected mission count. at crash time that effective count was zero. that does not mean the generated list on disk contained zero rows. it means the game's effective selected list state was empty or unresolved at the moment the ui needed it. root cause 1: a request can arrive before the active slot is published the r1c trace observed a legitimate cri resource request: /cri_bind/mission/missionlist_missionpack06.offline.list.sgo at the file-open callback, missionmgr+0x14fd0 still held -1, so a resolver that relied only on the manager's current active pack could not route the request to the custom provider. it incorrectly fell through to native lookup even though the requested path itself explicitly identified mp06. the bounded r2 request-identity fix parses an exact managed missionpacknn in the requested path, validates the managed slot/provider, and uses that identity before falling back to missionmgr state. this fixes a timing race without globally routing arbitrary resource strings or requiring an extra native setmode transition. the distinction is crucial: changing list contents or the compiler cannot repair a file lookup that never reaches the correct provider. root cause 2: old donor parity is a separate compatibility condition the authored bundle used source slot mp03 (odd). the historical mppp 1.0.2 validation path treats odd custom slots as the mp01 validation class and even slots as the mp02 class. the allocator had incorrectly assigned the bundle physical mp06, changing the parity of a legacy/donor-derived mode. a parity-preserving transaction migrated it to mp07, recorded mp06 as retired and prevented silent reuse of an old save namespace. these are two independent, previously confounded problems. correcting request routing does not automatically make the selected pack compatible with its donor validation profile. equally, moving mp06 to mp07 without correcting the early request lookup could still leave an unresolved list read. evidence sequence stage observed result scope initial mp06 selection 0xc0000094 at dll +0xdd2a9 direct windows/runtime negative r1c request trace mp06 list requested while missionmgr+0x14fd0 == -1 exact native callback evidence r2 request-identity patch exact windows dll build and runtime integration prepared; later redirect observed source/native patch plus runtime observation migrate source-mp03 authored bundle to physical mp07 odd parity retained; mp06 retired transactional allocation evidence mp07 selection under r2 list appeared; two request-identity redirects; no 0xc0000094 direct runtime pass for list selection alias-free provider + corrected list path mission opened, 10 giantant01 spawned, were killed, mission cleared; map restored direct runtime pass for this offline end-to-end case do not conflate the historical r17 legacy-composer experiment (which never separately demonstrated a parity-flipped mp03→mp06 runtime pass) with this later a2z authored-mp06 negative and mp07 positive lineage. both reinforce caution, but they are different test fixtures. generalizable debugging rules when a pack-selection ui divides by a selected mission count of zero, first prove the runtime list read and resolved provider, not only the file's presence on disk. resource-request identity can precede missionmgr active-slot state; an exact validated request path may be the only available authority during selection. preserve original legacy donor parity and save/progression identity unless a separate supported conversion policy overrides it. the later normal base_owned authored path has different entitlement rules. stop at the earliest failed gate: opening the list, launching a mission path, running ac/rmpa, and reaching mission clear are different boundaries. prefer transactional provider migration and retained namespace tombstones to silent slot renumbering. see alias-free provider versus list mission paths, missionpack07/08 tests, and donor-free base_owned policy.

fencer armor limits: mission-entry caps versus earned armor edf separates the armor value selected by the player, the maximum permitted on mission entry, and persistent armor growth earned by collecting crates. a mod that brings edf5 campaigns into edf6 must not confuse these mechanisms. the values below are observed in the tested edf5-content port running under edf6, not a universal table for every installation or arbitrary mission. what the mission-entry cap does when armor limits are enabled, the observed fencer mission-entry behavior is: mission_start_armor_raw = min(selected_armor_raw, translated_mission_cap_raw) a selected amount below the mission cap remains unchanged. the cap is an upper bound; it does not fill armor up to the cap. selecting more than the cap clamps the value before entry. the same cap was observed both in the user interface and in actual gameplay in the tested cases. edf5-content campaign hosted in edf6 tested mission/difficulty observed fencer mission cap evidence base mission 47, easy 1069 hp ui and gameplay; below/above-cap controls dlc1 mission 11, easy 1644 hp gameplay; below-cap preservation dlc2 mission 3, easy 2034 hp gameplay cap on base mission 47, deliberately selecting 250 hp entered at 250 hp; selecting approximately 900 hp entered at that selection; selecting above 1069 entered at 1069. a wing diver control remained at 559 hp in both the ui and mission, showing that the tested fencer-specific translation did not inadvertently change that class. for comparison, independently checked native edf6 control values were 1382 hp (main campaign mission 116, easy), 2012 hp (dlc1 mission 18, easy), and 2286 hp (dlc2 mission 38, easy). these native controls are separate from the edf5-port translation and must not be substituted for the port's limits. armor limit off is a different branch the native edf6 missionsync path uses a negative cap sentinel -1 for an unrestricted room. in the examined binary, the mission cap candidate is initially 0xffffffff; it is replaced with a normal nonnegative cap only when cap-lock conditions apply. at the gameplay serializer, selected raw armor is loaded from loadout+0x24. the cap sign is tested (test ebx,ebx); the js branch skips clamping when the cap is negative. thus the native behavior for cap = -1 is to preserve the selected armor value. the examined fencer translation path explicitly ignores negative caps and therefore preserves this branch. this is exact static evidence, not a separately completed runtime test of armor limit off for every lobby topology. a safe translator must never silently turn an unrestricted room into a restricted one. armor crates and saved progression are not mission caps a runtime test credited seven fencer armor crates and observed a maximum-armor gain of 4 hp. this is consistent with the edf6 fencer growth factor retained in the research (0.595 hp per credited armor crate, versus 0.80 for edf5 fencer), subject to the game's normal accumulation/rounding. the intended port behavior was to keep edf6-native persistent armor progression, even while translating the mission-entry cap for edf5 campaign content. in other words, changing soldierinit, armor-box rewards or save progression merely to imitate edf5 armor gains would be a separate behavioral change, not a required part of fixing the fencer mission limit. why a shared raw cap cannot reproduce all edf5 class hp limits for the examined difficulty profile, the native engine computes a common raw cap from mission position, then applies class-specific armor conversion. the useful simplified relationship is: cap_hp(class) = base_hp(class) + floor(common_raw_cap * class_growth(class)) the measured class conversion parameters are: class edf5 base hp edf5 growth edf6 base hp edf6 growth ranger 200 0.64 200 0.56 air raider 200 0.64 200 0.56 wing diver 150 0.40 150 0.35 fencer 250 0.80 250 about 0.595 for ranger, air raider and wing diver, the edf5/edf6 growth ratio is the same: 8/7 ≈ 1.142857. fencer instead requires 0.80 / 0.595 ≈ 1.344538. therefore one shared change to the raw armor_limit curve cannot recreate all four edf5 class caps while keeping native edf6 soldierinit growth. this is a structural consequence of the class parameters, not an arbitrary tuning preference. a retained source-profile example demonstrates the difference. the observed raw cap came from mission index divided by mission_count - 1, not from the list source's progression float (field9). with profile endpoints [4500,8000]: edf5 original: 4500 + 3500 * 5/110 ~= 4659 raw port layout: 4500 + 3500 * 6/111 ~= 4689 raw the one-row offset is associated with preserving the technical tutorial mission m000 in the installed port's list. it is a small independent ordinal shift; changing or removing m000 to hide it can break saved mission identity and is not a legitimate fix for the fencer class-growth mismatch. at approximately 4689 raw, edf6 class conversion gives 2825 hp ranger/air raider, 1791 hp wing diver, 3039 hp fencer. with the original edf5 raw value around 4659, edf5 class conversion gives 3181 hp ranger/air raider, 2013 hp wing diver, 3977 hp fencer. these numbers belong to this specific profile/mission example and must not be mixed with the separate 1069/1644/2034 gameplay-cap controls above. important boundary: the synchronized missionsync message carries a common raw cap, not a hidden fencer-only network cap field. the observed class difference is due to later class conversion, so changing network packet shape is not a justified cure. the class field and player slot identity must also be kept distinct: an earlier interpretation of networkuser+0x48 as soldiertype was withdrawn; the more complete dataflow identified a player/slot index instead. implementation boundary apply a class-specific cap translation only where the pack identity and requested cap are proven; do not rewrite all classes. preserve player-selected armor below the cap and preserve cap < 0 unchanged. keep mission-entry clamping separate from persistent armor growth and rewards. do not infer that a user-interface-only success guarantees gameplay behavior; the observed cases were checked inside missions. do not infer multiplayer safety or foreign missionpack/namespace collision safety from single-player or isolated online checks. still unqualified in the retained evidence: cross-provider namespace rebasing, unrelated third-party missionpack false-positive controls, and the full two-peer host/client/rejoin/transition matrix. the underlying arithmetic for the tested three edf5-port campaign families is runtime-positive. native game reference guides edf4.1 online cap enforcement edf5 online cap enforcement edf6 knot-based limits

player-state networking: periodic transforms, jumps, eos and rudp a player's walking position, a class-specific jump action, and a projectile collision event are not equivalent kinds of network messages. edf has separate gameplay packet classes, ownership and delivery rules. understanding these explains how a jumping player can briefly appear to snap into the correct position while ordinary walking state remains stale for other peers. three gameplay traffic classes the audited edf6 implementation separates the following paths: gameplay path packet / receive route application delivery what it is used for ordinary scene/player state class 3 / 0x3300, sceneobjectreceiver mode 1, no retained sequence/ack/retry periodic actor snapshots and ordinary transforms immediate gameplay events class 4 / 0x3400, eventcontroller mode 0, sandlot rudp retained reliability actions and class-specific state changes, including jump transforms projectile-state publication class 5 / 0x3500, networkbullet/bulletmanager mode 0, sandlot rudp retained reliability later projectile and contact state, according to selector all three can eventually use the same physical ordinary gameplay transport. reliable class 4/5 messages are wrapped in the game's own rudp records before that lower transport. therefore an underlying eos unreliableunordered call does not mean class 4/5 traffic lacks application-layer retransmission. periodic walking transforms (0x3300) the measured soldier state is an absolute current transform/state, not a delta that mathematically requires the previous packet. one inspected wire path compresses xyz to approximately six bytes. transforms are generated on a cadence (approximately one transform bit every six network updates), rather than only when a dirty baseline changes. the class-3 record is fire-and-forget: no pending reliable record or ack is retained after the physical send. if a packet is lost, a later successfully delivered and applied snapshot should correct position. persistent drift therefore demands something beyond one isolated loss: repeated failure/suppression, stale receive queues, a gate that discards decoded updates, or another ongoing defect. the receive path is staged. 0x3300 payloads are copied into a pending queue, later parsed, and then offered to a target networkobject through an apply gate. the pending flag can be cleared before the target gate is evaluated, so a false gate can discard that particular decoded batch. however, the basic soldier gate was found structurally homologous to edf5; treating its mere existence as an edf6-specific regression was a rejected hypothesis. why a jump can temporarily correct a position for fencer/heavyarmor, the audited path is: base_high_jump_start -> immediate soldier message 0x15 -> transform mask = 1 -> class 4 / 0x3400 -> retained rudp delivery ranger/assaultsoldier has transform-bearing 0x14-family messages, and wing diver has 0x16/0x17-family messages. the common result is that a class-specific action can publish a strong transform through a lane different from ordinary walking snapshots. in observed multiplayer desync, the jumping player's outward position corrected on other peers, but the jumper's view of the other players did not globally recover. desync could then return. this is a directional/per-sender event, not evidence that jumping resets the whole connection. important correction: a jump transform should not be generically called “message type 5” or “message 19.” those strong correction paths also exist but are not the identified class-specific jump route. edf5 steam versus edf6 eos physical delivery the audited edf5 physical interface distinguishes steam unreliable from unreliablenodelay. the shipping edf6 ordinary gameplay path uses the eos adapter's ordinary slot and ultimately eos unreliableunordered. in the inspected eos wrapper, the two logical unreliable methods had effectively converged on sends with ballowdelayeddelivery = false. this difference is a candidate loss/reconnect mechanism, not a runtime-proven universal cause. it may remove establishment/delayed-delivery behavior expected by the original ordinary path. in another observed code branch, eos_noconnection prompts connection acceptance but does not resend the failed original packet inside that wrapper. edf6 also adds a per-peer physical aggregation buffer that normally flushes on roughly 90 ms, or earlier when size requires. one physical loss can therefore discard several bundled lower-layer records. the buffering interval alone is much too short to explain sustained positional drift; its significance is the common loss domain beneath the gameplay lanes. normal class-3 payloads are not plausible 1400-byte limit overflow by themselves: the audited scratch record is 0x484 (1156 bytes) at maximum, and an ordinary walking xyz field is much smaller. the historical idea that legitimate rudp records routinely exceed the eos maximum was also rejected after checking the actual builder/aggregate envelope. the legitimate shipping class 4/5 retained record is bounded to 1156 bytes, first physical aggregate to 1164 bytes, against the audited 1170-byte eos path limit. rudp recovery and peer ready state for class 4/5 and normal networkbullet selectors 0/1/2, sandlot rudp retains sequence-tagged data until an ack. in the researched framing: 0x1200 — retained data; 0x1300 — ack for a matching pending record; duplicate received data is acknowledged again but not reapplied; 0x1400 — removes a receiver deduplication marker; its general role remains unresolved. retries start after 700 ms and add 1000 ms per retry. the edf6 fault interval threshold is 7000 ms, yielding about 25.9 seconds cumulative no-ack history in that failure chain; the directly compared edf5 threshold is 20000 ms, approximately 204 seconds cumulative. neither figure is simply a single 7-second/20-second timeout. the physical p2p::link object is replaceable while the higher-layer usersession, sender and reliablemgr persist. a transient remoteconnectionclosed can replace the link without discarding outstanding reliable messages. but the studied edf6 path can retain ready=1 during this replacement, causing the newly created link to bypass its normal initial recovery flow. this is a concrete binary-supported reconnect defect candidate; runtime repair qualification remains separate. what is confirmed, and what is not exact-binary findings: the three packet routes; non-retained class-3 snapshots versus retained rudp class-4/5; class-specific jump messages; 90-ms physical aggregation; the inspected ready/link behavior; and the compared retry thresholds. observed gameplay symptom: jumping briefly corrects the jumper's position outward, not every direction or peer. aim/firing state and hp can also diverge, so not all symptoms are transform-only. not established: that the delayed-delivery difference or stale ready individually explains every real-world desync; that restoring either is universally safe; or that eight-player multiplayer is already qualified. runtime traces must correlate physical sends, per-lane enqueue/drain/apply and rudp acks before assigning a singular root cause. for deeper bullet-specific behavior see networkbullet selector/contact semantics and rudp ownership and retransmission. event protocol registry and evidence-based diagnosis outer class 0x3400 is not an event protocol id. in the audited edf6 registry, damageobject=1, generator=2, mission=3, synchronizegate=4, sceneobject=6, noteeventsceneobject=7, itemdrop=8, system=9, talkmanager=10, and debug=100. protocol damageobject belongs to the retained class-4 eventcontroller path; it should not be conflated with fire-and-forget class-3 position snapshots. the literal 0x2b observed later in the damageobject handler is an internal event/job code. see full event registry. the comparative investigation also explicitly rejected the inherited bandwidth scheduler, inherited lightsync, a supposed networkbullet reliability downgrade, watchdog_session as a proven pc keepalive, and legitimate
