diagnosing edf6 multiplayer desync without reopening discarded theories the edf5→edf6 network investigation produced several exact binary differences, but no universal, runtime-proven fix for every desync symptom. treat a player's pose, aim, hp and projectile motion as separate state flows that share some transport layers. the evidence below tells a debugger what to instrument and which historical assumptions were already disproved. verified architecture by layer ordinary scene transform → class 3 / 0x3300 ───────────────────┐ damageobject / game event → class 4 / 0x3400 → retained rudp ───┤ networkbullet update → class 5 / 0x3500 → retained rudp ───┤ ▼ edf6 ordinary eos physical send (coalescing, then unreliableunordered) the fact that the lower eos send uses unreliableunordered does not mean that class 4 and class 5 have lost their application-level reliability. they are acked by sandlot rudp before being physically sent over the same lower layer. in edf5, the matching rudp flush likewise reaches the ordinary steam unreliable physical slot; it does not use the unreliablenodelay slot. which hypotheses survived the source comparison? candidate explanation retained result what to test next edf5 and edf6 use different central 150/350/450/20 scheduler constants rejected: both have a homologous low-priority scheduler with carry/debt and one low-priority packet per cycle do not blame constants alone edf6 invented lightsync rejected: the same lightsync concepts were found in edf5 check actual configured use, not name existence an ordinary walking packet encodes only a delta rejected: observed soldier xyz is an absolute compressed transform, roughly six wire bytes for its component if drift persists, look for repeated loss, staging/gating or another state stream jumping globally repairs a broken session rejected by user observation: a high jump sends an immediate reliable transform outward from the jumper, without resyncing the jumper's view of others correlate direction, owner and message lane edf6 downgraded networkbullet from reliable to unreliable rejected: audited normal edf5 and edf6 projectile paths use sandlot rudp examine missing class-internal state/selector payload a normal rudp record reaches an invalid 1400-byte packet rejected for qualified sender: 1144-byte payload → 1156-byte retained record → 1164-byte physical aggregate; eos limit 1170 do not revive oversized-packet theory without a new, different path sender mode-0 retransmissions repeatedly consume eventcontroller budget rejected: retransmission is below the event scheduler observe rudp queue rather than treating event budget as repeated debit watchdog_session removal is proven cause rejected for studied pc build: edf5 pc functions are stub/residue-like avoid using script-text absence as runtime proof eos ordinary physical send lost the edf5 delayed-delivery distinction binary-confirmed difference, potential repair candidate scope runtime a/b experiment to the ordinary physical send only remoteconnectionclosed replaces link without clearing ready binary-confirmed candidate defect; initial recovery can be bypassed correlate link creation, ready transitions, handshake and ack receipt reconnect and retry are separate lifetimes the native physical p2p::link can be replaced while the logical peer usersession and reliable send/receive state survive. if the old ready bit remains set when a new link enters initial, the normal retry and handshake cycle can be skipped. this is different from removing a peer, which destroys the logical session. do not reset rudp sender sequence numbers or dedupe tables simply because the physical link changed. retained rudp data is 0x1200; its sequence ack is 0x1300. the timeout interval starts at 700 ms, grows by 1000 ms after each resend, and marks fault after the running interval passes 7000 ms in edf6 (versus 20000 ms in the studied edf5 homolog). the roughly 25.9 s vs 204 s cumulative no-ack exposure follows from the progression; these are not seven-second and twenty-second one-shot timers. minimal evidence to collect for an actual reproduction record monotonic timestamps from both peers, local/remote object identity and which peer owns each object. track physical eos result, aggregate size, link ready, initial entry, and reconnect notifications. record outgoing/received class3 0x3300, then the deferred sceneobjectreceiver enqueue → parse → apply result; the receive path clears a pending flag before the target apply gate, which can drop one staged batch. independently record class4 0x3400 eventcontroller protocol ids and rudp sequences/acks, especially damageobject protocol 1. record class5 0x3500 bullet selector/mode and the projectile's serialized versus private state. repeat an ordinary walk and a class-specific jump. observe the outgoing jumper's state separately from the jumper's remote view. no plugin build, trace run or in-game reconnect repair was performed during this reconciliation. the reported results are retained earlier observations and source/binary reconstructions; the two candidate repairs still require clean windows game a/b qualification. see packet/event registry, player-state lanes and rudp lifecycle. cross-layer causal interpretation of captured desync the retained r7 two-pc physical-payload matches and the approximately 183-world-unit remote-position divergence are detailed in sceneobject's r7/r8 receive-frontier study. they rule out a simple missing physical eos packet as the sufficient explanation for that captured run, not all connection-related faults. a successful physical receive is not proof of sceneobject staging, soldier transform application or a successful damageobject event. the practical diagnostic separation is: class 3 positional divergence: distinguish 0x3300 physical delivery, individual fragment/type staging, 16-bit sequence freshness and concrete soldier application. different fragments may legitimately share a sender batch sequence, so a global equal-sequence filter is unsafe. class 4 event divergence: use the 0x3400 event identity plus sandlot's reliable data sequence and ack; a recovered reliable message may still be applied to the wrong object or with wrong game state. class 5 projectile divergence: 0x3500 retained selectors cannot replace flame/lightning/solidexp constructor-internal rng or detonation state that was never serialized. transient reconnect failure: separate physical p2p::link replacement/ready from the packet controller/usersession/reliablemgr lifetime. a persistent ready flag and no ack can create a different failure chain, but has not been proven to cause ordinary r7 position drift. the later r8 29-hook and r9 31-hook diagnostic candidates are static-qualified only in the retained sources; they did not retroactively repair or re-run the r7 two-computer capture. this source lineage is not an argument for automatically installing a global transport rewrite or for treating a per-type staging hypothesis as fully proven. source boundary: network/edf6_network_rc1_r8_maxcap_static_checkpoint_2026-09-11.md; network/edf6_desync_r9_protocol_aware_candidate_2026-09-29.zip. no new game run was conducted for r169.

edf6 native event protocols are not the same thing as packet classes when reconstructing multiplayer behavior, distinguish the gameplay packet class, the event protocol within class 4, and internal engine/job codes. they have different identifiers, different receiver paths, and different meanings. the native-binary census here is for the qualified edf6 dll studied in the 2026 research; do not treat these numbers as a universal cross-build abi. three game traffic routes outer route receiver/owner application delivery typical responsibility class 3 — 0x3300 sceneobjectreceiver mode 1, not retained periodic state, ordinary player transforms class 4 — 0x3400 eventcontroller mode 0, sandlot rudp damage, hp-related events, mission/object events, immediate actions class 5 — 0x3500 networkbullet / bulletmanager mode 0, sandlot rudp for studied shipping senders projectile creation, publication and later contact state for the gameplay controller id 3, the class-4 route is assembled as (controllerid << 12) | 0x400 = 0x3400. the event is then identified inside the event protocol, not by replacing the outer packet-class header with the event id. native eventcontroller protocol registry the following ids were recovered by native static analysis of edf6's event-protocol registration, not invented from editor enums: protocol id observed registered name 1 damageobject 2 generator 3 mission 4 synchronizegate 6 sceneobject 7 noteeventsceneobject 8 itemdrop 9 system 10 talkmanager 100 debug do not synthesize protocol id 5: its absence from this measured registry is not proof of a general reserved-slot rule. nor should one infer the wire schema or stable field abi from a symbolic protocol name alone. damage and hp are not simply part of walking position the native event_damageobject is registered at protocol id 1. its eventbase dispatch path hands the event to the eventcontroller builder, which uses the class-4 0x3400 lane and mode-0 retained rudp. the numeric value 0x2b seen in a later damageobject::onevent path is an internal event/job code, not protocol id 0x2b. thus a user can report apparently correct positions while still seeing incorrect hp, hit reactions or target destruction. do not diagnose all of those observations as one missing 0x3300 movement snapshot. confirm separately whether the relevant damageobject event was generated, serialized, reliably acknowledged, received, and actually applied. projectile data has its own third lane edf6 networkbullet registers a class-5 0x3500 receiver. in the audited shipping binary, all 23 direct send callsites of the public networkbullet sender selected mode=0, hence the reliable per-peer rudp path, not ordinary class-3 mode-1 delivery. edf5 had a homologous rudp projectile path, so a claim that edf6 simply made normal bullet traffic unreliable is unsupported. however, retained delivery only recovers serialized bytes. it cannot restore omitted class-internal projectile state. separate flamebullet02, lightningbullet01, and solidexpbullet01 investigations demonstrate that initial motion, rng/path state, and detonation countdown can be missing from the published selector payload. evidence and testing boundary the names, ids, event routing, outer class ids and mode selection are static binary evidence; the route is not a new endpoint established by independently sniffing a current live two-player session. for a network diagnosis, correlate both players' timestamps and the same object id across class 3 snapshots, class 4 event records, class 5 bullet records, rudp acks, and final in-world apply calls. see player-state packet lanes, rudp behavior, and projectile reconstruction. further native-game references edf6 hp deltas vs killing-hit events

edf6 weapon rng, batched fire and remote projectile reconstruction a remote weapon shot is not necessarily a copy of a sender-owned projectile. edf6 supports direct fire and batched fire with receiver-local reconstruction; the latter may reproduce the number of shots without reproducing all of their original random or class-internal state. this distinction is important when investigating mismatched firing direction, lightning paths, flame motion or explosion timing. the offsets below belong to the analyzed edf6 edf.dll build (sha-256 prefix 0d5092393a1b…). they are observations of that build, not portable structure offsets for every release. the weapon random-number generator the process has a global rng state. construction of a new weapon derives its live seed from an advance of that global state. the weapon instance then maintains its own 64-bit state at weapon+0xbc8. the recovered linear-congruential update is: state = (state * 0x5d588b656c078965 + 0x269ec3) mod 2^64 for the analyzed common firing path, rng consumption depends on the event: event weapon rng effect weapon onupdate one advance firespreadtype 1 or 3 spread step one additional random-spread advance firespreadtype 0, 2 or 4 no random-spread advance at this step each created projectile another advance; an upper-derived value is handed to the projectile a new weapon instance a new seed lineage derived from process-global rng in the analyzed direct-fire packet policy, flag weapon+0x153c & 0x08 causes the sender to transmit the pre-spread weapon rng value. the receiver restores that value before calling the shared projectile-creation logic. that is a concrete mechanism for deterministic spread when this bit is active. not all fire policies include that bit. a receiver calculating a shot later with a different rng history need not reproduce the sender's original outcome. direct subtype0 versus batched subtype1 property direct subtype0 batched subtype1 initial transform policy-dependent direct sender/local transform recreated locally on receiver; no equivalent transmitted sender muzzle transform pre-spread rng can be transported/restored when the direct-policy bit is enabled no active pre-spread seed restoration in the examined basic, charge, precharge or gatling paths timing direct fire action publication deferred for six subsequent weapon updates after delay arm delivery record direct fire may select retained/non-retained path by policy non-retained lower fire lane loss behavior depends on selected direct policy a lost final publication is not automatically retransmitted by the subtype1 sender subtype1 tracks a locally realized shot counter (weapon+0xbd0) and a received cumulative target (weapon+0x1544). a later higher target can make a receiver catch up on missed projectile-count positions, and lower received targets are rejected. this is count reconciliation, not exact replay of each historical shot. for charge / precharge, extension data is read as pending state and committed only for accepted count updates. a later cumulative counter does not reconstruct every missing intermediate charge value. accordingly, a later reconstruction can use a newer accepted charge state, changing fire count, accuracy, speed, damage, explosion or size parameters on affected weapon paths. weapon configurations that can change policy with stars a qualified scan of 1,315 active weapontable configurations, including roughly 2.9 million correlated reachable star states, found 157 weapons always using subtype1, 172 capable of reaching subtype1, and 15 that can switch from subtype1 to direct fire depending on star-scaled values. examples include penetrator, buster shot, double lance, twin lance, lightning bow variants and raijin. a weapon's base sgo or name is therefore not sufficient to infer its active networking policy; the evaluated star parameters matter. the detailed evaluator and all policy counts are documented in weapon synchronization policies. the six subtype1 weapons with rng-sensitive initial spread the complete active-weapon scan identifies six always-subtype1 weapon configurations with firespreadtype 1 or 3. this is a bounded list of initial-spread cases, not a list of every subtype1 weapon with rng-sensitive projectile behaviour. active sgo weapon name weapon family firespreadtype aweapon194.sgo wide acid gun basicshoot 1 mpack_b_weapon016.sgo extreme acid gun basicshoot 1 pweapon019.sgo phalanx u1 chargeshoot 3 pweapon032.sgo phalanx w2 chargeshoot 1 pweapon068.sgo destroyer blaster w prechargeshoot 1 pweapon117.sgo lightning rapid bow t2 chargeshoot 1 the class-method audit found no additional seed-restoring weapon+0xbc8 writer in basicshoot, chargeshoot or prechargeshoot. gatling's class packet helper is called with its seed-serialization flag cleared. these findings apply to the analyzed four ordinary weapon-family paths; specialized drone/subdrone implementations are separate. the current weapon rng stream can reconverge after delayed receiver catch-up when seed, update and projectile-step histories match, while the original spread sample does not: the receiver samples at the later reconstruction phase. random spread reduces an upper-state sample into one of 10,000 buckets, so accidental equality is possible but not protocol-enforced. new weapon construction reseeds from process-global rng; ordinary reload does not reset the same weapon instance to a fixed seed in the audited paths. the projectile has its own rng state the initial random value for a projectile is stored at bulletbase::initparam+0x1a0. the constructor copies it to the final live bulletbase+0x130. these are different address bases: interpreting +0x1a0 as an offset in the finished bullet object is incorrect. three observed projectile classes consume random state or the resulting constructor values beyond their initial trajectory: projectile class rng-dependent internal behavior what later ordinary network state does not restore flamebullet02 constructor-initialized motion scalars used by onupdate class motion scalars (including +0x11d0/+0x11d8) lightningbullet01 randomized path/current position and further state advancement bullet rng/path history, including bullet+0x130 solidexpbullet01 randomly initialized detonation countdown; expiration launches a blowhit01 effect detonation countdown (+0xf00) of the evaluated active weapon corpus, 40 weapons can reach subtype1 while using one of these three ammoclass families: 30 always subtype1 and 10 with star-dependent subtype1/direct switching. an additional subtlety: this problem can occur even with non-random initial firespreadtype 0. the divergence is then caused by post-construction projectile behavior, not initial aiming spread. later synchronization of the current weapon rng value does not rewrite an already-created bullet's historical rng-derived constructor state. a receiver may ultimately have the right shot count and still simulate different class behavior. what networkbullet can and cannot repair edf6 can send later projectile updates under several selector bits at bullet+0xe8c: selector transmitted class of state consequence 0 (bit 0x2) common spatial position/motion snapshot can update common trajectory state, not hidden class history 1 (bit 0x1) external-object contact/reference frame can re-anchor projectile position to a contacted object 2 (bit 0x4) missile collision/contact record (point, normal, object identity) can affect reflection/trajectory; only enabled by examined missilebullet01/02 constructors shipping networkbullet selectors use sandlot mode0 retained reliability over physically unreliable eos p2p. sequence/ack/retransmission can recover serialized selector bytes after a transient physical loss. this does not create the missing flame, lightning or solidexp fields, which are absent from those payloads in the examined paths. see selector payloads and contact behavior and application-layer reliability. how to investigate an apparent aim/shot desync trace these layers separately, rather than forcing the soldier's orientation everywhere: the local and remote weapon identity, firespreadtype and current star-evaluated sync policy. the sender muzzle/per-shot transform and whether a direct packet transports the pre-spread rng. whether creation follows direct subtype0 or six-update subtype1. the weapon+0xbd0 realized count and +0x1544 target; if charge/precharge, pending versus committed extension state. the projectile's initial constructor rng-derived state and the later class-specific consumers. only then, networkbullet selector delivery, later trajectory/contact updates and sandlot reliable-message acknowledgment. evidence boundary: these are exact static/native binary reconstructions for the specified build and a qualified shipped-weapon corpus. they do not demonstrate that a runtime fix for live network desynchronization has been implemented or validated. the minimum state to add to the protocol and the safest injection point remain open. controlled verification examples, without treating the plan as a runtime result for a practical same-build comparison, use four source-studied cases: m2 raven as a non-random-spread subtype1 control, mr111 fang as full-sender direct subtype0, penetrator f as a single weapon with three star-dependent policies, and wide acid gun as a receiver-local rng-sensitive subtype1 control. the full source-derived star-slot states, event rvas and expected timelines are in fire-sync runtime discriminator matrix. those traces were proposed and statically qualified as a probe, not reported as successful paired gameplay observations. why most rng-sensitive projectile state is not random initial spread the r14 shipped-data crosswalk found 40 active weapons capable of entering subtype1 with flamebullet02, lightningbullet01 or solidexpbullet01: 30 always subtype1 and 10 star-dependent. their firespreadtype distribution was 38 spread0, one spread1 and one spread2. this is a bounded intersection of those three projectile-class families with subtype1 reachability, not the same set as the six always-subtype1 weapons with rng-sensitive initial spread discussed above. consequently the main post-spawn divergence mechanism in this class subset can occur even when the weapon itself fires with nonrandom spread. the sender and receiver may create the bullet at different points in their weapon rng progression; the initial value is passed via bulletbase::initparam+0x1a0 into live bulletbase+0x130. the three derived classes can then initialize flame motion, lightning path or explosive fuse time differently. later equal shot counts or successful sandlot acks do not reconstruct that missing constructor history. source authority: engine_re/edf6_engine_re_r14_projectile_rng_consumer_checkpoint_2026-09-29.md, preserved and delimited by later r15–r17 findings. this count is a source-static weapon-corpus result, not an observed 40-weapon network runtime trial.

edf6 vehicle-mounted weapons: dynamic fire_model_direction mode 2 the fire_model_direction parameter is not simply a constant that can be read once from a weapon's sgo/mab record. edf6 has a runtime override used by the vehicleswingshoot weapon family. a model converter or weapon inspector that treats every value as static can therefore miss an active firing-direction mode. static configuration versus effective mode in the qualified vanilla corpus, the recovered classic sgo fire_model_direction values embedded in dsgo extra/mab were: static mode number of configurations 0 1,708 1 125 2 0 the normal configuration parser only creates modes 0 or 1. however, the native vehicleswingshoot code deliberately selects mode 2 at runtime, so zero mode-2 entries in the shipping configuration scan does not mean the mode is unused. runtime mechanism the analyzed vehicleswingshoot class uses the common per-shot transform/vector table: table stride: 0xf0 bytes per entry; entry+0xd0: dynamic override direction/basis; entry+0xe0: direction selector, set to 2 by vehicleswingshoot; shared 0x6969a0: consumes the mode-2 override basis on its direction path; weapon+0x370: fireburstcount; weapon+0xe18: remaining burst count. the swing progress is derived from remaining shots relative to the burst count, allowing the firing basis to change through a burst. the examined class does not immediately restore selector mode 0/1 within the same instance after selecting the dynamic mode. the exact native configuration examples are v605_barga_c_cannon.sgo, its _ai counterpart, and _dlc. they are statically mode 1 but dynamically mode-2-capable. consequences for tools and modding read the configured mode and the effective per-shot runtime mode separately. do not validate a weapon inspector by counting only static fire_model_direction=2 records. when investigating a barga cannon's shot orientation, capture the dynamic basis and remaining burst count instead of interpreting the configuration value as the whole firing contract. do not generalize this override to every weapon with a burst counter: the exact writer evidence is class-specific. for the rest of the firing pipeline see weapon fire transforms and weapon rng / batched projectile reconstruction. evidence: exact edf6 native binary tracing for the analyzed edf.dll build, plus three identified shipped vehicleswingshoot configs. other uninspected implementations and game revisions are not implied.

mdb loader dispatch and cmpl — valid models that still crash a model can have a valid mdb0 header, survive an elementary parser check, and still crash the target game for two independent reasons: the game selects the wrong resource loader, or the archive decompressor supplies a corrupted model body. both failures were isolated in an edf5 → edf6 desert-map port. they illustrate useful diagnostic methods, not universal conversion rules. 1. resource registration selects a typed consumer the map's registration table is not merely a list of filenames. its resource names and suffixes participate in type selection. in the studied desert map, mapb/mac t1 registration indexed one object under .trb, while the actual decompressed resource was an ordinary .mdb model. the observed chain was: map t1 entry 37 → sk_ptree007_11m_shuro.trb rab archive payload → sk_ptree007_11m_shuro.mdb actual payload → mdb model bytes, 53,806 bytes target consumer → trb/tree header parser, not mdb parser a crash dump showed the in-memory resource buffer was byte-for-byte identical to the deployed mdb (53,806 bytes). the normal edf6 model validation path accepted that mdb. the faulty path instead treated base+0x28 as the trb entry count and base+0x2c as a trb table offset. in this model the value at +0x28 was 0x300000, which led to nonsensical tree-table traversal. the useful rule is match the requested resource type to the actual resource; do not conclude that the model payload is malformed merely because the crash occurs during resource loading. a second t1 entry used a .mosb suffix; it too required separate role checking. other entries used .mdx and .fmep roles. do not globally rename every .trb to .mdx—this source-specific mismatch is not a generic conversion law, and valid trb resources must retain their real type. 2. a valid mdb header is not evidence that the whole body survived decompression a separate error occurred when the historical cmpl_compress_lz encoder in rab_mdb_upgrade2.py rebuilt compressed rab entries. an independent strict decoder confirmed that 45 of 76 mdbs failed round-trip: their first eight bytes, including the mdb0 version marker, remained readable, but their remaining model bodies were corrupted. an mdb version/dispatch check could therefore pass while later vertex, mesh, material or offset reads were using garbage. the offending historical encoder was withdrawn; that failure must not be attributed to the mdb abi itself. for the checked desert rab, a literal-only cmpl stream was used as a safety workaround. each group of up to eight literal bytes was preceded by a flag byte 0xff, consistent with the decoder's bit-0-as-literal convention. after rebuilding from pristine source, verification reported: post-rebuild content measured result mdb entries 76/76 recognized as mdb0 version 0x20 mdb bodies byte-identical to pristine source except the sanctioned version edit dds textures 348/348 byte-identical reported remaining problems 0 in the offline file audit the literal-only encoding was a tested historical fallback, not a recommendation that all edf archives should permanently abandon lz compression. a correctly specified, separately round-trip-tested exact encoder is preferable when available. 3. a converter's validation checklist for every transformed archive entry, check each layer independently: entry identity: exact resource name, type, expected role, and registration reference. decompression correctness: a strict independent decoder must reproduce the full expected payload, not just its magic/version bytes. payload abi: validate every offset, length, record count and expected semantic field after decompression. container consistency: rebuild entry tables, offsets and cross-file references without moving unrelated resources unexpectedly. runtime scope: a reproducible offline round-trip is stronger than a parser smoke, but cannot by itself prove all rendering or gameplay paths in the game. the two cases explain why a crash labelled “mdb loading” can have a typed-dispatch cause or a compression-payload cause. they also explain why extension-wide replacement, changing only mdb0 version bytes, or checking only the archive header are unsafe repair strategies. evidence boundary these are recovered observations from one historical edf5 desert-map port and its archived source handoff. the 45/76 and 76/76 counts refer to that rab content set, not all mdb assets or all cmpl encoders. later production versions may use different encoders and resource tables. the general lessons are type-matched dispatch and full-body round-trip verification.

weapon parameters the game's weapon data is not stored in a single table. the weapon resource sgo, weapontable.sgo, and localized weapontext.??.sgo are separate layers. vehicles add further distinction between the object, the mounted weapon and the vehicle request/weapon record. resource map resource purpose practical note weapon/<weapon>.sgo actual weapon and ammunition parameters names and units are not necessarily unchanged across edf 5 and edf 6 weapon/weapontable.sgo internal identity, resource path, category, rarity, level, upgrade caps, restrictions do not assume an imported weapon exists merely because its sgo was installed weapon/weapontext.??.sgo localized display name, descriptions and formatted statistics languages are stored separately; the exact internal mapping is not fully established in the source memo object/<vehicle>.sgo vehicle geometry/physics and durability vehicle-specific durability may be defined here weapon/<vehicle-mount>.sgo weapon mounted on a vehicle, e.g. v_602heli_gatling01_l similar broad form to soldier-weapon sgo weapon/<vehicle-request>.sgo vehicle call-in and multipliers includes damage/armor multipliers and fuel-consumption rate the notebook traces weapon names through weapontable → weapon sgo path → localized name → weapontext. it does not prove the internal game uses this as its sole runtime index. see also sgo/dsgo schema boundaries. fields and units firespreadwidth denotes the full angular span between the outermost dispersed shots, not the angular gap between two adjacent shots (source: 解析 rows 25–26). the source notes an edf5→edf6 difference for ammospeed: edf6 values can represent distance per frame rather than meters per second; at the observed 60 hz convention, m/s = ammospeed × 60. check the bullet class before applying this conversion universally. the sample weapontable weapon-level value uses a ×25 scale. this is a sample interpretation in the memo, not an independently tested rule for every release/build. in the sampled record, a smaller rarity parameter was reported to correspond to rarer drops; 1 is ordinary and 3 is used for dlc mission weapons. do not assume all equipment follows the same economy table. a display eligibility field can make a weapon's label red/white for underground or ruined missions. this display status is separate from the actual in-mission support/equipment restriction. see missionpack underground support restrictions. compatibility pitfalls the contributor reports that removing a weapon-adding mod while its added weapon remains equipped in a save could crash after selecting a missionpack. unequipped variants did not produce that observed crash. treat this as a reproducible-case report, not a proof about every save format; avoid silently removing inventory entries or weapon definitions. version scope and evidence edf 5 / edf 6: weapon-level and resource relationships are discussed. edf 4.1: not independently validated by this workbook. the source is a community-authored research memo with experimental observations, not a formal sandlot specification. source: 解析!b7:c26, 解析!b33:k61, and 解析!b239:d295 in mod製作メモ.xlsx. native game reference additions edf5 end-of-mission weapon choice related game mechanics (native-source references) edf5 and edf6 weapon-table schema edf6 weapon mab muzzle transforms further native-game references edf6 weapon secondary-action and firing gates further edf game documentation edf5 npc soldier weapons edf5 ai vehicle weapon and reload values

weapon upgrades (stars) edf 5 introduced a weapon upgrade/star system that the research memo reports as retained in edf 6. individual weapon statistics can level independently. a weapon's stars are data in three places, not merely a label in its description. sgo upgrade record: seven numeric fields a star-upgradeable field is represented by a ptr whose payload is a seven-number record. index meaning notes 0 base statistic the contributor identifies this as the value at star level 5, not necessarily at maximum stars 1 stat type correlates with kind/direction of progression; numeric enum is not exhaustively decoded 2 save/stat position index must agree between weapon sgo, weapontable, and weapontext 3 maximum star level each statistic can have a different cap 4 coefficient 1 (a) controls deviation from the base value 5 coefficient 2 (p) exponent controlling progression curve 6 display precision mode 0 integer/truncate; 1 one decimal and rounding, as reported for display formatting example: aweapon001 / minion buster uses separate records for ammocount, ammodamage, fireaccuracy, reload, range, velocity and firing rate. weapontable stores the maximum stars in the matching position order. weapontext uses placeholders such as $0 with an accompanying data record. progression formulas documented in the workbook let b be the base value, l the actual star level, a coefficient 1 and p coefficient 2. the memo uses 5 as the normalization level: increasing statistic: v_inc(l) = b * (a * (l/5)^p - a + 1) [ v(l)=b\left[a\left(\frac{l}{5}\right)^p-a+1\right] ] decreasing statistic (reload time is an example): v_dec(l) = b * ((1+a) - a * (l/5)^p) [ v(l)=b\left[(1+a)-a\left(\frac{l}{5}\right)^p\right] ] at l=5 both formulas produce b. for example with b=100, a=0.8, p=1.5, the increasing curve starts at 20 for star 0 and gives 100 at star 5, while the decreasing curve starts at 180 for star 0 and reaches 100 at star 5. important: the workbook spreadsheet deliberately evaluates levels up to 10 and yields negative values for the decreasing curve at levels 9–10 with these example coefficients. this is a mathematical consequence of the formula, not proof that edf allows a negative in-game reload time. validate caps and coefficients before editing. editing checklist choose the actual field and its type/position mapping; do not reorder records casually. keep the same stat-index correspondence in weapon sgo, weapontable and weapontext. preserve maximum stars and display formatting in each of the three locations. validate increasing or decreasing direction using the game's target field, not just the enum guess. avoid extrapolating beyond the configured maximum star level. test a newly obtained item and an existing saved item; a static sgo round-trip cannot establish save compatibility. source: 星システム!b1:k38, 星システム!b42:l69, 星システム!b69:l235 and 星システム!b242:e278 in mod製作メモ.xlsx. formulas and sample values are reproduced as reported by that source; item drops edf6 item drops have at least two separable parameters in the contributor's memory-patch experiment: how frequently a drop is emitted and how an emitted pickup is distributed among item types. threshold and weights the note describes each defeated enemy contributing points; once accumulated points exceed a droprate threshold, a pickup is emitted. smaller thresholds yield more pickups. setting the threshold to zero or extremely small values is explicitly discouraged in the original note. a second array controls the relative category weights: category source default example edit weapon 6 22 armor 15 21 small healing 14 14 large healing 3 3 total weights 38 60 the workbook's example changes threshold from 0.947 to 0.600. for a simplified expected-value approximation matching the sheet: [\operatorname{share}(i)=\frac{w_i}{\sum_j w_j}, \qquad \operatorname{drops\ per\ 100\ points}\approx\frac{100}{t}.] category count per 100 points is then 100/t × share(i). the sheet reports 105.60 total drops per 100 points at default threshold and 166.67 for the example edit. weapons rise from ~16.67 to ~61.11 per 100 points. these are spreadsheet rates; actual random outcomes and point quantization may differ. implementation boundary the workbook notes two approaches: memory patch: changes a threshold and category-weight table globally, in the tested game build. resource replacement: changing all relevant per-enemy resource settings may require a much larger asset edit. the sample aob/memory patch is version-sensitive and is not presented here as a universal signature. validate against the exact executable before using any offsets or byte patterns. scope and evidence source アイテムドロップレート!b1:s31 contains the japanese explanation, default and example weights, formulas and one patch example (attributed in that sheet to redone). the statistical model and editable values are reproduced from the sheet; native implementation beyond that experiment remains unverified here. native game reference additions crate spawning and category weights across three games edf5 result-screen weapon and armor rolls edf6 local and online collection further native-game references edf5 mission result commits related game mechanics (native-source references) weapon table rows and level scaling edf6 new-weapon and upgrade flags

audio cues & custom sound an edf6 sound cue is not equivalent to its .acb filename. the game may refer to a cue name through a preset, an object resource, a weapon resource or a mission script. presets describe playback settings; the actual waveform normally lives in acb/awb/hca data. loader path overview sepreset.sgo acts as a list of cue/preset settings (name, volume and other playback options) and does not contain the original audio waveform. an acb may contain multiple cues, and a cue can select several samples or different playback properties, including random pitch and looping. in weapon sgo, the memo reports a working path by naming the cue and declaring its actual sound file as a resource. in object sgo, preset-form sound references were also used. for mission angelscript, preload(...) is the documented way to load a resource first; some proposed combinations of playse/bgm remain not directly verified in the memo. negative results and caveats merely referencing sepreset in a weapon resource failed in several trials. the author suspected the preset might be loaded only at game startup; this mechanism was not proven. acb output produced by a tested newer cri adx atom craft le 3.55.00 was incompatible with the author's edf6 player test. they instead replaced sound data inside an existing acb using tools and re-encoded hca content. a format-version mismatch was suspected, but the exact validation cause remains unverified. existing cue-level loop settings can complicate replacement; copying a simpler cue structure was the reported workaround. the notebook includes direct positive/negative experiments on weapon eweapon049 and the vehicle vehicle403_tank. do not generalize one cue test into universal support for every audio format. for sound positioning and doppler see spatial audio. source: 解析!b1164:e1365 in mod製作メモ.xlsx. findings are attributed to the contributor and have not been reproduced from original edf6 audio archives during this r84 editorial pass.

weapon stat text & localization edf6 weapon statistics have a display/localization layer separate from the underlying weapon sgo parameter. for star-upgradeable values, the source describes placeholders such as $0, accompanied by the same upgrade parameter record used by the weapon. what must agree weapon sgo: technical value, star-upgrade record and its position index. weapontable: internal resource name/path, category, level, eligibility and star caps in matching position order. weapontext language variant: human-facing title, description and stat label/formatter, sometimes with a $0 substitution backed by the seven-field star record. translation of the visible label does not change gameplay. conversely, changing a gameplay statistic but leaving a hardcoded display string unchanged can mislead players. localized labels — examples from the contributor's comparison table japanese english label use 弾数 capacity magazine capacity 連射速度 rof rate of fire ダメージ damage damage リロード時間 reload time reload duration 有効射程距離 range effective range 弾速 shot speed projectile speed 精度 accuracy dispersion/accuracy 効果範囲 aoe area of effect 爆破範囲 blast area blast effect ロック時間 lock-on time lock time 誘導性能 homing capability homing behavior 起爆条件 detonates by trigger condition the source sheet also contains korean, traditional chinese and simplified chinese columns. it is a working comparison table, not a complete localization file; the full sheet is not an official global game-string registry. reference/r154_weapon_text_translation_id_directory.csv identifies each source row/id, populated language columns and english short label. it is a navigation/index aid, not wholesale redistribution of the workbook's multilingual text. placeholder and formatting strings such as $0 remain exact when modifying actual game resources. the 192 count describes numeric-id sheet entries, not unique labels or guaranteed live weapontext keys.

edf5 camera modes, vehicle ride and first-person hooks r86 cross-build qualification: edf5 camera offsets/hook sites do not transfer directly to edf6. camera reconciliation. overview edf5 does not treat a vehicle camera as a new scene-tree parent of the soldier. the camera keeps the soldier as its target while its mode changes from follow to ride. this matters for camera mods, especially when extracting the final view matrix or attaching first-person view to a head bone. format, api or behavior the studied steam build uses a mode object at camera +0xae0; follow and ride have separate routines. the final rotation rows are at +0x1a0/+0x1b0/+0x1c0, while the eye is at +0x1d0. a per-frame hook at the tail of characterghostcamera::update was tested. the suggested first-person implementation is not itself established as a working complete mod. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. camera mode state machine — static the player camera runs one of two modes: update calls the mode object at camera+0xae0 (call [vtable+8], edx = 1, at 9f45f); follow mode 9f590 switches to ride mode a0130 when the target's ride control block [target+0x1170] has users (9ffdc-9ffee: lea of a0130, state installed through camera+0xae8, old state called with edx = 2), and ride mode switches back when it has none (a033c-a034e). member-function-pointer state at camera+0xae8 (state object [+0x10]). ride mode reads the seat record [target+0x1160]: [seat+0x200] == 1 builds the camera from the bone matrices at seat+0x208 / +0x218 (a01a2); the ride update switches on [seat+0x200] at a03b4. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 camera final matrix — static the final world matrix is camera+0x1a0 / +0x1b0 / +0x1c0 (rotation rows) and +0x1d0 (eye position, w = 1). follow mode writes +0x1d0 at 9f7e4, 9fb03, 9ff9c and the rows at 9ffad-9ffbc; ride mode writes them at a077d-a07a8; the optional shake a5900 (called at 9f49d) multiplies the rows by +0x200; nothing writes them after the tail. the render submit (vtable slot 5, a0e00) copies them into the render record at a1068; slot 3 9eb50 copies them to +0xa90..+0xac0 (probably the previous-frame copy, unverified). systems that find the camera through the per-view table [125ab68] (0x188 bytes per entry, camera weak pointer at +0x238) read +0x1a0..+0x1d0 directly (e.g. 302760, 47a670). exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 camera tail hook site — verified the end of update, inc dword ptr [rdi+0x424] at 9f4f3 (6 bytes, rdi = camera), is a working per-frame hook site: the target is still locked in the local [rsp+0x20] and the camera fields are final for the frame. hook: e9 to own code, replay the inc, jump back to +6. only one patch can own the site. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 camera target stays soldier — verified while the player rides a vehicle the camera target is still the soldier, and the soldier has no scene parent (the vehicle is not its parent in the scene tree); edf5 input, keyboard snapshot and ime integration r86 qualification: internal locking does not independently establish arbitrary external thread coherent/atomic snapshot reads. input reconciliation. overview edf5 has a game-owned keyboard snapshot, dynamically loaded controller input, and special handling of windows ime composition. reading keyboard state from a hook on another thread is not equivalent to reading the game input frame. format, api or behavior the message pump fills a 256-byte getkeyboardstate snapshot at rva 0x1253600. the game does not statically import getasynckeystate or xinput in the form an external patch might expect. for japanese text, edf5 temporarily detaches the native ime from its window and renders its own composition/candidates while the game text ui is active. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. keyboard snapshot — static the game keeps a keyboard snapshot: a 256-byte getkeyboardstate table at 1253600. the message loop 60bc90 (peekmessage pump) fills it when flag 12535db is 0 and sets the flag; the input reader (60e04e in the source; input-pump-focus starts it at 60df50) copies the table under a critical section (lea rcx,[0x1253600] at 60e184, anchor keyref) and clears the flag, so it is refreshed once per input cycle on the pump thread and is safe to read from any thread. it can be read instead of calling an api. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 input xinput dynamic — static the game loads xinput dynamically: the utf-16 string xinput9_1_0.dll is at rva edffa0 (ede7a0 is its file offset, which an earlier version of this line gave as the address; checked in edf5.exe 2026-10-19), so xinputgetstate can be resolved the same way for controller combos. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 input getkeystate thread — static getkeystate would only be correct on the pump thread (the game's own ui calls it at 49324f, 5a25e9, ...); the keyboard snapshot avoids that question. the getkeystate slot c977a0 has five callers: 49324f, 493f97, 5a25e9, 5a28da, 5a471b. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 input not imported — static getasynckeystate, xinput and directinput are not imported; a patch resolves them at runtime, for example getprocaddress(getmodulehandlew(l"user32.dll"), "getasynckeystate"). exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 input ime detach — static edf5 detaches the ime from its window right after creating it and re-attaches it only while its own text input is active, through a window-procedure hook that swallows the composition messages and draws its own composition and candidate list; so by default no windows ime window can appear over the game. ime imports (iat slots): immgetcompositionstringw c97060, immreleasecontext c97068, immsetopenstatus c97070, immgetcontext c97078, immassociatecontext c97080, immgetcandidatelistw c97088 (also defwindowprocw c97770, sendmessagew c97768). window creation: createwindowexw at 60bba3 stores the window at [125a9c8]; immgetcontext at 60bc06 saves the context at [12535e8]; immassociatecontext(hwnd, null) at 60bc1c; flag [12535fc] = 0. window procedure 60ae90: unhandled messages go to a hook pointer [12535f0] if set (60b2b8), else defwindowprocw (60b2f6); on wm_close (60af7a) it re-attaches the saved context (60afbf), releases it and destroys the window. the game's text input: setup near 491856 installs the hook 491eb0 (at 49188a) and sends custom message 0x1000, on which the hook re-attaches the saved context (491f58) and sets the flag to 1; message 0x1001 (sent at 492ec9) detaches again (491f11); 4918c0 removes the hook. the hook swallows wm_ime_startcomposition / endcomposition / composition and passes wm_ime_setcontext on with lparam 0 (hides the system ime windows); its own drawing is in 493040 (via 491e10), which also detaches at 4930a5 when bytes +0x109 and +0x10c of its object are set. no per-frame re-detach was found. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 input ime no candidates in game — verified in game, the windows ime candidate window does not appear over edf5 while an overlay's text field has keyboard focus: the ime switched to hiragana but no candidate window appeared and no japanese text reached the field; edf5 radar projection, colors and marker scaling overview the minimap is a distinct projection and marker-rendering pipeline. entity world positions are projected onto a 2d radar plane, clamped to its range, and classified by a color/marker dispatcher before drawing. format, api or behavior in the inspected implementation the position scale defaults to 0.6, marker size scale to 1.2, and the planar range comparison uses 200.0 m. a helper computes 2d coordinates, relative height, and an inside-range flag. the source identifies where team colors are loaded and used, which is useful for hud overlays and special markers. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. radar scales — static the constructor sets [this+0x8e0] = 0.6 (position scale) and [this+0x8e4] = 1.2 (marker size scale, the game's normal dot size), read by the marker drawer 4ce730, the teammate-icon drawer 4ced00 and 4cf560. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 radar position helper — static 4ce5c0 returns radar-plane x, y, a height term and a flag at [rbp-0x14] (1 = inside range, 0 = clamped to the rim). the 2d distance is compared with 200.0 m (constant ee66fc, loaded at 4ce64e); positions are scaled by 0.6, so the rim radius is 120 radar units. height term = scale^2 x 2.25 x dy, clamped to +-80. the radar rotates with the player's heading (object [this+0x768], rows at +0x80 / +0x90; the source called it the camera object, but it is the player soldier: #radar-own-player-object, settled 2026-11-08). exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 radar colors — static the six colors are static float4 globals 125b400..125b450, filled once at 4cd89c from .rdata (ee7920 white, ee7900 cyan, ee7550 green, ee7470 red, ee7560 yellow). only the dispatcher uses them, through eight lea instructions at 4cdaee, 4cdb29, 4cdb69, 4cdc20 (crates), 4cdc5b, 4cdcc6, 4cdd01, 4cde0c; the drawer copies the color (16 bytes, no alignment needed). as rgb 0-255: hostile 255 0 0, team 2 0 191 255, team 4 and team 0 255 255 255, team 5 255 255 0, crates 0 255 0. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 radar marker drawer — static marker drawer 4ce730: rcx = radar object, rdx = hud draw context, r8 = list, r9 = a rotation matrix the dispatcher builds at [rsp+0x60], [rsp+0x20] = color pointer, [rsp+0x28] = pointer to the reference (player) position built at [rsp+0x50]. list: [r8+8] data, [r8+0x18] count, 16-byte vec4 elements; list in r13, index in r15d, next-element code at 4cec60. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 radar w lane — static position helper 4ce5c0 ignores the w lane of an element, so a patch can carry per-entity data there (floats such as 0..4 and 5/6/7 can be carried there). exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 version notes and limitations the report that an ignored vector w lane can carry extra information is an implementation trick in the studied helper, not a guarantee that all users or future builds ignore it. contributed sources: edf knowledge hub snapshot 54f89cd by novae (ajane), with third-party credits in the linked evidence pages. this editorial page is a synthesis and does not claim new binary or runtime experiments. related reference earlier wiki documentation remains authoritative for its own explicitly tested game/runtime scope; edf5 item drops, collection limits and online authority overview edf5 item boxes are managed by a native crate manager with separate live-field and collected-count limits. in multiplayer, spawning is authority-gated and the network sends spawn identity; edf5 deferred lighting, reflections, water and window materials overview the rendering path uses a g-buffer followed by deferred lighting, with some transparent materials rendered afterward in a forward path. embedded shader names or blobs alone do not prove that a feature is enabled in the shipped render graph. format, api or behavior the examined exe carries multiple deferred-lighting compute variants. its embedded ssr programs include a ray-march, resolve and blur pipeline, but the source reports no code references that would run them. building windows instead perform interior mapping from a texture; forward water and glass use their own reflection inputs. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. deferred lighting cs — static the dxbc blob at 1165260 (rendering.md#underground-shader) is one of three variants of the deferred-lighting compute shader, the pass that turns the g-buffer into the lit picture: the variant with sun shadows is 116e780 (0x39ec bytes), the other shadowless one 1172170 (0x3374 bytes); all three are created in 5d6bd0 (lea at 5d8185, 5d8165, 5d8145). environment reflections are applied here, per pixel, from a grid of local cubemaps (rtti localcubemap@ren@xgl). bindings: all write uav0:g_color_out; inputs t0 g_albedorgb, t1 g_specularrgb, t2 g_normalxyz, t3 g_smooth_reflection_specpow, t4 g_metallic_roughness, t5 g_viewxyz_id, t6 g_light_accumulate, t7 g_specular_accumulate, t8 g_local_cubemap_array (texturecubearray), t9 g_ambient_occlusion, sbuf10 g_local_cubemap_grid, point-light arrays and masks (sbuf11-14), t15 g_shadow_depth (only 116e780); cbuffers xgl_system (b0), xgl_additional_light_setting (b2), localcubemapworldaabb (b10: g_min_point, g_unit_size, g_cubemap_grid_divide_count, debug flags g_debug_is_used_local_cubemap, g_debug_preview_env). other blobs created in the same function: 1164ab0 (5d828c), 1168610 (5d80ae), 116a0b0 (5d77de). that darkunderground's blob is the variant used underground is inferred, not traced. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 dormant ssr shaders — static edf5.exe carries a complete screen-space-reflection (ssr) compute-shader set that no code references: a hi-z ray march with local-cubemap fallback (115af80, 0x104c bytes, and 115bfd0, 0x1f14), a resolve (115aa80), two ssr blurs (115ffa0, 1161630), a reflection-over-color composite (11562f0) and a cubemap-array pass (11567d0); so ssr was most likely cut, not hidden behind a setting. bindings: 115af80 / 115bfd0 t0 m_hi_color, t1 m_hi_z, t3 m_normal_map, t4 m_interscetion (sic), t5 m_cube_map_array (texturecubearray), uav0 m_out_reflection, cbuffer param (272 bytes: m_inv_proj_matrix, m_inv_view_matrix, m_cubemaps (cubemapparam), m_used_cubemap_count, m_debug_cubemap_miplevel); 115aa80 m_hi_color, m_interscetion -> m_out_reflection; 115ffa0 / 1161630 m_src_texture, m_depth, cbuffer ssrblurparam (m_blur_fall_out, m_threshold); 11562f0 m_reflection, m_color -> m_out, cbuffer param (m_param); 11567d0 m_src (texture2darray) -> m_out, m_cubemaps, m_used_count, m_camera_pos. file offsets are rva - 0x2200 in .data. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 window interior mapping — static building windows use snd_map_build_window.sgo, an interior-mapping g-buffer shader (a 2d interior_texture drawn behind the glass with a view-dependent offset, varied per instance) that samples no cubemap itself; any reflection on the glass comes later from the deferred-lighting pass's local cubemaps, driven by the material's metallic and roughness. g-buffer ps (6 targets; plain and instanced with instancing_interior_random_seed): t2 window_frame_texture, t3 interior_texture, t4 normal, t5 window_normal, t6 param_reflect_xxx_spec_hspec, all texture2d; xgl_user_param (80 bytes): normal_amount @4, window_normal_amount @16, window_normal_uv_scale @24, specular_pow @32, specular_color @36, light_smooth @48, metallic @52, roughness @56, fall_off_amount @60, fall_off_scale @64, fall_off_offset @68, interior_wrap_count @72, interior_random_seed @76; techniques deferred, deferred_instancing, deferred_skinning1, zpass*. other reflective-looking families in dx11.cpk: snd_map_object_glass, snd_map_water_transparent, snd_map_lod / _noenv pairs. which on-screen layer of a window (the interior picture or the cubemap) shows the city image is not settled. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 water glass forward — static the water (snd_map_water_transparent.sgo) and glass-object (snd_map_object_glass.sgo) shaders are forward shaders (techniques forward* and zpass*, one color target), drawn after the deferred-lighting pass; they take reflections from the single global cubemap g_xgl_environment_map, not from the local cubemap grid, so a change to the deferred-lighting shader cannot reach them. water ps: three scrolling normal maps, three parallax maps, bubble_albedo, t9 g_xgl_environment_map (texturecube), t10 g_xgl_viewxyz_id_texture (scene view positions, so it can read the depth behind it), t11 g_xgl_shadow_depth, point lights; edf5 decals, destructible map objects and debris overview decals and shattered map objects have related visual effects but separate ownership and lifecycle rules. modifying a decal lifetime alone does not stop its eviction by overlap or manager budget. format, api or behavior decalbase tracks age, lifetime, strength and undrawn duration; every spawner passes 20.0), +0x148 age/lifetime, +0x14c strength (removal rank factor), +0x1e0.. shader parameter blocks, +0x20c dissolve (= 1 - fade value, written each frame), +0x310 bounds (oriented box data used by the overlap test 19f220 -> 5bf340). fade value: +0x344 (splash), +0x340 (splashprojection); edf5 mission vm, script states and showlayout overview mission bytecode does not execute as a list of human-readable commands. a native interpreter dispatches opcodes into game systems, and ui instructions such as showlayout have both interpreter and layout-manager lifecycles. format, api or behavior the source follows the edf5 bvm opcode dispatcher and the missionscript state transition from created to started, playing and ended. it also identifies opcode 0x27 as a showlayout path. such details matter when transpiling mission scripts or testing when a ui element is safe to create. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. bvm interpreter dispatch — static the bvm interpreter 114f38 dispatches with movzx eax,dl; edf6 damage event pipeline and on-screen numbers overview damage numbers are presentation generated from native hit/damage events; they are not the same as the engine’s hp accounting. some hit paths do not produce the same display event, so overlay mods can miss legitimate combat interactions. format, api or behavior the source maps the built-in damage display and its option flag, event payload, style variants and missing-event cases. separate damage-model analysis documents multipart targets and conversion paths. a mod should join these only where the event data explicitly supports it. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. native damage display — static edf6 has a native damage-number display (huihuddamage, one per player hud). the options-menu setting option_damageuitype picks its style: 0 none, 1 hitpos (every hit at its point), 2 fixedpos (a fixed stacked list), 3 target (one number per target); the code switches on it at 88e640 and 892463. fixedpos works almost exactly like edf5 mods' fixed display: hits within a merge window add into the newest line, otherwise a new line is pushed; lines stack upward with the newest at the base; each line expires a set time after its last hit; a pop-in scale plays on every update; vehicles get their own size and optionally their own position, and soldier classes their own positions. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 native styles in game — verified vanilla's per-hit and per-target styles work with the patch's v0 red total next to them; edf6 fixed simulation step, presentation and high refresh rates overview edf6 update cadence and rendered presentation cadence are distinct. increasing display refresh or using a new swap-chain presentation mode does not by itself make the simulation run more often. format, api or behavior the measured game loop counts whole 1/60-second periods, may catch up with bounded multiple updates, and presents through a separate graphics path. at steady 60 fps, approximately 99.5% of reported frames advanced one simulation step. the contributor compared borderless blit-model presentation with an independent-flip setup; they behaved differently for vrr and pacing. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. edf6 game loop steps — static the game loop 11a2e90 asks the period counter 11dae60 twice per loop (at 11a2f4f before the wait, at 11a2f6b inside the sleep(1) loop); the counter returns n = whole 1/60 s periods since [2139d18] (period = qpc frequency x 100 / 6000) and advances the base by n periods; the loop runs min(n, 3) update steps (lea ebp,[rsi+3] at 11a2eda, cmp ebx,ebp / cmova ebx,ebp at 11a2f76 / 11a2f80; the count at [rsp+0xbc] goes to the scene's virtual +8 at 11a3006), so a late loop catches up by at most 3 steps and drops the rest. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 edf6 game loop tail — static when n > 1 the loop sets [rdi+0xc] = 8 (11a3079), counted down by one per loop, and passes [rdi+0xc] == 0 as a flag to 111d890 (meaning unread). the loop's end calls the getter 1183310 at 11a30bc and 1129c10 with 2139a90 (the render command queue) at 11a30df. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 edf6 content cadence even — verified at a steady 60 fps in a mission the loop runs exactly one update step per loop and one loop per present, so each shown frame advances the game by one 1/60 s step (about 99.5 % of frames; the rest a 2-step frame next to a 0-step one, about one pair every 7 s), with the window hidden and vsync off or visible with the game's vsync; the catch-up (2-3 steps) fires only while the mission loads. so on a 165 hz screen edf6's uneven look comes from the display side (#edf6-present-mode-pacing) and from 60 hz motion, not from its stepping; a refresh that is a multiple of 60 gives every frame the same screen time. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 edf6 present mode pacing — verified in borderless mode edf6 presents with the legacy blit model (presentmon: "composed: copy with gpu gdi", syncinterval 1, no tearing), so dwm composes it at the desktop's refresh and vrr (g-sync / freesync) cannot engage; on a 165 hz desktop its steady 60 fps reaches the screen as an uneven 3-3-3-2 refresh pattern. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 edf6 special k pacing — verified started through special k (120 hz, its own 60 fps limiter, flip discard, tearing allowed) edf6 presents as hardware: independent flip with syncinterval 0, but about 2-2.5 frames a second are held 25 ms or 8.3 ms (|msanimationerror| p95 7.95 ms); with special k's latent sync (each present timed to a scanline in the blanking) the displayed time has sd 0.96 ms and 0.13 hitches a second. reading (unverified): a frame paced by a free cpu clock lands on either side of a refresh boundary as it jitters. nvidia's g-sync indicator showed on although the captures stayed on 8.33 ms steps (unresolved). exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 version notes and limitations presentation measurements are hardware/driver and configuration specific. they are not a blanket safe120 runtime certification or evidence that physics, ai and scripting can simply be uncapped. contributed sources: edf knowledge hub snapshot 54f89cd by novae (ajane), with third-party credits in the linked evidence pages. this editorial page is a synthesis and does not claim new binary or runtime experiments. related reference earlier wiki documentation remains authoritative for its own explicitly tested game/runtime scope; edf6 eos datagram framing, reliability and state flush r86 scope note: for the ordinary audited shipping class-4/class-5 path, the native builder capped the first physical aggregate at 1164 b; a 1400 b defensive check alone does not prove oversize reachability. current reconciliation. overview edf6 uses eos p2p as a transport while the game’s own controller manages record framing, acknowledgements, replay suppression and periodic state flushes. “eos unreliable” does not mean every game-level record has no retransmission. format, api or behavior the contributor’s static reading reports an eos size limit of 1170 bytes against a looser native 1400-byte record rejection threshold. native outgoing state is flushed around 90 ms. records use a packed size/type header; reliable records include sequence envelopes and acknowledgements. a hypothesized six-frame state-phase interaction is marked unverified despite reported measurements. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. net eos packet cap — static one eos p2p packet carries at most 1170 bytes (the eos sdk's limit); the game neither splits larger data nor reports it, so anything above the limit is lost. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 net size check 1400 — static the game's own size check is looser than eos's: the packet controller refuses a record only above 1400 bytes (12d0be6), so a reliable message between 1170 and 1400 bytes is accepted, refused by eos on every try and resent until the room drops its members (packetfit.h: eight times over about 26 s; netclass.h gives a reliable record 6 tries, #net-record-format; the two counts were not reconciled). exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 net flush 90ms — static the game flushes its outgoing packet queue on a 90 ms timer and sends only the newest state record then, not every frame's. the interval is a float written by the packet controller's constructor 12cb5f0 at 12cb66c (41 c7 46 58 00 00 b4 42, mov dword [r14+0x58], 90.0f), fixed at start; the controller's update is 12cecc0, its flush 12cea10. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 net datagram format — static a datagram of the packet controller (eos::packet::controllerimpl, vtable 1af4ff0): records gather per peer in a buffer (12cffd0) that is flushed (12cea10; called from the send path 12ce99a, the acknowledgements 12cedbb and the per-peer builder 12d0020) when the next record would pass 1100 bytes (0x44c) and on the 90 ms timer. the flush writes an 8-byte header (two random bytes, a 16-bit datagram number, a crc32c of the plaintext records taken at 12cea79), encrypts the records with aes-ctr (7b8060, called at 12cebaa; same length) and hands the datagram to eos on the same thread (12d0120 -> vtable slot 3 12d2ef0 -> 12c8bc0, always eos_pr_unreliableunordered). the receive 12cdf20 decrypts with d2360 (at 12ce16b), checks the crc and drops a datagram whose number and crc it has seen (12ce1f3..12ce1fe). exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 net record format — static records inside a datagram start with a u32 size << 20 | type and size bytes follow (the receive loop 12ce515 advances by size + 4). sendunreliable (12d1040) writes the data record alone, lost with its datagram. sendreliable (12d0ac0) first writes an envelope, u32 0x00401200 (type 0x1200, size 4) and a u32 sequence number, and keeps the record until the peer acknowledges it: 6 tries, the first resend after 700 ms (1fef040), the wait growing by 1fef048 each try; the receiver acknowledges every envelope (12ce4ff -> 12cfcd0) and drops a record it already has. types 0x13xx, 0x14xx and 0x18xx are the controller's own (acknowledgements and the like, 12ce2b7..12ce2d7); a data record's type is ((sub & 0xf) | id << 4) << 8 (12c2e59); the event layer's batches are type 0x3000. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 net event batch builder — static event messages queue in a per-peer builder that sends only once it holds more than 250 bytes (761e60, the 0xfa from 74ed6d), so small messages of one frame share a record; 761e60 sends unreliable when the builder's +0x628 is set. framing costs at most 26 bytes per message (750380 / 7504a0 at most 12, 74d3e0 at most 14), then 12 for the reliable record and 8 for the datagram header. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 net position every 6 frames — unverified a player's machine puts its own position and facing into its sync record only every 6th frame; with the 90 ms flush (#net-flush-90ms) at 60 fps the two periods lock together, so another machine either gets the position in every packet or in none for seconds: measured, 1.3-5.9% of a remote player's packets held a position and 6% a facing, and remote players were drawn a median 1.57 m (up to 17 m) off and up to 117 degrees turned. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 version notes and limitations the 1170-byte transport limit and frame synchronization findings derive partly from third-party mod source/readmes; edf4.1 engine singletons, weapon fire and bullet objects overview native object ownership and weapon firing in edf4.1 are distributed among game-global systems, weapon classes and bullet instances. the source’s constructor and virtual-method data helps locate lifecycles without assuming edf6 class or allocator identity. format, api or behavior the global builder constructs xgs engine services before recreating game singletons. weapon_basicshoot dispatches through a per-shot record and target weapon matrix; bullet objects have their own vtable/update behavior. a port must preserve the source-visible timing and ownership, not just the resource names. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. edf41 globals builder — static 3442b0 calls 341ec0, the builder of every game singleton. it first calls 5647f0 (at 3422da), which builds the engine (xgs) systems, then for each global: calls the old object's virtual destructor (call [rax]), stores 0, allocates through the import _aligned_malloc [918698] (msvcr120; size in ecx, alignment 0x10 in edx), calls the constructor, stores rax. the teardown functions store 0 into the same globals: 342f30 for the game singletons, 564baa for the engine systems. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-57aab039 edf41 global engine systems — static cc89d0 xgs::umbra::system (constructor 5740a0, also stores systemservices and graphicsservice); cc84a8 xgs::controller::system (55fd70). built inline in helpers 5647f0 calls: cc8520 xgs::ui::system (565270), cc8530 xgs::havok::system (5651d0), cc8a80 xgs::user::signinmanager (565300). exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-57aab039 edf41 weapon shot — static shot (weapon_basicshoot slot 13 314d20) calls 30fc50(weapon, index, r8): returns for a remote copy's weapon; edf6 camera view matrix and ride mode overview edf6 inherits the broad idea of follow-versus-ride camera behavior but uses different native offsets and function sites from edf5. reusing an edf5 tail patch byte-for-byte is not valid. format, api or behavior the contributor locates edf6 follow and ride mode routines and the final camera rotation rows at +0x220/+0x230/+0x240 with eye at +0x250. it also records camera and vehicle-related vtables for precise source-to-target comparisons. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. ghost camera follow ride modes — static follow mode is faf20 and ride (vehicle) mode is fb9f0. follow switches to ride at fb93e-fb97c when the target's ride control block [target+0x1550] has users; ride switches back at fbbf3-fbc33. the mode state slot is camera+0xbf0, set by fadf0. the riding predicate f7210(camera) -> bool (camera+0x358 users, +0x360 non-null, [[+0x360]+0x1550] users) has no direct callers; the same test is inside vtable slot 9 f7500. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 ghost camera final matrix — static the final camera matrix is camera+0x220 / +0x230 / +0x240 (rotation rows) and +0x250 (eye). the ride mode writes it at fc0db-fc106 and the follow mode writes the rows at fb907-fb919. after the mode call, update multiplies the rows by the shake matrix +0x280..+0x2a8 when shake is on. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 camera class vtables — static primary vtables useful for camera and vehicle work: characterghostcamera 1768c10, gamecamerabase 1769178, tracecamera 1769218, freeviewcamera 1768fa8, vehiclebase 17dd720, assultsoldier 17cdf28, soldierbase 17d24d8, humanbase 17cfd20, dummyvehiclerider 17d7320, rideinfo@vehiclebase 17d9868. edf6 adds the vehicle classes vehicle601_tank, 603_flak, 607_robotruck, 60x_truck, 612_nix (see how for their prefix) and vehiclebigbegaruta to edf5's set. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-678ccb46 version notes and limitations some camera behavior is only statically observed; edf5 menu layouts, settings callbacks and ui notices overview edf5 settings and ui notices are message-driven native systems. a layout sgo specifies the c++ ui object class and callback names rather than fully describing the screen’s behavior. format, api or behavior ui::huilayout subclasses register named callbacks, with game settings implemented by huihqgamesetting. a separate notice dispatcher fans event 12 to ui listeners, including uinotice, which enqueues strings for presentation. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. hui layout framework — static edf5 menu screens are ui::huilayout subclasses created from layout files. the .sgo names the c++ class (xgs_ui_object_class) and the callback names its buttons use; the class registers handlers for those names; the hq main menu opens its submenus from paths stored in its layout data. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 gamesetting class — static huihqgamesetting: vtable ecfee0; factory create 515f60 (0x7b0 bytes); constructor 516110; update (vtable slot 1) 5172a0. callbacks registered by name in the constructor (4e9610): callinitializesetting 517ea0, callkeyconfigselect 518f10, chatshortcutcustmoize 518f00, receivekeyconfigselect 519690, request_manual 5198d0. this+520h is the player index (0/1). the +e8 flag hides buttoncallmanual; edf5 havok body properties and motion operations overview the studied edf5 runtime uses the havok physics2012-style hkp* body/motion system, with native wrappers and collision filter layers. this is not the same runtime body layout as edf6’s hknp* path. format, api or behavior the source identifies body wrapper, collision filter field +0x4c (low five bits as layer), and virtual setters for linear/angular velocity and linear impulse. these operations belong to the motion interface and need correct object alignment and lifetime. evidence and exact technical details the following selected source observations retain their original evidence level and build-specific details. follow their links for the complete evidence method, addresses and attribution. havok body wrapper — static the game's havok body wrapper is 0x2c0 bytes: hkpentity vtable cde138, with an embedded hkpmaxsizemotion (the concrete motion) at +0x150. crates point to it from unit +0xa0 (drop-items.md#crate-unit-body). exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 havok body filter info — static body +0x4c is collisionfilterinfo; the collision layer is value & 0x1f. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 havok motion vtable slots — static motion vtable slots, called as call [vtable+off] with rcx = body+0x150 and rdx a 16-byte-aligned vector: +0x90 setlinearvelocity (a plain store to motion +0xe0), +0x98 setangularvelocity (+0xf0), +0xb0 applylinearimpulse (v += imp × invmass, invmass = [motion+0xd0].w), +0xc0 applyangularimpulse. for keyframed and fixed motions +0xb0 / +0xc0 are no-ops. exact source: view evidence and source details · build steam-5d11de53 version notes and limitations do not use edf5 body/motion offsets against edf6 hknp bodies. format-level deserialization is not collision-semantic parity;
