id: patcher-one-pass-labels the patcher reads a .txt once, top to bottom, and resolves a label when it reads the line that uses it, so a label must be defined (by aob, alloc or label) on an earlier line; only the alloc line that defines a settings block has to come before that block's value lines, and aob anchors the settings do not name can follow them. parseaddress (about line 222) looks the base name up in labels; not found and not hex gives "malformed patch input: undefined label: x" and sets patch = false, so the whole file writes nothing (no second pass, no forward reference). alloc name size with two arguments starts its search at target = mmodule (near edf5.exe), independent of any aob; only a three-argument alloc name size label needs that label first. alloc runs only while patch is still true, and a failure later in the file leaves the block allocated but never written (a few kb). writes are collected (addpatch) and applied only at the end, and only when nothing failed; aob scans cover the module image (mmodule, mscanrange), so they see unpatched code and never the allocated block. a value line with no address before any address line writes at the current offset, which starts at 0 (the module base). the minimum order is therefore: alloc (plus any aob named by an in-code setting such as label+1: u32! 128, or by the alloc's third argument), then the settings, then every other aob, the code and the hooks; in a patch with 20 anchors and a 10-line banner that moves the first setting from about line 34 to line 14. the grammar table in methods/patch-format.md section 1 agrees (alloc row: an optional third argument asks for memory near that address); its section 3 puts "game anchors" before alloc, which is a convention, not a requirement. basis: when it hits, the path end is moved to the hit point and the bullet stops. flag 2 (m_icollisionflag2, +0x894 / +0x9d4, default layer 11) says what the bullet hits: a sphere shape-cast of the bullet's size along the (already shortened) path; a hit does damage, and a penetrating bullet passes through. a target hit by neither is passed through. shields are the exception: a flag 2 hit on a shield stops the bullet. basis: ktaro's 2,800-cell test; edf6 packet size, eos transport and native rudp current conclusion the eos p2p datagram limit, a packet-controller defensive size check, and the actual maximum built by a particular shipping sender are three different quantities. they must not be used interchangeably. in the qualified native class-4/class-5 application-reliable sender, the original research bounded the reachable physical aggregate to 1164 bytes, below the reported 1170-byte eos limit. a separate community analysis identifies a 1400-byte rejection check. that check does not establish that ordinary, legitimate native traffic reaches 1400 bytes. this is a reconciliation of separately contributed, build-scoped static/native analyses, not a new live packet capture. third-party mods may build larger packets or alter flush/fragmentation behavior; claims about those paths must be tested in those paths. the three size layers layer reported size meaning and applicability physical eos p2p packet 1170 b reported eos transmission cap in the knowledge hub; see community claim native application's defensive check 1400 b guard cited at 12d0be6 in the contributed analysis. a higher guard is not an observed payload size; see source claim qualified native source payload 1144 b builder limit in the previous native rudp analysis qualified native retained record 1156 b application-layer reliable wrapping, same audited path qualified first physical aggregate 1164 b transport envelope in the audited native path, 6 b below reported eos cap community per-peer builder flush trigger 1100 b datagram builder flush threshold; not maximum total datagram size; community record description implementation rule: do not apply the general statement "records between 1170 and 1400 are routinely resent to disconnection" to unmodified class-4/class-5 shipping sends. it is a plausible out-of-envelope scenario, e.g. if another builder, injected plugin, oversized extension or altered call path can actually produce such a record. prove reachability and exact build before treating it as a cause. physical transport is not application reliability the knowledge hub's datagram description says the controller calls eos with eos_pr_unreliableunordered. this is compatible with native class-4/class-5 application-layer retained rudp. sendreliable adds a record with 0x1200 envelope and sequence; acknowledgements (0x1300) retire pending records, with duplicate suppression at receiver. it does not turn physical eos delivery into a reliable mode. the routes have separate semantics: game route outer class delivery at application level ordinary player/scene state 0x3300 class 3 mode 1: latest snapshot, no retained reliable message immediate gameplay events, damageobject 0x3400 class 4 mode 0: retained sandlot rudp normal networkbullet selectors 0/1/2 0x3500 class 5 mode 0: retained sandlot rudp in audited native senders see player-state lanes and native event registry. event protocol id 1 (damageobject) is inside class 4; it is not a substitute for its outer 0x3400 class identity. retrying packets can only recover data actually serialized, not missing projectile rng, movement or detonation state. retry counts and disconnect the community note describes six tries for a reliable record, whereas a third-party source refers to eight over roughly 26 seconds. the supplied records did not reconcile those counts. the earlier native analysis independently derives about 25.9 s cumulative no-ack for its measured edf6 retry/fault progression (700 ms, then +1000 ms after each resend, final interval guard 7000 ms). these statements cannot be normalized to an unqualified "six" or "eight" send-count policy: attempts, resends, retry interval checks and higher-level peer faults may count different events. current rule: use the native qualified state-machine and cumulative timing for that exact sender/build, but retain the contributor's count discrepancy as unresolved pending an instrumented per-peer trace. remoteconnectionclosed replacing a physical link does not destroy the logical reliablemgr; a stale ready bit can obstruct initial recovery. see reconnect lifecycle. timing: 90 ms is not proof of a permanent phase lock the contributor locates a 90 ms controller flush timer (source) and separately proposes that a six-frame transform rhythm can phase-lock with flushes at 60 fps (unverified claim). the previously audited player-state reconstruction describes a transform bit approximately every six network updates and a staged receive/apply path. the unit of cadence matters. a period similarity alone does not demonstrate indefinite starvation; the observed remote-player drift and phase-lock mechanism remain contributor-reported and unverified for the qualified native path. verify the exact update counters, flush timebase, queued state overwrite, send events and receiver apply gate before making a root-cause claim. practical investigation record build hashes and whether the reproducer uses stock game, edf6coop, multislot or other hooks. log actual built physical datagram lengths, reliable record types and the sending source path, not just the defensive guard's constant. separate eos transport failures, reliable records pending ack and class-3 periodic state. capture the same actor/object across send, wire/receive, pending queue and apply gate; correlate with time and peer id. for oversized candidates, prove that normal shipping producer can reach the candidate byte count. for persistent drift, distinguish lost snapshots from repeat suppression or never-applied batches. provenance and limits sources: knowledge hub contributor appendix (steam-678ccb46, novae/ajane with original third-party citations); earlier native rudp reconstruction; native player-lane reconstruction. their executable hashes/build families were not independently cross-matched in this editorial pass. scope-dependent findings are retained rather than silently overridden. no new runtime tests were performed.

the vehicle is discovered through the ride link, not inferred from scene parentage. the contributed source marks this as verified in the named edf5 build, while the edf6 mapping is largely static. do not universally transplant the edf5 parent/link assumptions into edf6 without confirming the owner chain and seat record. in edf6 ride mode the seat data participates in camera construction; an edf5 hook that only adjusts follow-mode distance may have no effect in ride mode. the reported f7210 riding predicate has no direct callers in the contributor's binary reading; the corresponding condition is also present in a vtable method. lack of a direct callsite alone does not prove that the predicate is globally unused. hook placement and visual stability the edf5 camera tail site 9f4f3 was contributor-reported as a working per-frame hook after matrix update. the edf6 update and shake sequence must be located anew. a literal port of that patch can point into unrelated instructions, and only one installed patch may own a particular hook site without chaining/coordinated dispatch. the edf5 contributor also reported that the scene camera's projection could read invalid for whole frames during heavy close combat, with the cause undetermined; do not present a speculative render-thread race as demonstrated. see edf5 guide and camera source fact. safe conversion / plugin workflow match exact executable/build and re-identify the camera object, vtable and update routine. compare member accesses instruction-by-instruction; do not add one constant to every edf5 offset. validate follow, ride, death/spectator, pause and camera shake individually. distinguish a writable final view matrix from the authoritative input/look state that may overwrite it next frame. for first-person proposals, verify eye/head-bone source and weapon visibility/aim behavior rather than declaring first-person compatibility from a possible tail write. evidence boundary the mapping above is a reconciliation of knowledge hub observations and its crosswalk. edf5 hook/site and ride target lines include contributor-reported runtime verification; it does not validate replacing the entire action system. build-specific landmarks question edf5 contributed static analysis edf6 contributed analysis / earlier native investigation game-owned keyboard array 0x1253600, 256-byte getkeyboardstate snapshot (steam-5d11de53) 0x21360e0 buffer (steam-678ccb46); 0x11847ea anchor loads its address update/pump message loop 0x60bc90; input reader near 0x60df50/0x60e04e; flag 0x12535db separate keyboard polling/ui paths: see edf6 ui controls and system xinput xinput9_1_0.dll loaded dynamically; no static xinput import in source reading xinput9_1_0.dll; the contributed pad poll checks xinputgetcapabilities before xinputgetstate relative mouse acquisition stock cursor-based center/recenter path in prior analysis provider edf+0x11831f0, direct consumer edf+0x1188479 in the raw input contract do not copy edf5 0x1253600 into an edf6 mod. the 0x1253600 address is reported as array storage, not a pointer to a heap buffer. the 0x21360e0 location is similarly build-specific; verify both anchors again for patched executables. see edf5 source notes, edf5 global, edf6 global. threading: what is known and what is not the contributor reports that edf5 fills its array from the message pump and copies it under a critical section before clearing the refresh flag. this establishes an internal producer/consumer synchronization path, not automatically a guarantee that arbitrary external readers can safely read all 256 bytes lock-free at any moment. the claim "safe to read from any thread" in the source appendix is preserved as contributor-reported, but has not been independently race-qualified by this wiki. a robust external hook should sample at a defined frame boundary or arrange appropriate synchronization if consistency matters. windows getkeystate semantics are thread/message-queue sensitive, and cannot simply be substituted for the game's frame snapshot. getasynckeystate not appearing in an import table is only a statement about static imports, not proof that no dynamic call can occur. edf5's ime association and candidate rendering are a separate ui text input pipeline; do not rewrite them as if they were gameplay key polling. see input and ime source. edf6 overlay can replace import hooks the community source describes eosovh-win64-shipping.dll rewriting several edf.dll import slots after launch and periodically afterward. if reproduced in the selected build, this explains why an import-address-table hook installed early can appear to work and later disappear. the source also describes a crash caused by overriding the entire user32 getkeystate export; do not interpret that as a blanket recommendation to patch user32. prefer minimally invasive, build-checked hook points, proper chaining and an explicit coexistence policy. contributor source. raw input does not mean unbounded aim rewrites the separate native modernization raw input contract replaces edf6 relative delta acquisition (wm_input counts), leaving menus and downstream sandlot aim shaping intact: /24 scaling, saturation/carry, class-specific response and turret inertia where applicable. do not equate acquisition quantization with downstream intentional mechanics, nor turn an input hook into an implicit safe120 simulation-rate patch. suggested tests under the same build, compare foreground/focus state, keyboard snapshot and action event in the same frame; test ui typing/ime separately. for hooks, test cold launch and several seconds after eos overlay initialization; trace who owns the import slot. for raw input, test absolute cursor ui and relative gameplay paths separately, and check menu-to-game transitions for stale deltas. confirm two independent axes: key correctness and frame coherence. correct individual bytes do not prove one coherent snapshot if observed asynchronously. evidence boundary the source addresses above are contributed static analysis unless the original claim explicitly says otherwise; the earlier modernization contract reflects native binary reconstruction, not an assertion of universal in-game mouse parity. no new executable tests, full race analysis or hooks were run here. additional native game-system references edf5 message pump and xinput edf5 binding code domains

0.6 gives slight ascent. big bang core's unusual altitude behavior is associated with 204=0.4. contributor's experiment/interpretation; source 解析!b292:d295 210 possible recoil reduction; the big bang core example uses 4. the author explicitly says this is not the cause of big bang's altitude restriction. hypothesis; 解析!c294:d294 201 boost energy-consumption multiplier. the author lists specific changes for custom cores, such as 2.25 for vm jet and 0.55 for assault; not a universal baseline for every core. workbook configuration notes, 解析!a836:k855 205 flight energy-consumption multiplier, e.g. 0.9/0.8 in two experimental surface cores. workbook configuration notes 209 emergency recharge multiplier in selected examples; effect direction depends on the consumer, not just the numeric label. workbook configuration notes 206 normal recharge multiplier noted in the exam reverse example. workbook configuration notes keep 210 tentative: its japanese annotation includes “thought to be recoil reduction” (反動軽減と思われる). do not relabel it as an independently verified native symbol. ratios and capacity calculations the workbook's core stat table lists maximum energy, absolute consumption, and percentage of maximum energy for charging, emergency recharge, flight and boost. the percentage columns are calculated as: percent = absolute value / max energy × 100 for the workbook's example vz core (解析!a840:j840), maximum energy is approximately 1405.5222; displayed rows contain normal charge 84.3, emergency 210.8283, flight 210.8, and boost 63.2. those yield roughly 6.0%, 15.0%, 15.0%, 4.5% of capacity respectively. this is a reconstruction of the workbook's example, not proof that every gameplay subsystem consumes energy using these exact per-action values. the author hypothesizes that base percentage relationships are hardcoded and that a core's custom parameters then multiply them (解析!a845). in the experimental “jailbreak” core, a flight multiplier of 10 and boost multiplier of 25 give very large displayed costs (解析!a854:k854), but the workbook does not establish how every resulting edge case is clamped in-game. editing and validation rules treat customparameter identifiers as measured source annotations. retain them numerically until the binary consumer and data path are validated. distinguish takeoff impulse from sustained hover ascent: 204 can permit lift-off and still result in a gradual fall afterward. test flight, hover, boost, recharge and weapon recoil independently. a visible change in one does not imply the others share the same parameter. do not extrapolate edf5/edf6 semantics to edf4.1 without a paired native case. source: mod製作メモ.xlsx, sheet 解析, ranges b292:d295, a836:k855; user-relayed permission to incorporate research publicly. the workbook author’s preferred published name is not known. no fresh in-game tests were performed for this article.

air raider drones: formation, movement and attack-order sgo fields resource structure the contributed japanese workbook analyzes a portable bombing drone whose object resource string is app:/object/pd605_drone_grenade.sgo. it transcribes a custom_parameter tree with drone, formation, movement and order sections. the worked example is not an exhaustive schema for all air raider drones or an assertion that every named field is consumed identically across edf versions. the source distinguishes a drone's waiting/follow formation from attack-order area placement. do not combine the two offset lists into one coordinate system. formation / idle-follow data formation holds a list of per-drone offset vectors, rather than a single offset for the whole swarm. the author notes an example with 24 offsets for a 24-drone formation, and describes the waiting drones as following the air raider. for the excerpted first formation member, the source records the triple [1, 2, 1] (stored as doubles). the exact axis convention of this idle-offset triple is not proven by these cells; do not assume the attack-area axis descriptions below automatically transfer to it. source: 解析!b893:k925, especially b901, b905:k923. movement / aiming fields path or field worked example source interpretation movement.linear.max 30 maximum forward speed, per author movement.linear.accele 0.10000000149 acceleration parameter; numeric unit unknown movement.linear.lerp 0.05000000075 interpolation parameter (lerp) movement.angular.ratio 0.10000000149 angular steering field movement.angular.mix 0.94999998808 angular mixing field aim.speed 0.10000000149 source notes question what is being aimed (possibly mounted gun); purpose not resolved equipment / aim_target 1 / 4 numbers visible in this example, but their enumerations remain unknown the field names come from the example sgo tree; the physical units, interpolator timebase and enum mappings have not been independently established. see 解析!b925:k976. attack-order fields and directions the sample attack order contains type=4, trigger=1, a flight/attack offset, radius=5, delay with min=0 and max=60, an area list and is_end_to_suicide=0. the author's directional annotations distinguish two different offsets: aircraft approach offset relative to a warning zone (order.offset): sample [0, 18, -9], described as left/right, height and depth. the annotated sign convention is positive = left, positive height = up, positive depth = farther inward (解析!b1009:k1016). individual attack area offset relative to a specified strike point (order.area[*].offset): sample [40, 0, 0]. the author again describes positive x as left, positive depth as farther inward, positive height as up; a height change can shift landing points because mounted weapons aim at an offset altitude (解析!b1029:k1038). for each listed attack area, angle=0 changes the fan orientation when modified; a positive change was reported to rotate left. distance=250 specifies strike-range length in this example, apparently influencing aircraft motion along with projectile count. this is author-observed behavior, not a verified equation for aircraft speed. see 解析!b1040:k1047. safe editing rules preserve the number and pairing of formation entries when changing the drone count; investigate producer/consumer bounds before adding hundreds of offsets. measure values after changing only one field, and separately observe waiting formation, flight to target, warning-zone geometry and strike position. do not assert the exact meaning of aim_target=4, type=4, trigger=1, equipment=1 or is_end_to_suicide=0 without exact-build runtime evidence. cross-game/multiplayer serialization of these fields remains an independent question. source: mod製作メモ.xlsx, 解析!a893:k1059, specifically b901:k1056. editorial translation of named cells, no new game tests or extracted game assets.

air raider bomber requests: sgo record parameters and failed laser-guidance experiments data layers the japanese workbook compares bombardment request examples km6z4, phobos z, phobos z4 and a westa da entry. their sampled sgo records contain an object resource, multiple scalar parameters and a pointer to a subordinate projectile. the annotated mapping names fields such as bomber type, aircraft count, delay between aircraft, altitude, speed, attack-direction offset, distribution type and subprojectile node (解析!a417:o447). the excerpted object paths include app:/object/bomber501_2.sgo and app:/object/bomber401.sgo, but their presence in sample rows is not a universal list of allowed bomber objects. do not infer game-wide aircraft class ids or network protocol ids from the displayed record positions. source-supported behavior, not yet a general formula the workbook notes an attack center shown as a blue inverted triangle. one sampled field is thought to select a point from the base toward the tip of the warning zone (zero at the base; approaching one toward the front). another value apparently influences a forward/downward release trajectory: 0 gives a downward orientation, while increasing it is reported to lead in front of the aircraft. an additional field may describe spacing of aircraft. the author explicitly uses uncertain language for parts of this mapping (解析!h439:h443). accordingly, an editor should expose these as observed fields with uncertain semantics, rather than promising a physically accurate predicted impact location. the author notes a visual difference between phobos z and another attack that might be caused by gravity, but does not isolate the cause (解析!a481). laser-guidance negative experiment the author asked whether bombs released by a bomber can be actively redirected through a laser guidance device. the experiment reports a negative result in the tested configurations (解析!a483:e491): released class or nested construction what the source reports missilebullet01 guidance itself did not operate, even with the laser-guidance flag set to 1 clusterbullet01 → efsbullet some guidance was observed, but not by the laser-designation tool clusterbullet01 → missilebullet01 some guidance was observed, but not by the laser-designation tool the author proposes that the bomber's white radar marker, hence perhaps a different team id, may prevent it receiving laser-designation information. this is explicitly a hypothesis, not a diagnosed root cause. it must not be converted into a rule that all white-team entities reject laser targets. for exploratory team settings see community team matrix. tooling recommendations keep bomber request / aircraft object / projectile instance as separate entities in the authoring model. do not assume the visible warning-zone triangle uniquely determines actual landing points without trajectory and gravity tests. mark laser target forwarding as not demonstrated for these examples; avoid silently turning the failed experiment into a successful mechanism. if testing guidance, log the projectile owner/team, actual target selection, guidance flag, target acquisition callback and emitted nested projectile class separately. source: mod製作メモ.xlsx, 解析!a417:o491. the experiment is reported by the contributor; no runtime was repeated in this wiki revision.

fencer recoil and shield protection angles: empirical workbook measurements gatling spin/recoil experiments a japanese community worksheet records the interval between start of firing and the weapon model/camera reaching straight up for two fencer weapons. at the assumed 60 frames/second conversion used by the sheet: tested weapon start frame straight-up frame difference workbook conversion fireblast gatling 614 1529 915 frames 15.25 s flame revolver dc2 144 246 102 frames 1.70 s these are observations from a particular experimental setup, not evidence that their native recoil parameters are expressed as a raw timer or that the game always runs at a fixed 60 fps. the worksheet later comments that a more negative value in a sampled custom parameter increases the tendency to aim upward, and that setting another recoil-decay parameter to 1 could allow continuous upward drift after shooting (解析!q664, q670). another field appears to govern spin-up and may interact with firing interval; the author warns that some combinations fail to fire (q672). the underlying fields were not recovered as a complete validated enum. shield protection display values the workbook compares a shield's resource scalar with the angle shown in its description: variant raw scalar displayed protection angle standard 0.175 20° b 0.2625 30° f 0.35 40° source: 解析!a858:e865, especially a860:d863. the workbook calculates display_angle / raw ≈ 114.2857 for each row and states that 1.57 would show approximately 180°, suggesting a radian relationship. important qualification: the ordinary radians-to-degrees factor is 180/π ≈ 57.2958, not 114.2857. the observed ratio is approximately twice that factor (360/π ≈ 114.5916) within the samples' rounding. therefore a plausible editorial hypothesis is that the resource stores a half-angle in radians while the text shows a full protection cone. this is an inference from values, not a verified acos/clamp or engine angle implementation. avoid labeling the field simply “degrees” or simply “radians” without noting the factor-of-two ambiguity. for example, the author uses 0.7 for an experimental shield, yielding a calculated description of approximately 80° in the sheet (解析!a865:d865). whether runtime protection boundaries exactly match that ui value was not tested here. validation procedure verify whether the scalar changes displayed text only or also the actual shield collision/defense cone. test left/right and vertical incoming projectiles at controlled angles, keeping the same weapon and game build. check 60/120 fps regimes separately before converting recoil frames into seconds or using a fixed-step assumption. preserve the worksheet's uncertain field names; a negative recoil sign does not establish the formula for all fencer weapons. source: mod製作メモ.xlsx, 解析!a649:q675 and 解析!a858:e865. the half-angle explanation is labeled as new inference; original source measures remain unchanged.

team ids, radar colors and ai: community test matrix scope the japanese source notebook includes a test table for team ids 0–6, with separate columns for alien/character and ant test objects, radar display, ai movement, proactive attack, counterattack and an additional column labeled 味方npc (friendly npc). this is a contributor test matrix, not a native engine enum or universally defined faction system. observed row labels team id radar entry in alien/character column alien ai field preemptive attack counterattack 0 white working yes yes 1 red working yes yes 2 blue working yes no 3 hidden working no yes 4 hidden working yes yes 5 yellow not working no no 6 hidden working no yes these are readings of source labels, not independently repeated in a new exact-build test. the japanese table includes a separate 味方npc column with non-obvious yes/no values, for example team 1 (red, explicitly marked “enemy” elsewhere) is marked yes. that column's operational predicate is not established from its short heading alone. do not infer that the table marks red actors as friendly npcs or that the game universally maps team 2 to allied actors. the ant columns show different ai/hostility observations for several teams and have blank/dash cells; no entry should be filled in from the alien columns merely because the team id matches. the notebook questions the status of some ant behavior (“does not move?”). preserve those question marks. practical use in tools and scripts separate radar marker rendering from actual target selection, ai update enabled, attack authority, and alliance relation. never reconstruct a binary teammanager relation matrix from a seven-row test spreadsheet alone. match class, mode, exact build and native team callsites. a white bomber marker was suggested as a possible reason for missing laser guidance in the contributor's bombardment experiment, but team ownership was not experimentally isolated there. do not assume historical edf5/edf6 team values share edf4.1 native semantics. provenance source: mod製作メモ.xlsx, 解析!a1840:n1848. english labels here are editorial translations of the table. the raw workbook does not document a full engine-wide 0–6 enum contract. for separate exact edf6 native relation work see team-manager relation matrix.

acidbullet rgb: observed test patches and an unverified channel-weight hypothesis workbook observations the japanese workbook groups several acidbullet color experiments under 解析!a1851:..., including examples annotated rgb=2,2,2, rgb=1,1,2, rgb=1,1,3, rgb=1,2,2, rgb=1,2,3, rgb=1,2,5 and other sample triples (解析!a1885:fc1896). those examples originally used embedded screenshots; the public wiki does not redistribute the screenshots. the author reports that an input ratio r:g:b = 1:2:4 appeared to produce zero saturation and therefore proposes possible channel factors of r×4, g×2, b×1. this is a hypothesis derived from one family of visuals, not a measured shader constant or guaranteed linear light-space transformation. the workbook explicitly phrases it as “seems there are the following coefficients” (解析!a1887:b1890). why a global rgb multiplier would be unjustified many effects may vary in texture mask, material/shader family, hdr tonemap, fog, source-color space and per-particle state. a screenshot matching one neutral triplet cannot establish a universal color conversion for every acid projectile, let alone every edf material. in particular, no test here separates raw parameter handling from final display color. implementation guidance: preserve source rgb values, annotate the proposed coefficients as hypothesis, and test calibrated input/output values under a controlled build and effect before baking factors into a converter. a screenshot-based perceived hue is not a direct measurement of a floating-point register or texture sample. remaining questions is the effect's color field interpreted in linear or gamma-encoded space? does the hypothesized channel factor apply in the projectile code, the material/shader, or only the selected texture/effect? are the displayed examples measured at identical exposure and under the same color pipeline? source: mod製作メモ.xlsx, 解析!a1851:fc1896. no new image analysis or edf runtime measurement was performed; screenshot assets were intentionally excluded from public redistribution.

sentrygunbullet01: nested projectile experiments and missing child ammomodel data-backed sentry weapon families the workbook lists these sentry weapon ↔ child ammunition classes (解析!b2015:g2021): weapon sample direct child bullet class zer-gun, ze sniper, zera-gun solidbullet01 ze launcher rocketbullet01 ze blaster laserbullet01 fz-gun flamebullet02 the third table column indicates that an ammomodel entry was not necessary for those reported direct children. this is a tested-sample list, not a complete mapping of every possible sentry profile. reported limitation and workaround the author could not find a node within sentrygunbullet01's ammo_customparameter that specifies the child bullet's own ammomodel, which appeared to constrain sentry spawning a sentry. a proposed workaround is to have the sentry emit a different ammunition class capable of emitting subprojectiles itself: sentrygunbullet01 -> clusterbullet01 (reported to run without its own ammomodel) -> grenade-like child (reported successful test) the source states that clusterbullet01 worked without an ammomodel in the tested profile (pweapon230 example), and that a grenade child was demonstrated through this nested approach (解析!b2026:b2029). it also says “sentry from sentry is not possible” in that experiment (b2030); this must not be presented as a universal engine impossibility without a class/serialization audit. tooling boundaries sgo fields are class-specific; a child bullet model or custom-parameter block cannot always be inferred from the parent. successful nested grenade emission is not proof that arbitrary recursive sentrygunbullet01 trees are valid or safe. if a converter is asked to produce unsupported nested sentry behavior, it should fail visibly rather than silently dropping missing child resource references. separate projectile construction, actual firing, model instantiation and replicated/network publication when testing in multiplayer. source: mod製作メモ.xlsx, 解析!a2013:g2031. this article expands the earlier projectile/ammunition guide; original experiment reported by author, not rerun in this release.

e507 gold ufo ammunition records: observed fields and crash-sensitive unknowns two separately recorded profiles the japanese source contains a bullet_big_bomber_info pointer example for e507_goldufo_big.sgo (解析!a1665:a1690) and a longer bullet_info xml-like record for e507_goldufo_ace (解析!a2037:j2086). they must not be assumed to share a single identical parser or flat abi merely because their asset identifiers begin with e507. ace bullet_info record excerpt the source's comments identify only a subset of its positions: record index sample value source label / interpretation 0 integer 30 burst projectiles per attack, according to note 1 integer 1 fireinterval 2 integer 1 firecount 4 float 0.40000001 ammosize 5 float 30 bullet speed (弾速) 7 integer 15 ammoalive 13 float 0 changing this reportedly makes attacks aim above or below the target the nested ptr at index 6 contains additional integers/floats whose purpose is unknown. the author noted that one inner integer sample 8 (bullet_info[6][2][0] if the xml nesting is read literally) caused a crash as soon as the aircraft spawned when changed (解析!a2060:j2062). this is a critical negative experiment; do not treat the value as a safely tunable color/selector enum. the author also says that a nearby float is probably not ammocolor (j2052:j2054). implementation rules preserve unknown pointer nesting and indices when round-tripping sgo/xml; do not “normalize” it into a documented bullet class schema without evidence. a field annotated ammoalive does not automatically establish seconds, frames or lifetime tick units; preserve raw values until runtime measurement. unchanged native structs are the safe default for fields whose mutation is reported to crash on spawn. keep goldufo_big's bullet_big_bomber_info separate from goldufo_ace's bullet_info. they are different textual source excerpts. source: mod製作メモ.xlsx, 解析!a1665:a1690, a2037:j2086. the source includes uncertain annotations and reported experiments, not a full binary reverse engineering proof for these records. no original resource binary is redistributed.

edf 4.1 mapo component transforms: quaternion, translation and tint evidence scope: selected source mapo rows involved in r1d navigation reconstruction. evidence class: native source-data enumeration plus offline conversion experiments. this is not a universal format schema for every edf map. the three vector lanes the selected mapo rows expose several vector-like fields. their observed interpretations and confidence levels are different: source field current evidence what not to infer vec08 rotational component: 3,415 non-null selected rows; 3,415/3,415 unit-length within 1e-5, with pure y-axis xyzw quaternion form it is not an independent rigid-body selector vec0c component-relative position, varying within 1,675 repeated (placement,group) instances a repeated instance must not be silently collapsed to its first slot vec10 rgb/tint-like values: 11,918 non-null rows, fourth component always zero, rgb values within [0,1], none unit-length within 1e-5 it is not established as a collision transform the vec08 quaternion rotations, after q/-q normalization, form four observed values in the 3,415 non-null sample: y-axis rotation rows identity 1,327 +90 degrees 1,046 180 degrees 693 −90 degrees 349 the total is 3,415. 610 repeated (placement,group) instances vary in vec08. in a 1,675-instance repeated-row analysis, all 1,675 vary in vec0c, and 667 instances also vary in non-position vectors. of those 667, 114 had exact-zero mapb placement rotation. these distinctions matter: mapb placement rotation and mapo component rotation are separate fields. component transform versus rigid-body identity matching a component quaternion/translation to an arbitrary mad rigid body is not justified by the source evidence. in the selected corpus: 479 active r32 rigid bodies contain zero non-identity motionstate rotations. in the larger set of all selected-group bodies, 17 have non-identity body-motion rotations. among 11,988 selected referenced mapo slot/group pairs, 215 component-position vs body-motion-translation pairs match within 1e-5. only 5 match the full transform under the additional identity-quaternion requirement, all trivial zero-transform cases. edf5-derived underground missions: historical ui-hook and host-refresh diagnostics scope: a historical, source-scoped diagnostic sequence, not a recommended current patch. later direct runtime tests of custom m000, m001 and dm019 confirmed the native-like flags=40 restriction. read the current underground flag/runtime rule before applying any older hypothesis. why the first diagnosis was misleading the early mp03 m001 investigation observed air raider equipment restriction offline but apparent online permission, even with mission-list flags=40 (0x08 | 0x20). the initial interpretation treated red menu presentation and real weapon/support activation as if they had the same semantics; later in-game checks refuted that blanket conclusion. two independently plausible interference paths were examined. both remain useful diagnostic examples, not confirmed fixes for a newly observed issue. 1. global onlinelimitsdisabled ui setter the inspected mod patch replaced a shared native ui setter (the studied binary's mov byte ptr [rcx+0x71], dl; ret) with an unconditional 1 write. twenty-three call sites use that setter, including unrelated item, cursor, room, mission and difficulty controls. consequently, removing the disabled appearance for online armor/weapon-limit buttons could also re-enable unrelated ui states. a proposed narrower alternative targeted only the two identified room-setting calls for button_armorlimit and button_weaponlimit, without changing the common setter. its exact match positions were binary-build-specific (0x91c8bf and 0x91c9ab file offsets in the studied dll); these addresses are not portable across versions. that proposal had static pass / runtime pending status and was conditional on an a/b test proving this hook caused the actual symptom. rule: never modify a shared ui setter globally when only two specific room controls are intended, and never infer in-mission weapon authorization from a red/disabled equipment entry. 2. host-side mode refresh the compared source flow was: edf5 playmission_common: called applymodeno(new_mode_index) for host and client before setusedweapon. studied edf6 playmission_common: called applymodeno(sync.getnewmode()) inside !isgamehost(), relying on earlier lobby selection for the host. the r5 candidate made online call the common routine with a refresh flag and preserved the native client-only rule for offline. this was an intentionally isolated mainscript-only static pass / runtime pending candidate. the later r6 diagnostic explicitly labeled that r5 mainscript as runtime-negative for the symptom and proposed removing it after the a/b unless new evidence justified it. neither r5 nor the subsequent per-mission r7 setweaponcondition(no_support) experiment may be promoted to a mandatory authoring rule. what later evidence actually settled the actual in-mission support-request test, not loadout selection color, confirmed native-style flags=40 enforcement for m000, m001 and dm019 in the tested deployments. maintain the established metadata 0x20 path; do not globally rewrite it to 0x200, inject forced condition calls into all missions, or deploy an untested mainscript override based on the early symptom report. for a fresh regression, isolate variables: record the actual selected pack and mission, host/client and offline/online modes, deployed list flags, custom patch state, plus whether a conventional air raid/vehicle request succeeds in mission. distinguish a menu-only discrepancy from a state/write discrepancy before modifying game code. primary sources (retained diagnostics): /edf5_edf6_research/research/active/mission_meta/r6_online_underground_restriction/r6_online_underground_restriction_diagnostic.json .../r6_online_underground_restriction/r6b_narrow_online_limits_audit.json .../r6_online_host_mode_refresh/online_host_mode_refresh_audit_r5_2026-09-03.json .../r7_runtime_no_support/r7_m000_m001_no_support_audit.json evidence hierarchy: exact source/binary and historical static candidates, corrected by later scoped in-game runtime positives. historical candidate != current product requirement. mission identity is not only the visible loadout state see the complete underground map-reference census for the 15 source-derived mission ids, map uris and 30 final mode-specific list rows. a red equipment entry, flags=40 in a list file and a successful in-mission no-support check are separate pieces of evidence.

its msvc dll build and two-computer runtime qualification were not completed in the source record. do not treat a proposed hook or predicted event as an observed gameplay repair. first classify the traffic lane on-wire family retention/ownership in the audited shipping path what can still go wrong class 3, 0x3300 ordinary sceneobject movement mode1/non-retained; edf6 fire-sync: four controlled weapon discriminators edf6 can use direct subtype0 or deferred, receiver-reconstructed subtype1 for a weapon shot. the decisive variable is the evaluated runtime policy, not simply the weapon name or its base sgo. the following four-weapon matrix comes from exact binary inspection and correlated shipped-weapon star evaluation. it is a read-only test design, not a claim that the probe has passed on two live pcs. build scope: canonical edf6 edf.dll sha-256 0d5092393a1b9d8f1b75b0c93d8a8f65615a36a92c46e40349c2b66c733d0916. rvas must not be transplanted blindly to another game build. four high-value comparisons weapon / source asset static policy prediction why this case isolates a failure m2 raven — aweapon016.sgo always batched subtype1; sync_level=-1, bit4=1; solidbullet01, spread type 0 baseline for receiver-local projectile construction without random initial spread mr114 fang — aweapon108.sgo always direct subtype0, full sender transform (sync_level=1, bit4=0); spread type 0 control for direct sender transform authority penetrator f — aweapon104.sgo can be subtype1, direct sync0 or direct sync1 solely as correlated upgrade stars change strongest same-weapon three-state test of policy selection wide acid gun — aweapon194.sgo always subtype1 (sync_level=-1, bit4=1); acidbullet01, spread type 1 tests receiver-local random spread when the subtype1 packet lacks pre-spread seed restoration exact penetrator f star discriminators the source evaluation identified these three representative correlated star states (key = star slot index): star slots expected network path transform authority {0:0, 2:0, 4:0, 5:3} subtype1; sync -1, bit4 set deferred receiver-local {0:0, 2:0, 4:0, 5:0} direct subtype0; sync 0, bit4 clear sender orientation, receiver-local translation {0:0, 2:1, 4:0, 5:0} direct subtype0; sync 1, bit4 clear full sender transform these are derived source-config states, not a guarantee that a tester can select each exact combination with a standard in-game inventory ui. the relevant state must be established and read back before comparing traffic. read-only trace checkpoints the historical probe kit was built and statically checked but had runtime pending. its entry probes are observational: it was not designed to edit fields, packet bytes or scheduling. record at least: function rva event distinguishing observation 0x767150 policy synthesis weapon+0x153c flags, +0x1540 sync level, star-evaluated parameters 0x694910 direct sender bit4 early suppression vs actual subtype0 packet 0x695f20 batched sender +0x1544 target count, +0x154c delay, +0x1550 dirty state 0x690420 batched receiver accepted target and owner/proxy role 0x6947e0 deferred remote realization local count, target, cadence, count catch-up 0x698500 / 0x6969a0 shot selection/transform named-node transform provenance and selected muzzle/source entry optional short timing samples: soldierbase::onupdate 0x59abb0 and common weapon onupdate 0x6934f0. do not turn a short ordering comparison into a permanent per-frame logging load. the read-only probe instructions use f8 to arm and lock the next weapon event, f9 to reset/unlock and f10 to toggle a short soldier/weapon ordering sample. these are tool controls, not edf gameplay mechanics. expected interpretation m2 raven: direct-sender function may execute but should take the bit4 suppression path; eventual subtype1 tx and later remote count-based reconstruction are expected. mr114 fang: the direct packet should contain the full sender transform; ordinary shots should not follow the delayed subtype1 realization path. penetrator f: one source weapon should demonstrate all three effective policies if the exact source star states can be reproduced and logged. this is an explicit counterexample to a static “one weapon → one network policy” mapping. wide acid gun: a later cumulative count can repair the number of reconstructed shots without reconstructing the sender's original per-shot random spread. keep initial fire and later networkbullet selector0/1/2 records separate: sandlot can retransmit the latter while subtype1 initial creation still lacks historical rng/charge/class-internal state. a matching shot count, player orientation or ack does not establish full projectile equivalence. qualification boundary: the historical source documents static/linked/cold-extract probe qualification; no corresponding successful paired runtime trace is contained in the reviewed material. for the underlying formula, rng progression and individual projectile classes, see weapon rng and batched fire and star-dependent policy evaluation.

edf6 missionpack identification: native verification, modelist and online room dlc field an edf6 missionpack has several distinct identities. the selected numeric missionpack row, the native validation-name family, the network-room field named dlc, and license/entitlement checks are not interchangeable. the following facts come from a specific studied edf6 binary and historical custom-pack diagnostics, not from a universal rule across all builds. native membership and validation-name paths the retained binary study identified these build-relative entry points: studied native function edf.dll-relative address observed role missionpack membership/verification lookup +0xd92b0 resolves the native dlc/pack membership check missionpack validation-name mapper +0xe3f80 uses the missionpackname1 and missionpackname2 classes these offsets are build-specific. neither implies that every custom missionpack is natively licensed, or that the correct solution is a global dlc-check bypass. official mp01 and mp02 follow their native paths. historical compatibility extensions used odd/even missionpackname1/missionpackname2 classification for higher custom slots. that is an observed extension requirement, not evidence that the unmodified game natively supports arbitrary packs 03–99. why the room attribute dlc does not mean entitlement the native room-attribute table includes search_type, dlc, mission_no, difficulty, armor_limit and weapon_limit. in the studied path, the published dlc value is the selected modelist row's missionpack id. a room using custom mp03 therefore publishes dlc=3, even when the custom mission is not paid dlc. the corresponding room lookup compares the requested missionpack id and online mode type. no 0–2 clamp was found on this specific path. this proves only how that lobby-field path is interpreted; it does not prove successful two-peer joining or universal native custom-pack entitlement. resource path identity can precede active-mode identity during one mp06 custom-pack selection, the game requested /cri_bind/mission/missionlist_missionpack06.offline.list.sgo while missionmgr+0x14fd0 still read -1. a lookup using only the currently active manager slot therefore missed a resource whose exact request path already contained missionpack06. the resulting ui later tried to divide by an effective mission count of zero and raised 0xc0000094 at edf.dll+0xdd2a9 in that binary. see the full native failure case. reported two-pc incompatibility in a custom extension the contributor knowledge hub records a reported hf5.48 custom-missionbundle two-computer test in which peers loaded different missions/cutscenes. this is negative evidence for that specific extension and custom mission setup, not proof of a native vanilla edf6 lobby defect. a local successful offline or host-only launch cannot substitute for a successful remote-peer join and synchronized mission start. observed config modelist and cross-file reference fields in the studied edf5-port / edf6 custom-missionpack config schema, the static research identified: field observed interpretation 0 gamemode_offline/online_missionpacknn class identity 5 missionpacknn.mst save/progression namespace 6 companion list/localized txt/image references 8 offline 0, online 1 9 logical missionpack id, shared by offline/online pair 12 retained profile shape in official and custom rows; exact meaning is not asserted the generic config modelist loader read the runtime row count dynamically in the studied binary. this observation does not establish that arbitrary custom packs bypass license checks or that any pack number is universally supported. the network-room dlc field and the modelist pack id should be compared with actual list resource identity rather than inferred from a directory name. later tested custom-pack boundaries in september 2026 modded-game checks, mp03→mp07 and mp04→mp08 custom relocations reached an offline mission. mp08 progression was separate from mp04 and mp08 permitted creating an online host. a real second-peer join/start was not tested. an earlier mp07 black screen was traced to an incomplete ac-only fixture; it was not evidence of a numerical pack-id ceiling. these findings concern the tested extensions, not stock edf6. what cannot be inferred a game lobby field called dlc is not sufficient evidence of paid ownership. a valid on-disk list is not sufficient evidence that the selected runtime modelist references it. an online host creation result does not establish a remote-peer join. one extension's parity rules do not automatically describe stock edf6. source boundary: the native offsets and room-field relationship were audited statically for the retained binary. the custom-slot workaround and later mp07 result belong to separate historical modded runtime tests, not a new validation performed for this wiki. native manager versus network-room identity — deeper detail the studied native findoutermode(manager, modetype, missionpack) lookup uses the selected modelist row's +0x74 missionpack and +0x80 mode-type fields and returns an outer mode index. this is distinct from the room attribute named dlc and the currently committed pack stored at manager +0x14fd0. for the exact build-specific offsets and call chain, see native mode selection and package memory and async response pack publication.

edf6 missionmgr mode transitions: config loading, lobby state and save risks edf6 distinguishes loading mission-mode metadata from changing the active game mode. in a studied custom-pack runtime, invoking an extra high-level missionmgr::setmode from a callback not used by vanilla triggered a destructive save/progression regression affecting armor and collected weapons. that historical negative result demonstrates why these operations must not be treated as harmless substitutes. config and the native mode loader the studied game path loads its base config first and uses missionmgr::loadconfig for modelist source loading. additional custom modelist rows were demonstrated through this existing lifecycle in a later historical candidate, rather than constructing private missionmgr objects or replacing the loader's internal tables by hand. the native behavior of the stock game is a distinct question from the behavior of an extended config-less custom-pack loader. the latter is not evidence that base edf6 distributes arbitrary custom missionpack rows or that direct reallocation of native mode tables is safe. setmode is a state transition, not a harmless setter a withdrawn experiment injected an additional high-level missionmgr::setmode call in the custom-pack callback. on a real game run it produced a regression to saved armor/weapon progression. a later narrower interception of the script-wrapper transition avoided inventing a second native setmode call, but this must be understood as an extension-specific repair. the reusable native lesson is to preserve call counts and transition ownership when tracing this path. online room state is asynchronous historical tracing separated room change into request, response and commit stages. a menu selection or pending custom-pack request is not proof the room's committed missionpack or public/private family has changed. the room's creation family and subsequent committed selections can matter to policy decisions. for diagnosis, compare the requested missionpack, selected modelist row, committed room attributes, and actual loaded list before changing save/progression state. the precise request/commit details may differ across game builds and third-party extensions. evidence limit the reported save regression is a direct historical runtime negative for one candidate, not a claim that unmodified vanilla edf6 spontaneously loses progress. the later config-less loader branch was a separate qualification path; no new run was performed for this article. reconstructed entry-point distinctions the retained native-code study separated loadconfig at edf+0xda8e0, mode selection/transition at +0xdc460, and loadpackage at +0xe2ad0 for one specific edf6 dll. the loadpackage path materialized active package state at manager +0x130; that object included a std::wstring-style save/mst namespace at package +0x68. the response callback at +0x8ed9dd could later republish the selected missionpack at manager +0x14fd0. these are different transitions, not synonyms for a write to a single mode number. read the full native mode/package layout and asynchronous lobby publication for the verified evidence boundaries.

edf6 native winmm imports and startup call-path observations a bounded static audit of one edf6 binary set inspected imports of the windows multimedia library (winmm) to determine where the game itself depends on the api. studied binary direct winmm imports found edf6.exe none edf.dll waveingetnumdevs, waveoutgetnumdevs launchgame.exe none umbra_sandlot.dll none for this exact set, the audited edf.dll entrypoint/attach path did not directly call either imported winmm function. their examined normal call sites lay outside the entrypoint path. the result is not a universal guarantee about startup timing: transitive dependencies, os loader behavior, different builds and third-party dlls were not exhaustively covered. it also says nothing about whether a particular injected mod loader succeeds. this page records the bounded first-party game-binary fact only.

edf6 weapontable.p8: loot classes versus missionpack identifiers edf6 weapon drop classification does not use custom mission-pack numbers as the loot-class values. in the retained binary/mission compatibility research, weapontable.p8 used three native loot classes: p8 loot class observed native role 0 base-game weapon drop class 1 dlc1 weapon drop class 2 dlc2 weapon drop class for the tested edf5 content hosted in custom edf6 mission packs, the required correspondence was: custom content pack loot class missionpack03 (base edf5 content) 0 missionpack04 (edf5 dlc1 content) 1 missionpack05 (edf5 dlc2 content) 2 the pack identifier (03/04/05) and native class (0/1/2) serve different roles. the native loot class is not necessarily inferable by truncating the pack number, and this translation is not a general rule for arbitrary missionpacks. observed in-game discriminator the retained modded-game mp05/dlc2 test admitted p8=2 weapon rows at the expected late-game progression levels. that test supported the class translation for the tested installation, not the behavior of every stock/modified edf6 build or a global mission-pack namespace policy. when this distinction matters a mission can compile, reach the first frame, spawn enemies and award boxes while producing the wrong weapon family. diagnosing that case requires separating: the active game's logical mission/content pack; its associated native weapontable.p8 loot class; the weapon level/progression conditions of the mission; any modded loader's custom mapping, which is not equivalent to stock behavior. for missionpack list/config lookup and save identity, see native missionpack id semantics. for resource table parity, see missionpack list/txt/image evidence. native candidate filter and observed dlc2 rewards in the examined edf6 binary, weapontable.p8=0 passes the class check for any evaluated pack. nonzero values must match the active logical pack id in the original candidate path; the class gate precedes the level-range gate. as a result, a dlc1-class pool can include p8=0 and p8=1, while dlc2-class pools can include p8=0 and p8=2. the additional dlc rows are not automatically available merely because a mission's reward level overlaps their levels. an instrumented modified edf6 runtime running a custom mp09 test explicitly mapped to dlc2 class 2 recorded 110 p8=2 candidates, 34 newly admitted rows and two actual lv 107 air raider rewards: n9 eros vulture zam and gigantocopter 3 delta. the source acceptance report does not demonstrate a lv 110+ drop or native unmodified mp09 dlc2 behavior. for the exact binary path, p5/p8 decoded offsets and evidence distinctions see p8 candidate filtering and runtime test.

edf6 native mode lookup, missionmgr state and active package this reference separates three different native operations in a studied edf6 executable: loading the game-mode definitions, choosing an active mode, and materializing the package that supplies mission/character/weapon resources. treating these as one interchangeable setter is unsafe, particularly in reverse-engineered compatibility work. binary/build scope the specific edf.dll used for this study had sha-256 0d5092393a1b9d8f1b75b0c93d8a8f65615a36a92c46e40349c2b66c733d0916, image timestamp 0x678ccb46, and pe sizeofimage=0x022ce000. all addresses below are offsets relative to this edf.dll image, not portable signatures, game-version-independent api declarations or absolute addresses. two research names, missionmgr and gamedatamgr, are sometimes applied to the same central manager. this article therefore uses the neutral term manager where the exact rtti class name is not independently proven. native entry points and state image-relative entry point observed purpose evidence classification edf+0xda8e0 loadconfig-style loading/registration of a config.sgo source and its modelist entries static call-flow reconstruction edf+0xdbd00 findoutermode(manager, modetype, missionpack); looks up the outer-mode index static signature/caller analysis edf+0xdc460 mode transition (setgamemode / setmode in the research notes) static disassembly plus negative modded-runtime evidence for misuse edf+0xe2ad0 loadpackage-style materialization of the active package for the selected mode static call-chain reconstruction edf+0x20b2890 global manager-pointer reference static binary reference the manager also stores the active physical missionpack at manager+0x14fd0. this is not the outer-mode index and may be republished by a later response callback; see the separate lobby-lifecycle article. these names are semantic labels inferred from the investigated native code, not claimed exported sdk symbols. lookup layout — source-backed offsets findoutermode was reconstructed with the following logical signature: int findoutermode(manager* manager, int modetype, int missionpack); its observed traversal is: read the outer collection from manager+0x20 and its count from manager+0x30. for each outer item, follow its +0x10 modelist-like pointer. read the selected row offset/index from that modelist-like object at +0x08. compare the selected row's missionpack at +0x74 and mode type at +0x80 against the requested pair. return the matching outer index, or -1 when there is no match. the native direct-call census for the lookup named four call sites: edf+0x70e704, +0x70e74c, +0x8efef1, and +0x954333. this is a build-local call census, not a promise that indirect calls or later builds cannot introduce other paths. the outer index returned by this function, the missionpack numeric id stored in a selected record, and the active physical missionpack are distinct fields. a value read from one cannot be substituted for another without a lookup. active-mode transition the native transition at edf+0xdc460 expects rcx=manager and edx=requested outer-mode index at the observed entry point. in the examined control flow it selects the outer record and invokes the package-building path at edf+0xe2ad0 (call observed around +0xdc4b3). later, it publishes the selected outer index to manager+0x38 (around +0xdc4c5) and emits an event identified as 0xe in the retained reconstruction. the direct native call-site census for this transition found +0xac21a, +0xd6722, +0xdb6bf and +0x70fac9 in the audited .text. a function that changes the active mode is consequently not equivalent to setting a menu selection integer or appending an extra modelist row. active package and mission/save resources the loadpackage path materializes the active package at manager +0x130. the following child fields were identified in the studied layout: active package field supported interpretation +0x20 soldierinit-related node +0x28 weapon-category/map-related data +0x68 msvc std::wstring-style package / missionpack mst namespace +0xf0 dsgo/node reference to the mission table this explains why a valid modelist row alone is not sufficient to establish a playable/complete game mode: later package materialization can still require related packagename, soldierinit, soldierweaponcategory, config files. for the on-disk mst layout and class difficulty bits, see gst/mst save and progress tables. for the cross-file list/txt/image requirements, see edf5-derived missionpack metadata. why armor and collected weapons reset, and the damaged state was written on game exit. later analysis found the high-level call also enters loadpackage and rebuilds the active package. the exact edf6 asynchronous missionpack publication and hui room-state lifecycle an edf6 online room can contain three different representations of a selected mission pack: the local ui/modelist selection, the request sent through the room-mode change path, and the pack committed back to the central manager after a response. these do not necessarily update simultaneously. this distinction was recovered while investigating custom pack selection in a studied edf6 build. the native call and field observations below are distinct from the room restrictions created by third-party extensions: nothing here proves that stock edf6 imposes the exact same modded-room family rules. build-specific state references the binary examined in the retained analysis is the same edf.dll documented in native modelist and package memory. the global manager pointer was referenced through edf+0x20b2890; its active physical missionpack field was at manager+0x14fd0. an audited response callback near edf+0x8ed980 contained this sequence (image-relative instruction addresses): 0x8ed9c3 mov r8, [manager_global] 0x8ed9ce mov rdx, [r8+0x148] 0x8ed9d5 movsxd rcx, dword [rdx+0x8] 0x8ed9d9 mov edx, [rdx+rcx+0x74] 0x8ed9dd mov [r8+0x14fd0], edx the instructions use the selected row of a modelist-like object to republish the active pack id later in the request/response lifecycle. consequently, observing the earlier menu/request value or filtering one earlier store is not sufficient proof of the final active missionpack. the source study enumerated nine direct stores to the active pack field in that binary: +0x708a06 +0x70c331 +0x791567 +0x8ed9dd +0x90090a +0x904b65 +0x91aa62 +0x925a32 +0x925cf7 the nine addresses are a direct-store census for that build; they should not be presented as nine separate online room transitions, and no undocumented meaning is assigned to an individual store here. distinguishing the stages stage typical evidence to inspect what that evidence does not establish requested mode ui selection, request arguments, selected outer-mode index that the server/room has accepted the change selected modelist row row fields including mode type (+0x80) and missionpack (+0x74) that the manager's active pack and the loaded mission resources match async response the response callback and currently selected row that an earlier local state filter remains authoritative committed pack manager's +0x14fd0 after response processing that the resource pathname, mission count, package and save namespace are consistent resolved content actual missionlist_missionpacknn... request, mission table and package that remote peers selected identical content or that progression is safe for an independently observed resource-request-first failure in mp06, see missionpack identity and mission count. in that case the requested missionlist_missionpack06.offline.list.sgo pathname already identified the content while the manager's active pack field was still -1. native room/ui object lifetime is not room lifetime a huiroom destructor-like wrapper was located around edf+0x8f7510; it calls code around +0x8f5950, which installs the examined huiroom vtable (0x18180ac40) and operates on an object of size 0xca0. these data support a class identity and destructor-like operation. they do not show that destroying or rebuilding a huiroom ui object always means an online room was closed. the ui may outlive or be recreated independently of a lobby session. other researched lifecycle seams were room exit near edf+0x9049be and roomcreate_join near +0x8e69a0. their applicability as room-ownership reset points was established in a specific extension analysis; they should not be treated as general-purpose stock api functions without checking their native callsites. ui visibility and room-publication presentation in the same source study a native huiroom synchronous refresh function occupied edf+0x902b30..0x90315d. its public-visibility code lay near +0x902f8b; the researcher identified a direct caller at +0x8ffe67. this explains how a ui presentation event could lag behind an already-normalized visibility state in the tested extension. it does not establish a stock edf6 warning-message policy for custom content. a separate native room attribute named dlc was observed to carry the selected modelist's missionpack id, not a generic boolean 'user owns dlc' flag. that field is therefore useful for comparing published room state to local selection, while license/entitlement checks remain separate. see native missionpack room identity. diagnostic reading order when an offline mission appears but online room selection behaves differently, determine which value diverges before attributing the failure to packet transport: source row — does the intended modelist row exist and have the expected missionpack and type? request — is the selected mode/pack being requested, or is the previous value still being sent? response commit — was a later callback allowed to republish a different active pack? resource identity — does the subsequent list/config/package selection use the same pack? remote peer — has a real second participant joined and loaded the same mission, rather than merely observing that a host lobby can be created? evidence boundary: the native field addresses and assembly come from build-specific static analysis. the public/private room safeguards, warning timing and save-loss incidents used to discover these paths occurred in a modified runtime. they are not asserted to be native policies or bugs of unmodified edf6. there is no new multiplayer capture or in-game validation in this wiki release.

edf5 → edf6 mission numeric globals: ten identified scalar type mismatches what fails: edf5 source mission.bvm distinguishes floating-point scalars from integer counters. in an earlier edf5→edf6 mission.ac reconstruction, some global variables holding fractional values were declared int (or remained ambiguous object during inference). a fractional 0.8 or 0.9 then became integer 0 before being passed to allied-unit, enemy or generator scale parameters. this is a gameplay-visible type error, not a mere formatting difference. source and evidence boundary an independently regenerated 141/141-source-mission census compared the reconstructed edf5 bvm semantics against the effective early compatibility corpus. exactly 10 missions had global scalar declarations that needed float rather than int. the source reconstruction and static syntax checks passed; this was not a ten-mission in-game acceptance sweep. later conversion builds may differ from this particular early baseline. the inferred target types were: assignments containing only integer-valued numeric literals: int. numeric-only assignment sets containing at least one fractional (., f, exponent) literal: float. assignments with nonnumeric/object-like values: remain object until a better semantic type is proven. the prior heuristic incorrectly handled mixed branches such as 1 and 0.8f. a variable can be declared incorrectly even when its current path happens to use 1.0f; distinguish type drift from a proven visible symptom. complete ten-mission global census original mission (port pack) display number incorrect global declaration source-meaningful effect and limitation m026 (mp03) 29 friend_level 1.0 on lower difficulties; 0.8 on hardest/inferno. a wrong int yields 0 before createfriend/createfriendsquad on the latter difficulties m042_5 (mp03) 57 friend_level 0.9 below hardest and 0.8 above; wrong int yields 0 on every difficulty dm003_3 (mp04 / dlc1) dlc1 #13 friend_level 0.8 fed to multiple createfriendsquad calls; wrong int yields 0 dm023 (mp05 / dlc2) dlc2 #11 friend_level, enemy_level, enemy_dur allied level falls from 1.0 to 0.9/0.8 on higher difficulties; integer truncation can explain empty hp bars, ineffective healing and near-immediate allied deaths. enemy level/durability typing also differs m017 (mp03) — friend_base_level source type is float, but the observed path uses 1.0; no fractional truncation symptom inferred m039 (mp03) 89 begaruta_level, tank_level, soldier_level source has fractional allied levels, but the earlier r7 global audit saw values overwritten by 1.0 before use; do not attribute a specific hp failure to these globals on r7 evidence alone m065 (mp03) 68 generator_level fractional generator scale may truncate; this is an enemy/generator configuration case, not directly an allied hp bar issue m069 (mp03) 92 ufo_level fractional ufo scale may truncate; enemy scaling case dm009 (mp05 / dlc2) — g_generator_level observed source literal about 0.6 truncated to 0 in the affected ac dm012 (mp05 / dlc2) — g_level observed source literal about 0.4 truncated to 0 in the affected ac important separate m039 finding: a later, broader direct bvm→ac review found two int local variables forwarding fractional allied scales to nine npc construction calls in the then-current 1.0.6 corpus. that is a different, later and stronger value-flow finding from the earlier global-variable audit. the r7 statement about globally declared m039 variables must not negate the later local-variable finding. see the 141-mission direct value-flow review. why dm023 matters in the source-derived dm023 branches, the level multiplier is a real value: about 1.0 at lower levels of difficulty, 0.9 on hardest and 0.8 on inferno. when a variable carrying that multiplier is forced into an int, the caller may receive 0 instead of a fractional scale. a character may then appear to have no normal health budget even though the spawn succeeds. the enemy-level 1.2 on inferno was also mistyped in an earlier branch. a mission reaching gameplay is not proof of correct difficulty scaling. scripting implications treat float/int parity as end-to-end value flow: declaration → assignment under each difficulty → temporary locals → argument type at createfriend/createfriendsquad or generator construction. count-based script audits will miss a numeric-value error when the same api calls are present on both sides. the later backward-layout switch audit is complementary: even correct floats cannot rescue a difficulty switch reconstructed into if(0 == 3) constant comparisons. the ten-name declaration-only repair was validated as a minimal syntactic change in the historical compatibility corpus (10/10), but does not establish current retail edf6 behavior or end-to-end mission parity. for the distinct switch/branch issue see difficulty-switch reconstruction. source provenance primary record:
