layer-names-update. see also area damage versus direct bullets. attribution: edf knowledge hub / novae (ajane) and original community contributors credited in that appendix, snapshot 54f89cd (2026-11-14). native game reference guides edf6 supportable moving-body collision layers

edf5 versus edf6 physics: havok body models, world rules and motion limits evidence: exact binary-level inspection reported by the edf knowledge hub (edf5 steam-5d11de53, edf6 steam-678ccb46, 2026-11-14 snapshot) plus existing native mad/shkt research. this page compares observed game behavior and memory structures, not sdk headers. no new physics runtime trial was performed. a real engine transition, not just a file extension change feature edf5 inspected engine edf6 inspected engine havok family older hkp rigid-body architecture; reported version string hk_2015.1.0-r1 havok 2020-era hknp bodies and world per-body main object hkpentity with embedded motion; 0x2c0-byte wrapper in the audited class xgs::havok::body wrapper 0x110 bytes plus separate hknpbody 0xb0 bytes motion representation hkpmotion embedded at body+0x150 in the studied instance hknpmotion 0x80 bytes, with ids into a shared hknpmotionproperties library material/shape data older hkp layout hknp shapes, materials and collision filters requiring re-encoding this is why a model with a correct visible mesh can still have nonfunctional collision when its shkt/mad data are migrated incorrectly. renaming a havok class or editing a version string is not a valid conversion. edf5: measured world and body characteristics gravity in the analyzed world constructor: (0, −14.7, 0). world broadphase aabb: approximately −1000 m to +1000 m; border behavior do_nothing rather than automatic body removal. a native game tick is reported at 60 updates per second for the inspected game logic. the original body stores linear and angular damping as half-precision values and velocity limits as hkufloat8 bytes at motion offsets +0xca/+0xcb. in a crate example, the recorded 60 m/s nominal linear limit encodes to approximately 57.4 m/s. an attempted 80 m/s launch can be clipped by the physics solver. these are edf5 source measurements. it would be incorrect to copy its gravity and speed-limit numbers into an edf6 physics specification without examining the edf6 world independently. edf6: motion-properties library, not arbitrary per-body floats the recovered hknpmotionproperties entries are 0x70 bytes in the studied live library; a separate 104-byte serialized motion-properties record is documented for the compatible mad file profile. these should not be conflated as if they were the same structure or storage location. the default runtime library contains five named presets: static, dynamic, keyframed, frozen and debris. observed properties include: preset measured property dynamic max linear speed 200, max angular speed 100, gravity factor 1 keyframed gravity factor 0 debris max linear speed 100, angular speed 10, linear/angular damping 0.01 / 0.5 all default entries time factor 1.0 the source's runtime field offsets within a motion-properties entry include gravity factor at +0x08, time factor at +0x0c, max linear/angular speed at +0x10/+0x14, and linear/angular damping at +0x18/+0x1c. these addresses are build/structure-specific, not a universal external file format. a body can be assigned a different properties-library entry, but the analysis warns that a shared motion can make a nominally “per-body” change affect more than expected. a method being registered does not prove it is used by the original game. body lifecycle and gameplay contact are separate edf6 has distinct object-body paths: many vehicles retain a ragdoll component, eventanimationobject has its own ragdoll, buildings and breakable map objects keep their own body ownership, and visual modeldebris can use a layer that ordinary bullets never hit. the native game also exposes contact-signal callbacks for map objects and helicopter landing interactions. do not assume every collision or falling body produces character hp damage. the source analysis found no general native fall-damage rule in the investigated walking/cling paths, while contact handling of map props has its own ownership and event semantics. this is a scoped finding, not a proof that no conceivable script can damage an object on impact. the practical cross-generation rule when comparing edf5 and edf6 collision: confirm the game-owned body shape and world membership separately from the rendered model. distinguish source hkp collision filters from target hknp filters and target motion-properties ids. keep runtime memory offsets apart from file serializer offsets. interpret speed caps and gravity against the correct game's native world, not an inherited constant. test contact, damage and animation lifecycle separately from whether a body appears in the havok world. original evidence edf5 — physics havok: havok-world-cinfo, crate-body-limits-stored, hkufloat8-decode, crate-speed-clip, related world/body notes. edf6 — havok runtime: motion-properties-library, body-wrapper-functions, object-body-places, hknp-contact-signals, no-native-impact-damage-2. mad/shkt cross-version collision contract. attribution: novae (ajane), edf knowledge hub revision 54f89cd, and original community contributors identified in its per-fact annotations. runtime behavior not remeasured for this page.

vehicle boarding across edf4.1, edf5 and edf6: seat masks and ownership evidence: native vehiclebase/soldier analysis in the edf knowledge hub, with build-scoped observations for edf4.1 (steam-57aab039), edf5 (steam-5d11de53) and edf6 (steam-678ccb46). this is a comparative game-mechanics reference, not a guide to any custom vehicle plugin. the same sgo concepts do not imply identical runtime structures all three games recognize source concepts such as vehicle_riding_position, vehicle_weapon_setting, animation_model, ragdoll and vehicle_damage_effect. however, the in-memory structures and native seat authorization changed: observed detail edf4.1 edf5 edf6 seat record stride 0x180 bytes 0x340 bytes 0x340 bytes seat table within vehiclebase data/count at +0x328/+0x338 data/count at +0x418/+0x428 seats at +0x608; count +0x618 boarding class gate human.vehicle_mask & seat.mask richer seat authorization (source also compares player class/team) human+0x31c & seat+0x34 & seat+0x30 != 0 team test in seat eligibility absent from the examined edf4.1 canride present in the native seat authorization family present; includes the special team-5 and bit-7 rule ai vehicle rider dummyvehiclerider in identified creation paths dummyvehiclerider-based path includes native rideai/vehicle-specific behavior these are memory-layout observations, not offsets to use indiscriminately in a different game version. edf4.1: a comparatively simple class-mask and distance test canride checks that the human's game_object_vehicle_mask intersects the seat mask, that the seat has no rider, and that the human is close enough to the mab-derived riding point. in the examined build the point-radius threshold includes an additional 0.5. unlike edf5/6, this particular canride path has no team gate and no second seat mask. a separate findseat route chooses the first eligible seat and updates a per-seat change-bit field. the vehicle's team may follow the highest-numbered live occupied rider in the audited update loop. this is relevant to native ai/vehicle relation changes, not evidence of a universal player-vehicle command system. edf6: masks are class identities, not seat numbers the inspected edf6 game_object_vehicle_mask values use one bit for each infantry class: class source mask bit ranger 1 wing diver 2 fencer 4 air raider 8 a seat is eligible only if the intersection of all three masks is nonzero (human class mask, seat class mask and seat access mask). occupancy is checked through the native weak rider control. vehicles in team 5 have a special eligibility path; for a different team, an additional seat bit-7 permission can apply. the precise checks are in the source appendix; the team relationship is not equivalent to a bare “vehicle friendly/hostile” bool. the edf6 vehicle stores the rider at seat+0x260. seat change bits are separate from occupancy and allow the native code to select boarding versus leaving sounds; hearing a boarding sound on a non-boarding action may therefore indicate a stale or misapplied seat-change state rather than an audio resource problem. displayed seat name and rider animation are different resources in the audited edf6 seat configuration, vehicle_riding_position[i][3] is a text-table key such as “pilot seat” or “machine gun - left”. it is not the animation name. the rider's visual pose is selected using the seat locator's mab parameters (animation, dispcharacter) and the rider's cas animation state. this distinction matters when an imported vehicle shows the right seat label but the wrong character pose, or plays a boarding sound despite no actual rider transition. network ride events are distinct from physics ownership edf4.1 has explicit online vehicle ride/leave events with a seat index and sequence/counter; edf5 likewise has online ride events. edf6 retains event-driven ride state with its own native fields. a visible vehicle in the scene does not prove that a remote player has the same seat assignment or weapon-input authority. cross-generation multiplayer parity therefore requires a seat-event and entity-owner check, not just geometry. source and limitations edf4.1 native vehicle observations: edf41-vehiclebase-ctor-keys, edf41-boarding-checks, edf41-ride-net-events. edf5 native vehicle observations: edf5-vehiclebase-ctor-keys, edf5-boarding-checks and ride events. edf6 native vehicle observations: boarding-checks, seat-class-masks, seat-name-rider-pose, vehicle-seat-change-bits. edf4.1 vehicles ported into edf6: separate class contracts. attribution: novae (ajane), edf knowledge hub (2026-11-14, revision 54f89cd) and original per-fact third-party contributors. no new online or vehicle runtime test is claimed. related native edf6 networking systems online vehicle delivery and registration additional native edf6 mechanics references gear, fuel and recoil data in edf6

edf5 and edf6 radar: rendering scale, team colors and player slots evidence: build-specific native hud research in the edf knowledge hub (edf5 steam-5d11de53, edf6 steam-678ccb46, snapshot 2026-11-14). this article separates the game's observed drawing logic from third-party changes to hud palettes. no new runtime validation was performed. edf5 world position → radar position the studied edf5 huihudrader stores these defaults: field native value interpreted function position scale 0.6 multiplies planar displacement from the player before drawing marker-size scale 1.2 normal dot/icon size multiplier world-distance limit 200 m planar range comparison and rim clamp nominal resulting rim radius 120 radar units 200 × 0.6; not a claim that all modes share the same hud pixel dimension the native position helper rotates relative positions with the player's heading. it returns planar x/y, a separate relative-height quantity, and an inside-range flag. a point outside 200 m is clamped to the rim rather than simply disappearing in the examined helper. height is calculated separately and clamped to approximately ±80 in the source rule. edf5 reads these sprite resources from app:/effect/hud.rab: radar_item.dds, hudraderpoint.dds, hudraderarea.dds. hud layout is app:/ui/lyt_hudrader01.sgo. sprite identity and position conversion are different components. edf5 team colors and drawing order the native dispatcher creates per-category lists and renders them in an observed order: team 4, item crates, team 2, hostiles, team 5, teammate icons, team-0 entities, mission points and area circles. because the source pathway has no depth test for these markers, later categories may visually cover earlier ones. the examined native palette includes red hostiles, green crates, cyan team 2 and yellow team 5; teams 0/4 have white entries. the color associated with one game team is not necessarily a unique player slot color. edf6 hud colors are a different table edf6 has a set of native rgba float constants for neutral, allied, item, enemy and vehicle categories. the community's patch research found the color table and the item-class loop, but the colors written by those patches are custom choices, not evidence of edf6's original defaults. the edf6 player-icon path selects from four player-id entries, independent of the player's soldier class: player id in the studied icon path native icon rgba 0 yellow (1,1,0,1) 1 green (0,1,0,1) 2 blue (0,0,1,1) 3 red (1,0,0,1) the class can affect the icon's rotation/shape path, but color selection is by id. it is not proven that ids always equal lobby list order or that the host always occupies a specific id. edf6 distinguishes item categories in the hud loop: category 0 weapon, 1 armor, 2/3 health. the exact native drawing and optional per-category color override belong to separate stages. what the radar cannot tell you alone a changed dot color does not establish a changed game-object team relation, and a radar bearing does not guarantee ai line of sight. hud projection, teammanager relations, physics collision and target visibility use different source systems. do not merge their ownership logic simply because all can refer to the same object. sources edf5 radar source appendix: radar-hud-class, radar-scales, radar-dispatcher, radar-position-helper, radar-colors. edf6 radar source appendix: radar-color-constants, radar-item-loop, radar-player-slot-colors. edf6 team relation matrix. attribution: novae (ajane), edf knowledge hub revision 54f89cd, kittopiacreator and other cited contributors where noted in the original appendix. static and reported game tests are not conflated.

edf5 and edf6 native camera: fov, zoom, ride locators and clipping evidence: source-attributed reverse engineering and contributor-reported experiments from edf knowledge hub (snapshot 14 november 2026). offset and routine names belong to the named builds; the wiki has not independently repeated every disassembly or executed new gameplay tests. vertical field of view and native projection both games use the characterghostcamera / scenecamera family. the base vertical fov is approximately π/4 radians (45°). in the examined edf6 build (steam-678ccb46), a normal scope update computes: live_vertical_fov = (π/4) / camera_zoom the calculation in characterghostcamera::update f86a0 writes camera +0x24 from camera+0x410 (f890e–f8916). therefore, for zoom 1×, 2× and 4×, the mathematical camera values are approximately 45°, 22.5° and 11.25°. these are fov values, not a claim about the actual number of zoom settings of every weapon. a separate state transition may blend fov; observed mode-dependent behavior must not be flattened into a universal one-line rule. the edf6 projection builder 118d9f0 uses: edf6 camera member meaning evidence +0x20 reference/base vertical fov static +0x24 live vertical fov, radians static +0x28 near plane, normally 0.1 m static constructor +0x2c far plane static; scene farclipz varies +0x198 / +0x19c width/height used for aspect in the projection path static; exact ownership of dimensions inferred +0x410 current target-derived zoom in ordinary follow update static edf5 steam-5d11de53 uses the same +0x24/+0x28/+0x2c scenecamera projection fields, with the examined constructor values fov ≈ 0.785, near 0.1 and far 1000. the surviving field locations do not imply that entire camera class layouts are interchangeable between games. the final camera matrix is at +0x1a0…+0x1d0 in the studied edf5 build but +0x220…+0x250 in edf6. zoom reaches the camera through the weapon and soldier edf6's weapon resource fields secondaryfire_type and secondaryfire_parameter are loaded into weapon state. a supported scope toggle changes a per-weapon zoom value from 1.0 to the configured magnification and back. soldier update collects the maximum active weapon zoom into human+0x1d0; the camera's target/look block then supplies camera+0x410. this chain explains why weapon zoom is not a blanket camera setting shared by every vehicle or seat. in the examined edf6 code, the ride input path is distinct from infantry aim input, and the investigators did not find a seat/vehicle writer of the scope-toggle input bit in the inspected range. some vehicle weapon sgo resources contain a secondaryfire_type value, but that alone does not demonstrate a functioning native vehicular scope toggle. the native ride state also does not simply repeat every follow-state fov update. zoom, view-distance scaling and culling edf6's projection / far-view code uses a zoom-related view-distance ratio of the form: distance_ratio = tan(live_fov / 2) / tan(reference_fov / 2) the reported routine 118dcd0 computes this ratio and view-submission paths 1197f31 / 1197fbd pass it to later distance tests. a zoomed image and the range at which models are submitted are therefore related in the examined renderer. do not treat a fov-only modification as proof that every form of object culling and far drawing remains unchanged. the exact view variants and special byte-state paths still matter. native vehicle ride camera and model-authored locators edf6's ride camera uses vehicle_riding_position and locator records in the vehicle animation model (mab). its seat constructor can record an eye locator, a look-target locator, parent bones, easing parameters and xangleadjust. the frame's camera view is constructed from these locations and the current vehicle bone transforms. the relevant examined seat fields include: seat field native interpretation +0x200 ride camera type; 0 for missing specialized mode +0x208/+0x210 eye locator and parent bone +0x218/+0x220 look-target locator and parent bone +0x228 camera easing parameters +0x230 pitch adjustment factor xangleadjust, default 1.0 selected values reported from vehicle mab game assets (positions are local to the relevant parent bone, not global scene coordinates): vehicle eye offset (x, y, z) look offset (x, y, z) eye easing xangleadjust blacker 403 (0, 1.65, −7.05) (0, 1.55, 0.3) 0.05 0.9 titan 404 (0, 6.3, −40.45) (0, 2.7, 1.25) 0.025 0.5 naegling 402 (0, 3.45, −9.52) (0, 1.85, 2.08) 0.025 1.0 begaruta / nix (0, 4.21, −12.74) (0, 2, 0) 0.1 not stated proteus (0, 5, −23) (0, −0.65, 5.95) 0.01 not stated this explains the reported behavior where raising the gun can move a gun-bone-attached eye behind a vehicle component and allow the hull to obstruct the view. it is a model/seat/animation interaction, not evidence that edf6 supports a universal hardcoded first-person optical sight. camera collision and obstruction the edf6 ride camera routine identified as f6760 uses collision queries between the desired look point, final look point and camera eye. a hit can move a point to the contact point plus the contact normal multiplied by the current camera offset (reported as 0.1 m for one initialization). the edf5 follow-camera investigation separately reported havok shape sweeps used to bring the eye closer to the character when a building obstructs it. camera collision, projectile collision and enemy ai line-of-sight are not the same test. an obstructed vehicle camera does not prove that the vehicle's gun or ai is blocked by the same surface. reported frame/input behavior one contributor's edf6 offline gameplay test observed uneven mouse-look steps despite even frame pacing: the right stick produced equal angular steps at the tested deflection, while mouse yaw changes were quantized to cursor pixels and intermittently larger. that is a specific observed run and input configuration, not a universal performance diagnosis. it does not establish which internal stage caused the irregular steps. scope and sources native code/fields: edf6 camera source appendix, edf5 camera source appendix, edf5→edf6 camera layout comparison. native ride seats: edf4.1/5/6 seat records. fact identifiers in the knowledge hub: camera-projection-fields, ghost-camera-get-projection, scope-zoom-chain, scope-zoom-details, ride-camera-locators, ride-camera-locator-values, camera-near-plane-writer and edf6-mouse-look-uneven. original contributors: novae (ajane), hajisensai / all forces camera re, momotori01's edf6vr source, and the other individually credited knowledge hub contributors. camera source facts are mostly static; the mouse test is contributor-verified, not independently reproduced here.

edf6 enemy eggs: hatch targets, shell models and damage flags the examined edf6 egg objects are data-driven: their sgo entries identify which creature appears and which shell object remains or breaks. these are object definitions, not mission-owned spawn groups or hidden probabilities. the recovered class is giantantegg; a related giantantegg_break object follows a different model-parameter path. egg species encoded in stock object sgos sgo family (base / b form) object — creature to hatch shell/model clue observed durability giantant01egg / giantant01eggb giantant01 (black ant) antegg.mdb, white egg 1 giantant02begg / giantant02beggb giantant02b (red ant) antegg_red.mdb, larger bounds 1 goldantegg / goldanteggb goldant (golden ant) antegg_gold.mdb 1 e619_squid_small_egg / e619_squid_small_eggb e618_squid_small (haze) a separate tall model 1 object selects the hatched enemy, while break_object names the shell/broken representation. the sample includes eight edf6 names in four base/b pairs. a source comparison also found the same relevant values in the six edf5 ant-egg sgos studied, but the haze family is not thereby proved to exist in edf5. b variant and friendly damage the observed b variant differs from the corresponding plain one in is_friendly_damage_activate: plain 0, b 1. this is an sgo field value, not proof of every possible in-game friendly-fire interaction. in particular, do not infer that the monster which hatches is friendly, that all projectiles damage the shell, or that every mission uses the b variant. those conclusions require a mission placement and runtime hit test. changemodelparam distinction the native giantantegg path loads a changemodelparam entry, whereas giantantegg_break did not use that path in the examined build. a separately documented kittopiacreator patch looks up changemodelparam and applies it to the break object's animation model. the patch is evidence of a difference in the original routines, not a stock feature of giantantegg_break. where an egg actually appears the object sgo tells you which creature it could hatch. it does not independently prove the egg's mission position, activation event, health scaling or spawning frequency. these come from mission ac/bvm and mission rmpa or other objects. see mission-owned spawn records and enemy-generator semantics. evidence and credit: source-read sgo values and kittopiacreator's static patch note, edf knowledge hub (novae/ajane, 14 nov 2026), fact ids ant-egg-hatch-object (kh chat 120) and anteggbreak-changemodelparam (kittopiacreator). address examples such as 0x41114e are build-specific to steam-678ccb46. no new game runtime test was conducted.

edf6 shield bearers: barrier collision, teams and projectile stopping a shield bearer barrier in the examined edf6 build is a physical collision/query object, not merely a transparent visual effect. it also is not the same mechanism as a hector's carried, breakable shield. native owners and layers the relevant e513_shieldbearer variants (_l, _xl, _fixed*) are alientrailer objects. each includes an alientrailer_barrier subobject. the source identifies two barrier layers of 0x680 bytes, one at owner +0x18c0 and one at +0x1f40 in this build. a layer holds an havok body and barrierinfo. the examined body uses collision layer 14 and carries a key-2 reference to barrierinfo. the barrier info includes the team, copied from the owner each frame. the projectile collector considers a key-2 barrier when the barrierinfo team is hostile to the projectile side. the subsequent contact handler stops the shot at the barrier surface, including rounds that otherwise pierce normal targets. this is why a barrier can be visible yet not block every object equally: a collision layer, a team relation and the bullet's collision-handling path are all involved. what the shield does not prove question what static evidence supports hostile projectile reaches barrier eligible for barrier hit/stop handling piercing projectile the studied handler still stops it at barrier contact friendly projectile hostility filter can exclude barrier interception vehicle hull enters barrier stock vehicle collision blocking not established; the examined helicopter barrier query was gated on a field without a proven native writer shield is invulnerable to every possible attack not proven by the interception routine alone the source lists model radius families around s 50 m, l 100 m, ll 200 m and xl 470 m, but those are inferred from model data, not independently game-measured collision radii. use them as approximate model context rather than hard-coded universal barrier spheres. distinguish other collision questions a barrier hit is not the same as a direct bullet's stop/hit layer filtering or an explosion's area-damage query. see edf6 projectile filters and direct versus area damage. a historical edf4.1 mission incident involving a shield bearer and airstrike also needs its own mission-specific proof; the barrier mechanism alone does not establish the outcome. evidence and credit: shield-bearer-barrier, source analysis by hajisensai / all forces (shield-re.md) in edf knowledge hub, build steam-678ccb46. static, with some radii and byte interpretations marked as inference. representative gameplay combinations not rerun here.

edf6 humanoids: weapon slots, fire-mask messages and dropped guns colonists, martians, venus variants and other humanoid-like enemies do not necessarily carry a single hard-wired gun. in the analyzed edf6 data and runtime, weapons can be independent scene objects and, for newer families, independent child slots under the owning humanoid. weapon ownership: single-gun example the humanoid_basic (colonist/frog) constructor reads weapon from its object sgo, creates a separate gun object and attaches it to a weapon_node such as arms_r. the part named by weapon_constraint_parts is looked up in the owner's body/part table. the owning humanoid's +0x1120 list contains weapon weak-reference rows and +0x1130 is its count in the scoped build. the identified gun-family types include humanoidweaponbase, humanoidweapon_basic and humanoidweapon_heavy. their own sgo settings and bullet factory determine firing; the object is not simply a muzzle mesh on the humanoid. multiweapon sgo records the humanoid_base_weapon_ex.list field contains independently configured child entries with: field role in the examined object model object child weapon/shield object node model attachment / bone node constraint_parts logical body-part binding resolved against humanoid_base_parts_config rotation data attachment orientation observed stock families include e616_venus*, e664_armor_venus*, e601_martian*, e661_martian_leader* and e602_berserker*. a venus variant can mix two weapon children with two shield children. the important distinction: constraint_parts is a logical body-part reference, not automatically the name of an havok constraint or a softbody-only special field. which child actually fires? a native per-slot fire mask is sent through object message type 0x11 in the examined parent humanoid logic. the receiving dispatch fires the child slots indicated by the mask. thus a two-gun humanoid can fire left, right or both children without changing the weapon classes. relevant read sites in the one surveyed binary: message construction near rva 0x4716bf / 0x4716d6 and reception near 0x4740b0. this is a static message-path observation, not a completed online replay test. do not claim that arbitrary simultaneous firing across peer clients was proven by this disassembly alone. why weapons fall off the gun's enabled state is updated from its associated body part. on a transition to disabled, the original object code hides the in-hand weapon and can create a separate dropped gun scene object with its own model and ragdoll. in an online session the owning side also sends a drop counter/event; other peers can create their own drop using that sequence. the inspected humanoidweaponbase::drop object survives 600 frames (10 s at 60 hz), with physics/presentation; it has no recorded player pickup behavior. an isolated source investigation found no universal "enemy dies, always drop gun" shortcut: the observed event originates from the relevant part's loss of the enabled condition. therefore don't treat a dropped model, a recoverable player weapon item and a mission itemdrop packet as equivalent things. evidence boundaries fire_setting indices and several body-part byte interpretations were partly inferred from observed stock values and instructions. the source has stronger confirmation for the child-object ownership, 0x11 dispatch, weak-reference handling and drop creation. these offsets are not stable cross-build public api addresses. sources and attribution: humanoid-weapon-ex-list, weapon-ex-constraint-parts, humanoid-fire-mask-message, humanoid-weapon-objects and humanoid-weapon-drop in edf knowledge hub; hajisensai / all forces (humanoid-weapons.md and gravity-re.md), edf4.1→edf6 hector carrier source research. static evidence; no new game runtime tests.

edf6 ufocarrier508: native movement, flight states and route transitions the surveyed ufocarrier508 is a separately configured dropship object, loading app:/object/e508_carrier.sgo, and inheriting parts of the ufocarrier flight/ai machinery. understanding its position, target and velocity fields is more useful than interpreting it as a model translated directly to a coordinate every frame. flight is eased toward a requested velocity in the examined object update (reported rva 0x4f74d0), the active flight mode uses an approximate per-frame easing operation: velocity += (requested_velocity - velocity) * 0.01 position += velocity the named fields are +0xb40 (requested direction/velocity command), +0x5c0 (current velocity) and +0x90 (position), with heading adjustment through +0x600. this is the source's static reading of the normal active flight branch; not every state necessarily runs that branch. the unit and update cadence should not be generalized outside this code path. the parent ai slot can compute +0xb40 from a target/explorer direction, turn rate and speed. the ship itself performs the easing, which explains why forcing position directly would bypass its native flight model. named state-machine families the source identifies a state value at +0x16f0 and these handler functions in the examined build: state reported role 0 idle 1 follow route at +0x1728 2 follow route at +0x1740, then delete 3 fly to target at +0x1760, with radius +0x1780, then state 5 4 fly to +0x1770, then delete 5 additional state (function identified, exact gameplay label unresolved) 6 additional state (function identified, exact gameplay label unresolved) the inferred meanings of states 0–4 come from code and script usage; the exact caller that advances the state machine during every frame was not fully closed. specifically, a prior source note misidentified the damage-flame burst update as the state-machine tick. this later interpretation supersedes that mistake. the fly-to helper chooses a point on a horizontal circle about the target (radius 0 means the target itself), creates a desired 3d direction, adds a turn penalty and multiplies by its speed. the surveyed code did not implement a general smooth slowdown near the target point in that helper. model, bounding box and damage context in the analyzed model, catapult_a (the core) is approximately at local (0,-5,0), a hatch ring of eight hatch_a through hatch_h nodes is around local y -16.814, and its model collision box has approximate half-extent (47,43.5,75.9) with a small negative y centre offset. these are model-space measurements, not a universal collision radius for every carrier variant. the carrier's hp is maintained independently of its movement state. additional fire/damage effects are handled around an update separate from the flight-state logic. the model's physical shape, scripted spawn event and generated enemy occupancy belong to other subsystems. source and credit: ufocarrier-flight in novae/ajane's edf knowledge hub, static source by hajisensai / all forces (carrier-laser-re.md). all offsets/handler rvas apply only to the identified steam-678ccb46 build. no new runtime flight demonstration was performed.

edf6 corpse, severed-part and weapon-debris lifetimes edf6 uses different disappearance timers for different kinds of objects. a corpse timer is not a shared engine-wide constant, and debris persistence is not equivalent to a mission's enemy spawn cap. the following table summarizes values recovered from the specified stock edf.dll code sites. stock object/family inspected timer what the evidence actually measures spinner ufo 30 seconds float threshold in the death/disappearance path shellfish / nacre 30 seconds float threshold in the examined path giant ant 15 seconds float threshold giant spider 15 seconds float threshold giant bee 15 seconds float threshold dragonsmall (tadpole) 15 seconds float threshold humanoidbase 20 or 30 seconds two native code values; exact decision context is not fully resolved here berserkerbase (androids) 1,800 frames frame-count threshold, 30 s if the counter advances at 60 hz detached humanoid limbs 1,800 frames frame-count threshold, 30 s at 60 hz humanoidweaponbase::drop 600 frames frame-count threshold, 10 s at 60 hz the distinction between stored seconds and stored frame counts matters. a frame threshold does not guarantee real-time seconds under every variable-rate, paused or modified-timing scenario. a display fps limit is not automatically the tick rate of these objects. why all disappeared objects are not alike a humanoid gun dropped from a destroyed part is its own scene object with physics and a roughly ten-second lifetime in the default path. an insect death body, humanoid limb and a boss state may have entirely separate duration policies. cleaning up visual corpses does not prove the object was removed from a network scene registry, removed from all navigation blockers or eligible for reward drops. those are distinct engine systems. a patch that repoints float loads or changes frame comparisons documents the original constants but is not evidence that the patched timeout is stock. reference and attribution source fact despawn-timers, edf6 steam-678ccb46, independently read in the edf knowledge hub from kittopiacreator's adjustobjdespawntimers code and edf.dll instruction sites. credit kittopiacreator and novae/ajane. values are static baseline readings, not gameplay timing remeasurements. frame time conversions assume 60 ticks/s.

edf6 mothership cores: open-state timers and genocide cannon parts a giant edf mothership is not one undifferentiated object. in the examined edf6 build, its hull, large genocide gun, small genocide gun and core states map to distinct classes and data paths. a field on one of these classes should not automatically be attributed to the entire ship. grandmothership core opening the source's static instruction audit finds a normal core-open state that ends after its state-time counter crosses 0x708 = 1800 frames (30 s if the counter advances at 60 hz). an object-message handler covers the related state transition. a separately documented edf6_grandmothership_ex patch makes object action 100 (0x1000000d message) set an open-state byte so the core stays open until a later explicit close. the sustained-open override is patch-added behavior, not evidence that the original grandmothership always keeps its core open on action 100. equally, the 1800-frame threshold is not automatically a fixed 30-second wall clock in all gameplay conditions. genocide cannon is not a single untyped projectile surveyed component class / evidence relevant sgo details large genocide cannon ufomother511corebigcannon e511_mothership_genocide_l.sgo; durability 6000; rocketbullet01 bullet; fire0 muzzle; numeric parameters include 6000, 1500, 2400 (their meanings should not be guessed) small genocide cannon ufomother511coresmallcannon e511_mothership_genocide_s.sgo; durability 1200; no bullet setting in the cited record main hull ufomother511 separate parent identity and body paths these are static sgo/rtti observations for the named edf6 511 family. they do not prove which actor id is assigned as the attacker to the eventual hit. the surveyed source did not close the large cannon's actual firing site; it may be the gun part or another owner that performs the hit registration. distinguish animation, hit and explosion the existence of rocketbullet01 in the large cannon sgo is not proof that a genocide hit in every earlier edf4.1 conversion runs a particular effect, death explosion or network event. firing script, projectile class, impact-effects, and object destruction are distinct chains. the edf4.1-to-edf6 genocide cannon missing-explosion symptom must remain a port/runtime observation, not a proven fault in a stock edf6 511 cannon. evidence and credit: grandmothership-core-hold (kittopiacreator) and genocide-cannon-classes (hajisensai / all forces, subcarrier-re.md) in edf knowledge hub, novae/ajane export 14 nov 2026. source build steam-678ccb46; patch additions separated from shipping behavior. no new in-game test.

edf6 common clip and common light: native material profiles two ordinary map-model shader families in the examined edf6 mdb corpus are especially easy to oversimplify: snd_brdf_map_common_clip for alpha-cutout surfaces and snd_brdf_map_common_light for the basic illuminated/emissive path. both use a 60-byte, one-uv native mesh declaration in the bounded source examples, but they have different material contracts and texture slots. family native shader observed slots in the qualified reference mesh stride / uv common clip snd_brdf_map_common_clip albedo, normal, param_r_m_xxx_hr 60 b, one uv set common light snd_brdf_map_common_light albedo, normal, param_r_m_light_hr 60 b, one uv set the material includes its own ordered parameter records, exact type/size values, flags, layer, priority and native default values. a shader name and vertex stride alone do not supply that information. in the studied common_light family, light_color can be hdr (components above 1); clamping to a normalized editor color can alter the appearance. cutout is not generic transparency a 44-material sample of native common clip configurations had alpha_clip=0.5 for 42 instances and 0.3435 for 2 instances. this is an observed distribution, not a universal engine default. a sk_pshrub003-df.dds asset provides a concrete bc1/dxt1 one-bit-alpha example. other cutout and glass families use different render states; a cutout material is not equivalent to snd_map_object_glass or brdf window. known valid format versus observed in-game image the source qualified complete mdb geometry/material profiles structurally and reproduced the native-observed parameter abi in offline tests. it did not verify in-game rendering for a newly generated model. therefore native-like record ordering and exact values are stronger evidence for correct serialization than a generic pbr viewer, but not themselves proof of the final pixel appearance, clipping threshold interaction or glow intensity. for other profiles see native windows/glass/parallax family contracts and typed mdb material serialization. sources: edf5_edf6_research/research/active/map_authoring/r54_cutout_emissive_productization_2026-10-16/map_studio_r54_cutout_emissive_productization_2026-10-16.md and the native mdb corpus summarized in native mdb materials; no new game runtime. r54's project/frontend wrapper and adapter fixes are deliberately not subjects of this game-format article. what the exact pixel shaders establish beyond the mdb records native material serialization and the shader's arithmetic are distinct evidence. two pinned common_clip pixel-shader paths have the static alpha test equivalent to: if sampled_albedo_alpha < alpha_clip: discard this strengthens the interpretation of the named alpha_clip parameter for those compiled paths. it does not imply that all native clip materials use one threshold, nor that cutout is blended translucency. the material-level distribution above (42 of 44 at 0.5, two at 0.3435) is a bounded census, not a global default. for one exact common_light pixel shader, the recovered mrt write has the shape: sv_target6.rgb = sampled(param_r_m_light_hr).b * light_color.rgb crucially, the pinned write does not contain an extra multiplication by diffuse/albedo. a broader contributed renderer guide describes emission as depending on pre-emission color; that more general account must not override this specific compiled program. the scene compositor may combine other colors later, but the recovered target write alone cannot establish that later behavior. both shader families remain distinct from legacy snd_chara_basic, glass/window translucency and the separate terrain/fieldrender path. identical mesh strides do not imply identical gpu outputs. for the broader static-vs-frame evidence matrix see edf6 rendering and shader evidence.

edf6 online rooms: four slots, member indices and ready handshake the original edf6 online room is a four-member system in several separate layers: eos::users, per-peer packet sessions, the mission context, hud widgets and loadout tables. the four-player limit is therefore more than one menu setting. the details below refer to the examined steam-678ccb46 build and are not a description of an eight-player modification. user slots are not always hud player numbers the room's eos::users collection assigns a new member the first available slot (users::add, rva 0x12b7f50). removing a member empties a slot; it does not compact everyone upward. a later join can reuse the vacancy. the user+0x40 network/member slot, used in packets and initial synchronization, must not be assumed to equal the user+0x48 hud/loadout player index. the latter is assigned through mission and roster synchronization. a source harness observed a lost start-sync record after different machines saw leave/join slot orders differently; this is not a reported stock-production crash in every session. original room construction and ui also use four entries for the voice-talk display, status lamps, packet sessions and other per-member arrays. a larger mod has to reconcile these independent limits; changing a single room-capacity integer is insufficient. ready is a state machine, not merely the host pressing start the huiroom screen exposes request_readywait. members enter a ready handshake that tracks the roster count, content entitlement/availability checks and a short start countdown. the examined handshake states are: state meaning in the source investigation 0 idle 1 start initiated 2 own ready state submitted 3 roster locked / counting down 4 mission-start commit the exact state-object names are inferred from call sites; their numeric values and branching are from code. a changing member count or incompatible selected content can cancel or block the transition. the source reports a 1000 ms countdown stored when the ready flow starts; it is not a complete guarantee of wall-clock start latency under loading or network delays. huiroom's transition to mission start is a local screen/state commit; it should not be confused with the native missionmgr::loadpackage or a fresh setgamemode call. see missionmgr package model for those separate responsibilities. can someone join during a mission? in the source contributor's actual online gameplay, players could leave mid-mission, but a newly joined member stayed in the room until the next mission, rather than materializing mid-combat. that observation is contributor-verified gameplay; the separate four-slot limits and ui/state details are static binary research. do not use a room-entry observation as proof that a live mission supports dynamically rebuilding every player object. sources and credit: kh net-room-four-slots, net-member-slots, net-room-ready-handshake, net-no-mid-mission-join; edf6coop binary-site audit, hajisensai / all forces, novae/ajane. only the last claim is a reported gameplay observation, not newly reproduced.

edf6 mission start: loadout packets, player records and weapon ids edf6 does not spawn an online squad purely from whatever a player's local equipment menu last displayed. at mission start, the game synchronizes per-player loadouts, then constructs the online player objects from the received gamestatus records. this explains why client weapon-table compatibility matters even when the lobby and mission resources appear to load correctly. the examined native loadout record the code audit identified a 0xd4-byte (212-byte) stride for gamestatus player records beginning at gamestatus+0x14c78, with four native slots. eight audited indexing sites use this stride in creation, mission synchronization, colors or ui. the small +0x118 pickup count discussed in the source is a record-relative memory field used on the appropriate object/access path, not an additional 0x118 bytes that must be appended to a 0xd4-byte on-wire record. every participating machine calls missionsync_begin() and advances missionsync_update() until the synchronized start state completes. the host gathers player replies and produces the start message, including the player count and compact serialized loadout entries. the receiver reconstructs records and then creates player objects. the wire representation varies in size and is not automatically identical to the fixed 0xd4-byte in-memory stride. layer observed distinction gamestatus in memory 4 × 0xd4 record stride in the native build mission-sync wire records compact fields; varying lengths, not direct raw record memcpy player count separate synchronized value at gamestatus+0x14ff8 room member slot network identity used to match replies, distinct from the hud player number weapon ids: negative values matter the examined native equipment lookup has a nonobvious convention: -1 means empty weapon slot. ids less than -1 can encode a table row as abs(id) - 2. regular ids resolve through the weapon table according to the observed native lookup path. the source documents a mixed-mod session where a stock-table guest crashed after a host equipped a weapon added to the table by a mod. this is an observed cross-installation incompatibility, not evidence that ordinary matching stock edf6 installations crash from standard weapon choices. the problematic remote path lacked a sufficient bound check for the host's weapon index. resolving a weapon in a packet and rendering its name in the lobby are separate operations. record size and eos packet limits the source discusses a modified eight-member test reaching an estimated 1180-byte mission-start message, exceeding the separately audited 1170-byte physical eos bound. that result is reported as unverified mod-configuration evidence and must not be attributed to the four-player stock message size. it does illustrate why adding more members stresses serialized start records, not just the room ui. evidence and credit: kh facts net-loadout-records, net-mission-sync-flow, net-weapon-id-unchecked, net-mission-start-message; edf6coop/multislot investigators. static field layout and contributor mixed-mod crash; no new network-session reproduction.

edf6 enemy multiplayer: local ai, owner decisions and insect rng edf6 multiplayer does not transmit every enemy's full ai state at every frame. the examined engine runs enemy ai and physics on each machine, then uses object ownership and selected network messages to reconcile important decisions. this is why two games can show the same enemy model yet gradually disagree on its exact motion or random choices. simulation is local; authority is selective the static survey found that enemy ai/physics updates continue on guests, while selected decisions check an owner/remote-copy bit. examples include an owner-selected monsterbase random action and messages for insect hit reactions. a guest's weapon firing can be separately gated: when a shooter is a remote-owned copy, the examined 0x690cc0 path returns without generating its own projectile, so the copy uses replicated owner fire instead of firing the same shot a second time. therefore these two statements can both be true: each machine updates the enemy's local animation/physics/ai trajectory. a selected side owns an authoritative shot, random action or network event. do not infer "owner sends every movement coordinate" or "clients must all independently generate identical bullets" from either statement alone. insect pose update thresholds the surveyed giantant network-object writer has different thresholds according to state; it does not send a fresh pose every rendered frame. static constants include 40 or 90 frames in the non-moving-target cases and 12, 3 or at least 9 frames in specific moving/ai-mode branches. exact branch meanings for some status bytes remain partly inferred. source investigators corrected an earlier reversal of the 40-versus-90 condition. at 60 simulation ticks per second, 90 frames are 1.5 seconds and three frames are 0.05 seconds. these are thresholds on particular branches, not a guarantee that a changed pose is sent on that cadence under every condition. insects and random-state restoration the analyzed insect network path sends message 10 with an old seed and current rng state. the receiver consumes it and advances the state according to the same lcg step. other surveyed enemy families did not expose this same rng-resynchronization message; they may rely on shared initial seed and equivalent execution paths. a missing or additional rng draw on one peer can therefore change future enemy decisions, even if the player sees a recent pose correction. it would be wrong to claim that "all edf enemies continuously synchronize rng" or that a single missing packet explains every persistent aim/hp desync. a separate observed limitation an edf6multislot source report describes ants, spiders, dango and berserker-type robots not publishing ordinary pose updates during certain blown-away / downed phases, followed by guest-visible correction when standing. that observation is reported but not independently verified here, and the report specifically distinguishes bees. it should not be silently generalized to every insect or to a missing havok collision body. sources: kh net-ai-everywhere, net-copy-ai-no-own-fire, net-insect-pose-periods, net-insect-rng-resync, net-enemy-down-no-sync. credits: edf6coop binary work, novae/ajane, edf6multislot. build-specific offsets and branches; no new gameplay validation.

edf6 air raider deliveries: replicated smoke, transporters and vehicle ids a delivered vehicle in edf6 is not necessarily a vehicle object fully serialized by the host and transmitted to the client. in the examined native chain, every peer can create a corresponding local object using the same mission and sgo resources, then register it under a derived network identity. this applies to the studied smoke-candle / transporter508 delivery path, not all game vehicles in every circumstance. source-observed object chain the smoke-candle/bullet mechanism creates a transporter and, in a room, establishes a derived registration id. transporter508 creates its container and registers that container in the online object system. the container's unloading state loads the vehicle from a referenced sgo object path. the game sets the delivered vehicle's team/state, initializes/equips it, derives its network identity from the parent and a counter, and registers it. the delivery container is subsequently removed. the source identifies an sgo vehicle path at the container's +0xb80 and a registration counter at +0xc30 in the examined build. those are build-scoped object offsets, not universal sgo file offsets. why identical game resources matter a synchronized event and object identity do not include a complete copy of the vehicle's sgo/model/archive resources. the receiving machine still needs the appropriate game resource path. this explains why a modded delivery can work on one computer but crash another computer that lacks the referenced sgo, despite their network session itself having started successfully. the stock/source-derived chain creates each local copy, then the engine assigns ownership roles. the source reports owner/guest values in the network copy flags, but the precise downstream control/seat behavior remains a separate system. what this does not establish it does not prove that every custom vehicle object is safely synchronized just by using an equal sgo filename. it does not prove that the host sends the entire sgo to peers (the analyzed behavior indicates the opposite). it does not override vehicle seat eligibility or per-seat camera locators; those are separate native data. it does not imply that object registration, vehicle physics and local equipment input all use the same authoritative peer. for the other native pieces, see vehicle seats and masks, vehicle ride camera, and object network ownership. source and credit: kh net-vehicle-delivery, hajisensai / all forces online-re.md section 2.3. source-only code reading in steam-678ccb46, with some derived-id rationale inferred. no new peer test.

edf6 world snapshots: serialized state versus online player identity the examined edf6 executable contains an in-memory world snapshot facility via xgs::snapshot. its presence does not mean that ordinary online gameplay has a complete, safe save-and-resume of its multiplayer session. state restoration, peer identity, player ownership and lobby membership are different responsibilities. native build and restore wrappers the static source investigation identified a snapshot creation routine (rva 0x6b4820 in the surveyed build) that checks state/context, creates a write recorder and invokes a shared world-serialization root. a corresponding restore routine (rva 0x6b48a0) checks for a retained snapshot, restores relevant renderer/world state and invokes a read recorder over the same root. the fact that a wrapper exists proves serialization code is present. it does not prove that an arbitrary multiplayer match can be rolled back or migrated live to a new host. the source's context guard was not identified as a blanket prohibition of online snapshots; its precise state eligibility requires separate proof. known serialization boundaries component relevant finding soldierbase::onsnapshot dispatches to the general humanbase::onsnapshot implementation in the examined build soldier local/remote role at +0x128 not included in the inspected snapshot record playerinfo holds actor references; no retained puid/network-user identity in the observed record missionmgr::onsnapshot includes a record named script rather than the complete active content package lobby/session / eos users not demonstrated as reconstructible from world snapshot contents this explains the chief limitation: a restored actor is not automatically a correctly owned online player. the engine's normal joined-room handshake publishes the active pack and assigns player/member identities through other mechanisms. those mechanisms are not replaced by merely restoring the snapshot bytes. do not confuse three systems world snapshot — in-memory serialization of selected game/world state. mission sync — the roster/loadout/mission-start exchange among online peers. application-layer reliable packets (rudp) — retention/retry/ack of already serialized network records. a snapshot alone does not transfer the reliable-manager sequence state; reliable transport alone does not restore missing user ownership; a correct lobby package selection does not imply every scene object was recreated. evidence and credit: kh net-world-snapshot, net-world-snapshot-limits and net-join-shell-path; source analysis from edf6 network/desync investigation and novae/ajane, 14 nov 2026 hub export. static analysis only; no world restore was executed in the game for this guide.

edf6 shkt and sgo: ragdoll bones, binding tables, hit zones and weak points an edf6 ragdoll is not self-contained in an .shkt file. the havok shkt describes physical bodies, constraints and collision shapes; the accompanying sgo connects those bodies to the animated model, selects the data file, and describes many part-specific damage rules. understanding that division is essential when examining enemy hitboxes or apparently misplaced ragdolls. what points to the shkt? a game sgo refers to a physics object with a value such as ["app:/object/ragdolltest_ari_has_hka.shkt", { ... }]. the source corpus uses keys including ragdoll, body_ragdoll, armor_ragdoll, heavy_armor_ragdoll, barrier_collision, ragdoll_d, subparts and bullet_*. multiple character-color sgos can reuse a single physics file: ant color variants are a documented example. the bodies are identified by their names, not solely by array position. typical names are ragdollproxys.kosi, ragdollproxys.head or ragdoll_<part>. the engine's ragdollcontroller::binddependency finds the named body and associates it with an animation node; a related native lookup indexes body names using a fnv-1a hash. a contributor verified in the game that leaving an sgo reference to a removed shkt body can crash before mission start. renaming a body and updating the corresponding sgo references worked in their test. two mappings, opposite directions sgo table relationship gameplay phase ragdoll_from_animation animated bone → physical body following the living character's animation animation_from_ragdoll physical body → animated bone displaying a physics-driven corpse a row contains [body, bone] or [bone, body] followed by relative position, rotation and scale. quaternion rotation combines with the parent body's orientation; position is transformed into the parent's local frame. the joint hierarchy and shkt shapes are not a substitute for those mappings. the source investigator compared 44,159 rows to mdb bind poses. approximately 81% of animation_from_ragdoll and 98% of ragdoll_from_animation rows were within 1 mm and 0.5° of the bind pose. the exceptions often describe fingers, mouths or weapon bones in an authored alternative pose. these percentages apply to the surveyed sgo/mdb corpus, not every game release. coordinates and body-specific damage the studied shkt and mdb use metres, +y up, +x to the model's left (_l parts); the physics body transform, collision-shape local coordinates and model bind pose must still be distinguished. no general xyz axis swap is required between these two file families. for part damage and weak spots, inspect the sgo, not only shkt. the source includes a weak_point object with a named body, effect and separate damage multipliers (e.g. berserker ragdoll_eye), and humanoid_base_parts_config with part names, parents, hp, damage multipliers, model nodes and shkt body-name suffixes. the shkt supplies the shape that gets hit; sgo decides much of the part-specific response. evidence boundary the code-name lookup and corpus counts are static/binary research. body rename, sgo mapping and missing-body effects were tested by original contributor ktaro, but have not been repeated in this wiki revision. the exact lookup rvas 0x6e6a50, 0x6ea4b0 and 0x51e500 belong to the cited steam-678ccb46 build only. the source also notes that moving all ant bodies with corrected sgo maps largely preserved behavior, but the living hitbox's exact use of each mapping element remains unresolved. sources and credit: edf knowledge hub kh-edf6-physics-shkt, facts sgo-shkt-reference, sgo-body-names, body-name-lookup, missing-body-crash, ragdoll-bone-mapping, mapping-row-placement, shkt-mdb-coordinates, body-move-rename-tests, sgo-part-weakpoint-structures; ktaro's shkt reports, 2026-10-15–19. see native shkt structure. native game reference guides edf6 cling control and robotic enemies

edf6 accessory ragdolls: cloth, hair, joint chains and simulation ownership edf6's swaying clothes, hair and similar body attachments can use an accessory_ragdoll declaration inside the character's sgo model settings. this system is distinct from the normal animated body ragdoll: the game spawns accessory physics bodies, attaches them to a bone chain and updates them from particular character classes. the actual data relationship the observed sgo value is a four-part group: maximum camera distance, per-part motion table, accessory shkt path, and an embedded bone-mapping sgo. across 39 source sgos declaring accessories, the declaration occupies animation_model[4], before effect and outside the inner [mrab, mdb, lod] model-file tuple. the source corpus always uses a 20-metre max distance, not a per-file mix of lengths. placing the group inside the model-file tuple can make the game interpret it as lod data instead. the source investigator observed crashes or silent omission, depending on tuple length; those are reported game experiments, not inferred from an editor's ui. why accessories move for some classes but not others animationmodel::loadfromsgo constructs the accessory (source rva 0x6b4fb0), but the actual accessoryragdoll::update (0x6b61d0) is reached through humanbase::onupdate in the examined code. this explains why human-derived soldier classes have moving accessories while a constructed accessory on an ant or frog can remain stationary or at its spawn position. the contributor reports working movement for ranger and wing diver attachments; heavyarmor/engineer share the code path but were not separately confirmed in their game test. the accessory loader puts its bodies on collision layer 23 at runtime. the motion table in sgo, rather than shkt's default physics fields, supplies damping, gravity factor, friction, restitution and a collision toggle. one contributor-verified working example used linear damping 0, angular damping 0.1, gravity factor 1, friction 0.08, restitution 0.5 and collision 0. it is an example, not a universally recommended or default profile. root-body chains and attachment stability an accessory shkt must include the fixed root-side bodies that form a connected joint chain to the parts intended to sway. adding only the moving tip bodies can leave an insect's antennae invisible while alive or stranded where the model spawned. the contributor tested a ranger arm chain and wing diver booster arms with root bodies: both remained attached and moved. the game data includes accessory shkts for both older and edf6 soldier outfits. a source inventory notes all six surveyed *_accessory.shkt bodies have motiontype = 2 (dynamic). their being dynamic in a file does not imply the same update method runs for a non-human enemy. interpretation boundary an sgo declaration being parsed is not proof that the attachment will sway for every enemy class. the exact 20 m value, placement census and loader path are source data; sway/visibility examples are ktaro's in-game observations. repeating them under another edf.dll build, another rig or online mode has not been done here. sources and credit: edf knowledge hub kh-edf6-physics-shkt facts accessory-ragdoll-layout, accessory-placement, accessory-root-chain, accessory-gravity-test | confirms: accessory-values-from-sgo; ktaro research and field tests, 2026-10. see shkt/sgo ragdoll binding.

edf6 shkt: havok system layout, collision filters and measured shapes a native edf6 .shkt contains havok physics 2020 objects for character and vehicle hitboxes, joints and rigid bodies. its class format differs from the legacy hkp structures used in edf4.1/edf5: the studied edf6 files use an hknpphysicssystemdata, or a hknpragdolldata wrapper where a skeleton field is present but not shown to drive the game's binding. core records area native meaning bodycinfos body transforms, masses, motion and material references constraintcinfos joint relationships, with bodya the child and bodyb its parent materials friction and restitution; their encoded hkhalf16 is the upper half of an ieee float32 motion properties limits, damping and related rigid-body simulation fields shapes spheres, capsules, boxes, cylinders, convex hulls, compounds and compressed meshes motiontype values observed: 0 static, 1 keyframed, 2 dynamic. materialid and motionpropertiesid refer to local tables; 65535 can mean absent/none (including static-body cases). a source census found one physics system per shkt in all 316 files in that survey. the largest surveyed system had 111 bodies; a ragdoll example had 94 bodies and 93 constraints. packed collision filter field the body-side collisionfilterinfo encodes subsystem exclusions separately from the runtime collision layer: bits field 0–4 layer slot (game can override) 5–9 subsystem id 10–14 subsystem id to exclude 15–30 system group the game derives the effective layer during registration; the source found the serialized layer slot 0 for all 4,954 surveyed bodies, though actual player, enemy and map layers differ at runtime. ragdoll body exclusions commonly refer to the parent body's subsystem id; when the character contains over 31 bodies, 5-bit subsystem ids are necessarily reused. do not interpret a serialized layer zero as “this body collides with nothing.” the code's collisionfilter::collisionfilter path uses a fixed layer-pair matrix. some examples from the investigator's table: player/vehicle layer 1 collides with map-prop layer 20; enemy layer 2 collides with terrain layer 17, but not generally with prop layer 20. layer 26 is a special bullet-penetrable map category: it collides with several character/query layers, not the listed bullet layers 10–13. these statements refer to code and surveyed modded-runtime observations; see the separate 32×32 collision matrix if available in the published edition. shape census from 317 surveyed shkt/hkt files shape type count convex 8,034 compound 1,925 capsule 1,033 box 559 compressed mesh 439 sphere 71 cylinder 59 total 12,120 across that same census: 4,954 bodies, 4,444 materials, 4,230 motion-property entries and 3,059 constraints. all values are corpus counts, not global limits for arbitrary expansions. the source identifies simdtree in compound shapes as a four-way bvh; aabbtree is empty in the examined files. the largest source-observed convex hull has 252 vertices; up to 250 were separately reported working in the game, while 253–256 remained unqualified. do not confuse the maximum observed size with a universally validated engine limit. sources and credit: edf knowledge hub kh-edf6-physics-shkt, facts shkt-system-structure, collision-filter-info-bits, collision-layers, shkt-shape-statistics, shkt-size-limits, map-prop-layers; ktaro/bartey, 2026-10. binary addresses are build scoped and no game was run for this revision. native game reference guides edf6 walk support state and velocity edf6 cling movement

edf6 physics: mass distribution, inertia, wheels and suspension edf6's havok collision shape is only one part of rigid-body response. a body can have a mass value, a separate stored hknprefmassdistribution and a set of motion properties. vehicles then apply their own aggregate mass and wheel/suspension settings on top of that body-level description. stored mass and inertia a census of object and weapon found 2,052 null massdistribution references among 4,251 bodies. with a null entry, the studied native engine can derive center of mass and inertia from the collision shape. a non-null hknprefmassdistribution stores centerofmassandvolume and principal axes/inertia, with inertia expressed per unit mass. changing bodycinfo.mass therefore changes the effective inertial response even when the distribution record itself is unchanged. the original investigator found that stored mass distributions often differ materially from naive shape-based calculations: on the surveyed population, center-of-mass offsets had a roughly 2.5 cm median discrepancy and inertias about 45% at median, although volume matched. that is a description of the research corpus, not a recommended multiplier or evidence of a file bug. in their gameplay tests, changing shapes, friction, damping, joint limits or mass affected collisions and ragdoll dynamics. by contrast, shkt's saved collision layer was overwritten by the game, and a stored gravityfactor often did not act as a universal per-body gravity setting. some shell-casing and subsystem-exclusion experiments remained inconclusive. native files contain both inertia factor 1.0 (often newer e6xx assets) and 1.5 (many inherited edf5 assets); both were observed functioning in the contributor's tests. what a vehicle does with shkt masses car_base does not simply use a sum of shkt body masses unchanged. it takes those as relative weights, normalizes them to the sgo's car_base_all_rigid_body[0] total vehicle mass, then applies per-body factors from car_base_rigid_body. wheel rows carry: cast mode (0 ray, 1 cylinder), wheel attachment offset, suspension length, length addend, spring strength, two damping fields, radius and half-width. the studied suspension force is approximately: [f_{\mathrm{spring}} = k_{\mathrm{spring}},m_{\mathrm{vehicle}},x] where x is compression. consequently a simple stationary compression estimate is g / total spring strength, roughly 9.8 / total strength, in the source's chosen convention. this is a model-level relation, not a guaranteed observed compression for every moving vehicle or contact geometry. under-soft suspensions can let the chassis intersect climbing obstacles or be thrown off; the exact effect depends on the wheel and hull shapes. tested versus unresolved the investigator reports normal vehicle behavior for a rewritten v601 tank's compressed meshes and reports standing on a newly added invisible collision plate. these are contributor-verified game tests. by contrast, the hypothesis that very thin/open compressed triangle meshes cause vehicle sinking and shaking is unproven, so no root cause is asserted here. sources and credit: edf knowledge hub kh-edf6-physics-shkt facts mass-distribution-null, mass-distribution-details, shkt-effective-values, car-base-mass, car-base-wheels; ktaro, october 2026. see vehicle drivetrain and fuel and shkt structure.

edf6 ground and air vehicles: gears, fuel, recoil and ai data edf6's drivable vehicles do not all share one throttle or resource model. the studied code distinguishes multi-gear ground vehicles, simplified tank gearing, fuel-bearing vehicles, and seat-dependent gun recoil. their values reside in vehicle sgos, seat definitions and derived runtime state. ground-engine gear records a carbase vehicle stores a forward gear vector with 16-byte rows (speed, upshift threshold, downshift threshold, drive force). the source identifies additional neutral and reverse rows. runtime gear index -1 = reverse, -2 = neutral, 0+ = forward gears. a native sgo can provide car_base_engine_gear (full rows plus reverse data) or car_base_engine_simple_gear (used by tanks, with one basic speed/force and fixed ratio constants). the exact thresholds and control flow are source-derived; a simple-gear tank is not a regular car that merely happens to have one forward gear. the surveyed build uses a vector beginning at carbase+0x1758 and a gear index at +0x1b24. these are object-memory offsets for one edf.dll build, not positions within the sgo byte stream. fuel resources the native fuel object has an enabled flag and three floats: capacity, remaining fuel and consumption per unit of input. its update consumes a quantity proportional to absolute input × usage coefficient, reducing the effective control input when fuel is exhausted. the source documents fuel-bearing helicopter classes and two bike families; not every vehicle must implement it. the vehicle_setup example uses [999900, 1.666] as capacity/use values. those are data examples, not an assertion that every helicopter has that amount of usable fuel. the hud's v_fuel01 weapon-like gauge reads the vehicle's corresponding resource. a native code census locates the fuel state on helicopters at +0x1690, one bike at +0x29b0, and another at +0x2b00 in the examined build. recoil is partly a seat property a vehicle's gun seat can contain a bodyrecoil or aimrecoil object; the original weapon's sgo firerecoil is a separate signal. the source characterizes bodyrecoil as push/sway parameters attached to that gun seat, rather than only to its bullet. this matters when comparing a player-summoned vehicle with the npc mission version. concrete native-data comparisons include: family player-facing recoil npc/mission recoil epsilon 403 bodyrecoil [0.1, 0.05] ai [0, 0.05] blacker 505 [0.1, 1] ai/mission [0, 2] nickelinger 402 [0.025, 0.1] ai [0, 0] these values come from the source investigator's root.cpk read, not fresh gameplay measurement. they illustrate why the same vehicle family can appear steadier when driven by mission ai than when used by a player. scope the gear/fuel/recoil details are static code and source-data analysis, largely credited to hajisensai/all forces. civilian-car input uses the seat's steering/throttle rather than a universal weapon aim; this was separately reported tested in-game. no handling performance benchmarks were run for this release. sources and credit: edf knowledge hub kh-edf6-vehicles facts vehicle-gear-table, vehicle-fuel-tank, vehicle-body-recoil, npc-vehicle-recoil-data, civilian-car-input; hajisensai / all forces, november 2026. see native vehicle seat eligibility.

edf6 lock-on weapons: target search, multi-lock, firing and network cancellation edf6's lock-on mechanic is a weapon-local target state machine, not just a circle drawn on the hud. its sgo describes target filters, cone, range, time, lock distribution and expiry. the surveyed source code tracks searching, an unfinished lock, a list of completed locks, shot assignment and network cancellation as distinct steps. weapon parameters sgo key meaning in the examined build lockontype chooses lock behavior; 0 and 5 are treated as no lock-on in the observed paths lockontargettype determines candidate type; in a surveyed mapping 0 → search kind 3 (all), 1 → kind 2 lockon_distributiontype 0 = target per burst shot; otherwise target per pellet lockonangle horizontal and vertical half-angles, radians lockonrange maximum targeting range lockontime duration converted to update ticks lockonholdtime retention time of completed locks lockonfailedtime grace duration while target exits the cone, in frames lockon_autotimeout whether used/held locks automatically age out; internally an inverted flag lockon_fireendtoclear lock list clears on a specific reload-start transition when enabled maximum lock count depends on distribution mode: in the surveyed computation, type 0 yields zero; distribution 0 uses min(ammocount, fireburstcount) while the other path uses firecount. soldier equipment may apply separate multipliers for range, speed and repeated locking of the same target. search, progress, firing the lock tick searches eligible registry targets only when not already locking one and the completed list is not full. the picker scores candidates in the cone. lock progress grows in ticks; if the target leaves the cone the fail counter grows until expiry. a newly completed lock is appended to the list. this makes multi-target acquisition sequential rather than acquiring every target simultaneously. the firing code refuses to fire a lock-required weapon if the list is empty. it then assigns locks to the created shots, taking older nodes first. in distribution mode 1 successive pellets use successive lock nodes, with excess pellets not necessarily receiving homing; in mode 0 multiple pellets in one shot can share that shot's selected target. some lock nodes persist after firing, depending on autotimeout and hold timers. online cancellation matters the code sends a weapon network message type 6 when a lock fails or is cleared. the recipient clears its remote copy's active locking reference and progress. without this notice, that remote copy can retain a ghost lock and skip the next new-target notice. this is a source-derived risk from the code paths, not a claim that every stock session suffers a visible ghost-lock bug. sources and credit: edf knowledge hub kh-edf6-weapons facts lockon-sgo-fields, lockon-search, lockon-fire-distribution, lockon-network-cancel; hajisensai / all forces code study, november 2026. key rvas 0x68a920, 0x6963a0, 0x690bb0, 0x695150 are specific to the examined steam-678ccb46 build. see missile guidance.

edf6 homing projectiles: steering modes, delay parameters and local simulation an edf6 homing bullet does not necessarily rotate directly toward its target as soon as it spawns. the native bullet classes use separate ignition/steering gates and at least two distinct guidance models. mislabeling their custom-parameter positions can invert the meaning of a missile's early trajectory. which classes are involved? the surveyed code identifies missilebullet01, missilebullet02 and hominglaserbullet01 as distinct homing families, with separate constructors and updates. their exact custom-parameter contract is class-specific. a missile class whose numeric type selects a rocket/non-homing mode must not be treated as having the same steering rules as type 1 or type 2. for missilebullet01 and missilebullet02, the source corrected an older interpretation of custom parameter cp[9]. it is not a generic homing-duration timeout: it can function as a second delay before steering, after the initial cp[8] gate. in the examined vanilla weapon data only the ranger mlra (aweapon143) had a nonzero cp[9], of 5. hominglaserbullet01 has a different, genuine duration check; the mlra finding must not be extended to it. two guidance models in missilebullet01 steering mode observed mechanism important consequence type 1 — pursuit own velocity gains acceleration up to a speed cap, then rotates toward line of sight by a clamped angular step direction of own velocity is turned; inherited velocity is added separately type 2 — thrust/inertia thrust is applied along current nose; the nose rotates toward line of sight within its angular limit momentum is not rotated instantly; trajectory curves from acceleration and inertia for both types, propulsion/velocity maintenance can occur even while the guidance gate is closed. type 2 in particular accelerates forward before it begins turning; when the nose rotates, the velocity follows indirectly. the source estimates an approximate maximum lateral acceleration from thrust magnitude, not from the nose turn-rate parameter alone. target loss and spread the code checks whether the lock record and its target/control block are still valid. when it is absent or expired, the missile can fall back to an ahead-of-itself aim point rather than inventing a new target. a missilebullet01 optional cp[12] mode arms an overshoot/give-up behavior; no surveyed vanilla weapon enabled it. some guided variants sample randomness when constructed, modifying live speed/turn parameters via interpolation from cp[10]. that means identical sgo constants do not necessarily produce identical per-shot values. the source also reports that homing bullets are simulated locally on peers;
