this should not be confused with full replication of every intermediate steering vector. evidence and boundaries these are static re findings with contributor calculations, not new trajectory captures. the shape of custom-parameter arrays and numbered slots must be checked per class and per build; these are not universal commands for every edf weapon. source code rvas: type 1 around 0x269af0, type 2 around 0x269ee0, and the shared missilebullet01 update around 0x26a880, scoped to the studied edf.dll build. sources and credit: edf knowledge hub kh-edf6-weapons facts homing-bullet-classes, mb01-guidance-gate, mb01-guidance-type1, mb01-guidance-type2, homing-bullets-local-sim; hajisensai / all forces, november 2026. see lock-on target state.

edf4.1 to edf6: friendly follower movement, formation offsets and routes a friendly soldier's follow behavior is not equivalent to finding a globally optimal walkable path to the player. across edf4.1, edf5 and edf6, the source builds a target from the leader's position plus a random, world-space formation offset. how the soldier then steers toward that target changed significantly between generations. three generations at a glance game following movement follow anchor / formation obstacle strategy edf4.1 direct virtual-stick movement written by soldierbase leader position + world-space offset local contact normal and periodic short forward box sweep; sidestep/jump-like response edf5 target handed to a movement/path controller on the soldier same leader-plus-offset concept controller-based pathing; some controller fields updated while following edf6 think and airouteexplorerbase/path controller cooperate leader anchor + world-space offset, with chaseleader state scripted route, navigation route and path-mesh branches exist separately these are descriptions of the examined code paths, not comparative performance benchmarks. a different navmesh or missing map collision may still make the newer controller fail. edf4.1: immediate steering and contact probes the edf4.1 follower state is soldierbase virtual slot 58, while guard is 57 and engage 59. move-and-look writes a virtual move stick into the soldier's movement-input fields and a separate pitch/yaw request toward a look target. unlike edf5, this call does not delegate its follow target to a persistent path-controller object. when touching an obstacle whose surface normal opposes the desired direction, the code periodically sweeps a box about 3 m forward. if it finds a free path it can request a jump-like response; otherwise it retains a sidestep direction for a bounded interval. the jump flag's exact behavioral interpretation was inferred from the write, not observed afresh in this edition. formation offsets across the series in the edf4.1 code, normal followers eventually redraw a random horizontal offset with radius about 3–10 m at a timer of 900–1799 frames (approximately 15–30 seconds at 60 updates/s), seeded from a local ai random source and synchronized through a dedicated ai message online. the offset is expressed in world coordinates: turning in place does not rotate it behind the player. a soldier can therefore appear in front of a stationary leader after a redraw without deliberately choosing to block the player. edf5 and edf6 retain the broadly similar world-space offset and timed redraw model, but have distinct object fields, path controller and route management. the edf4.1 mission-native formation spread can enlarge this radius for scripted squads; a balam leader can impose a minimum separation. the 3–10 m range is not a universal distance for every mission-controlled formation. navigational and script consequences a mission's setairoute, setairoutenavigate and following-leader states are not synonymous. edf6's airouteexplorerbase is also used by vehicles and enemies; the native isaimoveend family checks whether the explorer pointer is gone, which can leave mission events waiting if pathing never completes. an npc already under a leader can ignore some route commands until its follow state changes. these distinctions explain why fixing a 4.1 map's physical geometry does not automatically fix the edf6 ai route assigned to it. evidence boundary the three source appendices provide static decompilation, not a newly executed comparison run. relative rvas (4.1 0x2b48e0, edf5 0x30b610, edf6 0x596b50) refer to their individually studied binaries. we do not claim the 4.1 virtual-stick branch solves navigation or that a path-controller's presence guarantees correct traversal. sources and credit: kh-edf41-squad-follow (facts edf41-follow-spot, edf41-follow-offset-pick, edf41-follow-obstacle), kh-edf5-squad-follow and kh-edf6-squad-follow, plus the source's kh-edf6-soldier-ai route census; community researchers novae/ajane and hajisensai/all forces. see three-generation recruitment.

edf4.1/5/6 friendly npcs: recruitment, squad trees and combat states the squad system in edf4.1, edf5 and edf6 is implemented as parent/child links between game objects, not as an independent roster manager with an autonomous “squad entity.” a friendly soldier tracks a leader and a list of followers. its animation/combat ai chooses among guard, follow and engage states. state-machine outline game guard / follow / engage slots update entry edf4.1 57 / 58 / 59 soldierbase per-frame update, with direct move-and-look edf5 74 / 75 / 76 soldierbase state machine with path controller edf6 89 / 90 / 91 soldier think with navigation and chaseleader distinctions the common transition pattern is: a leader causes guard → follow, a valid hostile target can cause follow → engage, losing that target returns to following, and losing the leader returns to guard. a script may separately set route or aggression flags, and combat events can interrupt the visible behavior. recruitment is proximity plus eligibility the examined edf4.1 and edf5 recruitment loops scan the friendly player's team for the nearest living humanbase within 10 m; they skip remote player copies in online mode. the check is gated by an object-side “may join” field and by the fact that the soldier currently has no leader. it then links the soldier to the player and emits a join event/talk cue (合流). in edf6 a corresponding +0x540 flag and the soldierbase::think recruitment block were identified. this explains why simply spawning a ranger or wing diver in a mission is not sufficient to guarantee that approaching the character recruits it. the mission source must establish eligible team/flag/leader state as well as spawn an appropriate soldier object. a modded mission missing one of those conditions is a content problem until native runtime evidence proves otherwise. leader death and squad continuity in the examined edf5 and edf6 paths, a dead leader causes followers to unlink. an eligible soldier may subsequently recruit to the player, but the code does not demonstrate a universal automatic election of a new ai leader. edf6's auto-revive-related flags can affect which branch applies. online follow changes are messages handled through the host/remote distinction rather than only local animation updates. edf5 additionally contains a temporary cover/recruitment budget for some unrecruited mission squads. the source records a roughly 1800-frame (30-second) initial state with different detection/damage/weapon factors while still in an unrecruited ai root. because its gameplay meanings partly rely on the edf6-homolog interpretation, those precise factors should be treated as a source-backed cross-version inference, not an independently reproduced edf5 combat test. what these facts do not settle they do not prove successful movement on edf4.1 geometry imported into edf6. physics collision, nav graph and ai steering remain separate. they do not imply npcs obey a player-facing “stay” order. edf6 has setaichaseleader(bool) in scripts, but that is not automatically a manual player command. they do not guarantee every friendly type is recruitable; team, flag, mission and enemy-squad configuration can differ. sources and credit: knowledge hub kh-edf41-soldier-ai, kh-edf5-soldier-ai, kh-edf6-soldier-ai, kh-edf41-squad-follow, kh-edf5-squad-follow, kh-edf6-squad-follow. named native functions in the original source; no new in-game recruitment trial for this edition. see movement and formation. 
## edf4.1 mission-native recruitment commands and boundaries

in the examined edf4.1 mission-native surface the object-creation calls and the direct follower commands are different operations:

| native id | name in the retained source | what is asserted in the script contract |
|---:|---|---|
| 1010 | createfriend | spawn friend, retain the supplied canrecruit state |
| 1011 | createfriendsquad | spawn a scripted squad, retain canrecruit |
| 1012 | createfriendgroup | spawn a group, retain canrecruit |
| 3151 | setaiautofollow | explicitly arrange automatic following |
| 3152 | recruitobject | explicitly attach a follower/leader relation, mapped through setaifollow in the audited conversion |

a successful createfriend is therefore not equivalent to executing recruitobject, and neither guarantees that the independent 10 m proximity recruiter is eligible to run. the source state machine, original leader, recruitment flag and mission commands determine whether the soldier joins the player. in the historical edf4.1→edf6 conversion, the five native contracts were checked statically; no post-r18 in-game recruitment pass appears in that lineage. the audit is evidence of command identity/preservation, not proof of gameplay outcome.

another source boundary concerns animation: the edf4.1 friendly soldier does not automatically have the edf6 ledge-climb states merely because its actor is hosted by the newer soldier class. that is a cross-generation asset/state availability difference, distinct from the movement and navigation problems. source: friendly_npc_gameplay_fidelity_policy.md, reports/r16_friendly_fidelity.json and reports/r17_friendly_fidelity.json in the r18 source checkpoint; the r16/r17 records belong to the same 18-check offline result and must not be counted as independent gameplay tests.

edf4.1 ufomother301 mothership: separate parts, generator hatches and phases the classic edf4.1 mothership ufomother301 is not one static mesh with a single monolithic weapon script. native research identifies a hull, a shared parts base and separate hatch, panel, cannon and bigcannon classes, all derived from gameobjectbase. each part is a game object with its own durability, state machine and, where applicable, scripted handle. hierarchy and source data the hull's ufomother301.sgo references the body mrab/mdb, a cas animation, a ragdoll shkt, damage data, effects and named groups of child sgos. the observed assembly includes: part group source inventory role mp_bigcannon 1 primary heavy gun mp_cannon 10 secondary gun array mp_panel 125, arranged in four groups shield/armor-panel ring with weapons mp_hatchlow 4 enemy-generating hatches mp_hatchmiddle 4 covers covers sharing the hatch part class part placements use an sgo-relative euler rotation plus offset against the parent waist node. the independent parts lists permit an objectaction command to enable, disable or trigger attacks by type without respawning the whole hull. getpartsobject (mission native 3300) returns a handle to a named main-gun or medium-gun part; it is therefore wrong to model every gun as decorative geometry only. state machines and timed changes part state updates receive a phase 0 enter, 1 update, 2 exit and track elapsed time/frames. the source notes distinguish dt in seconds from 60-hz update-frame counters. selected sounds are throttled via shared hull counters (approximately 16-frame windows), preventing every panel from playing the same cue on one frame. the main bigcannon has closed, opening, ready, charging, firing and closing states. its ordinary direct bullet uses laserbullet02, with special parameters on every eighth shot; the source's recorded direct base damage is 5000, not a generic value scaled with the mission-level factor. the ten medium cannon objects have a separate rocket/beam cycle and projectiles. panels are a third family with type-specific laser or plasma fire. mp_hatchlow is not simply an sgo name for a spawn position. each real hatch owns an objectgenerator, and mission messages can configure its resident or one-shot waves. a named mab locator (発生位置) supplies its actual spawn transform. enemy creation is under host control in the analyzed network path. the hull's exposed weak point and fall the hull has a state machine separate from its parts. following the opening and loss of the main gun, its weak section can be exposed, then hide after a delay and reopen. the source finds a 540-frame hit-related countdown before a hide and a 30-second hidden interval in a particular state sequence. these are state-specific timers, not a promise that every scripted mission shows the same choreography. on hull death, the code changes glow, stops attacks and produces staged explosions before a falling phase with havok ground probing. the death choreography can extend well beyond the instant the durability reaches zero. evidence boundary: this is static analysis of edf4.1 native code and source sgo/mission data, not a new boss fight. exact native addresses such as 0x24ece0 (hull constructor) and 0x250870 (hull messages) are tied to the studied edf4.1 build. some mission-specific behavior depends on objectaction, object durability events and difficulty/level multipliers. sources and credit: kh-edf41-motherships, original facts ufomother301-classes, ufomother301-sgo-parts, ufomother301-state-rng-sound, ufomother301-hatch-generator, ufomother301-hull-states-death, with original community credit retained in the source appendix. see earth eater's different component model.

edf4.1 earth eater: panelbase, turret locators, weak points and phases edf4.1's earth eater (ufomother401) has a fundamentally different organization from ufomother301. its “hull” is mainly a layout controller: the visible ceiling and weapons are separate panels, cores, generators and turrets. the research source states that the top-level hull has no model, collision or durability of its own; scripts and part objects control the actual encounter. the panel family each panelbase can fly into place, shrink/disappear, break and fall, or fly away. a panel's damage gate checks a named shkt weak-point body from its sgo. panels with no qualifying weakpoint, including certain panel01 armor variants, can remain physically visible but invulnerable through that test. this is why hitboxes and collision layers alone do not determine whether a panel accepts damage. one source-defined weak panel death event destroys other panels within a 200-metre horizontal radius after local randomized delays. a core has a separate, extended death sequence with staged explosions. the code also has a non-reward vanish route distinct from genuine object death: its result should not be counted as the ordinary killing of a destructible enemy. where are its turrets attached? turret mounts named 砲台 are found in group 0 of an embedded mab inside the panel's sgo animation_model, not in the basic two-bone mdb or in the shkt collision file. the source inventory reports: panel type mounts main-game panel01, panel01s, panel01sc 10 each main-game panel02b, panel02c 11 each mission pack 2 dlc_panel01, dlc_panels01, dlc_panels02 21 each mission pack 2 dlc_panel02c 11 a mount does not guarantee that a turret will appear. parts_define contains weighted entries, with [0, weight] representing an empty mount. the native constructor rolls an entry for each 砲台 locator. hence actual blue/purple/red/green gun totals can vary in the investigated layouts; their exact per-run reproducibility was not fully demonstrated. cannons, generators and event wiring the research source separates smalllaser (target distance under about 700 m) from sniper, plasma and rapid cannon families (about 500 m in the surveyed path). their cooldowns and projectile types differ. the large cannon panels, finalcannon types, generators and final generators have their own attacks/encounters. the generator family uses a generic wave controller supporting periodic refill or one-shot waves. the original edf4.1 mission scripts configure these objects through panel layout and objectaction calls rather than assuming the entire earth eater comes from a single immutable asset. the source's mission counts sometimes come from all forces' converted mission dataset, and those counts are marked converted-corpus evidence, not fresh vanilla-game counts. for example, one m018 phase is recorded as 361 panels plus a set of turret parts, followed by final-form panels and generators; this is a source-matched layout example, not proof that every difficulty instantiates identical numbers of enemies. earth eater collision and effects: separate concerns a panel's shkt/body collision layer, a turret's mab locator, a script's active/inactive state and its damage filter are distinct systems. a recreated edf4.1 panel in edf6 may inherit the wrong collision layer (an investigated edf6 wrapper could set 17 instead of original panel layer 0) while still having correct visual locators. conversely, successful shots at the shell do not prove the core's hidden weakpoint behavior is preserved. source and credit: kh-edf41-motherships, facts ufomother401-hull, ufomother401-parts, ufomother401-turret-mounts, ufomother401-turret-roll, ufomother401-mission-data; plus edf4.1 panel collision classes. source-derived only; no new game runtime.

edf5 input: keyboard snapshot, win32 focus, mouse delta and dynamic xinput edf5 on windows uses a win32 message-pump keyboard snapshot, a separate dynamically loaded xinput pad path and a focus gate. these are separate from edf6's later raw-input behavior; replacing one input api does not imply every game input source has changed. the keyboard snapshot the studied edf5 executable maintains 256 bytes of getkeyboardstate data. its message-pump thread fills the snapshot under a critical section and the consumer copies it and clears a refreshed flag. the source observes a single getkeyboardstate call per pump refresh, not ad-hoc polling of every key by every gameplay subsystem. the code imports getkeyboardstate, getkeystate, getforegroundwindow, cursor and window functions. it does not statically import getasynckeystate, directinput or xinput. instead, the pad loader obtains xinput9_1_0.dll dynamically and uses xinputgetstate from its resolved function pointer. therefore the absence of a static xinput import is not proof that the game lacks controller support. focus gates keyboard and mouse, not all input the pump compares getforegroundwindow() against its own stored window handle and writes a focus byte. when not focused, the keyboard path is skipped, the mouse delta is zeroed and cursor recentering stops; the keyboard snapshot itself can continue to update. the observed xinput controller path is not gated the same way: contributor tests found pad gameplay could continue when another window was in the foreground while keyboard-derived hotkeys did not work. the focused mouse path uses getwindowrect, getcursorpos and setcursorpos to measure displacement from the window centre. a menu-controlled byte can temporarily suppress recentering. the source also describes special filtering for wm_syskeydown/alt in peekmessage dispatch and an ime detach/re-attach policy that affects text entry. performance note in one researcher recording, the message-pump thread remained 99.7% busy and accounted for a substantial share of sampled process cpu cycles; it included sleep(0) and repeatedly called the win32 pump. this is a particular profiler observation, not an edf5-wide constant, and must not be generalized into a fixed fps performance improvement claim. evidence: static win32 call tracing, binary reading and contributor-controlled focus tests; no new runtime in this edition. build-scoped example: message pump near rva 0x60bc90 and keyboard snapshot address 0x1253600 in the investigated edf5.exe. sources and credit: kh-edf5-input fact ids keyboard-snapshot, keyboard-snapshot-slot, input-pump-focus, xinput-loader, input-mouse-delta, input-pump-thread-busy; community researcher novae/ajane. see binding table layout.

edf5 controls: keybinding codes, class pages, conflict rules and cfg layout edf5 stores bindings as integer input codes, not textual key names. in the source's examined build, a per-player binding block contains 10 categories with 255 action slots in each category. the native menu exposes only named subsets of those slots, and the rest are not proof of usable user-facing controls. code domains code range device / meaning 0 unbound 1–0x0b gamepad a/b/x/y, triggers, shoulder buttons, sticks and back 0x0c–0x11 mouse buttons, wheel and side buttons 0x12–0x78 keyboard keys from the game's own lookup table the keyboard list includes letters, digits, numpad keys, f1–f12, modifiers, arrows, navigation/editing keys and several locale-specific keys. these are internal game codes, not windows virtual-key values and not automatically directinput scan codes. menu pages and action groups page kind native action range group 0–1 0x00–0x14 gamepad pages 2 0x15–0x20 common keyboard 3 0x21–0x27 soldier classes 4 0x28–0x2f fencer 5 0x30–0x34 drive 6 0x35–0x37 tanks 7 0x38–0x3c combat frame 8 0x3d–0x41 bulga 9 0x42–0x46 depth crawler 10 0x47–0x49 helicopter the source's per-class categories 0 ranger, 1 wing diver, 2 air raider, 3 fencer contain overlapping common actions. a given menu label can be class-dependent: “dash/boost” represents different movement for ranger and wing diver, and may not appear for air raider. duplicate bindings and reserved codes the menu's assignment routine swaps a chosen key with another action on the same page that already uses it, rather than simply permitting arbitrary duplicates. a separate conflict routine reports 0 reserved, 1 already selected, -1 available. some assignments are mirrored across soldier-class categories when the page item carries a shared-action flag. one action stores one int32 code. the surveyed table does not encode modifier chords such as alt+b as a compound key, even if the underlying os can detect modifiers; an external remapper and the native binding table do different jobs. persistent configuration and scope the source places the table in the game's common.cfg representation, following camera-setting fields, with an address formula based on player, category and action index. it also traces the menu text to localized optionplayer_keyboard* strings. these addresses belong to the studied edf5.exe; do not use them as universal offsets for every distribution or patch version. sources and credit: kh-edf5-input facts keybind-table, keybind-codes, keybind-pages-vehicles, keybind-common-ids, keybind-assign, keybind-no-chords; original edf5 source investigator's code reading. no input-mod experiments were run in this edition. see windows input path.

edf4.1, edf5 and edf6 — how item crates spawn a defeated enemy does not independently roll a simple yes/no probability for every crate. in the source builds of edf4.1, edf5 and edf6, a drop quantity from the enemy's game_object_drop_item contributes to a shared floating-point accumulator maintained by the pickup manager. the manager subtracts a fixed threshold for each crate due and then selects a crate category by weight. this explains why low-point enemies can apparently drop nothing for several kills, then one more kill produces an item. drop rate is a threshold for the investigated builds, the threshold is 0.947. the source describes the following approximate progression for a single drop event: add the enemy's configured drop amount to the manager's current accumulator. while the accumulator is above the threshold, subtract 0.947 and attempt to spawn one crate. if the map is already at the on-field limit, that attempt produces no crate, but the threshold has already been subtracted. retain the remainder for later enemy deaths. the formula for an ideal long-run average, before caps and other rules, is approximately expected crates = sum(enemy drop amounts) / 0.947. the accumulator is shared across kills, not a separate bucket for each enemy. a contributor compared edf5 enemy sgo drop values with a japanese community drop table: examples include 2.4 for a silver spider and 0.29 for a black ant, rather than 240% and 29% independent bernoulli events. category probabilities per emitted crate category edf4.1 weight edf4.1 share edf5 weight edf6 weight edf5/6 share weapon box 5 13.16% 6 6 15.79% armor box 18 47.37% 15 15 39.47% small recovery 12 31.58% 14 14 36.84% large recovery 3 7.89% 3 3 7.89% total 38 100% 38 38 100% these are conditional category shares after a crate is emitted. they are not the probability that a given enemy will drop an item. edf4.1's category weights were found at a96060, edf5's at e9cd00, and edf6's at 17a6ce8, each tied to its named executable build. all three source builds have an on-map limit of 128 crates and a mission collection limit of 1024. the latter is not the same as the former. hitting the 128-on-map limit can permanently waste a crate that would otherwise be created because the threshold is still consumed. what happens after pickup? collecting weapon or armor crates is separate from awarding a particular weapon or increasing armor. edf5's source shows that these categories initially increment mission counters; the final selection occurs in a separate mission-result roll. edf6 also distinguishes box pickup from result-screen weapon selection. health boxes are handled immediately by a different path. online edf6 adds host arbitration for pickup ownership, described in edf6's pickup lifecycle. evidence and scope this is a synthesis of static source research, not a fresh gameplay test. the edf6 workbook documents an expected-value calculation but does not list every enemy's drop amount, so no universal enemies-to-crates count is implied. the exact 0.947 threshold and category weights refer to the studied steam builds; do not treat their offsets as cross-version constants. sources and credit: kh-edf41-pickups facts pickup-limits, drop-rate, edf41-drop-accumulator, edf41-crate-kind-weights; kh-edf5-drop-items facts drop-rate-accumulator, crate-kind-weights, dropitem-field-limit, dropitem-collect-cap; kh-edf6-pickups facts pickup-limits, drop-rate, drop-category-weights, drop-rate-model, dropitem-life. research compiled by novae (ajane), including contributions credited to fevgrave, stafern, kittopia and redone.

edf5 — the weapon-and-armor result roll picking up a green or red item box is not the same operation as receiving a particular weapon or armor increase. in the investigated edf5 executable, dropitemmanager::unit accounts for crates during play, while the native 1991d0 result routine later allocates weapon and armor rewards into save records. this makes the result screen a second stage of the loot system. when boxes become rewards weapon and armor pickups increment distinct mission counts (dropitemmanager+0xa88 and +0xa8c). the result entry collects them, combines retained counts where applicable, seeds an independent mersenne twister and assigns the reward categories. weapon entries carry eight star bytes; persistence merges those into saved weapon progression by keeping each statistic's maximum grade rather than replacing a higher existing grade with a lower one. spawn and reward counts are subject to separate limits. the result routine cannot roll more boxes than were actually spawned in the current mission: the manager records weapon and armor spawn totals at +0xad8 and +0xadc. the original 1024 pickup cap does not mean 1024 distinct weapons are guaranteed or available. which class receives a box? the source's four-class weighted allocation starts each class at 100 for both weapon and armor. the locally played class is raised to 600 for weapon crates and 250 for armor crates. with exactly one local player: reward type played class each of the three other classes weapon 600/900 = 66.67% 100/900 = 11.11% armor 250/550 = 45.45% 100/550 = 18.18% these probabilities are for class assignment of an eligible box and change with additional local players and game state. they are not final probabilities for a particular weapon or star grade. level range and candidate eligibility a mission's position within the selected list gives a normalized progression fraction t = missionindex / (missioncount - 1). edf5 reads a low/high/spread triple from defaultpackage/config.sgo's modelist[mode][6][difficulty][2]. the source-derived model uses: center = low + (high - low) × t width = max(0.05, 0.05 × (high - low)) lower edge roughly max(0, center - spread); upper edge includes a narrow positive allowance for star-bearing weapons the routine also checks class category, acquisition status, source missionpack (modelist[mode][8]) and weapon-table row eligibility. ordinary weapons may appear across packs, whereas pack-owned weapon rows are constrained to their intended pack. a jp wiki comparison found exact predicted lowest/highest levels in 473 of 550 sampled cells and predictions within one level in the other 77; this is supporting correlation, not independent binary proof of every edge case. failure-state retention is different a separate edf5 mission failed routine calculates a fraction of collected crates that may be retained: easy 100%, normal 75%, hard 50%, hardest 25%, inferno 0%, truncating the number of crates. this is a result-screen count path, not a change to crate spawning itself. the source audit did not fully trace the later handoff from this screen to final rolling, so do not infer further award semantics from this fraction alone. sources and credit: kh-edf5-drop-items, facts dropitem-collect-counters, loot-roll-entry, loot-roll-class-share, loot-roll-level-window, loot-roll-level-window-check, loot-roll-candidates, loot-roll-caps-spawned, loot-failed-mission-kept; static reverse engineering by novae (ajane), supported by the referenced japanese edf5 drop-range tests. all rvas refer to steam-5d11de53. no fresh in-game roll was performed. further native-game references original edf5 failure and result path

edf6 — pickups, healing, physics and online claims an edf6 pickup box is a dropitemmanager::unit stored in a manager-owned linked list, not a general enemy gameobjectbase and not a hidden extra kind of hostile object. the manager owns the physical box instances, their category, their online ids, pickup counters and the running drop accumulator. four item models and their behavior type native model from app:/object/itemmodel.mrab when effect is applied 0 weapon.mdb counts a weapon crate for end-of-mission result 1 armor.mdb counts an armor crate for end-of-mission result 2 healingsmall.mdb immediately heals the picker: 15% max hp 3 healingbig.mdb immediately heals the picker: 30% max hp the item manager in the studied edf6 build has a list head at +0xde0, item count at +0xde8, a drop accumulator at +0xdf0 and a next-box id at +0xe00. individual unit objects hold category at +0xc0, picked flag at +0xc4, box id at +0xc8 and a physical transform. these are version-specific field locations, not a general edf engine abi. who can collect? the soldier update calls the pickup manager once per update for an eligible local player. the pickup is tested against a point roughly one metre above the soldier position, using squared distance and a radius assembled from the soldier's class/state, certain accessories and the vehicle seat while mounted. a default base radius of 3.0 metres appears in the examined constructor; other states can increase it. the actor must be alive and have the local player-controller field set. npc allies walking through a pickup do not collect it. recovery items can propagate healing to living recruited followers using a separate recursion and ratio rule. in the source's ordinary player configuration that follower ratio is 0.35; an equipment-derived factor may alter it. this does not imply an identical ally-healing rule for edf4.1 or edf5. pickups persist until a cleanup condition dropitemmanager maintains a physical box list, clamps horizontal positions into the map area, removes boxes after pickup or when their height falls below −1000, and clears the list on mission change. the source did not find a universal short crate timeout or an automatic map-wide magnet in the ordinary native path. the on-field limit is 128 crates and the collected-crate limit is 1024 for this build. online protocol and ownership the source distinguishes four message kinds: message native meaning 0 replicate a newly spawned crate, using an agreed seed/id 1 guest requests the host to claim a particular box 2 host publishes the confirmed pickup to participants 3 request that an enemy death create dropped items the picker applies the pickup locally, then communicates with the host. the host arbitrates which player first claims an unpicked id and prevents duplicated weapon/armor counts. the source has no rollback if a guest applied an immediate local pickup that the host rejects. box ids can be negative; they are not equivalent to an enemy owner id. evidence boundary: the state and message flow are static analysis of steam-678ccb46. an offline invocation of the game's own functions (83 checks) confirmed some radius and serialization behavior, but that is not a live multiplayer or complete game-run test. the original appendix labels those facts accordingly. sources and credit: kh-edf6-pickups facts dropitem-manager-layout, dropitem-life, pickup-update, pickup-update-caller, pickup-gates-effects, pickup-award-dispatch, pickup-online, pickup-limits; novae (ajane). see crate generation and end-of-mission rewards in edf5. further native-game references native healing and ally credit

edf6 efs/esb — anatomy of a particle effect edf6 has an efs effect graph that is distinct from ordinary model materials and audio. in the source's native examples, effect definitions are .esb resources inside .efarc archives whose layout resembles rab. an .efarc can hold its model, texture and sprite-setting resources alongside the effect definitions. the graph dispatches components, not one monolithic particle object. hierarchy and timing node role effect root references the effect to dispatch, an integer start delay in frames and an unknown field effect owns an array of components, a system lifetime and additional unresolved fields singleton one model, glow, quad or other renderer with transform and color emitter repeatedly creates moving particle instances from a shape and emission rule nodeparticle_particle2d defines lifetime, color, scalar curves and 2d-oriented particle rendering nodeparticle_particle3d defines 3d particle movement/scale/rotation evolution and lifetime the source observes effect root with the child effect reference before its timing/unknown values in the raw binary order. a third-party xml tool may present a different field order. tool output ordering is not proof of a different edf6 wire format. emitter anatomy the observed 17-field emitter includes nodetransform, emission nodeshape, a particle definition, color, initial rotation/scale, initial-speed curve, an emissionrate curve and a maxparticle limit. one field is labelled isrelative: in the source's interpretation, relative particles continue moving with the parent emitter, whereas non-relative particles can trail behind. several unclassified integer and float fields remain unknown and should not be given invented enum names. animationcurve contains a type/flags region of uncertain meaning, a float variance, a keyframe count and seven floats per keyframe. the source identifies keyframe time and value; the other five floats are not decoded conclusively. a time value is usually frames, but the source explicitly notes exceptions. rendering a particle renderinfo_texture uses a referenced texture, scalar size, a render-mode field and optional geometry such as a ring mesh. renderinfo_model uses an embedded .mdb model and can carry animation-driven shader parameter changes. renderinfo_locusextendline creates a trail whose length/lifetime and width can evolve over time; renderinfo_extline stretches a line between an earlier location and the particle's current position. some texture render flags appear to affect blend mode, screen-depth interaction or rotation, but their exact semantics are not settled. different language pages and experiments disagree on one rotation flag. a reader should preserve native values rather than normalizing everything into a guessed universal material type. evidence limits the node families, archive relationship and selected fields come from static inspections and documented community experiments. this edition neither generated new effects in edf6 nor tested every emitter type. efs and regular .mdb materials have independent lifetime and rendering contracts, even when an effect renderer references an mdb asset. sources and credit: kh-edf6-effects facts efs-overview, efs-effect-root, efs-effect, efs-singleton, efs-emitter, efs-animation-curve, efs-particle2d, efs-particle3d, efs-renderinfo-texture, efs-renderinfo-model, efs-renderinfo-locus, efs-renderinfo-extline; original japanese/english community research collected by novae (ajane).

edf6 — visual effects are not the damage event a convincing explosion in edf6 can include particles, lighting, camera shake, audio, damage and destruction. those are separate mechanisms. the native effectgenutil singleton is a visual-effect dispatcher in the examined edf6 build: its functions create flames, explosions, shockwaves and other visual treatments, but do not by themselves inflict gameplay damage or play the damage object's death sound. visual families found in the native effect test table effect family source-recovered purpose flame / flame2 flame visuals, including variant parameters blazing fire and smoke treatment explosion standard blast visuals with scale/color parameters explosion_big larger composite of blast, smoke, wind and camera effects explosionwind smoke and blast motion treatment shockwave expansion/shockwave rendering and screen response stencillight timed positional light, radius and colored intensity linestripobject trail generated and drawn with a retained transform the debug registration db::createeffecttest lists effect invocations and their arguments. it is a useful static catalogue, not a promise that every debug command is exposed to retail players. representative native game calls the investigated ufocarrier508 death invokes the large-explosion visual path near its center and separately performs area damage with a 60-unit radius through another native call. its sound is also handled separately. movingfortress death and ufomother511 destruction similarly use effect helpers as one part of a larger object-state transition. thus copying only an effect's identifier or animation does not copy a boss's damage, state machine or explosion sound. the source also identifies chargeeffect_stdparticle, used for weapon charge glows; and linestripobject, whose render task retains the matrix supplied when the trail was constructed. a trail's motion and orientation cannot safely be inferred from the moving owner alone if the renderable holds its own original transform. lifetimes and ordering effectgenutil is instantiated in scene initialization and may be null outside a mission. its visual emitter and light managers are distinct from sound-channel managers. a stencillight initializer includes position, colors, radius and lifetime in frames; an internal path changes those parameters before display. persistent emitters own update and draw jobs and should not be assumed to disappear merely because a parent model's draw call stops. boundary these are source-level observations from steam-678ccb46, not fresh edf6 visual or damage tests. in particular, a named explosion helper may invoke camera shaking or other sub-effects but its mere presence does not establish damage volume, sound cue, or player hit rules. examine the caller's separate damage and audio operations for those facts. sources and credit: kh-edf6-effects, facts effectgenutil-calls, stencil-light-emitter-jobs, particle-emitter-class, charge-effect-std-particle, linestrip-trail-matrix, linestrip-object-lifecycle; novae (ajane), all forces source research.

edf5 — why blood, scorch and bullet-mark decals disappear edf5 uses a decalmanager and several decalbase-derived objects for splashes, projected stains, bullet marks and explosion marks. these are world-space render volumes, not paint permanently stored on map geometry. their removal rules explain why a mark can vanish long before the nominal lifespan expires. different decal families native class typical effect decal_splash ground or death-pool-like aligned decal decal_splashprojection hit blood or acid projected into world geometry decal_bulletmark bullet impact mark, including glowing/smouldering transition decal_explosionmarks blast/smoulder marks fullscreen_rain, dust, fog fullscreen classes in the broader decal family, not identical to a wall mark the studied constructors receive an initparam with lifetime and strength. decalbase separately tracks age, time spent undrawn, fade/dissolve and bounds. the reported ordinary duration is 20 seconds, but that number is not a guarantee a particular decal remains visible for 20 seconds. the rules that remove marks early out of view: the examined update logic deletes a decal after approximately one second not drawn, irrespective of the remaining nominal lifetime. the researcher verified this effect in game by changing the comparisons and seeing decals persist much longer. global capacity: the ordinary pool has a limit of roughly 100 managed decals, with eviction when more arrive. stacking/overlap: about 6 overlapping marks can cause fading and 8 can cause removal in the observed configuration. a new bullet mark can thus evict an older blood stain on the same wall. this overlap behavior was also tested by the source investigator. normal age and fading: an older decal loses importance and ultimately ends its own lifetime, with special glow/fade curves for some mark classes. the manager ranks living candidates using a factor of remaining lifetime, decal strength and time undrawn. it compares general and overlapping candidates before deciding what to demote or remove. the source notes that one hard-removal path may unlink a decal from the manager without proving immediate visual destruction; that distinction remains unverified. projection and attachment the hit-blood spawner raycasts forward and creates a perspective-projected volume only after finding a surface. its ray reach, projection depth and weight are partly linked, which means changing range can change stain appearance as well as distance. the acid spawner follows a different, simpler distance/depth path. a decal is registered in world space and is not dynamically attached to the specific wall chunk or enemy limb it struck. consequently, a building fragment moving or disappearing does not imply the decal will move with it. performance and evidence each decal is submitted individually, and inserting one requires considering the manager's tracked set. high decal counts therefore have real cpu and rendering costs; the game does not treat 10,000 projected marks as an ordinary budget. the contributor reported a test in which many decals survived after changing removal rules, but that is not proof of normal performance or memory safety at such counts. sources and credit: kh-edf5-decals facts decal-classes, decal-fields, decal-life-cycle, decal-undrawn-in-game, decal-eviction, decal-stacking-in-game, decal-cost, decal-spawners, acid-reach, decal-world-space, decal-game-values; novae (ajane). static findings and source-reported gameplay tests are distinguished here; this edition ran no game test.

edf5 spider webs — rope simulation and capture an aranea's web is not just a line sprite with damage. in the examined edf5 code, spiderstringbullet01 and spiderstringbullet02 own rope-node arrays and render their strands through the game's line-strip path. a successful hit can create a separate grab object, modify the soldier's capture state and pull the target toward an anchor. the rope, graphics and warning color each constructed spider-web bullet receives exactly ten rope nodes. for the inspected type-01 path, 0x30-byte rendering vertices are rebuilt from the rope nodes every update, with position, rgba color, longitudinal texture coordinate and strand width. type-02 also has a separate vertex vector and draw path. consequently a strand's line is geometry updated by the bullet, not a static mdb pasted between two endpoints. type-01 webs attached to a locally controlled player can switch to a warning state: the renderer alternates ammo color and red with a phase advancing at approximately 10 hz. the source investigator observed that flashing when an aranea held and reeled in the player. not every white spider strand in a scene was successfully identified with one of these two callbacks; a level-placed spidernet object remains a possible separate source. capture requires a grab object on a qualifying web hit, a native callback tests the hit rope node and candidate target, constructs a 0x150-byte grab object and links it to the web's active capture list. the grab records the node, initial target–anchor length, stall/best-distance state and owner. capture messages travel through the soldier's game-object handler and transition it to a held state, rather than simply applying damage or changing an animation. the source notes that some shield and online conditions can refuse an attach. a particular spiderstringbullet01 online flag skips an attach path; do not generalize that into “spider webs never capture online.” the source also has a distinct kind-1 grab/guard condition. how the web reels in the player the type-01 held-target update reduces the rope's permitted length by about 0.05 metres per 60-hz frame, approximately 3 m/s, once taut. it updates a hold point; the held soldier then receives an additional velocity equivalent to roughly six times the gap per second between itself and that hold point. at sufficiently high pull speeds, the walk state is altered to prevent opposing movement from counteracting the pull in the same way. the web releases captures when the owner disappears, the target no longer exists, or the target's capture state no longer matches. it can play a reeling sound for a local player's target; release messages have their own talk-line logic. these interactions are separate from the drawing of the visible strand. evidence boundary the ten-node layout, grab structure and pull math are static reverse engineering of steam-5d11de53. the flashing appearance and some rendering changes are source-reported gameplay observations; no new capture test was performed here. some spiderstringbullet02 behavior and a universal on-screen direction arrow remain open. sources and credit: kh-edf5-stingers-webs facts web-classes-and-types, web-vertices, web-rope-nodes, web-blink, edf5-web-attach, edf5-web-grab-fields, edf5-grab-object, edf5-web-reel, edf5-web-pull, edf5-web-release-talk, edf5-web-open; novae (ajane) and the original edf5 web investigations.

edf5 — needlebullet01 bee stingers bee stingers in edf5 are represented by the needlebullet01 ammunition class. the research identifies both a line-based draw path and a model draw path, selected by an ammunition custom parameter. they share a physical projectile and impact lifecycle, but should not be mistaken for a conventional dropped model asset. the native draw geometry the stinger draws from a bullet-to-render transform: a position and an oriented z axis. the source reconstructs its segment as position ± (z direction × 25 × ammosize). in the model mode, a uniform matrix scale uses ammosize; in the line mode it affects both length and width. ammo_customparameter[0] selects the mode (observed 0 = stretched line, 1 = model); exactly which mode every bee variant uses was not exhaustively verified. the line's geometry is centered on the collision point. the investigator observed that when a stinger strikes the ground, reducing its size causes the visible tip to disappear below the surface, rather than retract uniformly from the pointed end. that is a reported game observation, not just a mathematical guess. fade is a material-and-depth operation a stuck needle can be faded by changing the alpha of its draw color. model mode loads a constant rgba (1,1,1,1) into the draw-utility shader path; line mode uses the ammo color. the source also notes that depth writing must be disabled during transparent fading, otherwise a transparent stinger can still occlude other geometry as though it were opaque. the contributor reported the fading approach as tested, rather than simply reading the call graph. the model uses the game’s draw-utility color-lighting shader. this is not necessarily the same material configuration as the environment mdb it appears to strike. impact smoke is spawned separately via a helper and fragment emitter; changing the needle geometry alone will not copy or remove all impact effects. stuck state and cleanup the source identifies a hit flag inside the needle's render subobject and a lifetime at projectile +0x3f8. once the original lifetime expires, a stuck projectile enters a 300-frame cleanup countdown; an unstuck expired projectile is removed by its own path. the hit flag's precise behavioral interpretation was inferred statically and was not separately reverified in game. the five-second countdown is derived at a nominal 60-hz update rate, not an independently measured wall-clock promise. sources and credit: kh-edf5-stingers-webs facts stinger-callback, stinger-geometry, stinger-has-hit, stinger-draw-and-fade, stinger-draw-paths, stinger-centered-on-hit, stinger-removal-timer, stinger-impact-dust; novae (ajane). investigated executable: edf5 steam-5d11de53.

edf6 — how a collision becomes damage a projectile collision, a gamedamageinfo record and an hp change are three different stages of edf6 combat. the source identifies a native hit message (0x10000000) that carries an attacker handle, team, damage, impact position, damage flags and a vector of individual contact points with rigid-body identities. a broadphase intersection alone is not yet that message. what the hit record contains in the examined steam-678ccb46 build, key offsets of the 0x90-byte record are: record offset meaning +0x10/+0x18 weak attacker object reference +0x20 hit type; type 4 forces an unconditional part rate +0x24 team, −1 means no team rule +0x30 world-space impact position +0x50 base damage; negative can represent healing +0x58 blast amount/radius-related field in relevant paths +0x60 bitfield affecting forced hits, rate and special treatment +0x68 shield multiplier +0x70 contact-point vector; 0x30 bytes per contact each contact entry stores a world point and havok body id. the id is local to that machine's physics world, not an online global identity. bosses that only accept hits on one specific part can translate the body id into a ragdoll body index and reject other contacts; checking only the collision position cannot reproduce that native rule. direct projectile hit sequence in a shape-cast hit, edf6 first obtains the world impact fraction, point, normal and body. it resolves the body to a sceneobject and, when eligible, records that object and its contact into the bullet's own direct-hit queue. a queue entry is keyed by target. a second collision against a target already queued merges the contact points and does not simply double the queued damage. the queue is settled synchronously in the relevant bullet update/collision path; it is not a universal all-frame deferred hit bus. the bullet's hit record lives in the bullet core (core+0x730, in the source the core is the bullet at +0x140), whereas the queue is at core+0x6e0. some explosion-only bullets clear the direct-hit queue and use a separate blast path. a render-only contact or nearest bounding-box candidate should never be counted as a confirmed gameplay hit. area damage is another query gamedamageinfo::applyareadamage performs a region query around its position and radius. depending on the caller, it uses a collision-layer filter, a team rule, optional ignored object and optional already-hit set. the area query produces candidate game objects; the damage path then queues hit events for those that qualify. stock caller examples include boss deaths and bullet explosions. a visual explosion_big call does not, by itself, invoke this damage query; see visual explosions. evidence boundary all offsets and call order refer to the surveyed edf6 dll. the source explicitly corrected an earlier mistaken identification of one stack argument: it is collision filter data, not a camera frame. this article follows that later correction. no new game or network capture was performed. sources and credit: kh-edf6-damage-model facts hit-record-layout, hit-points-bodies, bullet-hit-queue, direct-hit-to-damage-path, area-damage-call, damage-function-part-rate, vehicle-weapon-owner; novae (ajane), original contributors. see special body-part damage.

edf6 — armor and shields are different damage targets a visible enemy can contain multiple independently simulated parts. this is crucial for interpreting damage numbers and for understanding why a bullet can collide with a model while the target's main hp does not decrease. multi-part bosses and source body identity native deroy leg/core pieces, some queens and armored humanoids are not always one game object with a decorative material change. some boss components are separate game objects with their own hp and damage events. other targets, including ufocarrier508 and movingfortress in the examined source, use a ragdoll body's identity to determine which exact weak component accepts a hit. the gamedamageinfo contact vector includes physical body ids. a boss may demand that at least one contact maps to a particular core or open hatch part. without the correct body mapping, the visual appearance of a hit is insufficient to prove damage eligibility. armor on humanoids the investigated humanoid classes share a part lookup through their +0x6c0 part manager. each armor piece holds its own durability and state. the main damage function asks the target for a part damage multiplier (virtual slot byte offset 0x88); an intact armor piece returns 0 for body hp damage. that yields the native white 0 damage number on armored colonists and greys, rather than a missing hit event. when an armor piece's durability reaches zero it can break and change the effective part multiplier. this is distinct from killing the parent humanoid. a special hit flag 0x1000 skips armor-piece durability loss in the researched path; if the closest part still supplies a rate of zero, the result is zero damage to both armor and body. the source reports a game observation of white zeroes for certain gas and electric-line attacks against armored greys, but the mapping of that flag to every such projectile is not completely traced. carried shields use a separate receiver a humanoid's shield (edf6_softbodyweapon_shield) is a weapon-derived sceneobject, not a normal gameobjectbase. it receives the same hit-message family but handles it in its own shield routine, outside the parent's ordinary damage function. its guard_settings include maximum/current durability, per-hit cap, recovery delay/speed and reload time. a hit's shield damage is bounded by the shield multiplier and maximum-damage setting; reflection mode can also gate durability consumption. consequently, a hit absorbed by an intact shield produces no normal hud damage number in the source-reported vanilla gameplay, unlike an armored body-part hit that can produce a white zero. shield breaking and regeneration are state transitions belonging to that shield object; they should not be represented as merely an armor texture switching off. boundaries this describes static code plus source-declared observations on edf6 steam-678ccb46. the exact 0x1000 hit-origin classification is not fully proved, and this article does not claim that all enemy shields or every boss part share one abi. build-specific field offsets are not safe generalizations to edf5 or edf4.1. sources and credit: kh-edf6-damage-model facts multipart-boss-parts, hit-points-bodies, humanoid-hit-path, humanoid-parts-manager, hit-part-lookup, armor-zero-and-break, flag-1000-zero-hits, gas-electric-flag-1000, zero-hits-armored-aliens, enemy-shield-class, enemy-shield-settings, enemy-shield-hit, enemy-shield-no-number; original research compiled by novae (ajane).

edf6 online damage is not a stream of every hit edf6 does not publish every nonlethal hit as a full record with attacker, contact points and event data to all clients. the investigated native path separates local hit processing, killing-blow events and hp-delta or absolute-hp synchronization. that distinction explains why two machines can temporarily disagree on a floating damage number or hit reaction while the target's health later converges. which machine owns a hit? the applydamage path first tests whether the current scene is online; then it considers attacker identity, a remote-copy flag, an optional forced-hit bit and a target-specific virtual decision. ordinary game objects, controlled players and vehicles can answer that decision differently. a simulated bullet on a guest machine is not automatically authoritative merely because its collision system detects an intersection. the source identifies a guest pre-filter that suppresses certain attackerless, non-forced hits when the room is active. this is not a rule that an attackerless hit never deals damage: the host's corresponding path may process it. likewise, an attacker handle may refer to a vehicle rather than the player in its seat. network paths after local damage change audited transmission principle nonfatal hit accumulate health difference for a later delta message alive → dead transition send the killing-hit event with a new target epoch periodic or forced reconciliation send absolute hp with an epoch for the investigated target object, an outgoing delta is an integer truncated from the accumulated local float difference. the sender monitors thresholds relative to maximum hp, time and dead state rather than broadcasting each fraction immediately. the receive routine compares epoch counters and discards stale events. a received same-epoch delta can update a living object without replaying the original weapon hit or its contact location. in the source's implementation, the kill event is raised by the alive-to-dead flag transition. a later nonlethal hp delta with an older epoch can be discarded. this is one reason another machine may never visually reconstruct the exact sequence of hit numbers preceding a death. periodic absolute hp messages can repair health totals but cannot recreate a missed stagger or projectile-internal state. why hud observations can differ the original contributor reported an online session where each player saw their own damage numbers. the local ui event is not the same as the network event. a shield-hit absence or armored-part zero is also controlled by the local target's native hit implementation; neither implies the ordinary position snapshot was lost. evidence and scope these claims are sourced from static edf6 re plus that specifically reported online observation. they do not constitute a new paired packet capture or a proof that every desync is caused by hp epochs. the gameplay event packet layer, retained rudp and projectile-state serialization remain separate mechanisms. sources and credit: kh-edf6-damage-model facts online-damage-authority, online-hit-processing-decision, online-hit-kill-only, online-hp-delta-sync, online-guest-drops-attackerless, online-own-numbers, online-hit-send, online-hit-receive; novae (ajane). see network event classes and pickup ownership.

edf6 — healing, rescue and support are separate mechanics the original edf6 combat code distinguishes increasing hp, reviving a player, providing a support buff and crediting a healer's battle statistics. these actions share some recipients but are not interchangeable and do not all emit the same network or achievement events. ordinary healing and pickup recovery the native addhp routine clamps hp between a target's allowed minimum and maximum. it refuses to heal a target in a fully dead state. edf6 recovery crates (type 2 small, type 3 large) restore 15% and 30% of maximum hp, respectively, on the ordinary collection path. the pickup handler can also heal the picker’s living follower npcs with a separate configured fraction. these recovery paths do not necessarily credit a soldier's recorded healdamage statistic. source re explicitly notes that health pickups and revives do not send the same healer-credit message as healing weapons. healing messages and credit a healing hit can be expressed as negative base damage in the hit record. when it is applied, the game can send 0x10000007 to the healer with the target and float amount restored. native contributors found additional sources of that event: supportunitbullet01 type 0 (e.g. a healing support device) the vehicle507_rescuetank healing its riders and attributing it to the driver hit processing on a remote target, where the message amount may initially be an estimate because this machine does not own the actual hp the receiving soldier handler increments healdamage only when the healer is player-controlled, the target is not self, their teams are not hostile and the target accepts the credited category. self-healing by a life vent therefore does not automatically count in the same way as healing an ally. revival moves hp between players the native player-rescue function gives the revived player half of the rescuer's current hp, subject to the revived player's hp bounds, clears its dead-state flags and restores team participation. the rescuer loses that amount through addhp(negative value). it is not equivalent to picking up a large health crate or adding the same hp to both participants. support is not always recovery supportunitbullet01 types 1–3 are buff operations, not direct hp restoration: the source describes one as increasing a target attribute, another as lowering incoming-damage multiplier and another as increasing a further gameplay multiplier. their object fields are build-specific; the source does not prove a universal ui label for every subtype. evidence boundary all named routines and message fields are from the investigated edf6 binary, not a new rescue or online healing test. the source warns that the healer-credit message can be produced even in an edge case with an amount at or below zero; do not treat every observed event as proof that a player gained hp. sources and credit: kh-edf6-damage-model facts addhp, health-pickup, heal-credit-message, heal-credit-receiver, player-rescue, support-unit-buffs; novae (ajane). see pickup owner and recovery.

edf5 — where the mission ends and results are committed edf5 stores campaign behavior in mission bvm bytecode interpreted by its mission runtime. the missionmgr object owns the active missionscript, and script state changes are distinct from which ui banner or result screen is currently visible. this matters when determining whether a mission has ended, failed, or actually committed its collected rewards and progress to save data. native mission-script lifecycle the investigated missionscript has states observed as 0 created, 1 started, 2 playing and later terminal/result states. its result flag is separate from its execution state. endmission(script, result) can be invoked from the mission bvm, debug control, pause menu, failed dialog and retry flow, with different result codes. a visible failure screen alone does not prove which exact final result has been committed. the angelscript mission() native yields while a mission remains in the started/playing states; once a terminal state is reached, it returns the recorded result for higher-level menu logic. the original scripts layer several fades, sounds, layouts and result dialogs around that event. failure and game over the source's missiongameoverevent script checks an all-players-down condition. its failure sequence draws lyt_huimissionfailed.sgo, plays the failure jingle, opens the failed-result ui and ultimately calls endmission according to the user's retry/exit choice. this is not the same as any arbitrary loss of one player's hp in co-op. on a failed result, edf5 retains a difficulty-dependent fraction of collected weapon and armor boxes: easy 100%, normal 75%, hard 50%, hardest 25% and inferno 0%, using integer truncation. the retained source did not fully establish how every failed-screen branch later reaches the actual reward draw, so this should be described as a retained box-count result rule, not a guarantee of a particular item award. save commit and result order applyresult(ismissionclear) first calls the pickup manager's loot-record commit routine. only after that does its clear-only branch mark progress and perform relevant online result synchronization. clearresult and a related reset routine clear mission counters. because the commit and clear-only progress branch are separate, testing only the visible mission-complete banner is insufficient to prove weapon save data and progression were both recorded. mission numbers are list positions, not directory numbers the folder mission/mnnn is an asset identifier; the on-screen mission number is the entry's position in missionlist.offline.list.sgo or missionlist.online.list.sgo. the source's original edf5 list audit finds 110 offline and 111 online main missions, with tutorial and two late online missions producing the difference. do not confuse those original-list measurements with the 112/111 and later 112/112 tables of a separately studied converted edf5→edf6 package. sources and credit: kh-edf5-mission-flow facts missionmgr-fields, missionscript-state-values, endmission, mission-native-yields, mission-gameover-event, mission-clear-bits, applyresult-native, clearresult-reset, result-tally-retention, mission-folder-not-number, mission-list-order, mission-lists-offline-online; community investigator novae (ajane), source build steam-5d11de53. no edf5 game test was performed for this wiki release.

edf4.1 — sound is driven by two distinct routes music playback, scripted radio speech and nearby soldiers' conversational cues are not the same edf4.1 subsystem. the original executable uses a soundcontroller for playback and a talkmanager for choosing and scheduling spoken cues. this distinction matters when a cue appears in several mission scripts or a speaker's line changes between soldiers. music and fade logic soundcontroller::playbgm at build-relative 0x3e7c10 receives a narrow cue name. its three traced callers are the debug bgm command, bvm native 300, and the menu/system angelscript playbgm function. a player handle stored on the controller determines whether music is currently playing. the cross-fade path (0x3e7c80) fades out the existing handle, releases it, starts the next cue and applies a fade-in. bvm native 302 performs this transition with a fade duration; native 301 fades out the current music without starting a replacement. the stop/cross-fade debug commands use the corresponding engine routes. these function addresses apply to the examined steam-57aab039 build, not arbitrary versions. why npc talk selection varies the talkmanager reads the speaker's talk sgo and chooses entries by weights, a bit-mask filter and a permitted numeric window. a selection can use either talkmanager's random generator or a per-call seed. a weight of zero makes that entry unselectable in the examined picker, though using this as a live data override was not tested. an npc stores a voice-variation index. cue placeholders such as u001e%s are resolved to variant suffixes (e.g. a–f) for the speaker, so two soldiers can select the same logical phrase but play different recorded takes. a selected line has a frame delay; the playback path chooses spatial or unplaced output, and can send an animation message to the speaker. radio dialogue uses a mission native bvm native 4000 invokes the radio-voice path rather than weighted npc chatter. the source census found 902 calls across 147 scripts, including musenbegin and musenend once each in every script. the radio route can stop the prior cue before playing a new one. this explains why a mission's radio click and ordinary soldier remarks need different interpretation, even if both ultimately use soundcontroller. evidence and credit: edf knowledge hub kh-edf41-sound, facts edf41-bgm-play, edf41-bgm-crossfade-stop, edf41-talk-line-pick, edf41-talk-voice-variant, edf41-talk-line-start, edf41-radio-voice-native; novae (ajane) and original kh contributors. static research only; no new edf4.1 game test.

edf5 — native audio banks and line scheduling edf5's surveyed windows build uses cri adx2 / cri atom, with the playback implementation linked into edf5.exe and a wasapi output path. this is not evidence that edf4.1 sound assets can be copied into edf5 unchanged. bank names, cue references, source voice variants and text/subtitles must be treated independently. bank and cue organization resource original logical path music app:/sound/adx/tikyuux_music.acb effects app:/sound/adx/tikyuux_se.%locale%.acb atom settings app:/sound/adx/tikyuux.acf voices app:/sound/adx/tikyuu5_voice.%locale%.awb and related banks a global soundcontroller owns the active music playback. music from bvm and menu scripts eventually reaches a shared play function. a cross-fade stops or fades the prior handle, releases it, plays a new cue and sets the fade-in duration. the native bvm calls in the studied scripts are 300 playbgm, 301 fadeoutbgm, 302 fadeinbgm, and 303 for a seek/start-offset variant. a survey of 141 scripts found 846 calls to 300, 747 to 301, 99 to 302 and six to 303. these are call-site counts, not the number of unique tracks. the npc voice tables are not dialogue text the examined edf5 dataset includes 20 talk sgo files, 1464 talk tables (135 empty), 10,792 entries and 5402 distinct audio cues. a table entry carries the cue, animation, selection weight, bit-mask condition, conditional numeric window and possibly a reply table. the manager selects a weighted entry, applies a speaker variant and schedules it through one of its channels. unlike edf6, edf5 has no general npc chatter transcript or corresponding edf6_voicetable in the surveyed resources. a small set of quick-chat ui messages pairs display text with voice cues, but ordinary soldier remarks' spoken words are in audio. a cue appearing in the sound bank therefore cannot automatically be treated as a subtitle identifier. the talkmanager updates four channels. while a line is playing it reduces a music-volume factor toward 0.3, restoring it toward 1.0 after speech stops. the precise interpretation of that controller float as the bgm multiplier is a static inference, not a separately captured audio measurement. evidence and credit: kh-edf5-sound facts audio-cri-adx2, audio-banks-paths, bgm-play-choke-point, edf5-bgm-crossfade-stop, edf5-bvm-bgm-natives, edf5-talk-line-pick, edf5-talk-entry-fields, edf5-talk-no-captions, edf5-talk-update-duck; source build steam-5d11de53 / novae (ajane). no r125 runtime test.

edf6 — the voice table is not the npc speech transcript edf6 adds a localized mission voice-caption table on top of separate dialogue cue selection and audio playback. three closely related objects must not be conflated: the npc talk sgo that chooses a cue, the cri sound bank that supplies audio, and edf6_voicetable.<locale>.sgo that supplies captions for selected scripted lines. soldier and alien speech selection the surveyed edf6 game resources include 30 talk sgo files with 2257 tables (281 empty), 16,289 entries and 8625 distinct cues. entries are now keyed dictionaries (with fields such as #0…#12 and mask) rather than edf5's flat 13-item lists. cue selection still uses weighted choices and speaker masks. a per-object talk variation determines which replacement letter is inserted into wildcard cue names such as aa001b*. the english mission edf6_voicetable contains 13,869 keys, but it principally covers scripted mission speech. only 11 keys use the observed ai-voice families; only seven of the 8625 talk-sgo cues were found with captions in that voice table. therefore the voice table is not a complete index of all casual npc dialogue, and the absence of a caption is not proof that a cue is unused or silent. music is semanager-owned the surveyed semanager stores the music handle at +0x20 and has distinct operations for ordinary play, cross-fade, play from a time offset and fade-out stop. the seek-play path converts the start offset from seconds to milliseconds. the native mission angelscript api exposes bgm, crossfadebgm, stopbgm, bgm2 and crossfadebgm2. in the decompiled mission-script set, the source counted 3277 bgm, 1165 crossfadebgm and 380 stopbgm calls; the two 2 forms had no calls in that corpus. these figures do not imply that every call is executed in a single playthrough. subtitle timing is separate from audio playback a voice/internal_voice call can play through talkmanager, but caption display depends on the queued voice group's caption key and a pending state. the subtitle builder looks up localized text by key; object.playse and some internal_voice use cases play only audio and are not general caption requests. the game can therefore correctly produce sound with no subtitle, even if a similar cue has a mission-caption entry. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-sound facts talk-variation-id, talk-wildcard-resolver, edf6-talk-sgo-entries, edf6-talk-no-captions, edf6-bgm-play-paths, edf6-bgm-script-natives, object-playse; and kh-edf6-talk-subtitles facts edf6-voice-natives, edf6-subtitle-when, edf6-subtitle-builder; build steam-678ccb46. no new game test. native talkactor countdowns and the 59.94 hz framework gate in the examined exact edf6 binary, two common caption actors use integer update-call countdowns, not elapsed-time subtraction: actor native update function countdown field initialization talkactor_object 0x1805db310 actor +0x7c caption lifetime metric × 60.0 talkactor_voice 0x1805db800 actor +0x40 caption lifetime metric × 60.0 each actor decrements its field once per actor update call. talkactor_wait::update (0x1805dba30) likewise decrements its +0x20 integer and sets completion bit 0x2 once the previous value is nonpositive. the public script api waitvoice has not been proven to construct this particular wait actor. do not identify them solely by name. the application registers its talkmanager callback into the central game-system dispatch. the recovered xgs::framework timer uses queryperformancefrequency * 100 / 5994, giving a scheduler gate of 59.94 hz. the talkmanager callback lies outside the inner loop which processes accumulated fixed ticks. hence a processing hitch can turn multiple missed fixed ticks into one outer talkmanager update, making the subtitle countdown run slower than wall-clock speech. merely raising render fps is not evidence that these actor countdowns update faster. this is a narrow, native-binary explanation for why sound, localized text lookup, caption lifetime and visible scroll timing can diverge without any missing dialogue cue. a global config.sgo/modelist timing control was not found in this recovered call chain, but that does not eliminate abnormal runtime hooks or resource-layout effects. the later separately qualified subtitle scroll correction adjusts presentation scheduling and is distinct from lossless voicetable compatibility additions. evidence level: static, exact-build edf6 edf.dll control-flow and class-layout audit (edf6_talkmanager_caption_countdown_scheduler_re_2026-09-05.md). build-specific absolute addresses above must not be transplanted to other binaries. pc/ps5 english subtitle timing: separate observed and suspected causes a control test of a native edf6 pc mission reproduced late english-caption scrolling with the whole mods directory disabled. that rules out mod-folder-only voicetable, mission ac, config and other custom mod-folder assets as necessary causes for that control. it does not demonstrate that a fully stock edf6 pc executable and graphics environment reproduce it. the tested root still contained dxvk d3d11.dll/dxgi.dll proxy dlls and a winmm.dll loader; canonical edf.dll integrity and removal of those root components were identified as remaining controls. the fps/dispatch evidence makes cadence a plausible contributing factor, but not a proven diagnosis: 59.94 / 55.07 ≈ 1.0884, so an actor decremented only once per outer update at a sustained 55.07 hz would run about 8.8% longer in wall-clock time than one updated at 59.94 hz. an older fps-unlock approach could produce the opposite effect by invoking outer-loop callbacks too often. neither arithmetic observation proves that dxvk caused the actual observed caption fault. community comparisons suggested ps5 english subtitles behaved differently, but the retained record lacks a matched pc/ps5 same cue + same language + timestamped scroll/audio measurement. consequently platform divergence is a hypothesis, not a proven universal pc-versus-ps5 fact. do not attribute every late-scroll case to the port, dxvk, or a general sandlot engine defect without a controlled installation-and-cue comparison. the missing-key voicetable problem remains independent of these presentation-timing effects. evidence: vanilla control/mods-disabled reports edf5_edf6_vanilla_subtitle_environment_frontier_r84_2026-09-06.md, edf5_edf6_pc_ps5_subtitle_divergence_r86_2026-09-06.md and native talkmanager analysis. the separate measured caption schedule has positive runtime tests without resolving this environmental root cause for all installations.

edf5 — native free-camera machinery in the retail executable not a user-facing photo mode: the source research uses “photo mode” as a section label. evidence here establishes internal debug code and post-processing behavior in the inspected binary, not an ordinary retail feature or publicly reachable menu. the investigated retail edf5 binary still contains a freeviewcamera class and control bindings, even though that does not establish a supported public photo mode. the existence of a debug class is a fact about native code, not a guarantee that it is exposed in menus or safe to activate during online play. pause flags and offline/online modes the game system maintains a pause-bit field and a separate mask of bits allowed to suspend updates. the mode setter changes that mask: in online mode it excludes 0xe (bits 2, 4 and 8), so the ordinary pause menu bit does not halt shared gameplay; offline mode restores those bits. other bits, including one assigned to the debug camera, remain capable of suspending local simulation. this is a native difference between pause request and effective pause. free-camera controls present in the code the debug camera reads left and right analog sticks and gamepad triggers. the left stick moves in the camera's yaw frame;
