triggers change height. x selects a movement-speed multiplier, the right stick changes yaw and pitch with pitch clamped to ±π/2, and shoulder buttons change the fov by an expression proportional to tan(fov/2). the source also identifies start for pause, back for single-frame stepping, a pose/fov reset, and a debug projectile/raycast action. those controls document an internal debug class; no user-facing workflow is promised. the captured post chain is not a full photo suite the source extracted 260 dxbc blobs from edf5.exe. the investigated shader set includes resize, bright-pass, gaussian blur, tone/exposure, final combine, depth helpers and ambient-occlusion passes, but no positively identified depth-of-field/bokeh/motion-blur/vignette implementation in that bounded set. the rest of the game's archives were not exhaustively searched, so this is not proof those effects cannot exist in any external or later resource. the final combine weights the scene by a single exposure/tone value and then adds two bloom buffers, rather than implementing a general focal-blur pipeline. the source's proposed photo-mode procedure was untested and is not part of this article. evidence and credit: kh-edf5-photo-mode facts edf5-pause-bits, edf5-pause-mask-offline, edf5-free-view-camera, edf5-free-camera-bindings, edf5-free-camera-update, edf5-free-camera-buttons, edf5-free-camera-zoom, edf5-post-chain-shaders, edf5-post-combine-formula; novae (ajane). build steam-5d11de53; no r125 game test.

edf6 — free camera and image post-processing are distinct systems not a user-facing photo mode: the source research uses “photo mode” as a section label. evidence here establishes internal debug code and post-processing behavior in the inspected binary, not an ordinary retail feature or publicly reachable menu. the investigated retail edf.dll has a freeviewcamera implementation with analog control, collision handling and a field-of-view value. it is an internal debug system, not evidence of an ordinary user-selectable photo mode. edf6's post-processing chain also has tone and bloom operations, but does not automatically provide photographic depth of field or an adjustable vignette. pause is mode-gated the game system stores both requested pause flags (+0xcd8) and an allowed mask (+0xcdc). missionmgr::setmode changes whether bits 2, 4 and 8 can pause simulation: they are excluded in the examined online mode and allowed offline. a pause request may therefore set its bit without stopping the game. listeners are notified when the effective paused state changes. build offsets refer only to steam-678ccb46. camera update and fov the class reads the left stick, triggers and right stick; yaw and pitch apply a fov-scaled rotational sensitivity, with pitch limited to ±π/2. depending on whether the game is paused, movement either changes the stored point directly or uses the debug camera's own collision-controller velocity. start toggles the class's pause bit, back advances one step, and the code retains debug hit/projection actions. fov adjustment uses a factor involving tan(fov/2) and the shoulder-button difference. these are structural code observations. they neither prove the controls can be used from a retail menu nor authorize changing a live game installation. bloom and exposure order the 490 examined dxbc blobs contain resize, high-pass, blur, tone-lerp, final combine, depth and ambient-occlusion shader paths. the inspected final combine computes roughly: result.rgb = scene * tone + bloom0 * strength0 + bloom1 * strength1 the tone value is a single scalar and bright-pass uses that tone before thresholding. the lightenv parser provides tone and bloom keys, and scene linear/view-space depth exists for ambient occlusion. the surveyed dll shader set did not reveal a native bokeh or depth-of-field pass; the study did not exhaust every external shader resource. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-photo-mode facts edf6-pause-bit-users, edf6-pause-mask-offline, edf6-free-view-camera, edf6-free-camera-update, edf6-free-camera-zoom, edf6-post-chain-shaders, edf6-post-combine-formula, edf6-bloom-tone-settings, edf6-lightenv-tone-keys; novae (ajane). no r125 runtime test.

edf6 — character appearance has a saved identity and a rendered preview edf6 does not treat the currently drawn soldier model as the sole authority for an outfit. the investigated game-state structure stores one outfit value per local player, while 3d room/hq previews build models from a description containing class, two colors, outfit variant and equipped weapons. outfit identity and variants the source identifies an appearance field with permitted values −1 through 3. a soldier-screen choice is converted into a saved outfit id, not simply a filename swapped at render time. the popup's five entries include modelindexmission, trainee, soldier, edf5trainee, edf5soldier. their callback values in the examined build are respectively −1, 2, 3, 1, 0. these ids are game-state values and must not be confused with the on-screen order of the popup or with another class's independent customization fields. room and hq preview models huihq3dmodel creates a view for each local player. its description carries class code, outfit value, two color values and weapon entries. the source shows a message-driven update path rather than a new model being built synchronously on every ui click. messages distinguish full model rebuilds, single-weapon updates, recolor and outfit changes. an asynchronous job performs the actual model update and tracks a completion flag. for the surveyed fencer example the description includes a left-hand shield entry before the main weapon, matching a weapon-slot convention rather than a generic two-gun visualization. other ui messages can temporarily lock and unlock rebuilds during a transition. a remote online participant is not automatically another local hq preview slot: its model description is derived through separate multiplayer state. boundaries those internal values and message ids describe source build steam-678ccb46. the source does not establish that every character class exposes each outfit variant in the same menu or that a custom model can be substituted without additional resource work. no ui gameplay observation was made in r125. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-player-outfits facts soldier-outfit-fields-paths, hq-3d-view-jobs, hq-3d-view-messages, outfit-popup-save-job; novae (ajane), original kh contributors.

edf6 — simulation ticks and displayed frames are different clocks an uneven-looking edf6 frame does not always mean the game simulated its movement unevenly. the source distinguishes its approximately 60 hz update cadence, its presentation call, and the external display compositor. in the studied build the internal timing loop counts elapsed 1/60-second periods and performs at most three catch-up update steps in one loop, dropping further excess time rather than accumulating unlimited simulation debt. what was actually observed a contributor captured the game at approximately 60 fps during missions and reported one gameplay step per present in roughly 99.5% of displayed frames, with occasional adjacent two-step and zero-step frames. it also reported 47–51 fps when a never-focused game window was held offscreen: disabling the present synchronization for that specific test restored approximately 59–60 fps, supporting a presentation wait rather than a wholesale slowdown of the internal clock. borderless window and refresh mismatch the contributor's presentmon captures at 2560×1440, 165 hz identified borderless edf6 as a legacy composed copy path using syncinterval=1, not a demonstrated variable-refresh direct-flip path. a 60 fps sequence displayed on a fixed 165 hz interval must distribute frames unevenly across 2 and 3 desktop refresh intervals. in the source's two one-minute traces, the displayed-frame timings clustered near 12.1 ms and 18.2 ms, rather than uniform 16.7 ms. thus a visual 60→165 hz unevenness can occur even if game simulation updates are stable. a refresh rate that is an integer multiple of 60 avoids that particular 2/3-interval pattern, but is not a universal solution for stutter, gpu stalls, shader compilation or online delays. external presentation changes are different evidence separate contributor tests with special k reported a flip-model presentation path at 120 hz but still showed timing outliers; a different latent sync configuration reduced variance in that test. these are observations on a named test system, not native edf6 settings, stock behavior or a generally verified optimization recommendation. they do not establish that an uncapped edf6 game loop would run animation correctly above 60 hz. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-frame-pacing facts edf6-game-loop-steps, edf6-game-loop-tail, edf6-content-cadence-even, edf6-hidden-window-vsync, edf6-present-mode-pacing, edf6-special-k-pacing; novae (ajane), build steam-678ccb46. static code analysis and separately attributed contributor tests; no r125 test.

edf4.1 — online caps are separate checks, not one generic setting edf4.1's weapon-level restriction and armor limit travel through different code paths. the restriction shown in the hq weapon list is not identical to the armor value applied when the host starts an online mission. neither should be inferred from offline mission settings. modelist and cap-state ownership the original config.sgo modelist main offline scenario carries zero for per-difficulty entries 6 and 7; its online-mode flag at node +0x5c is zero. the cap getters therefore return a no-cap condition. the cap tables for every separate offline dlc mode were not independently re-read in the source note. for the examined steam build, the session update at 0x377cd0 derives a weapon-cap-enabled byte from the room's weapon-limit switch and the current cap. the saved state flag is save+0xa7d5; the room's weapon and armor switches occupy distinct fields. game notices onlinesys_weaponcaplock/unlock and onlinesys_armorcaplock/unlock mirror these changes. the armor notice converts the room's armor-box limit into a displayed class-dependent hp value. above-cap weapons cannot be confirmed in edf4.1 a weapon beyond the cap is marked in the equipment screen and its text is rendered red. the uihqequipment_selectweapon confirm handler checks the over-cap marker and skips the selection. this is an important cross-generation difference: edf5 and edf6 also color above-cap levels red, but their equipment confirmation handlers do not reject on that marker alone. stage original edf4.1 behavior in the studied build display weapon above cap red text, flagged cell confirm that weapon rejected by selection-handler check host prepares online start serializes a per-player equipment record with a capped armor-box value spawn in online mode uses the received armor count and the class's per-box coefficient spawn in offline mode uses the local save's armor boxes, without online cap the host's start-message writer chooses min(cap, boxes) if the armor cap is active. the resulting hp follows base hp + capped boxes × class hp-per-box coefficient. the offline branch reads the saved armor count instead. this confirms the cap is enforced in the launch/spawn path, not simply by changing a menu label. what is not established this analysis does not prove a safe general method to activate online restrictions offline, nor does it test any patch. it is specific to steam-57aab039. the underlying room-message receive code was not fully read for one record-layout inference. primary evidence and credit: edf knowledge hub kh-edf41-online-caps, facts edf41-offline-modes-no-caps, edf41-cap-flag, edf41-weaponselect-cap-refusal, edf41-online-armor-cut, edf41-spawn-armor-paths; novae (ajane) / kh contributor research. static analysis, not a new gameplay test.

edf5 — equipment marking and mission-start restrictions edf5 retains two independent kinds of online limits. weapon levels are compared to a calculated ceiling for the selected mission/difficulty; armor boxes are limited when the host prepares each player's launch record. a red weapon cell is not a complete statement about whether a weapon can be selected in the menu. offline versus online metadata in the original config.sgo, the three offline modes (campaign, dlc1, dlc2) have zero in modelist's cap-list fields. the three online counterparts carry the indexed cap data. the byte save+0x24571 is set by the online session update when the room's weapon switch is active and the getter provides a positive cap. the armor switch is stored separately. the mode flag at node +0x5c is used to distinguish online from offline creation. red does not mean unselectable edf5's huihqweaponselect sets an above-cap bit on the relevant weapon cell; its level text is red. but the studied pressbutton handler rejects only cell bits 1 and 2 (cell+0x4c & 6). it does not reject bit 0, which represents being above the online limit. therefore the equipment menu permits that selection even though the online limit is visibly exceeded. it is incorrect to transfer edf4.1's stricter confirm-handler behavior to edf5. armor is bounded at online departure the host's mission-start record writer takes a limit in armor boxes and clamps each participant's count if a nonnegative cap is smaller. the receiver stores the transmitted count in the player-record area. the online spawn route then computes the character's hp using the received bounded count; the offline route reads the locally saved count. current and maximum hp are stored separately on the soldier. a useful semantic distinction: boxes are not hp. they become hp only after applying the class-specific coefficient and base. a data comparison of an armor-box count and displayed hp would mix different units. question observed edf5 answer does the offline campaign use online cap lists? no; its modelist cap entries are zero is an over-cap weapon marked? yes; its cell becomes red does the menu block confirmation solely for over-cap bit 0? no is armor merely a ui restriction? no; the online launch record clamps the count do the offline and online spawn paths read identical armor ownership? no; local save versus received online record evidence and credit: kh-edf5-online-caps: edf5-offline-modes-no-caps, edf5-cap-flag, edf5-weaponselect-cap-colors, edf5-online-armor-cut, edf5-spawn-hp-store, build steam-5d11de53; original kh curators / novae (ajane). these are static reverse-engineering observations. additional native-game references edf5 equipment and settings screen layout

edf6 — weapon/armor limits and loot-window hints are different numbers edf6 has a per-mode, per-difficulty online weapon limit, an armor-box limit, and a separate loot-level window. the equipment screen presents two visually different comparisons. a red weapon level means it exceeds the active online restriction; a yellow one can mean it sits outside an expected drop-level window. yellow is not another way to display the online restriction, and the two thresholds do not always align. source of the caps each modelist difficulty entry contains indexed weapon- and armor-knot lists. the native getters interpolate between adjacent values using the selected mission's normalized position t (clamped to 0–1): let x = (number_of_knots − 1) × t; let i = floor(x). for an interior segment, interpolate between knot i and knot i+1 if both are nonnegative; a negative knot denotes no applicable cap. weapon output converts the interpolated unit through trunc(value × 0.25 × 100) to the displayed weapon-level ceiling. armor output is an integer box count, not final hp. the main campaign's inferno weapon curve, for example, is the source sequence [2.4, 3.2, 3.999, 3.999]; the dlc1 and dlc2 inferno curves use [-1, -1] (no positive cap). these are values observed in the cited config.sgo corpus, not newly measured in game. what red and yellow actually mean ui indicator native basis consequence red level current online cap predicate and room flag marks an above-cap weapon; menu selection is still possible yellow level loot/drop-window range from other modelist fields can appear even offline; not an online-cap refusal normal color neither visual predicate applies does not by itself prove a weapon will drop or pass every room rule the red predicate is installed on the weapon-selection screen only for online mode and compares the cell's level to the computed cap. the confirm handler ignores the over-cap bit 0 and refuses the separate disabled bits 1/2. thus the highlighted red entry can remain selectable; the launch/runtime constraints are separate. as a concrete illustration from the static corpus, the original campaign hard range has a yellow boundary around 3.75 at its beginning while the online cap is 5. the exact placement depends on progress through the difficulty's knot curve. these values should not be extrapolated as a universal fixed maximum for every mission. armor is processed when the mission starts session room switches for weapons and armor are distinct. the live cap-state flag resides at gamestate+0x14fc8 in the examined build. its update path combines the room's weapon-limit switch with whether the computed limit is positive. when a mission starts, the departure serializer transmits the equipped weapon ids as they stand, but clamps the armor-box count if the current armor cap is active. the spawn path converts armor count into class hp using the native armor formula. the examined native offline-mode entries do not carry a positive online limit. an external offline-limit modification that compares a cap in boxes directly to hp would conflate units; its behavior cannot be described as stock edf6. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-online-caps: online-level-cap-enforcement, edf6-online-caps-code, edf6-online-caps-knots, edf6-yellow-vs-online-cap, edf6-red-level-online-predicate, edf6-offline-armor-spawn; build steam-678ccb46. the source's yellow-boundary arithmetic was not independently checked in-game for this revision. additional native-game references edf6 equipment cell bits and selection ui

edf6 — the walking character controller in the examined edf6 build, walking actors use xgs::havok::charactercontrol_walk. it is separate from havok's general rigid-body solver and from the charactercontrol_cling used by crawling insects and some robots. understanding the distinction explains why a generic knockback impulse does not necessarily reproduce player movement or wall-clinging movement. support detection and ground-state representation walk_checksupport invokes havok's character rigid body checksupport, which fills an hknpcharactersurfaceinfo. the record contains: relative offset native field interpretation +0x00 issurfacedynamic contact/support classification +0x01 supportedstate 0 unsupported, 1 sliding, 2 supported +0x10 surfacenormal world-space normal +0x20 surfacevelocity reported surface linear velocity +0x30 surfaceangularvelocity reported angular velocity the source identifies a 1/60-second support-check step. the walk-controller path uses its own cached support state and motion channels; it does not simply hand the final position to a physics body and wait for the solver. final velocity has several sources the walk_step path combines the internally maintained velocity channel (+0x30), projected movement input (+0x20), a step-scoped external contribution (+0x60) and the additional +0x1c0 channel, then publishes the result to the character body. the source also distinguishes a measured airborne velocity from the launch/accumulation velocity — these fields must not be interchanged. the support state controls whether a character is grounded, sliding or falling; the airborne path updates gravity-related motion. this system is used by playable soldier classes and the npc/civilian human controllers, though their higher-level input and animation behaviors differ. scope and limitations the values are not an api promise for another edf build. source paths were traced from charactercontrol_walk and original havok callbacks; they are static disassembly, not a new motion test. the separate article moving platforms explains why a valid support velocity is not necessarily incorporated into soldier movement. primary evidence: kh-edf6-character-control: walk-support-info, walk-controller-layout, walk-step-states, walk-all-characters, walk-external-velocity-slot. build steam-678ccb46; fevgrave and hajisensai / all forces research, kh curator.

edf6 — charactercontrol_cling is not a walking controller edf6 uses a distinct havok-linked xgs::havok::charactercontrol_cling for ground-attached and wall-attached actors. its users include the insectbase family (ants, spiders, bees, dango and small dragons), nephila, berserker-family walking enemies, and the player's vehicle502_groundrobo. the same actor may change to a flight-specific mode that bypasses ordinary cling velocity integration. native state model controller field meaning in the studied build +0x00 mode; nonzero bypasses ordinary velocity update (for example, giantbee flight) +0x50 / +0x60 attachment normal and smoothed normal +0x70 attached/grounded byte +0x73 contact recorded for current step +0x80 ballistic velocity (a vector, meters/second) +0xa0 gravity vector; default (0, −9.8, 0) +0xb0 / +0xb4 collision sphere radius and extra probe distance +0xb8 number of frames during which landing is suppressed when attached, the controller clears its ballistic velocity and relies on the attachment/movement branch. when detached, the update pushes ballistic velocity (plus temporary contributions) into the body and integrates gravity. the original ant/controller initialization scales gravity for one insect path; a single universal gravity constant for all enemies is therefore unjustified. launch is a velocity assignment, not a force impulse the observed cling launch native sets the attachment flag to zero, writes a supplied velocity and records a no-landing frame count. its callers use different counts: 2 for a sampled giantant blast-knockback path, 0 for a jump, and 4/8 on robot paths. a zero-count launch can immediately reattach on the next contact; a nonzero count temporarily suppresses that landing. the launch alone does not switch animation state. when the controller is in nonzero flight mode, this launch path does not provide the same result: the update bypasses its velocity integration, leaving movement under the actor's separate flight routine. that helps distinguish the handling of a grounded insect from a flying bee, without claiming a new gameplay experiment. primary evidence: kh-edf6-character-control: cling-controller-layout, cling-launch, cling-users. build steam-678ccb46. static source analysis credited to hajisensai / all forces and kh curators.

edf6 — a moving support body does not necessarily carry its passenger the stock edf6 walking controller asks havok whether its character body is supported. that query includes both surface linear velocity and surface angular velocity. in the studied implementation, the subsequent walking step uses the support state and normal, but does not add those reported surface velocities to the character's own movement. static code consequence the original walk_step final velocity is assembled from the walk controller's motion channels, not by appending surfacevelocity. a soldier standing on a sideways-moving body therefore tends to retain the character's own world velocity while the supporting body moves beneath it. physics contacts can still push the soldier up with a rising surface or sideways with an intersecting wall. the source derives these results from code; it does not claim a new systematic gameplay measurement for every platform type. the contact surface itself may be a moving vehicle part, a keyframed ragdoll body, a crate/container or an animated event object. the native collision table matters: the player movement layer 1 contacts layers 1, 6–9, 14–20, 25 and 26, but not all enemy movement or flight layers. for example, a helicopter's keyframed component might be supportable while its distinct flight body is not — that specific vehicle interpretation is source inference. why using havok's returned surface velocity is not trivial an earlier external moving-platform investigation found havok's reported surfacevelocity was zero on some edf vehicle contacts. the contributor then resolved the supporting rigid body and computed point velocity from the body's actual motion, including angular velocity. this is useful diagnostic evidence about which field holds the relevant motion, not evidence that the original game already incorporates it. this distinction is especially important for standing on animated bosses, vehicles and environmental objects: their keyframed body positions may move visibly even when the controller's reported support velocity is not used by gameplay movement. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-character-control: edf6-moving-ground-stock, edf6-moving-ground-effect, edf6-moving-ground-layers, walk-support-body; novae (ajane), fevgrave and kh contributors. build steam-678ccb46. external plugin behavior is provenance only, not a public tool guide or claimed stock feature.

edf6 — damage numbers have their own native layout and animation damage values are not displayed by a generic floating text routine alone. edf6's lyt_huddamage.sgo describes seven drawing styles and layout modes; the game projects world anchors into ui space, animates position/color/scale, formats decimal text and queues digit sprites. the original configuration file, not an external editor, owns these defaults. seven named sgo styles named style typical native behavior lifetime in source hit_every every hit; a moving per-hit number 0.8 s aboveiconhistory fixed recent-number history list 3.0 s hit per-target placement 0.8 s aboveicon one total over its icon 0.8 s reticlesidehistory recent history beside reticle 0.8 s reticleside one total beside reticle 0.8 s aim_stack stack beneath a target 0.8 s the source identifies these as damagedispparam_<style> rows. each row has lifetime, pop fraction and pop size, display rules, spacing and font parameters. keyframe records are (frame, value, ease); the aboveiconhistory opacity, for example, remains at one through frame 160 then falls to zero by frame 180 during its three-second lifetime. projecting world positions for on-target placement, the game projects both the contact position and that position with a defined world offset. it chooses a minimum 90-pixel vertical gap or the projected 1.25-meter offset, whichever produces the larger displacement. this means the text location depends on camera projection and is not simply a fixed world-space billboard. fixed list styles place more recent results first and space each line by a configured count; vehicle display mode additionally scales its displayed numbers. native default fixed positions differ for wing diver, other soldier classes and vehicle mode. pop and numeric text the original pop-size animation uses a cosine ease to shrink an initially enlarged number to normal scale. its digit formatter has thresholds for two, one or zero decimals rather than a uniform integer rounding rule: under 10, fractions of at least 0.01 use two decimals; under 100, fractions of at least 0.1 can use one. the number texture routine also accounts for a trailing fixed-width sequence when calculating visual alignment. a rendering quirk noted in source research is that the original digit material constants are applied before the per-number drawing loop. although each record has its own color values, the shared material can show only one of those colors at a time. the contributor identified this statically and separately tested a modified color-upload path; do not call that behavior a new r126 runtime observation. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-damage-numbers: damage-style-rows-vanilla, damage-keyframes, damage-placement, damage-fixed-list-layout, damage-pop-curve, digit-text-format, digit-color-upload; novae (ajane), build steam-678ccb46. source-file values and static reverse engineering; no new r126 game test. additional native-game references edf6 follower health bars and text rendering

edf6 — the achievement store is a typed set of variables and events the examined edf6 build does not save achievements by writing a free-form list of names and values. its original app:/etc/achievement.sgo declares the available variables and events, then the game loads values and unlock states into a fixed binary trophy.dat representation. the save uses ordered values, not per-entry textual names. achievement.sgo defines what can be counted the sgo includes two collections, achievementvariable and achievementevent. each variable is identified by a name, type (int or float) and initial value. the original source census contains 91 variables and 39 event definitions. only names present in the loaded registry can be incremented or read successfully; an arbitrary kill-counter name does not automatically create a new slot. an event has a name, comparison operator (==, !=, >, <, >=, <=) and numeric threshold. the unlocked state is kept separately for the steam and epic integration paths. the event checker traverses events associated with a variable whenever its value changes and, where appropriate, invokes the native platform-specific unlock routines. runtime in-memory store the store contains a std::map<std::wstring, variable> and an event array. a variable node carries a key, a type code (0 integer, 1 float), its current value and indexes of events watching it. a lookup of an unknown variable returns the map's head/sentinel node, not an automatically inserted zero-valued counter. trophy.dat serialization byte region native meaning in the studied build first 0xc8 (200) bytes event-unlock bytes, padded with zeros next 200 × 4 bytes variable values, ordered by utf-16 variable name total 0x3f0 (1008) bytes fixed record buffer used by save/load on load, the engine reconstructs the registry from the sgo and reads values in that same name order; the file itself does not contain the names. this means changing variable names or their sort order changes how the stored numbers are interpreted. the researcher also identified no count bound when writing additional variable entries beyond the expected 200: that is a format hazard, not a supported way to extend the game. scope this is a build-specific description (steam-678ccb46), not a prescription to modify player saves. no r127 game save was opened or written, and the identified overflow path was not tested as a live crash. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-battle-record, facts achievement-sgo-variables, achievement-store, edf6-achievement-event-fields, edf6-achievement-unlock-sites, trophy-dat-layout; novae (ajane) and original knowledge hub contributors.

edf6 — why a kill may not appear in the battle record the native edf6 kill counter follows an explicit object-name lookup. it does not count every destroyed object in a universal category, and it does not automatically inherit names from older edf releases. kill messages and accepted counter names the examined soldierbase kill-message handler processes message 0x10000006. for a soldier with a local controller/pad object, the handler looks up the killed object's sgo field game_object_kill_counter and attempts to increment that named variable in the achievement store. if the name is absent from achievement.sgo, the update does nothing. that path explains two distinct observations: an npc or a vehicle does not follow the local-player soldier's normal kill-message route, and a ported edf4.1 enemy may bring a name edf6 does not register. some familiar names have also been reused for different enemy families: dragonkillcount refers to edf6 tadpoles, carrier1killcount to teleportation ships, and anthillkillcount to teleportation devices in the examined data. exact name reuse matters more than apparent visual resemblance. the source notes suggest that the achievement registry is local to each machine and does not receive an independent online synchronization channel. however, the route from a guest's enemy-death event back to the guest's player kill message was not fully traced. therefore remote and guest kill ownership must remain partially unresolved. battle record is a fixed presentation table the huihqhistory page constructs 90 hard-coded rows; each contains a variable name, a display format and a scale factor. formatting modes include integers, hours:minutes:seconds, a count suffix, percentages and meter values. a first pass checks the store and skips a killcount row whose value is zero; a later pass looks up localized labels through statusinfo_<name>. this leads to two important distinctions: variables in the achievement registry and rows in the battle record ui are not the same set; a registered variable does not have to be shown, while a row that refers to an unknown name does not magically add that variable. the research also identified an unsafe sentinel-node read for a missing row name; the present wiki does not claim a tested gameplay failure from that path. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-battle-record: kill-counter-path, kill-counter-online (unverified), kill-counter-name-reuse, battle-record-page, achievement-sgo-variables; build steam-678ccb46.

edf6 — the equipment screen is both a data-driven layout and a runtime list the original equipment selection screen loads app:/ui/lyt_huihqweaponselect.sgo from the resource archive. its sgo identifies the huihqweaponselect native class and contains named visual templates; the c++ constructor instantiates one column for each weapon category and fills each column with entries owned by the current player. why five rows appear the viewport weaponselectarea has a 201-pixel height. each weaponsel_cellbase row is 40 pixels tall. therefore five complete rows fit in view (201 / 40). this is an sgo layout fact, not a native loop hard-coded to render exactly five entries. a parent stencil clips overflow. the basic column is 355×201 pixels, and the level/quality subcells sit in separate 43-pixel-wide areas. the columns scroll together the constructor locates whichever category column has the most cells, creates the vertical scroll information on that column, and shares its scrollinfo object with all other columns. this is why the stock equipment categories scroll in unison even when they contain different numbers of weapons. the source identifies scroll-margin fields for focus and display; the generic mouse hit test has separate clipping and does not simply apply those margins as-is. weapon cell status bits cell flag readable behavior in the studied build bit 0 online above-cap level; red text bit 1 weapon already equipped in another slot; gray/disabled bit 2 the corresponding content pack is not owned; dark red/disabled the confirmation handler rejects (cell+0x54 & 6), i.e. bits 1 or 2. it does not reject bit 0. thus the red online cap mark is informational at weapon-selection time, whereas a duplicate slot or missing content entitlement disables the selection. the source ties bit 2 to the content-pack field in weapontable, not simply to the weapon's category. for weapons that can be equipped, the selected weapon id is written into the current class's saved slot area; current-class and displayed-class indexes are distinct screen state. layout and mouse behavior are separate the hui generic button hit test walks the element's rectangle, parent clipping and scroll offset. the source identifies a few-pixel vertical strip that remains outside the interactive area at the edges of a scrolled cell. that is an input hit-test boundary rather than an absence of visible rows. exact offsets are specific to steam-678ccb46. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-ui-weapon-select: ui-layout-load-chain, ui-weaponselect-layout, ui-weaponselect-columns, ui-weaponselect-shared-scroll, ui-weaponselect-cell-bits-content, ui-button-hit-test, ui-equipped-weapon-storage. static source research.

edf5 — message log lines are dispatched to active ui listeners edf5's message-log/notification route is a ui event dispatch, not a console print. a native poster builds a wide-string payload paired with an optional game-object context, then emits manager event 12. the ui manager forwards that event to registered listeners; the in-game notice screen interprets it through its own handler. native event route 460be0 (build-relative) prepares the text and object context, then invokes 61e950(uimanager, 12, payload). the manager locks its critical section and iterates listener lists, calling a virtual handler for each. the notice listener is an uinotice object; its event-12 handler consumes the text rather than interpreting it as a hud draw command. a separate listener can be present in offline missions. thus the route is not exclusively tied to a multiplayer room: messages can appear during offline play as long as the receiving ui is initialized and its active listener exists. initialization is not equivalent to listener readiness source analysis shows a lazily created ui manager held in a global pointer. the uinotice listener, however, is constructed and attached as part of the current ui/scene lifecycle. those two lifetimes should not be conflated. one earlier contributor test posted a message from a first-frame radar draw hook during mission loading and observed an immediate crash, while a corresponding action-triggered post worked after the mission had started. that first-frame result was not independently isolated or repeated. it is evidence that initialization timing matters, not proof that all loading-screen notices crash or that a stable runtime bug has been identified. what a log entry proves if an entry appears in the message log, the active listener and event-dispatch route handled it. if a line does not appear, the absence alone cannot tell whether the producer never sent it, the manager was unavailable, or the correct listener was not active. no additional edf5 runtime testing was carried out in r127. evidence and credit: kh-edf5-ui-notices: notice-poster, notice-dispatch, notice-listener-uinotice, notice-listener-offline, notice-post-during-loading (unverified), ui-manager-lifetime; build steam-5d11de53.

edf5 — setting rows are data-backed ui components the original edf5 hq menu uses subclasses of ui::huilayout. a screen's sgo declares xgs_ui_object_class, identifies layout elements and connects named callbacks to functions registered by that native class. this separates visual layout from the screen's application-specific settings logic. game settings structure huihqgamesetting constructs its rows from a fixed set of setting ids 0–11. dedicated switch functions interpret each id as a name, range, current stored value, write destination or display label. unknown ids do not automatically become new supported settings: every relevant switch has an explicit case set. the normal constructor creates 11 visible setting rows, with a 12th row in the observed second-player/gamepad-specific variants. the class stores the player index separately, and some buttons are hidden depending on player/activation context. registered callbacks include initialization, key-configuration selection, chat-shortcut customization and opening the manual. visible rows versus full list capacity the settings-screen cursorarea has 631×630 pixels and each row is 45 pixels tall, so 14 rows fit in the viewport. this is not a maximum count enforced by the native setting-id logic. a layout flag 0x800 keeps focused child entries in view by adjusting the parent's scroll position, even when the scrollbar is not drawn; other flags control horizontal/vertical cursor behavior. this also explains the relationship to the weapon-selection ui: edf5 and edf6 share the same 201-pixel-high five-row list geometry for equipment screens. edf5's original sgo uses the misspelled scrool in some scrollbar element names, so those resource identifiers should be quoted literally if comparing the files. boundaries the source does not demonstrate that adding another arbitrary row to the sgo automatically installs its save/read/write logic, nor that the two game settings columns scroll together for rows beyond their native set. that behavior remains unverified rather than silently inferred. evidence and credit: kh-edf5-ui-menus: hui-layout-framework, gamesetting-class, gamesetting-rows, settings-row-capacity, settings-scroll-by-focus, weaponselect-layout-same; build steam-5d11de53.

three edf generations — familiar hud elements hide different limits the armor meter and short-chat input look similar across edf4.1, edf5 and edf6, but the original executables store their bounds and text differently. the figures below are code/data observations for the named steam builds, not universal constraints on all later patches or ports. native chat-input length game default character limit in the examined build width-related constant edf4.1 32 (0x20) 400 edf5 32 (0x20) 400 edf6 16 (0x10) 400 the width value is not a character limit. edf4.1's code compares a text-area width with a 400-unit baseline; edf5 has a separate text-input width path; edf6 stores a bounded window dimension in its input object. as a result, changing only the character count would not necessarily produce a correctly sized visual textbox. armor gauge is a display, not the complete gameplay value in the examined executables the native hud display truncates the current and maximum armor floats to integers and caps the displayed values at 999,999 (0xf423f). edf5 and edf6 additionally compare copies stored within their gauge state. edf5's bar fill still uses the underlying float ratio, so a capped label does not imply the combat model itself is capped at that number. game-specific storage differs; edf5's soldier keeps maximum and current hp in separate floats, while edf4.1's displayed values are fetched through its hud getter. a higher gameplay hp value and a six-digit printed value should not be read as contradictory evidence. vehicle aim lines and visibility in all three source corpora a cooldown state can suppress a vehicle weapon's aim line. the exact cooldown fields differ (edf4.1 +0xab0, edf5 +0xb40, edf6 its own draw logic), so copying one game's address or gameplay-state offset to another generation would be incorrect. the available sources do not establish one unified color rule for every vehicle weapon. evidence and credit: kh-edf41-hud (armor-gauge-cap, chat-limits, aim-line-cooldown), kh-edf5-hud (same three fact names), kh-edf6-hud (armor-gauge-cap, chat-limits, aim-line-cooldown); fevgrave, blueamulet and other original contributors. static source observations; no r127 gameplay test.

edf6 hud elements resolve data from several different owners the original edf6 hud does not draw every on-screen indicator from one central list. follower durability bars, text glyphs and the contextual spot/q marker come from different source objects and update paths. follower health bars hudplayer_followerdurability obtains the hud's live player owner and walks that player's linked follower list. for each follower it projects the object's position raised 2 meters, skips offscreen entries, draws a frame and fills the bar according to the follower's current and maximum hp. the same draw routine recursively visits each follower's own list. a vehicle that is not in anyone's follower list therefore does not get a vanilla follower-style health bar through this path. glyph and font fallback the examined resource manager loads four original ui truetype resources, covering japanese, korean, traditional chinese and simplified chinese. the font-chain order varies with the selected language. for each character, the rasterizer tries fonts until getglyphindicesw indicates a glyph is present, otherwise falling back to the first font. this is why embedded cjk glyphs can appear in interface strings outside the primary ui locale. this is a font fallback strategy, not a guarantee that every japanese/chinese symbol has identical metrics. the source notes distinguish monospaced latin advances in the japanese font from proportional latin advances in the chinese font variants. spot and player-name labels the player's spot (q) action takes its input from a soldier flag and follows a dedicated marker/effect and online-message path. a separate function looks up player names for labels. these should not be treated as a generic text-notice system: spot identity, follower bars and hud text all have different owners. evidence and credit: kh-edf6-hud: follower-bar-walk, hud-fonts, spot-mark-name-tag; static analysis of build steam-678ccb46 by original knowledge hub contributors.

how enemy hp is calculated in edf4.1, edf5 and edf6 the three game generations use a recognizably shared model: base object durability, a source level adjustment, a difficulty/mission-progress factor, and multiplayer scaling. the result is a floating-point number, not an integer automatically rounded by the enemy-spawn code. the shared ingredients in the studied edf5 executable, an object's maximum and initial hp are assigned from the same calculated float. for normal enemies the factor is assembled in this order: multiply the spawn's hp multiplier by the object's game_object_level_adjust (default 1). calculate mission progress t = mission row / (mission rows - 1) and interpolate between the selected difficulty's [l, m] level bounds. multiply the level-adjusted factor by l + (m - l) × t, then divide by 10. multiply by game_object_durability (default 100), the difficulty's enemy-hp factor and the multiplier indexed by the number of players. the scripted spawn factor can be different from 1. in edf5, the setmissionlevel/bvm mission factor can further affect spawns. in edf6, the same underlying hp pattern survives with relocated object fields and modelist indices. this is a source-level structural correspondence, not a claim that all three games use identical difficulty tables or health outcomes. studied build raw durability field max / current hp fields distinct qualification edf4.1 steam-57aab039 +0x160 +0x168 / +0x16c no equivalent of edf5's fixed-level override in the same location edf5 steam-5d11de53 +0x1f0 +0x1f8 / +0x1fc mission tutorial can use the fixed-level flag edf6 steam-678ccb46 +0x2ec class-specific stored fields a new modelist field shifts the per-difficulty node to index 7 why hp often has decimals the observed edf5 code uses single-precision sse operations at each step. the calculation is not equivalent to first multiplying everything at double precision and rounding once. as a source example, the edf5 black ant in offline mission 2 on inferno has calculated hp of approximately 966.6055, so the smallest whole-number damage amount that reaches zero is 967. the exact stored float and the damage comparison, rather than an integer hp stat, determine death. the edf4.1 shield bearer exception edf4.1's alientrailer (shield bearer) reads the second difficulty factor modelist[mode][6][difficulty][3][1] where ordinary enemy classes use [3][0]. in the source tables this makes its online hp approximately 1.2× the ordinary-rule result from normal upward; on easy the relation is about 0.83×. offline, both factors equal 1. this is not the same as adding 1.2 to a multiplayer multiplier. the edf6 alientrailer uses the ordinary helper and reads factor [3][0] instead. therefore carrying the edf4.1 exception forward unchanged would misrepresent edf6. mission-specific modifiers are real in a survey of 98 edf4.1 scripts, 34 included at least one non-unit enemy-spawn hp factor. the records contained 1,373 such entries across the surveyed difficulties; values ranged from 0.1 to 5. examples include difficulty-varying deroys in m119, transport ships in m304, and stronger charging bees in m137. these are script overrides, not a different hard-coded enemy species formula. evidence and attribution: kh-edf41-enemies (edf41-hp-same-steps, edf41-shield-bearer-online-hp, edf41-spawn-hp-factors), kh-edf5-combat (hp-formula-modelist, hp-float32-order) and kh-edf6-missions (edf6-hp-same-steps). the cited work is static re and file analysis; no new hp runtime measurement was performed here.

enemy kills, merit points and support-weapon reloads some support equipment and vehicles recharge through kill merit rather than elapsed time. the number displayed as an enemy's base hp or its level-adjusted durability is not automatically the number of credits earned. the mechanics also changed between edf4.1 and the later games. which object contributes merit? generation native rule established by the cited build notes edf4.1 raw game_object_durability no game_object_destroy_score_adjust key is read by the examined executable edf5 raw durability × game_object_destroy_score_adjust the adjustment defaults to 1; level adjustment is not part of merit edf6 raw durability × game_object_destroy_score_adjust same model as edf5 with different object-field offsets at an enemy's death, the engine credits the relevant hostile teams through the teammanager. an object without a team (-1) does not credit a team through this path. this is why the merit rule must not be interpreted as a blanket "every destroyed object gives every player the same credit" statement. for edf5, source examples are silver spider: 450 × 5 = 2250, gold ant: 30 × 5 = 150, and colonist: 500 × 0.84 = 420. the separate game_object_level_adjust can scale hp but is not multiplied into the merit reward. the original edf4.1 japanese merit table mostly agrees with object durability, with a few exceptions. retiarius webs are described as granting zero in the community source, but the reason that their destruction does not pass through the usual team-credit route remains unverified in the executable. do not infer it from the presence of an sgo durability field. why a huge kill does not give its full cost immediately in edf5 and edf6, credit-charged equipment (reloadtype = 2) compares the teammanager's accumulated merit against the total last observed by the weapon. for the new increment d, the observed conversion is: [ c(d) = \begin{cases} d, & d \leq 1500 \ 1500 + \operatorname{int}((d-1500)^{0.8}), & d > 1500. \end{cases} ] the code performs its integer conversion as part of the update. it then reduces the weapon's outstanding reload cost using c(d) and stores the latest team total. compression happens to the accumulated increment between two weapon updates, so a large batch of kills can be compressed together. source example (edf5) raw merit credited reload credit gained one silver spider 2250 1699 one erginus 32000 5367 100 black ants killed together 6000 2336 the edf6 source has the same 1500 threshold and exponent 0.8 at a different routine address. its teammanager total is maintained locally for the current machine's game state, so identical credit reload behavior on every online peer cannot be inferred solely from the equation. what remains uncertain the edf4.1 damage/death routine supports durability-only team merit, but the original edf4.1 call-in reload was not fully reversed in the cited study. the edf5/edf6 compression rule must not be retroactively asserted as edf4.1 behavior. also, source examples come from specific pc builds; field layouts are not portable offsets. evidence and attribution: kh-edf41-enemies (edf41-kill-merit-durability, edf41-wiki-merit-table, edf41-web-no-merit); kh-edf5-combat (kill-merit-team-credit, merit-from-sgo, credit-reload-merit-compression, merit-cut-examples); kh-edf6-combat (edf6-kill-merit, edf6-credit-merit-compression, credit-reload-tick).

edf4.1 uforobo (argo): one boss, two movement forms the edf4.1 giant argo ship, internally uforobo, is not two unrelated npcs swapped in a mission. the source describes one native game object and one object handle, with a body state machine and a higher-level ai state machine. mission scripts can subscribe to the object's durability events before and after its transformation. script actions objectaction native meaning 0 begin the transformation from flying ship to robot if alive; may be replayed 1 enter the robot form immediately, using stand and approach behavior 2 switch to approach behavior without performing the full transform these are action ids for edf4.1 uforobo, not generic action ids for other edf enemies or the edf6 movingfortress. body-state sequence state behavior s0–s3 ship idle and successive small, medium and buster attacks s4 transforming; the cited native damage check makes this stage invulnerable s5–s6 falling into robot form and landing s7 robot main state: plan a step, turn or attack s8–s9 execute a step/turn or execute an attack s10–s11 death sequence, followed by a wreck state and deletion in ship form, an ai steering state circles roughly 300–500 m from its target, about 250 m above it. heading changes are constrained, and sideways slip is part of the flight behavior. the robot uses animation root motion, turned into the chosen world heading; a downward map ray keeps its feet aligned with the terrain during stepping. gun groups and pacing native gun data distinguishes the knee beam weapons (beambullet01), shoulder rocket volleys (rocketbullet01), large hand weapons and the annihilation cannon. each group has idle, charging and firing phases. source parameters include a roughly 300-frame buster charge, with subsequent shots spaced by 31 frames during the firing interval. other guns run separate timers and have individual distance windows. the robot's high-level state selects attacks by distance and angle windows in robo_attack_table. an attack switches the body to s9, and the ai does not return to movement planning until the body returns to s7. consequently attack time does not count toward the ordinary movement-phase timers. the lengthy native animation clips help explain the boss's deliberate, stop-start walking tempo; they are not necessarily ai stalls. the original static analysis also found a possible edge case: when no valid attack-table entry exists (for example a target beyond the allowed range), a fallback assigns an ai function into the body-state machine. the source author considered this a probable edf4.1 bug; the wiki does not claim a newly reproduced crash or stuck state. evidence and attribution: kh-edf41-enemies, facts uforobo-states-ai, uforobo-guns-events-death, uforobo-attack-rhythm, uforobo-function-map; original re attributed to hajisensai / all forces, steam build 57aab039.

edf4.1's four-legged fortress is controlled by part groups the original four-legged enemy fortress is the native class alien4legtank, not a renamed edf6 movingfortress. both look like multi-part walking fortresses, but their mission commands and generators differ. what the seven script actions do the native action handler receives the mission's objectaction message and dispatches values 0–6 into a seven-entry table. each command targets one of three part groups or the body itself: action native response 0 / 1 enable / disable part group 0 — main cannons 2 / 3 enable / disable part group 1 — gatlings 4 / 5 enable / disable part group 2 — auxiliary bits 6 enter the destruction state if the fortress is not already dead the part enable routine walks records of 0x20 bytes beginning at the object's part table +0x920; it compares each part's group field at +0x18 to the requested group. mission 16's original script (m117) uses all seven actions, including a roughly 35-second interval between the cannon activation and deactivation. other missions use only subsets of this action protocol. the same numeric objectaction values in edf6's movingfortress have different meanings. a direct one-to-one translation of script action 1, for example, can turn an edf4.1 cannon-off command into an unrelated debris action in edf6. compatibility requires object-specific action translation, not a global numerical mapping. movement and generator layout edf4.1's alien4legtank begins standing; the original scripts do not send a separate stand-up command. it has one object generator at the belly hatch above its core (+0x1040 in the studied build). when idle and sufficiently clear of the map edge, the locomotion state makes a five-way draw: 0–2 select a walking clip, 3 turns left and 4 turns right. it moves by complete animation clips instead of freely steering in every frame. this clarifies several familiar gameplay observations: a wandering fortress may finish a motion clip before choosing a new heading, and the central generator is a separate concern from activating its weapons. neither behavior should be attributed to edf6's native fortress unless that game's own object is examined. evidence and attribution: kh-edf41-enemies, alien4legtank-object-actions and alien4legtank-stand-wander; original analysis attributed to hajisensai / all forces, steam build 57aab039. values are re findings, not new in-game tests.

why weapon table order matters in edf5 and edf6 weapons are not identified in saves merely by a unique text name. in both generations, the loaded weapon/weapontable.sgo row order is a critical identity: the row index is the weapon id. corresponding weapontext.<language>.sgo entries stay in the same order. the hq ui may sort what it displays by category or level, but that does not change the underlying save identity. edf5 uses eight fields; edf6 uses nine position edf5 table edf6 table 0 weapon identifier / name weapon name / identifier 1 weapon sgo path weapon sgo path 2 weapon category weapon category 3 rarity / acquisition weight rarity / acquisition weight 4 stored level float stored level float 5 acquisition class acquisition class 6 star-rating specification star-rating specification 7 content/source pack availability/display flag for underground/wasteland 8 — content/source pack the edf5 study counted 1187 table records; the examined edf6 table contains 1564 records. counts are build and data-set specific. the edf6 engine reads its table as a collection of rows, with row-name lookup case-sensitive in utf-16. table pointers are populated when a game mode loads its configuration; callers should not assume the table exists earlier. categories, starting equipment and dlc edf5 encodes a class/category family as approximately 100 × class + kind, with classes ranger 0, wing diver 1, fencer 2 and air raider 3. edf6 category numbers are also defined by defaultpackage/config.sgo; the category name shown on-screen comes from a localized text-table key, not from the numeric category itself. in the edf6 table, acquisition value 0 means a normally rollable item, 1 starting equipment and 3 dlc-granted equipment. the source-pack code 0 identifies the main-game pool, 1 dlc1 and 2 dlc2 for normal random acquisitions. the underground/wasteland cell is a display indicator, not the whole authority for whether equipment can actually be used in a given mission. a stored weapon level is not the screen number for edf5, the weapon's displayed level follows approximately floor(float32(table_level × 25)). the single-precision conversion matters: the stored 2.12f can display as level 52, not 53. a comparison with japanese community tables matched the rule in 1178 unambiguous cases. this detail should not be replaced by a simple decimal multiplication and rounding formula. identity and compatibility risks inserting a new row in the middle shifts the ids of all later weapons. removing a row referenced by equipped or owned save data can cause a load or menu crash. likewise, the game does not automatically register an arbitrary weapon sgo simply because it exists in an archive. edf6's implementation iterates up to a hard-coded 0x800 record slots in several save routines; exceeding that bound cannot be assumed safe. evidence and attribution: kh-edf5-file-formats (weapon-table-sgo, weapon-table-loading, weapon-level-times-25); kh-edf6-weapons (weapon-table-ids, weapon-table-entry, weapon-table-access), plus the earlier game-data guide by ktaro / edf modding wiki.

edf5 weapon stars: values, curves and display labels a weapon may show an overall star label beside an hq statistic, but the engine computes individual stat modifiers first. the stars for ammo count, damage, accuracy, firing interval, reload, range and related properties can progress independently. per-stat data the edf5 source describes an upgradeable stat as an array of six entries: [value_at_5_stars, stat_kind, star_slot, top_star, ra, mu] the first number is a stat's value at five stars, not at zero stars. star_slot selects which stored upgrade level applies to this statistic. ra is the deterioration share at zero stars and mu sets the curve. the source example for pa-11 ls damage is [16.0, 8, 1, 8, 0.5, 0.5]: approximately 8 damage at zero stars, 16 at five stars, and 18.1 at its top of eight stars. let s be the stat's current star rating. for a statistic where higher is better, the formula is: [ v(s)=v_5\left((1-ra)+ra\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)^{mu}\right). ] for a statistic where lower is better, such as reload time or inaccuracy spread: [ v(s)=v_5\left((1+ra)-ra\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)^{mu}\right). ] examples of stat kinds in the source: ammo count 0, damage 8, accuracy 13, projectile speed 16, reload time 21 and firing interval 25. a plain numeric sgo value without a star array is not upgraded by this mechanism. why the hq line shows a star average the equipment screen builds one line from one or more underlying stat kinds, then calculates a truncated average of their star levels and top levels. a stat whose maximum is under 5 can be rescaled for this display. this explains why an individual line can show an intermediate label or + even when some underlying statistic has already reached its own cap. the ui shows a filled star when the displayed average equals its corresponding top value, rather than directly checking each raw stored stat for equality. the display evaluator and the underlying weapon value evaluator are not interchangeable. an aggregated visual label cannot reconstruct the complete per-stat upgrade state of the weapon. evidence and attribution: kh-edf5-file-formats, facts weapon-star-arrays, weapon-star-label-average, weapon-star-label-examples, weapontext-hq-stats, weapon-level-times-25; static reverse engineering and jp-table comparison, build steam-5d11de53.

edf6 distinguishes ownership, use, newness and upgrades the examined edf6 weapon system keeps a per-row state in its game-save context. possessing a weapon is not the same as having equipped it, having seen it since acquisition, or having improved its stars. four observed flag bits bit meaning in the cited state updater 0 owned 1 used / equipped on a sortie 2 newly obtained, not yet cleared by the normal sortie transition 3 upgraded a normal new-game reset grants acquisition-class 1 weapons as owned/new and seeds their star fields from the defined starting policy. download-content refresh separately checks installed content packs, grants acquisition-class 3 items from eligible packs, and removes ownership for uninstalled pack-specific items. an equipped weapon that is no longer owned is replaced by a soldierinit default. mission rewards and stars a mission result passes crate acquisitions through the game-data reward handler. the cited route marks a newly granted item owned/new, initializes its star data and may subsequently upgrade it. zero stars is a valid state. the weapon stat evaluator clamps each stat to its table-defined cap; the weapon display and actual firing state are calculated from the same star inputs but can format them differently. at the start of a sortie, setusedweapon() marks equipped items as used and clears the new and upgraded presentation flags from the rows it visits. thus the new indicator is a short-lived presentation state; it does not constitute a separate permanent acquisition list. what installed dlc and the current mode change the game reads content entitlement separately from table acquisition class. weapon rows have a physical index in the currently loaded weapontable, and the active mode supplies the table context. the mode transition and save-load sequence therefore matter when interpreting ownership, displaying weapons, or applying localized weapon text. a save holding an old row number must not be assumed to map to the same item if the table order changed. the user interface's weapon count and weapon-acquisition percentage are based on owned records and use their own dlc exclusion rules; those numbers are not identical to the number of rows in the weapontable. evidence and attribution: kh-edf6-weapons, weapon-grant-paths, weapon-table-access, weapon-table-entry; source build steam-678ccb46. this article describes game behavior inferred from code and game data, not instructions for changing a save file.

edf6 mission progression has separate clear flags and difficulty-level state the engine records which difficulties a player/class has completed for each mission and separately decides the current mission level, which affects scaling. a clear flag, the selected difficulty and a script's setmissionlevelfix() are three different state variables. mission-clear flags difficulty stored bit easy 0x01 normal 0x02 hard 0x04 hardest 0x08 inferno 0x10 the native completion function loops from easy up through the just-cleared difficulty only when the difficulty is easy, normal or hard. clearing hardest or inferno marks their own bit, not all lower difficulties. this explains the familiar progression behavior without treating the flags as an ordered numeric level value. mission progress is used to interpolate enemy level the selected difficulty comes from gamestatus +0x4c in the studied build. the current mission's row position and total row count yield a progress fraction. the per-difficulty [lvmin, lvmax] bounds in config.sgo are interpolated using that fraction, with single-precision arithmetic. for the original main campaign the source reports bounds: difficulty level-factor bounds easy 5–15 normal 10–24 hard 20–60 hardest 70–150 inferno 160–280 dlc modes may use different bounds; dlc2, for example, has inferno 310–350. these are parameters of the game's scaling model, not necessarily weapon-drop levels or individual enemy hp values. a script's fixed-level flag is independent of difficulty the scripting interfaces getdifficulty() and setmissionlevelfix() operate on distinct fields. the latter sets a fixed-level flag at gamestatus +0x44 and does not change the selected difficulty at +0x4c. a bvm reset clears the flag on relevant mission lifecycle transitions, so a fixed-level tutorial cannot be assumed to change the following mission. edf6 carries both an older bvm call and native angelscript routes, but bvm native 20's shared mission factor is not the same operation as the angelscript setmissionlevel(float) enemy-team factor. these should not be translated by matching only names or arguments. modelist structure changed from edf5 edf5 uses a 12-field mode row; edf6 uses 13 fields, adding an explicit .mst filename in field 5. as a result, the mission-list triple and the difficulty array move one slot later, with edf6's per-difficulty values in field 7. a parser that applies edf5 offsets to an edf6 configuration would read the wrong data even when the visible mode name is the same. evidence and attribution: kh-edf6-missions: mission-clear-bits, difficulty-mission-level, difficulty-level-ranges, edf6-modelist-shape. anchors apply to build steam-678ccb46; prior source includes an instruction-level harness comparison but no r128 in-game validation.

edf4.1's save layout is package- and mode-aware the original pc edf4.1 executable constructs a save tree under the folder string my games/edf4.1/save_data, with a saveslot%02d folder for each save slot. the documented strings come from the game executable, not from guessed filenames. the base folder is acquired through a windows known-folder lookup, though the exact shell-folder constant was not resolved in the cited study. names visible in the original executable name or pattern role / level of evidence saveslot%02d save slot directory name pattern system.cfg shared system configuration; studied code builds a system folder in place of a slot name common.cfg save-related configuration name systemwin32.cfg windows-specific system settings name trophy.dat achievement/statistics save name main.gst the mode's principal game-state resource filename %ls_m%02d.mst mode-specific mission progress filename pattern the .mst filename is assembled using the loaded config.sgo packagename and the modelist row index, not only the visible campaign title. the stock package name is defp, so the first mode's progress name becomes defp_m00.mst. the main.gst string is read from an explicit modelist entry. what this does and does not prove the source establishes the filename constants, folder pattern and mode-name construction. it does not independently document all bytes inside these save files, all platform variants, or how concurrent writes are handled. the presence of trophy.dat in both edf4.1 and edf6 should not be taken as proof that their binary schemas match. in particular, the edf6 achievement layout has its own game/build-specific documentation. a modded package can alter packagename or mode rows, making filename identity a practical compatibility consideration. that is an observation about the game's native storage model, not a guide to editing or bypassing progression. evidence and attribution: kh-edf41-globals: edf41-save-files and edf41-save-file-names; original static source inspection by novae (ajane), build steam-57aab039.

edf6 defines muzzle positions in weapon animation data an edf6 gun's firing point is not necessarily a specially named muzzle bone in its mdb mesh. the studied game reads its muzzle description from the weapon sgo's animation_model[2] mab-related list. each entry associates a name, a model node and a local transform. the runtime turns that into the shot-origin matrix used when firing. source geometry and the runtime entry the native weapon construction code creates muzzle entries with a 0xf0-byte stride, accessed through a weapon field at +0x1d0. in a representative entry, offset +0x00 points to the node record, +0x10 stores a local matrix and +0x50 the resulting shot matrix. the data is derived from the node's transform, not simply from whatever bone pose the renderer currently shows. examples recovered from original edf6 resources: weapon/model example named mount node local position (x, y, z) assault rifle s_assault_af14d.mdb body (0, 0.089, 0.683) sniper rifle s_sniper_mmf01.mdb body (0, 0.105, 1.112) shotgun s_shotgun_buffalo01.mdb body (0, 0.087, 0.704) ranger stingray-type launcher root (0, 0.126, 0.672) wing diver lazr01 root (0, 0.078, 0.663) fencer heavy cannon h_cannon_normal01.mdb nozzle (0, 0, 1.486) fencer gatling h_gatling_normal01.mdb roll (0, 0, 0.956) these values are local to the model's own coordinate frame. they should not be interpreted as absolute positions in a mission map or reused as global weapon dimensions. why an attachment can look right but fire wrong the visual model can contain a node called body, roll or nozzle whose origin is not the projectile spawn origin. the mab attachment supplies a deliberate offset. therefore matching a screenshot of a muzzle tip does not by itself reproduce the native shot transform, and inspecting only the mesh bone table is insufficient for accurate projectile placement. evidence and attribution: kh-edf6-weapons, source facts weapon-muzzle-data, weapon-muzzle-entries, muzzle-shot-modes; static analysis and source-resource inspection attributed to hajisensai / all forces, build steam-678ccb46. no new firing test was run.

edf6's air raider energy wall is a projectile-backed collider the energy wall deployed by air raider equipment such as eweapon196 is implemented in the examined edf6 executable as barrierbullet01. despite its appearance as a stationary shield, its lifecycle and contact handling belong to a bullet-derived native object. shape and placement its ammo_customparameter carries five entries: an arc in radians, radius, height, three-axis scale and local offset. the wall's curved collision surface is divided into approximately int(arc / 0.0872) segments, centered along the object's local +z axis, with an additional 2 m skirt below it. the source identifies collision layer 14 and an associated barrierinfo metadata record. once the deployed bullet touches the environment, a state flag anchors its position. the update path still synchronizes its collision transform with its stored bullet transform rather than treating it as arbitrary static map geometry. why friendly and enemy shots interact differently the wall records a team at creation, inherited from its firing/support-unit context. its candidate selection filters hostile teams' bullets. this is the native basis for the familiar result in which enemy projectiles collide with the wall while allied projectiles can pass. the team is captured once at construction; the research does not establish an arbitrary dynamic team-change mechanism for an already-deployed wall. the object has a float durability/hp field. incoming damage messages reduce it, with an exception for the cited forced-replay flag. at zero hp or the object's deletion condition, the wall is removed; the original path does not create a generic shatter effect at destruction. in online play the object sends an appropriate delete notification unless its special state suppresses that send. evidence limitations the source includes instruction-level re and a private native-mapping test of damage reducing the wall's hp until deletion. that is not a complete gameplay test of every shield equipment, network peer or damage type. numeric offsets and vtables refer to the studied steam build and must not be applied to another executable blindly. evidence and attribution: kh-edf6-weapons, fact barrier-bullet-wall, contributed by hajisensai / all forces; build steam-678ccb46.

edf6 secondary actions are part of weapon state, not one global key command in the studied edf6 native weapon system, each weapon carries a secondaryfire_type field and the main weapon update dispatches that value through a fixed native table. the observed types include 1 = zoom, 4 = jumpjets, 5 = dash and 6 = shield reflect. this means identical player input can perform different actions depending on the equipped weapon. fencer movement from a weapon action for a fencer dash or jet action, the weapon sends a native message (0x2003) to the character object. the dash controller projects its movement input along the player's current aim yaw, and the associated network event carries yaw information. it is not simply a global player-speed multiplier detached from the weapon and aim direction. a shot also passes several independent gates native weaponbase firing checks rounds remaining, a firing-delay flag, cooldown and a separate state bit. the source records the cooldown as a float value counted down by weapon updates, not by a wall-clock timer independent of the game's frame cadence. a successful round reduces available ammunition and selects a muzzle based on a running shot index modulo the weapon's muzzle count. a lock-on weapon has an additional rule. except for documented lock types 0 and 5, firing is refused when the lock list is empty. with multi-lock targeting, a single trigger action can produce a volley whose shot count derives from the number of locks; the distribution mode chooses whether it controls fireburstcount or firecount. vehicle-mounted weapons can update their lock search even without an active trigger pull. these conditions help explain two otherwise surprising behaviors: a weapon can appear ready but refuse to fire without targets, and holding a burst trigger through a cooldown does not necessarily queue unlimited bursts. scope this is a source-derived description of selected native classes in edf6 build steam-678ccb46. not every weapon shares every vtable path or secondary type. no new gameplay input or multiplayer latency test was performed. evidence and attribution: kh-edf6-weapons, secondary-fire-dispatch, weapon-fire-gates-round-count, weapon-sgo-fire-gates; contributors edf6vr/momotori01 and hajisensai / all forces.

edf6 animation state machines: how cas controls poses and movement the edf6 animation system is more than a list of named clips. a .cas file combines an embedded canm6 clip container, independent animation groups, named controller variables and compact programs that assemble the pose each update. this account is based on exact-build code analysis and a multi-file parse census, not on new in-game animation testing. container and named state identity in the studied steam build (steam-678ccb46) a cas header is 0x30 bytes. all 323 cas files in the original sampling subset used version 516 (0x204), with an embedded canm, tcontrols, vcontrols, animation groups and bone-name references. the edf6 instruction format is 13 32-bit words (52 bytes), unlike the earlier 9-word form in cas 512. strings are terminated utf-16le; most record-local offsets are relative to the referring record. a tcontrol is a 12-byte, named ordered sequence of canm clips, not a bone channel. its length is the sum of clip durations; sampled files included valid empty tcontrols. the vcontrol records (20 bytes) supply float, int or matrix variables; the game finds inputs by name, including v_move_x, v_aim_target and weapon- or vehicle-grip ik targets. changing a variable name can sever the engine's intended input connection. a separate cas bonelist resolves node names against the model; a missing node can produce an initialization message. each anmgroup owns its own node/state list. code selects groups and nodes by name and changes them using setplayedanimationid(group,node,flags). main and weapon are examples; their names are not arbitrary metadata. node timing and cross-fades record observed native behavior animation node (0x24 bytes) holds state name, default and source-state transition records, and three programs: entry, pose and post-skeleton ik end kind 0 never expires; loops end kind 1 uses explicit float end time end kind 2 uses the combined duration of a tcontrol selected by tcontrol index, not by canm clip-name order transition (0x20 bytes) includes source-state match, fade time in frames, optional program and a start-time mode crossfade start mode 2 preserves current playback phase rather than unconditionally resetting it the source's 375-file census counted 6,037 kind-2 nodes, 577 kind-0 nodes and ten kind-1 nodes. a separate 323-file verification found 346 false out-of-range references if kind-2 end times were misread as canm clip-name indices. this is a concrete example of two valid index spaces inside the same asset. what the tiny vm actually does a program is a count plus an instruction-array offset. its native opcodes do not provide a normal branch/loop language: instructions execute sequentially, while node transitions provide state control. programs run at different phases: the global controller program runs after group times advance. entry parametric1 and transition programs run when a node is selected. parametric2 samples/blends the pose;
