group references can contribute more poses. the game updates bone/world matrices, then parametric3 supplies ik corrections. opcode family operations found in the source 0–5 sample a tcontrol, normalized samples, two/three-way blends, additive sampling 6–11 rotation compose/difference and weighted blends (some defined but not seen in sampled files) 12–22 float assignment, arithmetic, interpolation, clamping, magnitudes 24–28 integer assignment and arithmetic 30, 31 aim constraint and two-bone inverse kinematics 32 run the active node's post-update ik program 33 send a user callback to game code, e.g. weapon hand reattachment these are vm opcode numbers, not portable commands for arbitrary cas versions. the source documents a real ignored opcode 35 and invalid operand combinations that can crash the game. the embedded canm's own bonelist is not proven interchangeable with the cas bonelist. evidence and useful companion pages the source reports a 323-file parse and a separate 375-file state-machine census; these are not necessarily identical populations and must not be merged into one denominator. this is static / binary-researched knowledge for steam-678ccb46. attribution: edf knowledge hub, edf6/animation-cas.md; cas/canm specification (unnamed author), edf_tools (auk233), and novae (ajane). fact ids cas-header, cas-vcontrol, cas-node, cas-transition, cas-program-vm, cas-opcodes. see the cross-game cas/canm record comparison, game animation overview and original detailed source notes.

edf6 npc weapons: native sgo values versus reported on-screen damage the damage number stored in an npc weapon's sgo is not automatically the damage that an ally deals on a given difficulty. an edf knowledge hub comparison of 24 npc soldier weapon entries with the japanese edf6 wiki found a consistent factor-of-two difference in the quoted normal-and-above damage figures. that comparison is a strong data observation; the native code path that would independently prove the scaling factor was not identified. soldier weapons: measured pairs edf6 weapon sgo ammodamage in sgo figure in japanese edf6 wiki aisoldierrifle01 5 2.5 aisoldiershotgun01 3 × 10 1.5 × 10 aisoldiersniperrifle02 25 12.5 all 24 tested soldier-weapon rows followed that relationship. the likely explanation is that the game scales npc weapon damage to one-half of the sgo amount under the wiki's test conditions. that is an inference from correlated data, not a traced damage routine. edf5's comparable wiki historically used the full sgo figure, which helps explain misleading comparisons across generations. vehicle sgo mission_setup[0] is not a generic damage flag research compared the two-element mission_setup[0] list in several allied vehicle sgos. it found values that numerically reproduce the japanese wiki's vehicle-weapon reductions, notably: vehicle sgo observed pair supporting comparison v504_begaruta_ai, v504_begaruta_g_ai (nix) [1, 0.8] weapon figures 5 and 60 × 0.8 = 4.0 and 48 v608_oldrobot_ai (gravis) [1, 1] same base weapon figures listed as 5.0 and 60 v603_flak_weak_ai [1, 0.5] ordinary v603_flak_ai is [1, 1] vehicle403_tank_mission [1, 0.6] distinct mission actor preset v603_flak_mission [1.25, 1] first element differs; role unknown v614_proteus_mk2 and related mission variants [3, 3.5] not a standard [1,1] preset the second value behaving like a damage multiplier is plausible but still unverified. the reader of that pair was not traced. the first value's meaning is unknown; treating it as a durability multiplier would be speculation. vehicle base-value cross-check and exception a broader check found the japanese edf6 npc vehicle wiki usually agrees with the sgo base durability: e.g. blacker and varius 700, titan 2,400, epsilon 1,600, proteus 7,500 and war/armament barga 40,000. most weapon entries also agree, but the proteus buster cannon is unresolved: the wiki quotes 60, while one sampled v_407bigbegaruta_cannon_ai sgo has 35 and the associated mission setup is [1,1]. the combat wagon variants have difficulty-specific durability entries [700,700,2100], not one universal figure. evidence: sgo comparisons, not independent r130 gameplay tests; edf6 steam build steam-678ccb46. the japanese wiki's displayed figures are source comparison data, not original sandlot documentation. attribution: edf knowledge hub edf6/npc-data.md, facts npc-weapon-damage-half-wiki, npc-vehicle-mission-setup-factor, npc-vehicles-wiki-match; kh chat 117/118 and japanese edf6 atwiki page 343. see original source note, enemy scaling and vehicle physics.

edf6 insect contact queries: why a friendly swarm can still cost collision work in the examined edf6 steam binary, a particular insect-related contact check performs a full world collision query before discarding many non-hostile results. this is important for understanding the cost of a crowded scene, but it does not establish that the same call path is used by every insect attack or every swarm. observed query chain the study identified a candidate contact routine at edf.dll+0x429b00, called from +0x431b80 at +0x4322ac. it reads a collision filter, builds a list of 0xa0-byte hit entries and calls the common world-query routine +0x542860. the latter has five known direct callers; only one was associated with this insect-related site. the broad world query visits body ids, resolves a body and its owner, skips null owners and the querying object itself, invokes the narrow collision phase (+0x11aa270) and appends contacts that pass. these operations happen before the caller makes its later hostility decision. the function lies near rtti/vtables for giantdango, but the source did not confirm the exact in-game creature that owns this call site. the adjacency must not be promoted to a resolved class identity. post-query team filtering back in +0x431b80, the caller locks weak references for the recorded hit entries and reads team ids at object +0x314. if both ids are valid (not -1), it retains a hit only when the querying team's relation table says the target is hostile (2). otherwise the contact can be discarded after the more expensive collision work has run. this means that in a same-team swarm some narrow-phase intersections can be computed only to be thrown away. it does not imply friendly units collide or attack one another in the final gameplay result. where performance claims stop a separate contributor explored moving that hostility predicate to the candidate loop before narrow-phase testing. that explains a potential optimization principle, not a measured speedup: the original hub explicitly marked the claimed large fps gain unverified. counts of candidates and excluded non-hostiles would be needed to quantify it. moving the check can also change behavior if team ids are missing or relationship tables are inconsistent, so source equivalence alone is not gameplay parity. evidence level: static disassembly / known caller mapping for steam-678ccb46; no new profiling or runtime performance measurement in this wiki revision. attribution: edf knowledge hub edf6/insect-contacts.md, edf6swarmperf and novae (ajane), facts insect-query, world-query-loop, insect-hit-discard, swarmperf-filter, swarmperf-gain. see original source observations, native collision matrix and umbra visibility costs.

edf6 main script: title, hq and mission are coroutine-driven states the retail edf6 mainscript.as contains named routines for starting the title, entering headquarters and launching missions. the native angelscript registration coroutine createcoroutine(const string &in) resolves these function declarations by name, rather than hard-wiring every transition as a compiled c++ scene. this is the same underlying game mechanism for normal menu transitions and the retained debug path. native routine graph routine role in the observed script starttotitle() loads system save data and reaches the title route title() presents the title/press start stage that also initializes input ownership slotselect() chooses the save slot through createslotselectui2 hqmain() main hq/menu route, can return playmission_offline playmission_offline() starts the selected offline mission and eventually applies its result result_common(g_is_mission_clear) processes clear/failure after the mission and returns to hq debug_startoffline() retained internal function that omits normal title and slot selection playmission_offline() ultimately returns the name hqmain, so hq is reconstructed as the next script state when an offline mission ends. this is a fact about the native state machine, not evidence that chained unattended mission launches are an official gameplay feature. slot and mode are separate concerns the retained debug_startoffline() sequence calls initialization, boot-complete network location, title-save load, add-on/save readiness waits, an offline mode selection, then loadsavedata_modeselect(). a failed mode-save load returns to starttotitle. the debug route relies on the current engine slot index because it skips the usual slotselect() stage. for the studied steam build steam-678ccb46, the gamedatamgr offline mission row was reported at +0x48 and difficulty at +0x4c (values 0–4). the report maps m001 to row 1 and rm015 to row 13. these offsets come from a contributor's native/plug-in mapping and were not separately retraced in edf.dll during the knowledge hub audit. a revealing input-mode edge case a contributor runtime test found that entering via the preserved debug startup left actual gameplay in gamepad mode even without an attached pad: keyboard movement/mouse look did not respond, while some menu navigation keys still worked. repeating entry through the normal title press start using a keyboard initialized keyboard/mouse control; a subsequently observed mode byte read zero. that difference identifies title input-mode initialization as an important part of the genuine startup lifecycle. it does not by itself prove every detail of an alternative initialization path; a direct mode-byte change was specifically left untested. evidence and references static script line positions in the original source: starttotitle about 442, hqmain 894, playmission_offline 1087, debug_startoffline 1865, applymodeno(int) 1895. native routine registration: edf.dll+0x12946f0, overload with second any@ argument at +0x1294b00 (build-specific). all code offsets and line numbers apply only to the retained mainscript.as and binary build. attribution: edf knowledge hub edf6/menu-script.md; novae (ajane), edf6autopilot / hajisensai, source facts createcoroutine-menu-routines, gamedata-mission-row-difficulty, edf6-debug-start-offline-flow, edf6-offline-mission-chain, edf6-debug-start-pad-mode. see original study, missionmgr and mode identity and mission scripting.

distance and detail across edf4.1, edf5 and edf6 all three examined games use camera-distance-dependent model selection for map trees, structures and other props, but the default distances and engine controls differ. the same source also records a separate distance-dependent animation update skip, which should never be confused with mesh lod or with animation being absent. mesh → billboard → cull for trees in each studied generation the tree renderer compares a squared camera-distance metric to squared thresholds from the map's .trb definitions. below the near threshold it draws the mesh; in the near-to-far band it blends full mesh and billboard; farther away it draws the billboard where available; past the cut-off it draws neither. some pass types do not submit the billboard. the camera-distance factor has an additional view-dependent multiplier whose writer was not resolved consistently in all studies. game native .trb examples evidence scope edf4.1 most trees: 10 m near, far often 110–250 m; selected city street trees start at 50 m 96 .trb examples across the studied map set edf5 most trees: 50 m near, often 100–180 m far; bushes commonly 10/50 m 149 entries in the studied all-map enumeration edf6 trees on heigen507: 50 m near, 100–180 m far, usually 1000 m cut-off; bushes 10/50 m 19 local .trb entries in one named map the edf6 example is not an all-map census and should not be compared numerically with the wider edf4.1/5 corpora as if they sampled equally. a billboard texture must also exist; otherwise a far-distance selection may render nothing. buildings are not smoothly crossfaded in the studied builds placed building structures have up to three model choices. the engine selects a level based on lod distance fields in mapb and the corresponding part fields in mapo; when both specify thresholds, the larger defined value is used. the observed native renderer hard-switches between structure lods rather than smoothly dithering from one to another. a contributor verified a plainly visible edf6 building pop when walking a small step in a city scene. common squared-metre fields explain thresholds that otherwise look too large: field value equivalent distance 6,400 80 m 10,000 100 m 22,500 150 m 40,000 200 m 90,000 300 m across edf4.1, 3,011 of 4,632 sampled placed category-1 .mosb buildings used the 150 m first lod with no second lod; edf5's 8,365 placed buildings included 2,854 such 150 m/no-second-lod cases. edf6 included several frequent two-threshold pairs, such as 200/300 m or 100/300 m, and a separate 150 m/no-second-lod class. these are observed frequency tables, not map-independent rendering contracts. distant animation updates are another knob the generation crosswalk identified pose-job frequency reduction for edf5 and edf6 insect actors. in edf5, the native distance bands can update poses once every 1, 4, 8 or 16 normal job slots; for humans the corresponding path is gated by human_frame_skip_enable and is usually disabled by default. edf6 insects use corresponding bands, influenced by insectbase_animationlodadjust from sgo data. edf4.1 had the mesh lod selector but no corresponding animation skip was found in the inspected paths. that is a negative-search result, not proof no skip mechanism exists anywhere in the game. edf4.1 uniquely exposes set_lod_distance_scale, which changes several distance-scale globals (the chara family is treated separately). edf5 did not have the corresponding global distance-scale control in the researched build; edf6 uses distinct global structure scaling values. nothing here establishes that changing any of these controls is safe for performance, shadow passes or other map content. what this comparison does and does not establish three independent systems matter: tree billboard selection, building mesh lod and skeleton/pose scheduling. changing a mesh selection threshold does not force new animation frames, improve an existing source texture, or solve foliage alpha blending. likewise, retaining distant full-resolution meshes can increase draw or visibility cost. evidence: source-code/disassembly and named-map asset studies, plus one contributor's observed edf6 building pop. no new game run was performed for this article. attribution: edf knowledge hub crosswalk/lod-distance-animation.md, edf41/map-lod.md, edf5/map-lod.md, edf6/map-lod.md; novae (ajane), kh 00v/autorun contributors. exact fact ids preserved in the separate provenance ledger. see original edf4.1 lod source, edf5, edf6 and native visibility cost.

edf6 map collision: from mad bodies to physical surface types edf6's visual map geometry and its solid physical collision are separate resources. in the examined corpus each map's mad contains a collision.hkt havok payload; the map loader resolves that entry by its name's crc32, loads its physics-scene data and associates named physical bodies with their map models. the source counted 50 maps with collision resources in three cpk groups; that count belongs to the examined install snapshot, not all conceivable dlc or mod maps. how a map collision body identifies a model a body name can combine an mdb model name, a collision node and an optional render node. for example: com_ym_jihanki_panel1.com_ym_jihanki_panel1_colli|ym_jihanki_panel1 the native reader splits on . and |, reconstructs the asset identity and matches the named bodies with models from the map's rab. the body and the visible mesh are therefore not interchangeable, even if their names resemble one another. compact per-surface information some havok material names contain json under the source key 0xf201, for example: {"hkconfig":"p_material=2;p_penetration=0;ai_cost=0;","name":"aaa_panel01"} map::havok_fixupshape packs the three values into shape userdata: property packed portion source meaning or limitation p_material bits 0–7 surface material; 0 default, 1 glass, 2 metal in the studied configurations p_penetration bits 8–15 separate penetration/contact classification ai_cost bits 16–23 possible navigation cost input; the native consumer is not established the low byte is read on a hit by the game's material lookup. that routine descends compound shapes through shape keys and reads the leaf userdata (or a material field for a type-8 leaf). it is not simply reading the original json string again. source code for the hit lookup, including +0x1082e0 and +0x11a9b60, was traced on one edf6 steam binary. p_material=1 correlates with window/glass pieces and 2 with metallic panel/vending-machine components; collision-layer and effect-sound tests supported the mapping. the underlying hknpmaterial friction and restitution fields can be overwritten by global map settings during load, so a raw material's half-float values are not necessarily final runtime parameters. evidence boundaries the source reports a contributor-tested hkconfig reading, static code mapping for packed userdata, and many observed materials. it does not demonstrate a global use for every ai_cost, or that water on any arbitrary map is implemented as a special penetrable solid. do not generalize any function address to another binary build. attribution: edf knowledge hub edf6/map-collision.md; ktaro and hajisensai/all forces, facts map-collision-load, map-body-names, map-hkconfig, map-hkconfig-usage, hit-surface-material. see original map collision study and collision filters.

edf6 maps contain two distinct floor-navigation worlds on the studied edf6 executable and map corpus, each map has two havok navigation resources, with matching .nvmd metadata: resource suffix ai world native actor examples .navmesh_h.hkt 0 — human humanbase allied soldiers, vehicles, routeguide and bombbullet01 .navmesh.hkt 1 — big humanoidbase, large berserker/hector actors, merman, shellfish and giantdango the suffix _h maps to the human world, not the big world. the original route-building function chooses the names according to the inverse-looking selector in its caller; relying on alphabetical order or filename length would invert the maps. what these files really store each navigation hkt contains section-indexed triplets: navmesh<n> (hkainavmesh), graph<n> (hkaidirectedgraphexplicitcost) and mediator<n> (hkaiquerymediator). one studied edfroom file had 15 sections. both classes of navmesh were almost entirely upward-facing floor geometry (99.6–100% of measured face area). the _h mesh typically had 5–6× more faces than the big version in the reported corpus. these are not wall-climbing navigation meshes. enemy wall-climbing and attachment can be handled by a different controller, and the existence of a detailed collision body is not proof it has a traversable navmesh connection. a valid navmesh_h.hkt is also not enough to establish that an edf4.1 port has the correct paths on a different map geometry. runtime ownership and open limits maprabinit requests both variants, and the map manager creates separate ai worlds. createaicharacter takes a world id, so actors can end up using different route graphs within the same scene. a contributor tried replacing the human source mesh with the big one and did not observe a clear behavioral difference in that specific test. that was inconclusive: it neither disproves the world separation nor establishes that swapping the files is safe. evidence: source-level havok file inspection, static edf.dll analysis (+0x18f9a0, +0x121470) and the one inconclusive contributor experiment. build steam-678ccb46; no new r131 in-game validation. attribution: ktaro / edf knowledge hub edf6/map-collision.md, facts navmesh-worlds, navmesh-contents. see original evidence, navigation guide, and edf4.1 route-graph limitations.

why edf6's route guide can visually cut through a wall the moving arrow strip drawn by routeguide is not the navigation mesh itself. it takes an ai path's corners, simplifies and smooths them, then draws its own world-space line. thus a guide line that seems to cross a wall does not, on its own, demonstrate an invalid navigation mesh or physically permeable wall. native path and renderer routeguide obtains its path through a havok human-world ai::character search, not by reading mission.rmpa route names. the line renderer generates vertices and advances a texture phase based on time and accumulated distance; this is why the arrows appear to flow along the path. the separate routeguide_arrow sgo creates one arrow and is a different scene-object class. the route-guide object has two explicit target modes in the studied sources: mode 1: follow a target object and stop if that object disappears. mode 2: follow a fixed area/point location. a legacy edf5 bvm entry also reached a mode-0 route path in the studied edf6 binary, but the target-mode handler did not cover 0. that raised a source-level risk of a zero-origin endpoint in a converted mission. the hub did not report a game demonstration of this anomaly. why visually cutting corners is possible the draw route first prunes near-duplicate corners: in the observed default configuration, corners within approximately 15 m of the start are dropped and subsequent corners within 7 m of the preceding kept point are dropped. it then creates a hermite-style curve through midpoints rather than requiring every original corner to become an exact vertex. additional smoothing blends indexed points between frames, with factor 0.04 (or 0.08 in the alternate script condition). three distinct transformations can therefore change the visible line: dropping a near corner can bridge over the edge of a nearby structure. the smoothed curve can leave the exact polygonal ai route even when its original corners follow a corridor. when a path's number of corners changes, index-to-index interpolation can temporarily blend unrelated positions. the studied code also allows a straight player-to-target line after a failed/missing query result, which may cross obstacles. these are explanations from code and offline geometry reasoning; the original contributors did not perform an exhaustive gameplay qualification of every map and guide mode. keep navigation evidence separate do not infer that the rendered line is a test of obstacle clearance, enemy attack targeting or the navmesh graph's validity. a mission can have correct physical collision but wrong ai route data, or a correct route graph but inaccurate guide rendering. attribution: edf knowledge hub edf6/map-collision.md, facts route-guide-object and route-guide-wall-cutting; hajisensai / all forces, novae (ajane). studied build steam-678ccb46. see human and big worlds and source notes.

edf5 and edf6 walking controllers: ground support is not ground transport the examined edf5 and edf6 character controllers share recognizable physics concepts: a desired horizontal velocity, a separate vertical/ballistic velocity, a support-normal query and a 60 hz step. a key detail is that havok can report velocity for the supporting surface even while the character's stock walking code chooses not to inherit that velocity. edf5's native walking step in edf5 build steam-5d11de53, xgs::havok::charactercontrol_walk has its own rtti/vtable and a shared step routine at edf.dll+0x628b80. it is owned by several classes, including humanbase, humanoidbase, monsterbase, alientrailer, barga/balam-like fortress robotics and the nix/begaruta walking controller. it makes an hkstepinfo of 1/60 s and reads checksupport into an hkpsurfaceinfo. hkpsurfaceinfo field meaning supported state 0 unsupported, 1 sliding, 2 supported surface normal direction used to project movement onto a slope surface velocity velocity of the ground contact, available but not consumed by the stock walk step dynamic flag describes a moving/dynamic support-body property when supported, the controller projects desired movement onto the ground and adjusts ballistic motion. a launch flag protects jumps from being immediately treated as ordinary supported movement; when airborne, the vertical velocity changes under gravity. the stock controller combines these fields into one character-body linear-velocity update. the moving-platform trap the edf5 walk function reads the support state and normal but not the reported surface velocity or dynamic-support flag. edf6's studied controller likewise calculates an output from its own movement and external velocity slots rather than automatically carrying over the surface velocity from a moving support body. thus simply standing on a moving actor need not transport a soldier at the platform's speed. for edf5, the havok support query does populate the ground-velocity field. its getground route, however, is called with usedynamicbodyvelocities=0, which can limit which ground-body motions contribute. neither source establishes correct movement-on-every-vehicle behavior: whether a particular collision layer allows standing on a body and how that body's motion is represented remain separate questions. cross-generation differences and limits edf6's controller field offsets differ (for example desired velocity appears at +0x20 in the retained edf6 map versus +0x50 in edf5). directly reusing memory offsets or moving-platform assumptions across builds is unsafe. the edf5 source also notes that mode changes for ragdoll parts are a separate physical system from the ordinary walking controller. evidence: static exact-build reverse engineering, not a new test involving a moving platform. potential alterations to surface-velocity inheritance in the original source were unverified engineering hypotheses and are not presented as native game behavior. attribution: novae (ajane), edf knowledge hub edf5/character-control.md and edf6/character-control.md; facts edf5-walk-step, edf5-walk-fields, edf5-moving-ground-stock, edf5-get-ground-velocity, edf6-moving-ground-stock. see edf5 character source and edf6 walk controller details.

edf6 language settings: display text and voice are separate engine values in the examined edf6 executable, language selection is not one interchangeable scalar. the engine has a text-language integer and a neighboring voice-language integer, exposed by separate accessors. this distinction is relevant to ui strings, subtitles, voice lookups and localization testing. native text selection the original accessor at edf.dll+0xe4000 reads the text-language value at the build-specific global +0x20b2b30, while +0xe4030 writes it. the observed enum order is: value text language 0 japanese (ja) 1 english (en) 2 korean (kr) 3 traditional chinese (cn) 4 simplified chinese (sc) the source relates these numbers to option-string ordering and distinct chinese font resources. they are build-specific enum values, not a general locale identifier for all edf releases. voice language is normalized separately a nearby getter at +0xe4010 reads voice language from +0x20b2b34. its setter at +0xe4070 maps incoming value 4 to 3, so the two chinese text-language choices share one chinese voice-language selection in the studied build. this behavior does not establish that every line in each language has a voiced cue, nor does it imply that text and spoken language must always be the same. other globals for input and ui sit in the same overall engine environment but have separate update paths. for example the keyboard-state buffer and the current input-mode byte are not the language controls; changing one is not evidence of a problem with the others. evidence: direct static read of native getters/setters for build steam-678ccb46, not a new in-game localization test. the precise voice table resolution for each cue belongs to the audio subsystem. attribution: edf knowledge hub edf6/globals.md, facts text-language-global, voice-language-global, input-ui-globals, contributors novae (ajane) and original research authors. see edf6 dialogue and subtitle pipeline and original globals study.

edf5 map.mapb: where map objects are placed a map's visible objects are not simply stored as complete models at their world positions. edf5's map.mapb associates placement records with object definitions; the loader constructs a world matrix, chooses an object class by the definition's resource extension, and hands the resulting parameters to that class. edf6 uses a closely related format, but not the same placement record size. the placement record the studied edf5 loader walks the entries with 0x44 bytes per record. the corresponding edf6 record is 0x48 bytes. for a record at address r the source identified: offset from r edf5 meaning +0x00 relative offset to the object definition +0x04, +0x08, +0x0c translation x, y, z as 32-bit floats +0x10, +0x14, +0x18 euler rotation x, y, z in degrees the native function converts degrees to radians, applies the x, then y, then z rotations, and builds a matrix with the translation and homogeneous w=1. it does not read a per-record scale in this path. that does not mean no object in edf5 can have scale: generated foliage and mdb model internals use other sources of scale and pose data. an object definition includes a type (+0x00), a self-relative parameter sgo pointer (+0x04), a name (+0x0c) and other display/damage fields. the parameter sgo is checked against sgo and version 0x102. the corresponding mapo record, when present, is at base mapo+0x08 + placement_index*0x1c. which native class loads which resource? file-name ending edf5 preload owner what makes it special .mosb preload_structure composite building or structure, often with individual parts .fmep preload_fmex ground/field scene and its associated fmb and grass resources .mdx preload_animationmodel or preload_model has_animation in parameter sgo selects the animated branch .shfb preload_shf heightfield terrain, with .cols.sgo and .norm.sgo .trb, .mlb not spawned by this ordinary dispatcher generated through the grow-object visitors of the ground/heightfield the original notes also identify a build-specific global that can skip certain definition categories; the exact conditions were recovered statically. they should not be interpreted as universal edf5 authoring rules without the same executable. how the constructed matrix travels preload_base::initparam receives the object's world matrix alongside the parent loader, embedded parameter sgo, record, definition, mapo entry and original placement index. this establishes why resource-name identity, placement index, world transform and model part data are different pieces of the map format. evidence: static reading of edf5 steam build steam-5d11de53 (c3650 and its preload dispatch). the researcher explicitly did not independently compare every decoded byte to an untouched raw map.mapb; these offsets are engine-read semantics rather than a complete published binary grammar. sources: edf knowledge hub, edf5/map-placement.md, facts edf5-mapb-record, edf5-mapb-matrix, edf5-mapb-classes, edf5-preload-base. compare edf6 map resource layout and edf5 structure parts.

edf5 mapo is not a generic transform list map.mapo accompanies mapb placements. in the studied edf5 corpus each mapo entry is 0x1c bytes, and a part list uses self-relative pointers, distinct from the mapb object's own placement transform. this matters for destructible buildings and compound pieces: a single placed .mosb can contain many model components with their own transforms. record fields and measured corpus mapo offset observed role +0x00 fmep-specific piece pair +0x04/+0x08 pointer to and number of parts +0x0c distance-like float, often 1000 on .mosb and 0 on .mdx +0x10/+0x14 model/collision name pair; often names ending _gr +0x18 optional second part list, seen on some building entries the source counted 69,931 entries across 24 map macs; 16,771 entries contained model/collision names at +0x10/+0x14, consistently paired _gr names such as sk_bd1020_gr01.mdb / .hkt. the name suggests gareki, japanese for rubble, but the exact native reader of these name fields was not located. do not equate their presence with a proven break-to-rubble game event. in the sample, ordinary .mdx entries commonly had one part. .mosb entries ranged from one to 127 parts. one class of category-1 structure used the second +0x18 list for additional parts. these observations apply to the inspected files, not every edf5 stage or possible dlc. structure parts and local transforms a part record contains offsets to a quaternion, a position, an optional vec4 (default 1,1,1,1), and the mdb model name. preload_structure reads these values and constructs part transforms under the placed structure's world matrix. lod model-name/distance pairs and the definition's draw distance further control visibility. the structure's havok shapes are likewise assembled at part-local pose and combined into one fixed rigid body, rather than all being at the base placement origin. this distinction prevents three common mistakes: using a model's local origin as its world collision position, mistaking _gr paths for proof of runtime debris behavior, and assuming that 127 parts require 127 independent top-level mapb placements. source and scope: edf5/map-placement.md, edf5-mapo-entry and edf5-mapo-parts, static edf5 build analysis. this is structural re, not a fresh collision or destruction test.

edf5 map collision: how a placed prop becomes solid edf5 looks up many placed prop collision resources using the model or structure name, with a .hkt suffix. a map also has its own collision.hkt, but a placed model's resource path and its world transform have to be handled separately. two independent conditions: source resource and a collision role preload_model reads the object-definition name, derives its stem, and conditionally requests <stem>.hkt when a definition field at +0x10 indicates a collision asset. the same suffix is used by the fmex, animated-model and structure preload paths. the source counted 1,309/1,317 inspected definition rows with value -1 and eight with 0; interpreting this as a collision-presence switch is an inference, not an officially named file field. for a qualifying hkt, the engine builds havok rigid-body information, assigns a collision filter, poses the body from the mapb world matrix, and associates it with the object's placement index. recorded default physics data include friction-like values 0.8 and 0.5; the researcher inferred the fixed-body motion type from the stored enum. no universal collision-shape identity can be inferred from a matching mdb file name alone. observed layer selection by definition category object definition category observed collision layer 3 17 (0x11) 2, 4, 5, 6 20 (0x14) 10 water path, no ordinary body built here other categories 15 (0x0f) for composite .mosb structures, the native code merges multiple .hkt parts into a fixed body with local part transforms. generated trees use their own capsule collision, often on layer 20. the numeric layer does not alone establish every permitted pairwise collision: the filter matrix is a separate piece of havok state. limits of the evidence these findings come from edf5's object-preload functions and a 24-map tally. the source did not read all layer-to-layer pair rules in the same pass. do not substitute edf6's hknp material/layer semantics into edf5's hkp bodies simply because the class or object name is familiar. attribution: edf knowledge hub, edf5/map-placement.md, edf5-map-collision-by-name, edf5-map-collision-pose, edf5-map-collision-layers; build steam-5d11de53.

edf5 generates some vegetation from ground cell data, not mapb placements trees, grass and certain small props on an edf5 map need not have one ordinary mapb record per plant. the ground controllers read cell grids, identify plant type and jitter records, then create individual scenery objects at positions derived from the ground. fmex and shf ground use different grid layouts and height computations. fmex grid in the studied mapobject_fmex path, one plant group has an 0x88-byte description. it includes cell size, column/row counts, x/z origin, a jitter-index grid and a type grid; 0xff in the type grid is empty. type records are 0xc8 bytes; a separate jitter record is 16 bytes (rotation, two planar offsets and size). the visitor combines cell index, jitter, size and ground elevation with the ground transform. visitor implementations treat kind 0 as grass and kind 1 as generated objects. this is not a promise that all fmex resource kinds are understood, only what the recorded dispatcher actually branches on. shf heightfield grid mapobject_shf visits a different grow block with a compact two-byte cell (type and jitter index), 0x28-byte type records, and a jitter table. it does not pass jitter size into its tree visitor. its y-coordinate is obtained by casting downward from 505 units over 800 units at the chosen x/z; the ray results and the type record's vertical offset decide the placement altitude. fmex instead uses the ground cell's stored height. what .trb and .mlb do resource generated owner main behavior .trb mapobject_tree weighted tree/stump model, deterministic yaw, optional collision capsule .mlb mapobject_anyobject weighted small model, rotation/offset/color/scale attributes from rules tree selection uses a 64-bit lcg (state = state × 0x5d588b656c078965 + 0x269ec3), seeded by the placement or cell-derived index. a reload of the same seed can therefore reconstruct the same model choice and orientation. its yaw and model choice are randomized; the inspected tree visitor does not use jitter size to scale the tree. small .mlb objects have a scale branch, but the source's examples left that scale at 1. the source also distinguishes grown mapobject_tree from map-level mapobject_trees. these are not interchangeable names or the same damage handler; the independent tree-damage study is here. evidence: static edf5 loader and tree-rule re, not fresh tests of the visual distribution. source edf5/map-placement.md; facts edf5-grow-walker-fmex, edf5-grow-walker-shf, edf5-grow-object-matrix, edf5-tree-build, edf5-mlb-anyobject.

edf5 trees and buildings have different lod systems a tree's trb rule determines both its shape family and the values used when deciding when it becomes a billboard. structure models use a different part/slot lod table. treating a single distance in a map resource as a universal edf5 lod radius obscures those distinctions. trb rule anatomy in the ig_heigen507 corpus, 19 .trb sgos were observed. their rules and strings contain weighted model alternatives, optional stumps, trunk/branch identifiers and several numeric families. selected children of rule 0 are: rule 0 child observed contents supported interpretation 0 weighted model-name choices chooses the tree model 1 vec3, e.g. (0.5,9.0,0.5) or (1.0,33.5,1.0) collision/trunk size inferred 2 category such as 2 (tree) or 0 (bush) collision role 3 stump model or zero post-fall representation candidate 4 [1000], [500], [400] or [80] body property and display cutoff; not tree hp 5 two values, such as [50,150] billboard near/far switching values 6 樹木 (tree) category/name marker other rules describe the far billboard card, leaf appearance and sway by named bones (miki trunk / eda branch). model names such as sk_ptree013_40m_sugi encode characteristic heights; the engine picks from a finite set of models rather than continuously scaling each tree. the [1000]-type number is copied into a havok body property. its exact gameplay reader was not identified; interpreting it as ordinary durability is contradicted by the grown-tree hit path, which has no damage threshold. billboard and building lod the tree pipeline uses distance fields from trb rules and a billboard transition; the original notes include a per-map tally of rule values. building lod instead follows .mosb part names and per-part distance thresholds. material shaders include fade/dither behavior, so a visual disappearance can reflect lod choice, culling, or shader fade, not necessarily the removal of the physical body. boundaries: the distance fields were measured for inspected game assets and native routines, but drawing pass names and some per-parameter visual semantics were not resolved in the same study. sources: edf knowledge hub edf5/map-placement.md (edf5-trb-rules, edf5-tree-build), edf5/map-lod.md (edf5-tree-classes, edf5-tree-blocks, edf5-trb-distance-fields, edf5-tree-billboard-switch, edf5-trb-distance-values, edf5-structure-lod-table, edf5-building-lod-values, edf5-lod-fade-shaders).

edf5 scenery damage does not use one universal destructible-object class edf5 has a mapobject_base path with stored durability, child destruction and network messages. separately, generated trees are handled by mapobject_trees / mapobject_tree handlers with no ordinary hp threshold. mapobject_crashmodel also has a mesh replacement function; the existence of that method does not prove it is a physics tick. a mapobject_base hit in the studied executable the base object stores maximum and current durability at +0x124 and +0x128, respectively, with break state around +0x120. a hit record includes damage at +0x50 and a flag word at +0x5c (these are edf5-specific offsets). certain flags or definition categories allow damage to reduce durability, clamped to [0,max]; collapse can also be forced or triggered when durability reaches zero. the object provides a no-write hit check, a hit-application callback, a collapse callback and a network-message path. an object can refuse a hit due to its current state, category or the embedded networkobject. the collision code does not collapse every decorative object on every projectile contact. definition categories and observed behavior a 24-map tally included categories for buildings, trees, ground, poles, fences, vehicles/props, water and rocks, with different durability values. buildings could have values in the hundreds; light poles, fences and some small props commonly had very small values. in the native hit path category-specific masks control whether a normal hit counts, and explosion/break flags add another gate. a 0/1 distinction cannot be reduced to the model's visual size. collapse is a family of effects on collapse, the loader can traverse a mapb child-index list and signal child objects before the parent; mapobject_structure overrides the callback to step through its parts. mapobject_crashmodel has a mesh-swap override which loads a replacement resource while holding a win32 critical section. its fixed counterpart does not add a distinct override. an effects routine resolves numbered resources near the destruction point, but the source did not prove which spawned debris class owns that visual. modeldebris has an independent elapsed-time field (at +0x330) and cleanup threshold. that shows a timed lifetime; it does not establish that the class is the entire building-sinking mechanism, and the source marks its interpretation as unverified. why generated trees are different a generated tree handler resolves the contact body's identity through a map of registered trees. on a qualifying contact it can call the tree-fall handler without testing hp. the tree's fall geometry is constructed at its base, and its own body/pose path is used. the .trb rule's [1000] number is stored as a havok property and is not a normal health bar. evidence: build steam-5d11de53, reverse-engineered damage dispatch and class vtables; no new in-game test. class names and indices should not be reinterpreted as identical edf6 hknp behavior. sources: edf5/map-objects.md, facts edf5-mapobject-durability, edf5-mapobject-damage-check, edf5-mapobject-collapse, edf5-trees-damage, edf5-tree-falls-any-hit, edf5-trb-1000-body-property, mapobject-crashmodel-mesh-swap, mapobject-fixedcrashmodel-no-overrides, mapobject-structure-cascade, mapobject-destroy-effect-spawn, modeldebris-tick.

how reflections evolved across three edf engines all three edf releases ship precompiled dxbc shaders and a deferred lighting path. but where an object reflection comes from changed substantially. the same-looking model shader name can give a different result after a cross-generation port. directly observed architecture game deferred lighting compute shaders main environment-reflection source ssr status edf4.1 three identified variants one global environment cubemap no ssr shader set found in examined executable edf5 three identified variants grid of local cubemaps and texture cube array complete ssr-oriented shader set retained but unreferenced by recognized paths edf6 three identified variants grid of local cubemaps no ssr-oriented shader set found among 490 edf.dll dxbc blobs the edf4.1 deferred pass additionally produces a view-z component. edf5 adds a g_smooth_reflection_specpow g-buffer binding which is missing from the edf6 list; edf6 introduces brightness-fog parameters inside xgl_system. names and resource bindings were read from disassembled dxbc shader data, not guessed from screenshots. edf5's local cubemap path binds g_local_cubemap_array and g_local_cubemap_grid, with parameters such as the world aabb and grid cell size. edf6 retains the same concept but not the exact g-buffer or per-shader register contract. copying one game's reflection shader wholesale into another is therefore not a lossless swap. deferred versus forward reflective surfaces a deferred-combine change does not necessarily affect edf5 water or glass objects: their source shaders use a forward pass, read g_xgl_environment_map, and do not themselves sample the local cubemap grid. by contrast, building windows use an interior-mapped g-buffer shader and acquire environment lighting downstream in the deferred pass. evidence and uncertainty the three shader families were identified by resource bindings across the executables. one edf5 creation/dispatch chain was also traced; corresponding code paths were not traced to equal depth in edf4.1/edf6. the absence of a discovered ssr shader set is not proof that all forms of screen-space approximation are impossible; it is a bounded binary search result. no new picture-level comparison was performed. attribution: edf knowledge hub crosswalk/deferred-lighting-reflections.md, edf41/rendering.md, edf5/shaders.md, edf6/rendering.md; novae (ajane), hajisensai/all forces. see why edf5's ssr code is dormant and window/water differences.

edf5 ships an ssr shader suite that appears dormant the examined edf5.exe contains a coherent group of shaders whose resource bindings fit a screen-space reflections (ssr) pipeline. these are not merely shaders with a word like reflection in their file name: the rdef data identifies hi-z depth, intersection textures, a ray-march output, a resolve phase, blur phases and a final composite. detected stage function of the retained shader hi-z ray march samples high/low depth (m_hi_z) and color (m_hi_color) and writes m_out_reflection; can fall back to m_cube_map_array resolve combines intersection data and color into reflection two blur passes blur reflection using source texture/depth and blur parameters reflection + color composite combines m_reflection and m_color into output cubemap array pass samples a texture array and cubemap parameters the source supplies exact rvas for these stages, including hi-z at 0x115af80 and 0x115bfd0, resolve at 0x115aa80, blurs at 0x115ffa0/0x1161630, and composite at 0x11562f0 in the examined build. these are for identification only, not stable offsets across game builds. why “dormant” is the appropriate label the researcher scanned all executable sections for recognized rip-relative lea/mov references into the dxbc data and for absolute 8-byte pointers. other live lighting shaders were referenced; the ssr block was not. this is strong evidence that the observed ssr suite is unreferenced by the identified native call paths, and is consistent with a cut feature. it does not rule out every possible computed/indirect reference and does not prove the suite can be enabled through an ordinary settings toggle. edf6's examined edf.dll has no equivalent ssr binding family among its 490 dxbc blobs, while its local cubemap lighting remains. edf5's normal reflective appearance should therefore not be attributed to a confirmed live ssr renderer simply because the exe contains dormant shader bytes. evidence: static rdef and executable reference census, no in-game ssr toggle test. source edf5/shaders.md fact dormant-ssr-shaders, edf6/rendering.md fact lighting-cs-local-cubemaps.

edf5: water, object glass and building windows are not one shader a port or asset viewer can show multiple transparent or reflective-looking surfaces, but their source shaders do not necessarily execute in the same render pass. the edf5 dx11.cpk analysis distinguishes at least three common families. material family named shader observed drawing path reflection/interior data water snd_map_water_transparent.sgo forward, after deferred combine global environment cubemap, scrolling normals, parallax maps, scene view position standalone glass object snd_map_object_glass.sgo forward / zpass global environment cubemap, normals and reflect parameters building window snd_map_build_window.sgo g-buffer / deferred (also instanced and zpass variants) view-dependent interior texture; local cubemap contribution through later lighting combine the water pixel shader references three scrolling normal maps, three parallax textures, bubble_albedo, the global cubemap, shadow depth and the view-position texture. xgl_user_param includes water_color, reflection weighting, blend_depth, metallic and roughness. the glass-object shader exposes reflection and translucency falloff controls. neither of these forward shaders binds a scene-color input, so they cannot simply sample a hypothetical fully rendered scene for ssr without a separate binding/change. interior mapping is not a true 3d room the building-window shader samples a two-dimensional interior_texture with a view-dependent offset, including an instanced random seed. it uses window_frame_texture, window_normal, normals and a reflect parameter. that can create the impression of depth or rooms behind windows, but the source does not prove actual interior geometry or a physical space visible through the wall. the documentation preserves a remaining uncertainty: which visual component of some city images arises from the interior texture and which from the later cubemap combine had not been experimentally isolated. the shader resource bindings support the pipeline separation, not a complete visual attribution for every pane. source: edf knowledge hub edf5/shaders.md, facts water-glass-forward, window-interior-mapping, water-ps-math, window-glass-geometry where cited in the original source. static dxbc evidence only.

same shader name, different output: the legacy mech-material trap snd_mech.sgo and snd_chara_2colorchange.sgo exist across multiple edf generations. the examined deferred pixel shader implementations do not preserve the same base-color formula or output register contract. this explains why an old model's color and reflect texture cannot be assumed to look identical after a direct cross-generation import. base color formula let b be the base albedo times the diffuse/material color, and f a reflect-related component. the dxbc comparison found: version o0.rgb g-buffer target count other observed information edf4.1 b 4 reflect term also written to o3.y edf5 b 6 separate reflection contribution in deferred combine edf6 b + f × (1 − b) 5 sqrt(f) written to o3.x; roughness derived from prior specular power in o3.y the edf6 formula raises low-color channels toward white as the reflection factor grows. the source compares a legacy gold robot, where the base (0.25,0.13,0) can be pushed toward (0.72,0.68,0.63), against a native edf6 golden machine using a brdf material and stronger metallic behavior. the formulas were read from real shaders, but they do not alone prove the final pixels for every lighting, exposure and srgb configuration. texture color-space flags, environment maps and post-processing were not isolated to the same degree in the comparison. why a binary shader swap is unsafe the differences include the number of output render targets, semantic contents of o3, g-buffer resource binding order and some vertex outputs. the loader can resolve custom shader names from app:\shader\dx11, but simply supplying an older .sgo with the same material parameters would not restore compatible deferred-rendering semantics. for general materials, [metallic, roughness] fields also influence ambient and directional weighting downstream; changing an old shader's specular_color is not necessarily equivalent to changing the edf6 material's metallic parameter. source: edf41/rendering.md edf41-material-base-color-output, edf5/shaders.md edf5-material-base-color-output, edf6/rendering.md material-shader-load-base-color, plus the crosswalk assembled by hajisensai/all forces and novae (ajane). all claims pertain to the inspected shader builds.

edf5 creates shaders from precompiled dxbc and combines lighting with a compute pass the edf5 engine was observed to ship 260 dxbc blobs in its executable, alongside model shaders in dx11.cpk. it imports d3dcompiler_47!d3dreflect to inspect compiled shader resources at load time; the renderer creates shader stages and caches some objects by hash. the analyzed executable does not depend on rewriting hlsl source at every map load. lighting dispatch in the view loop three deferred-lighting compute variants were identified. their source numthreads is (16,16,1), and the main-view dispatch uses: dispatch(ceil(view_width / 16), ceil(view_height / 16), 1) the selected variant depends on scene parameters and sun-shadow state. the shader binds g-buffer albedo, specular, normals, roughness/metallic, view position, accumulated lighting, ao and the local cubemap grid. a sun-shadow variant adds a shadow-depth srv. the source identifies an additional scene-flag variant that may be associated with underground rendering; that association is an inference, not a separately observed gameplay mode. why this affects water and glass reasoning a deferred combine writes to the output uav before the later forward-material phase. the inspected frame region contained no detected scene-color resource copy or resolve between that compute dispatch and the forward phase. thus source-era forward water/glass shaders do not automatically receive a sampled copy of the lit scene; a shader requiring the scene color would need a corresponding resource binding or additional pass. this clarifies why material and shader discussions need to distinguish precompiled shader presence, resource binding, actual dispatch, and final on-screen effect. finding a dxbc blob in the executable is not itself evidence that its shader was used in the game. evidence: static reverse engineering and rdef inspection of steam-5d11de53, no current direct runtime measurement. source edf5/shaders.md: shaders-exe-blobs, shaders-reflection, deferred-lighting-cs, deferred-lighting-dispatch.

why the number of edf5 missions can appear to change three counts can all appear in project documents without describing the same file set. the original edf5 mission lists have their own offline/online membership. later edf5-derived content was expanded for an edf6-compatible mission pack, and a still later layout intentionally assigned the same number of progress slots to both modes. a source-sensitive comparison evidence corpus base offline base online meaning original edf5 active list tables, as counted in r37 source census 110 111 original mode-specific membership, with a 112-id union historical converted r41 edf5-content pack 112 111 expanded offline list, with original online-only ids also present offline later edf6-compatible shared-progress target 112 112 intentionally identical ordinal axes for save-progress compatibility the 112 original base-union ids are not the same as 112 original offline rows. tutorial m000 was originally offline-only. m082 and m083 were originally online-only. their presence in a later converted offline table does not retroactively change the original edf5 shipping list. dlc membership is separate: 15 dlc1 and 14 dlc2 missions, bringing the distinct primary shipping corpus to 141 scripts (112+15+14). the source census counted 335 bvm files overall, but this included 10 nonshipping source orphans, 126 edf4.1-subtree files, 56 test files and two tgs/demo files. a 145-script stress set is likewise not the shipping mission count. why the distinction matters a save system can attach clear marks to mission ordinal instead of to a filesystem mxxx name. a port that changes the list membership or row order without translating save progress can attribute a completion to the wrong mission. conversely, a converted mission-list table is useful as a study/reference order but is not proof that the untouched original edf5 offline list had exactly those rows. other resources—name tables, image rabs, config.sgo and each mission's script—must be compared separately. a valid script id alone does not prove it is offered in every mode. evidence: edf5 original source list census edf5/mission-vm.md, facts edf5 online drops: one decision, several local physical crates when an enemy dies, the edf5 drop system checks whether a drop should occur and, if online, whether this machine has authority to make that decision. the resulting crate is created locally, then enough information is sent for peers to create their own copies. it is not a single physical rigid body continuously synchronized across all computers. the spawning chain the investigated death paths pass a game object and location into a drop decision, which reads the object parameter game_object_drop_item. offline the drop branch executes without the online authority gate. online there is a session-related authority check; the original researcher inferred it represents the host, but the precise session callback was not exhaustively named in that study. when the condition succeeds, the manager creates a local crate. the network event includes seed, crate serial, position and two floating parameters. notably the message contains no killer/attacker field; the attacker can exist on the lethal-hit record, but it is not part of this particular crate creation message. receivers dispatch the spawn event to the same local crate-construction routine. as a result, each client can simulate its own crate physics after receiving the original seed and position. the source did not find a continuous per-crate position-sync stream in the inspected path. slight differences in the movement of local copies therefore do not themselves imply a different crate identity. the serial is the logical identity a crate's dropitemmanager::unit+0xb0 holds the serial assigned by the manager's +0xa80. that serial is the key used in later pickup events. the manager pointer at unit +0xb8 is not itself a network identity. the owning player/attacker, the local physical position and the shared crate serial are distinct fields and must not be conflated. evidence: static edf5 steam-5d11de53 analysis, facts drop-death-paths, damage-record-attacker, drop-authority-check, crate-spawn-broadcast, crate-spawn-receive, online-crate-serial. no new multiplayer session was run for this revision. source: edf knowledge hub edf5/online.md. follow-up: edf5 three pickup message types.

picking up an edf5 crate is a separate protocol from spawning it the edf5 item-drop event handler recognizes three different message types. this resolves a common misunderstanding: a client does not simply delete everyone else's crate because its local physics capsule touched something. it reports the pickup, and the authority-side route distinguishes a request from a confirmed collection. type byte meaning recipient's effective action 0 spawn build a local crate copy with the shared serial/seed 1 pickup request authority checks it, resolves the requesting player and can issue the confirmation 2 pickup confirmed award the pickup to the appropriate player locally and mark the serial's crate collected the local pickup reporter records serial, item category and player network id (soldierbase net id at +0xf8 in the studied build). on the authority machine it can publish a type-2 confirmation; elsewhere it sends a request. the host resolves the player and calls the local award path before broadcasting the confirmation. why one crate cannot normally be counted twice for weapon and armor categories the authority checks whether a requested serial is still an uncollected item. the first valid request marks it collected; a second request for the same serial is ignored. this is a source-established de-duplication rule, not a prediction based only on how pickup animations look. when a client receives type 2, it resolves the player by network id, applies the collection locally, finds its own crate copy by serial and sets a collected byte. the ordinary cleanup loop then deletes that copy. the source's note that it 'blinks out' describes this state change, not a physical teleport of one globally authoritative crate mesh. shared rewards and unresolved timing a contributor confirmed from play that online weapon/armor pickups are shared rewards. that agrees with the code: each peer processes confirmed collection to its local inventory/reward counters. the original notes leave one issue unresolved—whether a type-1 request arriving after mission result synchronization can be lost to the tally. do not present a deterministic late-pickup outcome without a controlled runtime trace. sources: edf knowledge hub edf5/online.md, facts pickup-online-report, pickup-protocol-host, host-dedup-pickups, remote-pickup-mark, loot-shared-online, late-pickup-requests. static protocol and one contributor-verified sharing observation, no new online test. related native edf game references full edf5 crate protocol sequence complete spawn-to-pickup state sequence (consolidated) the spawn and collection messages form different stages, even though the same logical crate serial is reused throughout. the following describes the investigated edf5 executable; message numbering does not prove a complete transport-layer wire schema. eligible enemy death └─ session authority check ├─ create local crate copy └─ send type 0 {seed, serial, position, two floats} └─ each receiver creates and simulates a local crate copy local soldier touches weapon/armor crate ├─ authority machine: validate serial -> confirm type 2 └─ other machine: report type 1 {serial, category, player net id} └─ authority validates -> type 2 ├─ award the appropriate player ├─ mark local serial collected └─ delete local crate copy during cleanup a type-0 spawn message is not a kill-credit/attacker message. the seed/serial establish the crate's reproducible logical identity; its physical trajectory is simulated locally after spawn. authority was inferred from the inspected native session gate, but the exact authority callback was not fully named in that study. this diagram is a reconstruction of native code flow, not a captured multiplayer packet log. sources: edf5 edf5/online.md, drop-death-paths, drop-authority-check, crate-spawn-broadcast, crate-spawn-receive, pickup-online-report, pickup-protocol-host, host-dedup-pickups, remote-pickup-mark (static disassembly).

edf5 online loot has both a pickup event and a reward counter a crate visually disappearing is not by itself proof that a player's final reward counter increased. edf5 performs item collection, checks authority/session state, then credits health, weapons or armor through different paths. the end-of-mission result subsequently applies a difficulty/mode-dependent retention factor. counted categories and native limits in the examined dropitemmanager the relevant fields include: field recorded meaning +0xa84 total counted weapon + armor pickups +0xa88 weapon pickup count +0xa8c armor pickup count +0xa90/+0xa94 additional result components included in the end tally for a weapon or armor pickup, the code increments category and total counters only when the authority test succeeds and the total counter is below 0x400 (1024). health categories instead heal the player via the collect path. this cap belongs to the inspected edf5 executable; the results of mods that change those immediates are not the game's stock behavior. mission result calculation the result routine reads the weapon and armor counters, multiplies by a retention factor indexed through the current mode/difficulty state, and adds the separate result components. one branch has a zero retention factor. the source inferred the index was difficulty, but did not prove every mode's displayed output via an in-game experiment. in multiplayer, do not assume every non-host copy's counters match: the same source left the non-host semantics of the session authority callback unresolved. confirmed shared item awards are a different claim from perfectly identical intermediate counters on every machine. sources: edf5/online.md, pickup-award-counters, result-tally-detail, nonhost-counters; steam-5d11de53 static disassembly. see pickup event protocol and edf5 weapon reward roll. related native edf game references edf5 result timing and local-player gate local-control gate and result-sync uncertainty (consolidated) the per-frame pickup check is local-controller gated: in the audited edf5 build, the player controller pointer at soldierbase+0x240 identifies local control. remote soldier avatars do not independently run the local pickup contact test on every peer. a confirmed pickup references a player network id (audited soldierbase+0xf8), not the crate creator or the last attacker. the 0x400 total limit is an audited stock executable counter threshold, not a statement about guaranteed result-screen rewards or equality of all intermediate peer counters. the code processes confirmed pickups locally, but non-host counter equality and a request arriving after result synchronization remained unresolved in the source study. the presence of a debug-console command named drop_item is not evidence that it runs during ordinary missions. sources: edf5 edf5/online.md, pickup-local-players-only, local-controller-slot, pickup-award-counters, result-tally-detail, nonhost-counters (unverified), late-pickup-requests (unverified), debug-command-table (static).

edf5 checks physical pickup overlap only for locally controlled players the fact that a game object has player animations or a soldierbase rtti type does not prove that a pickup test runs for that object on every peer. edf5 has a local controller slot stored on the player, and the player-update routine tests it before entering the pickup code. recognizing a local avatar the source identifies player +0x23c as a pad index and player +0x240 as a pointer to the corresponding controller-manager slot. assigning a valid controller stores both; clearing the association sets the pad index to -1 and the pointer to zero. the native mission-script player-creation path can create an avatar with no local pad. the normal player update skips the pickup block when +0x240 == 0. thus a remote avatar does not run the same spatial pickup test in your local player's update. in split screen, the test can run once per locally controlled player per frame. a player's network id used in a pickup message is not the same as the local controller index. why this matters for visualizing multiplayer each computer can have local versions of multiple avatars and crates, but the spatial check is gated by controller ownership. a remote player's confirmed pickup still arrives through the online event handler and can award shared loot without that remote avatar ever running your computer's local proximity check. the result is not contradictory: the local check and the network confirmation are two separate routes. the source notes that this distinction was recovered by static disassembly of the per-player update and four soldier-class update call sites. it does not establish the exact number of supported gamepads or a universal split-screen installation configuration. source: edf knowledge hub edf5/online.md, facts local-controller-slot, pickup-local-players-only, per-player-update-local-gate. build steam-5d11de53.

edf5's teammanager is not a list containing only the four players the game maintains an array of team records. each team has a container of game objects and a separate relation table used to distinguish hostility and friendliness. looking up an online player's network id therefore means walking team membership and checking the object's actual type, rather than indexing a fixed four-player array by net id. native layout recovered from static code item observed edf5 data teammanager lock critical_section at +8 team row array pointer at manager +0x38 team row size 0x38 bytes team count at manager +0x48 member node msvc tree node with object pointer at node +0x20 team relations dword array indexed by other-team number; 2 = hostile per-team merit total float at team row +0x30 the player finder walks team 0's object container, uses an actual dynamic_cast<soldierbase> and compares the network-player id at player +0xf8. this ensures a team object is not automatically treated as a player. the note's hypothesis that team 0 includes allies and vehicles is unverified; only the use of the cast is observed. a separate enemy-count approach sums member counts in teams whose relation from team 0 is hostile. this is a rough live container count, not guaranteed to match currently alive/visible enemies: the author explicitly notes that dead members might temporarily remain registered. mutating the team field does not update membership in edf5 the team id on a player is at +0x218. a contributor verified that directly changing this field could make enemy hits connect, but a mission restart could crash because the manager's object set still contained the player under the old team. the team number and membership set have to stay consistent. the native team-changing helper exists and updates membership; direct field mutation does not emulate it. evidence: static teammanager and player-lookup re, with one historical contributor-verified team-switch failure. this is not a recommendation to edit game memory or a claim of consistent behavior across versions. sources: edf5/online.md facts player-list-walk, team-records, team0-members-not-only-players, team-member-counts; edf5/combat.md team-id-field, team-switch-restart-crash, combat-teammanager-walk.

edf5 renders many map props through an instanced map-specific pipeline map props are not all drawn through the same animationmodel or character-renderer callbacks. the edf5 mapobject_* family contributes to a maprenderer::modelrenderer path which collects groups of models, lod units and per-instance poses before issuing instanced indexed draws. what one pose stores the author observed a cpu pose array with 32-byte entries: part type meaning entry bytes 0–15 float4 rotation quaternion x/y/z/w entry bytes 16–31 float4 translation xyz and uniform scale w the entry array has a bounded capacity noted as 0x1770 in the studied implementation, is uploaded to a gpu buffer, then sampled by shaders through g_instancing_array. the shader's instance index includes the draw's instanceid and a blend-index input; the separate g_instancing_inv_array supplies an inverse-node transform. this does not imply every mapb placement record itself has a scale field: the render-instance pose and the map-file placement are different layers of data. draw-group organization rendergroup points at a model and a linked list of renderunit objects, including an lod-linked next group. each unit has its placement and fade value. per-frame code chooses a model group according to distance, then creates draw batches in several phases. the source identified three maprenderer render-phase entry points, but did not establish an exhaustive correspondence to all commander phases. for an edf5 object that seems to disappear at distance, possible causes include the mapb/mapo distance rule, lod choice and shader fade; a simple character draw hook may never see this map object at all. evidence: static render-call disassembly in steam-5d11de53; source edf5/map-objects.md, facts map-objects-renderer, map-instanced-draw plus mapobject-primary-vtables. no new graphics capture.

edf5 and edf6 share object concepts, not an identical memory layout gameobjectbase, soldierbase and teammanager are recognizable by rtti across these two games, but field offsets and message identifiers changed. a value that means team or hp in one executable cannot be copied to the same offset in the other. selected game-object fields concept edf5 offset edf6 offset world-position matrix row +0xa0 +0x90 maximum hp +0x1f8 +0x2f4 current hp +0x1fc +0x2f8 team id +0x218 +0x314 local-pad index +0x23c +0x338 local-player link / controller +0x240 +0x340 object flag word +0x280 +0x380 the values are valid only for the versions and class contexts described in the native studies, not all arbitrary derived classes. in edf5, a dead-state bit appears in the flags word; edf6 also exposes a dedicated dead byte at +0x2e8. team membership and logical identity both games store team-member sets in an msvc tree with similar record sizes. edf6's native teammanager still uses 0x38-byte team rows, a lock and a relation table. its default constructor initializes seven teams, while the class's address and many surrounding object fields moved relative to edf5. a numeric team id also has relations (friendly, hostile or neutral) rather than representing a simple boolean enemy flag. hit records and lethality the original code sends lethal/damage-related messages through virtual handlers with different message ids: edf5 uses 0x80000000 in the studied object-hit path, whereas edf6 uses 0x10000000 for its corresponding path. that is an important abi boundary: a message tag is not a cross-generation serial format unless its handler and record structure match. edf6 also distinguishes forced hits that bypass immunity/spot-damage conditions. evidence: static field-by-field source re, historical edf5 contributor tests of invincibility/team-state changes, and native message-handler comparison. do not transplant offsets or hit-record byte layouts wholesale across versions. sources: edf5/combat.md combat-teammanager-walk, team-id-field, lethal-damage-message; edf6/combat.md teammanager-layout, edf5-edf6-object-fields, hit-message; edf6/objects.md gameobjectbase-layout.

a class name is not necessarily the name the game uses edf5 uses at least three naming layers for its enemies. the c++ class or xgs_scene_object_class is the engine's implementation family, an sgo is the particular configured object, and a localized name may be present in the statistics screen or a mission briefing. the three are not interchangeable. how names are grounded an enemy definition's game_object_kill_counter can name a statistics counter. the english text table etc/texttable_xbox.en.txt_sgo includes statusinfo_<counter> entries that describe the corresponding game statistic. examples from the source comparison include: source counter/class family english statistics label giantant aggressive alien species αs giantspider aggressive alien species βs giantdango aggressive alien species γs giantbee flying aggressors giantantqueen mother monsters giantbeequeen queens nephila araneas defeated humanoid frog / grey colonists / cosmonauts biggreyboss silver man ufocarrier508 teleportation ships movingfortress outpost bases the exact family/counter mapping is defined by each sgo; the names above are a reader-facing paraphrase of the recorded label census, not a claim that all subtypes get their own status counter. specific variants are sometimes named only in missionlist.*.txt.en.sgo briefing text, for example “red drones,” “heavy-armored aliens,” “bombers,” “golden aggressors” and “silver aggressors.” names that appear in an external radar catalogue but not in either game's localizable strings are catalogue/wiki names, not proven official ui labels. the anthillkillcount localization says “teleportation devices” even though the associated e517_anthill sgo is catalogued as a giant ant hill. important mismatches the edf5 class dragonsmall is the tadpole, not a dragon enemy in edf5's played campaign. nephila refers to the web-spitting aranea (the related edf4.1 type is often called retiarius). treating an internal class or filename as a literal bestiary label would misidentify both. the original contributor verified the general tadpole/aranea identification from game knowledge; the exact kill-counter localization and briefing scans are static source analyses, not a fresh screenshot comparison with the english game ui. source: edf knowledge hub edf5/object-classes.md, facts edf5-enemy-names, kill-counter-names, briefing-subtype-names, anthill-label-teleportation-devices. build steam-5d11de53.

ant and hornet variants are configured, not separate c++ classes the edf5 sgos distinguish ants and hornets through model selection, tint parameters, level adjustment, movement and ai settings. two definitions that share a model may behave differently, while two appearance variants can use the same engine class. ants edf5 sgo base game_object_durability defining source properties giantant01, giantant01b 60 black ant; 01b changes ant_aisetting to [1,10,30] giantant01netlightsyncmode 60 black-ant model; different ant_networkislightsyncmode giantant02b 180 red ant model, red-hit effect giantant03b 270 purple/dark-crimson variation of red model; diffuse (0.25,0.5,0.5,1); movement speed 0.45 giantant04 15 full-size ant model with green tint (0.5,1,0.5,1); movement speed 0.8 giantant04sb 15 half-size model ari_half.mdb; ant_ex_damagescale=2.5; grab/capture animation parameters the small green ant is not simply the full-size green ant scaled uniformly: it selects another model and has extra grab/capture parameters. gold ant base entries are included in the downloadable sgo catalogue; their runtime health is further modified by game_object_level_adjust and game difficulty. hornets edf5 sgo base durability difference giantbee01 and giantbee01charge 45 same model; differ in bee_flyangle and bee_flysidemovespeed giantbee02charge 90 red tint (diffuse starts 1.25,0.1); level adjustment 1.5 giantbeequeen 3000 ordinary hornet queen, no red-queen adjustment giantbeequeen02 3000 red/demon queen tint and level adjustment 1.5 for example, the red hornet's source-adjusted baseline is 90 × 1.5 = 135, not simply 90. these are source-side base quantities; online scaling, stage multipliers and per-mission overrides must not be ignored when predicting actual hp. evidence: native sgo root comparisons; edf5 knowledge hub facts edf5-ant-hornet-subtypes and edf5-hornet-subtypes, static. in-game subtype naming in the notes is attributed to contributor knowledge, not newly retested here.
