some edf5 variants are defined by a mission condition, not by a new enemy class tadpoles and the inherited dragonsmall name edf5's dragonsmall class covers the tadpole family. the source catalogue lists ordinary red tadpoles at a 50 sgo durability and green tadpoles at 20; the alternate *_hs variants can use smaller models. the source contributor identified three color-based tadpole types in play. these names do not imply that the edf4.1 dragon is present in edf5 gameplay. blue drones and bomb ships e507_goldufo_hi is the blue drone variant with diffuse tint (0.6,0.6,0.8,1) and game_object_level_adjust=1.5. the audited mission script for edf5 offline mission 7 spawns 50 of these on hardest/inferno only. that is a specific mission/difficulty source condition, not an assertion that all drone encounters change similarly. e507_goldufo_big is the bomb ship: its definition uses ai_big_bomber_info and base durability 3500. the dlc mission pack 2 source census records it spawning in missions 3, 10 and 13, with respective counts 3, 2 and 1. this is a mission-script count, not an independent runtime population measurement. armor-clad colonists the e503_armorfrog_* definitions add armor_model, armor_ragdoll and armor-break reactions not present in corresponding e503_frog_* definitions. humanoid class alone therefore cannot establish whether a colonist is the armored variant. inspect the sgo subfamily and armor fields. sources: edf knowledge hub edf5/object-classes.md, facts edf5-enemy-names, sgo-dragonsmall-20, sgo-dragonsmall-50, edf5-drone-colonist-subtypes; evidence static except contributor identity edf5-enemy-names verified.

a deroy filename's suffix is not its size edf5's deiroi sgos are differentiated by a body configuration and parts_config assembling the legs and weapons. the japanese bestiary distinguishes deroy (pulse-turret type) from deroy b (missile-equipped type), with short/long variants. in particular, the _m suffix in e509_deiroi_m refers to the missile version, not a medium body; a legacy raw catalogue glossed it “deroy (medium)” and is contradicted by the sgo parts list. edf5 root sgo base body durability leg weapon configuration e509_deiroi 1350 four pulse turrets e509_deiroi_m 1350 missile turret replacing the corresponding pulse configuration e509_deiroi_s 825 short legs, one pulse turret, level adjustment 0.7 e509_deiroi_sm 825 short legs, one missile turret, level adjustment 0.7 e509_deiroi_l 1500 three pulse turrets plus one missile turret e509_deiroi_xl 2250 ten pulse turrets plus one missile turret the short body adjusted baseline is 825 × 0.7 = 577.5. raw part durabilities are pulse turret 40, missile turret 200, toe 260 and leg joint 1. the deiroifalleffect definitions are separate objects that reference corresponding deroy sgos; they should not be counted as live deroy body instances. this explains why counting “deroy” sgo filenames alone may overcount actors, and why interpreting _m as a size mislabels the weapon configuration. the source cross-checks exact sgo parts against the japanese bestiary; source values are not gameplay hp after difficulty scaling. sources: edf5/object-classes.md, facts edf5-deroy-subtypes, atwiki-deroy-b-naming. build steam-5d11de53.

file presence does not imply campaign presence edf5's root.cpk includes monster501_king and its supporting resources. it uses monster501 as does ordinary erginus, but has different model, cas and ragdoll assets, a source durability of 64000 compared with erginus's 32000, an enlarged camera distance and an attack setting 1500 compared with 1000. that makes it a genuine retained resource; it does not make it an edf5 main-game encounter. the exact source scan found monster501_king in the edf4.1 mission subtree stored within edf5's archives (mission/edf4.1/mp004/mission.bvm). no edf5 campaign or either edf5 dlc mission pack script in that corpus references it. this is a narrowly scoped negative mission-reference finding, not proof that no mod or undocumented external script could spawn it. an earlier inventory row labelled monster501_king “used in official missions.” its broad scan included the edf4.1 subtree. the later explicit source-provenance scan corrects that misleading statement for edf5 release missions. the model's color in gameplay was not established from these resources. source: edf5/object-classes.md, fact edf5-erginus-king-unused (static sgo and full mission-reference scan); raw row sgo-monster501-64000 corrected by this later evidence.

an sgo number is a configuration input, not final observed health edf5 object sgos declare xgs_scene_object_class and, for relevant objects, game_object_durability. some enemies also contain game_object_level_adjust. the japanese bestiary's baseline tables agree with the product in the 45-value comparison described in the source analysis. variant raw durability level adjustment adjusted baseline red hornet 90 1.5 135 blue drone 75 1.5 112.5 short deroy 825 0.7 577.5 red/demon hornet queen 3000 1.5 4500 gold ant queen 2800 3.5 9800 these source-level baselines are not a complete runtime hp calculator. difficulty, online scaling, mission setup, independent destructible subparts and script changes can alter active enemy endurance. downloadable full grouped source inventory data/edf5_native_sgo_durability_82_groups_r134.csv retains 82 grouped source facts across enemy objects, npcs, vehicles and mission objects. each row records the native c++ class, raw durability (or its absence), variant labels, source grade, exact fact id and build. totals: 37 enemy groups, 24 vehicle groups, 4 npc/civilian groups and 17 object/spawner groups. multiple sgos with the same class/base durability are grouped to match the source census rather than inventing unique classes. the original inventory labels are retained for provenance. they are not authoritative official english names: the detailed subtype articles correct examples such as the deroy _m suffix and “ai-controlled” parked vehicles. a generic inventory “used in official missions” can include edf4.1-source missions retained in edf5's archive, so it does not prove the enemy spawns in the edf5 campaign; erginus king is a counterexample. source: edf knowledge hub edf5/object-classes.md, facts atwiki-enemy-durability-level-adjust, sgo-giantant-15, sgo-vehicle505-tank-700, sgo-generatorpoll-14000 and the cited 82 sgo-* records; native build steam-5d11de53.

an ally's uniform is less precise than its configured weapon sgo edf5's npc soldier sgos describe weapons in soldier_load_weapon, pointing to weapon/ and an ai* weapon sgo. the source census lists 22 carried npc weapon definitions. broad runtime classes are shared with player soldiers: assultsoldier for ranger-style ai, palewing for wing diver-style ai, and heavyarmor for fencers. sgo suffix/prefix interpreted npc loadout _af assault rifle _fl flamethrower _rl rocket launcher _sg shotgun _sn sniper rifle fencer _sc hand cannon fencer _smc galion autocannon fencer _ssg dexter shotgun fencer _sp pile bunker / spine driver family wing diver _lance power lance wing diver _lr mag blaster family wing diver _izn lightning bow wing diver _tb thunder bowgun wing diver _ms monster fencer definitions can carry two weapon definitions, including aiheavyshield01; grim reaper variants additionally name aiheavydash01. elite corresponds to the spriggan group, _s_ to sarge's squad, whose leader carries aisoldierlaserrifle02 (blazer) from offline mission 78 onward in the studied script data. npc weapon sgos contain plain ammunition, damage and reload numbers rather than player weapon star arrays. the original source comparison with the japanese npc weapon table found matching values where provided, but also found erroneous english first-pass catalogue labels (e.g. shotgun rangers called fencers). sources: edf knowledge hub edf5/object-classes.md, edf5-npc-load-weapon, classes-player-vs-npc, japanese edf5 npc weapon table. static source and community table corroboration; no new live npc damage experiments.

ai-driven vehicles and player-summoned vehicles have different sgo roots player-summoned forms generally use vehicle_setup. ai-driven forms additionally use a mission_setup root that names their mounted weapon sgos. the native class may be unchanged, but mission ownership, model choice and weapon setups differ. ai sgo family source durability weapons and native parameters v505_tank_ai (blacker) 700 105mm howitzer base damage 70, blast 8, reload 180 frames vehicle403_tank_ai (epsilon) 1600 penetrating railgun base damage 300, reload 180 frames vehicle404_bigtank_ai (b651 titan) 2400 requiem gun 750, blast 30, reload 1200 frames v510_maser_ai (emc) 1000 180-shot burst, base damage 10 per shot v507_rescuetank_ai (caliban) 1500 healing total 600 from mission_setup vehicle402_rocket_ai (naegling) 550 200 homing rockets, 100 base damage, bursts of ten, blast 8 v504_begaruta_ai (nix) 1200 arm guns base damage five each six frames; missile pods 60, 20 rounds in bursts of four, blast 6 v515_retrobalam_ai (barga) 40000 no sgo gun-style melee damage table identified the source revises community estimates with frame-based settings: naegling 240 frames (4 s) between bursts, nix missiles 420 frames (7 s), emc 180-frame burst plus 120-frame reload (five-second cycle at 60 hz). these are native parameter timings, not newly measured actual cycles during arbitrary lag or time dilation. the caliban's proposed “0.05 hp per tick” was not proved: the matching 0.05 in a weapon sgo is labelled fireaccuracy. the community barga melee-damage numbers also lack supporting native weapon sgos in this particular audit and must not be promoted as a confirmed table. sources: edf5/object-classes.md, facts edf5-npc-vehicles-wiki, edf5-npc-vehicles-wiki-diffs, edf5-npc-vehicle-variants.

_mission does not mean “this vehicle drives under ai” edf5 scripts can spawn empty, boardable vehicles with special *_mission or *_fw sgos. these are distinct from a separately configured *_ai vehicle driven by an npc. the static inventory was cross-checked against japanese mission tables marking vehicles 搭乗可能 (“boardable”). mission sgo model or role mission placement from source v505_tank_mission blacker tank offline 80 (three), 81 (one) v504_begaruta_mission gray nix (“blue” in community table) offline 80 (two), 92 v504_begaruta_g_mission standard/green nix offline 81 v504_begaruta_fw yellow nix with combat burners offline 96, 105 v513_trailertruck01cab tractor head offline 92, 96 v512_keitruck small/light truck present in source mission catalogue v515_retrobalam_mission barga mission-prop-like in offline 81; boardable later in 82 a coarse catalogue called v505_tank_mission a “scripted maser tank”; its model and mounted weapon identity show blacker. some raw rows marked _mission vehicles “ai controlled” simply because their class is shared with ai forms. the sgo setup and placement determine the role, not the class name. the original contributor separately reported a verified gameplay constraint: npcs do not share a vehicle with a player as driver or passenger. this is an observation for ordinary game play, not a claim that modified code could never implement it. sources: edf5/object-classes.md, facts edf5-mission-vehicles-boardable (static mission/wiki pairing), edf5-npc-vehicle-variants (static) and edf5-npc-vehicles-not-shared (contributor-verified).

not every durable sgo is an enemy edf5's native object catalogue includes mission scenery, destructible props, spawners and event effects. their sgo class and numeric durability settings are not automatically enemy health. native class / sgo raw sgo durability source interpretation generatorpoll e505_generator 1250 teleport anchor generatorpoll e505_generator_large 2500 large teleport anchor generatorpoll e505_generator_superlarge 14000 super large teleport anchor anthill e517_anthill 1500 giant ant hill; statistics counter is “teleportation devices” bignest hornetnest401 28000 hornet nest spidernet20, 40, 80 750 / 900 / 1200 spider-web configurations spidernet160, 320, 480 2400 (shared group) higher-named web configurations giantantegg 1 egg and spawn-related scene objects cavewall rockl, rockm 200 cave/rock props, not enemy hp edfdoor01 200 event animation door shootingtarget 100 shooting-range target deiroifalleffect, demoairstrike, demoindirectfire and eventparticle in the same source catalogue have no durability field; these are effects or event objects, not ordinary enemies. likewise the size number in a spidernet filename does not directly encode durability: the source explicitly groups three size-labelled web sgos under the same 2400 value. evidence: native sgo class/durability scan and text-table comparison, steam-5d11de53. facts sgo-generatorpoll-1250, sgo-generatorpoll-2500, sgo-generatorpoll-14000, sgo-anthill-1500, sgo-bignest-28000, sgo-spidernet-750, sgo-spidernet-2400, sgo-giantantegg-1, anthill-label-teleportation-devices.

the runtime class does not identify who owns the vehicle edf5 mostly uses the same c++ class for a vehicle's player-summoned, ai-driven and parked mission variants. its owner, driver, ride link and sgo setup determine whether it behaves as the player's vehicle, an ally-operated vehicle or an empty map object. native class vehicle family vehicle402_rocket naegling vehicle403_tank epsilon / menace railgun vehicle404_tank titan vehicle501_fortressrobo barga/balam vehicle502_groundrobo depth crawler vehicle503_bike free bike vehicle504_begaruta nix vehicle505_tank blacker vehicle506_helicopter eros vehicle507_rescuetank caliban vehicle510_maser emc vehiclebegaruta / vehicle407_bigbegaruta proteus vehiclehelicopter409 nereid vehiclehelicopter410 brute vehicle_car grape and civilian/light trucks v505_tank, v505_tank_ai and v505_tank_mission can all resolve to vehicle505_tank. npc soldier sgos similarly use player-style classes (assultsoldier, heavyarmor, palewing) while loading different weapons and behaviour settings. the source did not identify an in-game vehicle for vehicle511_bike; that mapping remains unknown. the grouping into tanks, helicopters, bikes and mechs is editorial rather than a discovered native base-class hierarchy. depth crawler is separated because its wall/ceiling traversal is mechanically different. source: edf5/object-classes.md, facts classes-player-vs-npc, vehicle-class-to-name, vehicle-class-groups (rtti/sgo inspection; contributor grouping convention).

final-boss warning: source structure contains more than one hp value the japanese bestiary places silver man / nameless (e516_biggreyboss) in a spoiler-fold within its archelus page, rather than under a separate heading. headings-only scraping can therefore miss the entry and wrongly report that it is absent. component or attack object reported source/bestiary baseline main body 32000 upper arm 2400 forearm 1600 thigh 1800 shin 1200 large meteor 336 medium meteor 168 small meteor 84 the meteor values were cross-checked with the corresponding e516_biggreyboss_meteor_* sgos. the japanese page describes 0.7× damage-through to the body from hit limbs and a drop-rate convention equivalent to 100 items. those additional figures are source attributions, not newly runtime-measured thresholds. japanese community names (for example 銀の人 and かの者) are not identical to official english localization: the english statistics counter identifies the boss as silver man. the internal class name humanoid_biggreyboss does not imply a common player-facing name either. sources: edf5/object-classes.md, atwiki-silver-man-spoiler-fold, kill-counter-names, sgo-humanoid-biggreyboss-32000. this page contains edf5 final-boss spoilers.

render phase 0 is a depth pre-pass, not the shadow pass edf5's scene traversal combines umbra visibility callbacks with per-object model drawing. the names of render phases cannot be assigned by guessing their index: a contributor specifically verified that phase 0 is the picture's depth pre-pass. when a model was skipped in phases 1 and 2 but still drawn in phase 0, its remaining on-screen appearance was a flat white silhouette. skipping all phases 0–2 removed the model cleanly in that experiment. this corrects older descriptions that grouped phase 0 with the shadow pass. animationmodel phase behavior native phase effect observed in code 0 opaque-list depth pre-pass 1 main opaque / g-buffer pass 2 translucent-list draw via second model callback 3 draw only materials marked to cast shadows (material flag +0x21 bit 0) 4 no animationmodel draw for phase 2, a source researcher inferred the use of the forward technique because a one-color-plus-depth render target is selected immediately beforehand. that technique mapping is unverified from a runtime shader capture, although the translucent callback is identified statically. the game routes animated characters, soldiers, enemies and vehicles through animationmodel slot 1 (0x3aef60) and translucent drawing through slot 2 (0x3ae990) in the studied build. rigid sgmumbraobject renderables follow another callback. the renderer also updates last-drawn bookkeeping after phases 1/2; that should be distinguished from whether an object actually appeared as a visible pixel. evidence: edf knowledge hub edf5/models.md, render-phase-0-depth-prepass (contributor-verified), models-animationmodel-phases (static), animationmodel-draw-callback (verified), render-phase-2-forward (unverified inference). build steam-5d11de53.

animated visibility bounds come from the model's bones in edf5, an animationmodel holds an oriented bounding box (obb) whose three axes/half extents are at model offsets +0xf0, +0x100, +0x110; the center is at +0x120. the post-update builds the box and passes it to umbra::object::settransform. this is not merely a decorative debug box: it is the geometry used by the umbra occlusion/culling object in the studied code. the source found two builder cases. a resource mode value equal to 1 uses one selected bone's transform scaled by the resource extents. other cases collect the transformed local boxes of all flagged bones, calculate their encompassing aabb in the model's coordinate system and store corresponding world-space center and half-extents. a model that has been animated can thus have a changing visibility envelope without changing its mesh file. the umbra settransform implementation stores the box center and a scalar based on the lengths of its axes. the researcher tentatively interpreted the scalar as a bounding radius but explicitly did not establish the normalized unit-box convention ([-1,1] versus [0,1] or half-units). treat that interpretation as a hypothesis rather than a confirmed radius formula. the same source distinguishes owner objects from embedded renderables. human soldiers, vehicles, weapon objects, insects and humanoid enemies embed animationmodel at different offsets; sceneobject parent/child links associate attached rigid weapons and wing parts. a renderable's address is therefore not automatically its owning game object's address. source: edf5/models.md, facts models-animationmodel-box (verified), models-box-builder, models-umbra-settransform, models-bones, model-embed-offsets (contributor-verified).

distant animation can update less often while game time keeps advancing edf5's animation pipeline can skip pose evaluation for distant insects and some humanoids. it does not necessarily skip ai logic, movement, damage or animation time. the insectbase code advances animation time each frame, but queues a cas pose-evaluation job only on frames selected by an object-specific modulo rule. source distance-metric band (not calibrated real metres) insectbase pose-job cadence near band, up to nominal 150 every frame (n=1) next nominal 150–300 every fourth frame (n=4) next nominal 300–600 every eighth frame (n=8) beyond nominal 600 / not drawn previously every sixteenth frame (n=16) the source chooses these bands from a renderer-scaled squared-distance metric; they should not be interpreted as calibrated metres without resolving that scale. the numeric thresholds are 22500 / 90000 / 360000 and an animation/model visibility bookkeeping field. eligible insect classes include giantant, giantspider, giantbee and dragonsmall (tadpole in edf5). the skip also has an sgo/controller flag and a state bypass; not every insect performs the same skip under every condition. for humanbase, the corresponding code has closer nominal metric bands 30 / 60 / 120 (squared 900 / 3600 / 14400), but the configuration human_frame_skip_enable defaults to 0 in the examined sgo loading path. therefore the presence of this branch in native code is not proof that all soldiers ordinarily render at the reduced pose rate. the study found this explicit pose-job skip in two update functions, insectbase and humanbase, and did not find it in the named nephila/fortress/robot/ufo families. such a negative code-scan result is bounded to the inspected classes; it is not a claim that every other effect in edf5 updates each frame. source: edf5/models.md, facts insect-pose-job-skip, human-pose-job-skip, pose-job-skip-scope (static disassembly, no fresh runtime a/b). this is distinct from the engine's fixed simulation step and actual display refresh.

four things called "lod" are not one system edf5 distinguishes animated-mesh lod, map-prop mesh lod, texture .lod.dds streaming and offline/dev impostor capture. their formats and selection mechanisms differ. animated characters: the animationmodel draw chooses full detail first, then walks 0xf0-byte lod records using per-record thresholds. these source distance thresholds are squared at load, then compared against the renderer's squared camera-distance metric. the source did not find a direct fov, display resolution or graphics-quality factor in this specific mesh-lod selector. the umbra distance field includes a commander-owned multiplier whose writer was not established, so no universal world-meter conversion follows. map props: maprenderer selects separate lod render units using distance ranges stored on the units. the source resolves _lod, _lod2, _lod3 suffixes as meshes inside the corresponding rab archive. this is a different pipeline from changing the animation-update frequency of a living enemy. texture .lod.dds: this name describes texture streaming and does not itself mean a mesh has changed lod. farclipz is a camera far-plane value, not the animated-model lod threshold. character impostors: classes called lodmodelobject, lodsgmumbraobject and lodcapturecamera are associated with the developer lod_capture operation, not with observed live character rendering. the source found runtime billboards for vegetation, not an equivalent generic character impostor stream. this is a bounded constructor/call-site finding; it does not prove no other visual trick exists anywhere in the engine. source: edf5/models.md, animationmodel-lod-select, umbra-object-distance-metric, map-prop-lod, no-runtime-impostor, lod-lookalikes. no new gameplay capture.

a friendly squad is a graph of native game objects, not a separate squad class edf5 allied soldiers execute statemachine::agent<soldierbase>. the state-machine's active state and elapsed counters live in the soldier object. its three primary state virtual functions correspond to guard, follow and engage; each receives an entry/update/exit phase. state native behaviour described by source guard return toward the stored home point, with a formation offset; switch to follow after assigning a leader follow move toward the leader's position plus a per-soldier offset; return to guard if the leader disappears engage choose and act on a live target; return to follow when target reference becomes null these states interact with a leader/follower tree. the leader pointer is soldierbase+0x3a0, a linked-list head of followers is +0x3a8, the count is +0x3b0, and +0x398 is the may-recruit flag. calling native setfollow first detaches a soldier from its old leader's list, attaches it to the new leader, updates its formation offset and releases its active route explorer. changing only the leader pointer would not reproduce this transition. the native online follow message identifiers are 0xb for host and 0xc for guest in this edf5 code path; the source contrasts edf6's corresponding 12 / 13. a network message id is not the same as the visible npc state id. the source also found enemy squad script natives using the same underlying follow tree. the result is that soldier “follow” is simultaneously a state-machine behavior, a leader-tree membership and a potential networked transition. all three have to agree to understand a recruited squad's movement. sources: edf knowledge hub edf5/soldier-ai.md, edf5-soldier-ai-classes, edf5-soldier-ai-states, edf5-squad-tree (static native code study). build steam-5d11de53.

recruitment is enabled by mission script, then resolved by nearby-player search edf5 mission natives createfriend (1010), createfriendgroup (1012) and createfriendsquad (1011) set the object's recruitability state. in a scripted squad, the leader gets the specified canrecruit setting and subordinates can later become recruitable after their original leader disappears. the separate recruitobject native (3152) can directly attach one unit to another through setfollow. an unled soldier whose may-join flag is set searches the relevant player/team group for the nearest live humanbase within 10 world units. the online branch avoids treating a remote avatar copy as the local recruit target in the observed logic. recruitment attaches the soldier, selects a formation direction at approximately 2–5 units from the player and uses a temporary reassignment timer. when a leader dies, the source shows an unfollow operation, route release, cooldown and potential new-player recruitment. it does not mean every unled npc is automatically recruitable; the original sgo/native flag must still allow it. the first-30-seconds source pattern the researcher also found a 1800-frame initial budget in certain un-recruited squad formations, with reduced factors for visibility/targeting, damage and weapon output while the formation remains rooted in its original npc leader. recruiting into a player-led chain removes that condition. the field meanings were interpreted partly by analogy with matching edf6 code and are not fully independently established in edf5. consequently the exact amount of incoming damage mitigation in live edf5 should not be asserted solely from these registers. source: edf5/soldier-ai.md, facts edf5-friend-natives-join-flag, edf5-recruit-near-player, edf5-unrecruited-squad-cover. static code, with some field semantics explicitly inferred.

npcs can track a hostile object without firing at it edf5 soldier ai separates target acquisition from line of sight and trigger authorization. this explains why a soldier can face or retain a distant enemy without continuously shooting. the hostile-target search runs approximately once every 60–119 frames. it visits teams hostile to the soldier's own team and retains the nearest eligible object as a weak reference. the native scan has no explicit search-distance ceiling or line-of-sight condition in this phase. a separate visibility ray begins roughly 1.5 metres above the soldier, points toward the target and is capped at 300 m. the source's collision query uses layer 22. the ray stage operates in blocks: about 30–44 frames of active checking followed by 60–89 frames of delay. its visibility byte can be cleared while off-cycle or in other character states. the engage state finally gates the trigger on visibility, facing (dot product greater than 0.8) and distance up to max(25, 0.5 × first weapon's range), provided no conflicting face-order is active. these are control-logic thresholds in the studied native build, not a promise that the gun's projectiles physically travel exactly this range, nor a full model of every npc subclass. external forced-target mission commands can be additional inputs. source: edf5/soldier-ai.md, fact edf5-target-and-fire (static disassembly, exact build steam-5d11de53). the note compares the logic with edf6 but does not claim byte-identical class layouts.

route completion is not equivalent to reaching any arbitrary waypoint name edf5 keeps an airouteexplorerbase shared pointer in the game object. the per-frame update lets the explorer supply a next point, destination validity and speed; completion clears the explorer pointer. the ai can also receive a separate facing-order target and direction timer. mission script conditions test this state through three different native event factors: script condition studied field meaning eventfactor_aimoveend (9300) route explorer has been released/completed eventfactor_aimoveendordie (9301) completion or qualifying death eventfactor_aifollow (9310) a leader link exists the same research maps the edf5 native setairoute to 3101. these distinctions matter when a mission waits on a squad: a follower can have a leader without a specific route having reached its final node. when an ai stops making progress a watchdog records the last best distance to the current waypoint. when a soldier fails to get 2 m closer for approximately 3600 frames (60 seconds), while the route point has not moved over 1 m and several safety/ownership conditions are satisfied, it invokes native position-related helpers using that waypoint. the source infers that the result is teleporting or repositioning the soldier, based on corresponding edf6 logic; the physical effect was not verified in an edf5 runtime trace. this is not a generic claim that edf5 npcs never get stuck. pathfinding routes, collision against map geometry, follower formation and the watchdog are separate mechanisms, and a single 60-second rule cannot repair an incompatible navigation mesh. source: edf5/soldier-ai.md, edf5-ai-route-fields, edf5-route-watchdog (static; watchdog effect inferred).

squad radio chatter is driven by ai conditions and cooldowns edf5 uses named talkmanager tables. the game object and the current ai state determine whether a line is eligible; it is not simply a fixed sound assigned to an animation. the source identifies the following native talk events: trigger source condition 合流 (joining) a recruit joins a player-led squad 体力低下 (low hp) first crossing below half hp ダメージ (damage) hp decreased; then approximately 300–599 frames cooldown, excluding certain state values リロード (reload) a weapon becomes empty and is reloading 増援出現 (reinforcements) hostile count increased by more than ten, or increased from zero; after at least 900 life frames 気付かれた (spotted) first target after at least 60 frames 勝利 (victory) at least 120 frames without a target 走り出す (start running) a following soldier has moved for around 90 frames under a local-player squad root; 300–899-frame cooldown the table names are native japanese strings present in the source. their english rendering here is an explanation rather than a claim about localized subtitle text. cooldowns describe the examined ai conditions; actual spoken lines can also depend on table selection and game circumstances. the native source identifies distinct sound talk tables for rangers, squad leaders, fencers, spriggans, grim reapers, civilians and alien types, so a per-actor fixed sound cannot capture the full event machinery. source: edf5/soldier-ai.md, edf5-npc-talk-lines, edf5-npc-talk-triggers, edf5-talk-sgo-tables. native code and root.cpk table census; no newly recorded dialogue session.

edf6 havok assets use a specific binary-tagfile generation edf6's native havok files are havok 2020.1 binary tagfiles, with tag0 as the container magic and sdk version text 20200100. the physics types are primarily hknp*; navmesh types are hkai*, and animation/ragdoll data may refer to hka*. these names matter because older havok 2014 hkp* files may be readable by a legacy parser without satisfying the data contract expected by a modern edf6 loader. section header each section begins with eight bytes: a big-endian u32 combining two high kind bits and a 30-bit byte count including the header, followed by a four-character section tag. kind=0 describes a container that can contain subsections; kind=1 describes data. the object's serialized data field values are little-endian, so byte order is not uniform across the file. section recorded role tag0 top-level tagfile container sdkv havok sdk version string 20200100 data serialized objects and arrays, little-endian values type container for tst1, tna1, fst1, tbdy, tpad tst1 type-name strings tna1 named type declarations and template arguments fst1 member-name strings tbdy field/layout definitions for types indx / item indexed object, array and string locations the surveyed edf6 files do not contain thsh type hashes or a ptch patch table. that is a finding for this native corpus, not a claim that the broader havok serialization format never uses such sections. source: edf knowledge hub edf6/havok-format.md, facts tagfile-identity, tagfile-sections, source sgo/build scope havok 2020.1 (static file census).

metadata descriptors and object values use different encodings the havok tna1 and tbdy streams use variable-length packed integers. ordinary leading patterns are 0xxxxxxx (1 byte, 7 bits), 10xxxxxx (2 bytes, 14 bits), 110xxxxx (3 bytes, 21 bits) and 111xxxxx (4 bytes). tna1 additionally recognizes 0xe8 followed by a big-endian u32, used for large numeric values. type and member names are referred to by an indexed string table padded with 0xff. tbdy is not a stream of ordinary c structs. it specifies a packed type index, parent, flag mask and optional sub-type flags, version, serialized size/alignment, member descriptors and interfaces. the known sub-type families distinguish bool, integer, float, pointer, class, array and tuple. for example the source identifies type flag 0x05 for floating point, 0x06 for pointer, 0x07 for class and 0x08 for array. these describe the serialized data layout, which need not equal x64 runtime class memory offsets. item references indx/item contains 12-byte records. record zero is null. each record stores the item flags/type index, offset from data's start and element count. pointer, array and string fields inside data store u32 item indices rather than native memory pointers. value concept native tagfile representation hkrefptr<t> and t* u32 index into item hkarray<t> u32 item index; length obtained from item hkstringptr u32 index to a nul-terminated char item hkreal little-endian ieee float32 hkhalf16 upper 16 bits of float32 (bfloat16), not ieee binary16 tuple fixed-size type-defined sequence the source has not decoded hkufloat8 in this corpus. it would be incorrect to describe it using a guessed ieee half/byte mapping. likewise an unused type declaration in tna1 may have no corresponding tbdy object entry when no instance requires it. source: edf6/havok-format.md, tagfile-packed-ints, tagfile-tbdy, tagfile-items-values. static tagfile format analysis.

a shkt is an object graph, not only a mesh or a skeleton the typical edf6 object/weapon shkt file has an hkrootlevelcontainer with a named variant called “physics data” or “physics scene data”. its class is hknpphysicsscenedata, which points to one or more system data nodes. those nodes hold material tables, motion properties, body cinfos, attachment relations, constraints and the overall physics-system name. the system node is either ordinary hknpphysicssystemdata or, for ragdolls, hknpragdolldata with additional skeleton, bone-to-body mapping and body-tag arrays. hknpbodycinfo properties are not identical to authored render-mesh metadata. some shape graphs use hknpconvexshape, hknpconvexhull, hknpcompoundshape, hknpcapsuleshape, hknpcompressedmeshshape and simple primitives. survey sizes the source enumerated 316 shkt/hkt physics scene files and over 100 native type classes (108 in the reported census). examples of files containing types: havok type files containing type hknpphysicsscenedata 316 hknpphysicssystemdata 238 hknpragdolldata 78 hknpbodycinfowithattachment 316 hknpmaterial 316 hknpmotionproperties 294 hknprefmassdistribution 151 hknprefdragproperties 145 hknpconvexshape / hknpconvexhull 288 hknpcompoundshape 212 hknpcapsuleshape 91 hknpcompressedmeshshape 58 the class list also contains legacy-named hkpragdollconstraintdata and hkplimitedhingeconstraintdata embedded as constraint schemas. their presence does not imply that the file's entire physics scene uses an old hkpphysicsdata root. a particularly useful negative finding: _has_hka in a filename does not guarantee an hkaskeleton. none of the eleven suffix-matched files in this census had one, while 78 other files did. only the actual tagfile type graph establishes this. source: edf6/havok-format.md, shkt-object-tree, havok-class-census. static native corpus survey, not a new in-game collision experiment.

edf6 compressed collision meshes encode coordinates with two quantizers a hknpcompressedmeshshapedata.meshtree contains one or more sections. each section supplies packed-vertex and primitive index ranges, a shared-vertex reference range and a local coordinate codec. in the source corpus, two vertex encodings coexist: vertex kind encoded width axis allocation reconstruction section packed vertex 32 bits x 11, y 11, z 10 offset_xyz + scale_xyz × integer_xyz mesh-wide shared vertex 64 bits x 21, y 21, z 22 domain.min + (domain.max-domain.min) × integer/(2^bits-1) a primitive is a 4-byte four-index record referring first to the section's own packed vertices, otherwise through an indexed mesh-wide shared-vertex table. if the third and fourth values match, the record is a triangle. otherwise it is a quad split into two triangles, (0,1,2) and (0,2,3). the first equals second sentinel is used in the separate convex-hull compressed-mesh family. the source census identifies two nonmixed classes of compressed mesh in object/weapon files: 82 convex-only and 214 triangle-only (296 total). edf6 maps contribute many more compressed-mesh sections in the separate map corpus. in triangle-kind sections the observed maxima are 127 primitives, 107 packed vertices and 198 shared-vertex references per section. mesh-wide shared vertices are frequently reused across sections and support boundaries without duplicating their coordinates independently. the source reports 174,419 quad records and 23,318 triangle records within the inspected triangle-kind corpus. those are encoded primitive counts, not a count of distinct physical bodies or on-screen graphics triangles. source: edf6/havok-format.md, compressed-mesh-encoding, compressed-mesh-kinds, compressed-mesh-triangle-kind. this is serialized collision geometry, not the edf6 visible fmb render model.

collision mesh primitives have a stable indexed key and a spatial tree in the edf6 compressed collision profile, the observed shape key is a section/primitive combination: section_index << 8 | primitive_index << 1, with the low bit selecting the second triangle of a quad. source fields numshapekeybits, maxkeyvalue and numprimitivekeys describe key storage and triangle coverage. the corpus has a recorded exception to one naïve key-width relationship, so using only the number of primitives to predict key width is not generally reliable. an all-ones value can also collide with sentinel use if key width is underestimated; the separate mad source research records this problem. the native aabb structure is hierarchical. each section has a packed aabb4bytescodec tree that divides its primitives. the mesh has a top aabb5bytescodec tree over sections. nodes are stored in preorder. an inner section-tree node encodes an offset to its right child while its left child is the next node; a leaf encodes the primitive index. a source formula maps each child min/max axis to low/high nibbles within its parent aabb. the author reconstructed the section-tree quantization from 2,400 axis values in the convex-only corpus with byte-identical results. that is strong evidence for these serialized field rules, but it is not equivalent to proving the game’s own physical collision outcome for newly constructed meshes. the top tree uses a different 5-byte codec and must not be decoded with the section-tree rule. the source also notes that an outer shape's numeric key does not by itself identify the visible object material or npc owner: those require the collision material and game-object context in the enclosing hkt/shkt graph. source: edf knowledge hub edf6/havok-format.md, facts compressed-mesh-keys, compressed-mesh-trees; independent mdb/mad key-width source guidance remains separate.

a recognized field is not necessarily a understood gameplay rule the hknpcompressedmeshshape source census contains mass properties, a mesh domain and triangleisinterior bit information. these can be extracted exactly; their physical purpose is not equally well established. mass properties. the examined source describes the domain bounding box as the basis of its stored volume and center. its inertial terms correspond to 1.5× those of an equivalent solid box, using a formula of the form 1.5 × m × (b²+c²)/12 for a principal axis. the body's configured mass and the mass field of a compressed shape agree throughout the 82 convex-kind meshes, but only in 86 of 214 triangle-kind meshes. therefore one cannot infer every body's active mass from that shape's mass property alone. the corpus also contains special source-specific density/mass selections. interior triangles. in the triangle-kind data, 112,419 of 372,156 possible keys are marked interior. the researchers found that flagged triangles do not have open edges in the surveyed files, but no tested combination of edge-closure, planarity, convexity, concavity or quad-half conditions reproduced the bit pattern well. the field was attributed to havok authoring tools; its exact semantic rule remains unresolved. do not replace it with a guessed geometry test and claim native identity. these distinctions matter for reasoning about static geometry and possible collision behavior, but the wiki does not claim that changing such fields has been qualified through an actual edf6 runtime test. source: edf6/havok-format.md, compressed-mesh-mass, triangle-is-interior (native file and disassembly census; open semantic question).

an edf6 .mad map file is an archive around a havok tagfile the examined map .mad files use a marc version-5 wrapper, not a raw havok file at byte zero. in the source corpus, each of the 50 map mads contains exactly one collision.hkt entry. the payload starts at byte 0x24 and is a native tag0 havok tagfile. the name block is utf-16le, stored after the payload aligned to a 16-byte boundary. mad field meaning in the observed 50 native examples +0x00 ascii marc +0x04 version 5 +0x08 payload offset 0x24 +0x0c name-block offset relative to +0x24 +0x10 payload byte size +0x14 file-entry table offset relative to its own field +0x18 file count 1 +0x1c absolute name-block offset +0x20 utf-16 name length including terminator (14 code units) +0x24 collision.hkt tag0 payload, padded to 16 bytes the trailing name text is collision.hkt\0 in utf-16le. the entry record holds a signed relative name offset, payload offset and length, then reserved zero fields. the native rule set reproduces the 50 scanned wrappers byte for byte. that establishes the wrapper format for this corpus; it does not prove every unknown modded or future mad has exactly one member. the hkt payload itself still has to be interpreted as havok physics data: understanding marc offsets alone says nothing about whether a body's collision layer, mesh bvh, mass or joint setup is accepted at runtime. source: edf6/havok-format.md, fact mad-marc-layout. static byte-level audit of 50 map archives.

constraint data is more than two attached body names edf6 shkt ragdoll joint definitions contain a child/parent relationship, local frames and limit parameters. the analyzed native constraints assign bodya to the child and bodyb to the parent; local joint-frame transforms reconstruct nearly coincident pivots in model space. across the surveyed constraint bodies the measured pivot mismatch was at most about 0.8 mm. the source's class census includes hkpragdollconstraintdata, hkplimitedhingeconstraintdata, hkpprismaticconstraintdata, hkphingeconstraintdata and hkpwheelconstraintdata inside the modern scene graph. motor enablement was absent for the surveyed ragdoll and limited-hinge pattern. the nominal target rotation records refer to the transformb frame rather than a second arbitrary world-space pose. angular limits are stored with redundant calculated values including inverse cosine and tangent terms, with special sentinels near singular angles, around ±π, for a cone without a lower bound and near π/2. the source derived these rules from thousands of native constraints and reproduced the numeric values using the appropriate single/double-precision order. one should not overwrite only a displayed angular limit and assume the dependent serialized values remain consistent. this is a format-level mathematical observation. it does not demonstrate that editing a joint makes a character's ragdoll behave plausibly in the game; mass, local transforms, body assignment, collision layers and constraint logic all matter. source: edf6/havok-format.md, facts constraint-value-rules, havok-class-census.

an engine that recognizes an old file format may not instantiate its physics bodies for edf6, source navigation companions *.navmesh.nvmd and *.navmesh_h.nvmd begin with bytes 44 4d 56 4e, the little-endian representation of the four-character value nvmd, followed by version 0x130. the native code checks the identifier and version. the remaining nvmd structure was not analyzed in the source chapter; treating its later bytes as decoded path polygons or point indices would be unsupported. the game's dll also contains a legacy havok binary tagfile reader named hkserialize::tagfilereadformat2014 and many old hkp* classes alongside the modern hknp* system. this is valuable compatibility evidence, but recognition of the old serialization is not proof that every old hkt or shkt is usable by every edf6 subsystem. a map collision loader and a character ragdoll path can enforce different root-type, conversion and solver requirements. this particularly matters for edf4.1/edf5 assets retained within later archives. a file's extension, a successful read of its old tagfile header and an actual functioning havok body in-game are three distinct gates. the source's older experiment with ragdoll_testvehicle401.hkt is explicitly documented as unresolved for that isolated reader test. later subsystem-specific evidence must be consulted instead of extrapolating. source: edf6/havok-format.md, nvmd-header, legacy-tagfile-reader. unresolved nvmd fields remain marked unknown.

equal objects do not imply equal serialized file bytes edf6 havok tagfiles are indexed object graphs. reproducing a native tagfile requires more than emitting each object's fields in any convenient order. the studied files use an item numbering and payload traversal convention that can change every downstream item reference if one reference is serialized too early. in the native source census, item 1 is the root. referenced pointer targets enter an object queue in discovery order. after an object, the writer emits what is reachable from it without crossing another object pointer (its local closure), visiting member references in serialized type order and base-class members first. for long arrays, the research found 1024-element chunks. strings are delayed until after the enclosing item and identical string values share one item. every payload item is aligned to its declared tagfile type alignment with zero-fill, and the overall data section is padded to a 16-byte boundary. an empty array is represented with a null item reference, not a non-null item with a zero element count. pointers can target the same object from multiple owners; these references must share the same item identity to preserve the graph. these conventions were reported to reproduce the native byte organization for 316 object shkts, eight navmesh test files and 50 map collision hkts. the counts belong to the researched corpus and should not be generalized to every possible file from different game versions. this page describes native serialized data invariants, not the architecture of any particular third-party editor. source: edf knowledge hub edf6/havok-format.md, tagfile-writer-rules, tagfile-items-values. static, source-corpus byte identity.

the multi byte changes which ready events execute the inspected edf5 bvm runtime stores a registration's delay at record offset +0x18, and its multi flag at +0x20. the scheduler's native comparison is exact: multi == 1 means append all ready registrations; otherwise choose one eligible registration with the greatest delay. this is not a generic nonzero/truthy bit interpretation. observed registration population multi=0 multi=1 total 141 shipping bvm scripts, raw 4,619 574 5,193 141 shipping bvm scripts, reachable 4,540 572 5,112 exact44 matched source set, reachable 1,993 221 2,214 no other multi values appeared in the shipping census. the corresponding edf6 angelscript scheduler uses event_type_sync=0 (one best ready event) and event_type_async=1 (all ready events). thus the appropriate source behavior comparison is multi == 1 versus any other value, not multi != 0. four official edf6 source ports—m015, m016, m024, m035—have event-type totals that differ from the edf5 source; these are observed port authoring deviations, not a discovered extra bit in the original edf5 flag. end-event time sentinel across the 44 exact original/official mission pairs, a special source end registration whose delay is exactly 100.0f becomes 100000000.00 in the official target representation. do not apply a blanket time unit multiplication to ordinary delays, and do not equate this special case with all references to 100 in arbitrary scripts. distinct factor operations the mapped factors include 9201 object destroyed, 9202 object encountered, 9300 ai movement end, 9301 movement end or death, 9116 group member count, 9117 group encounter, and 9205 ride vehicle. 9201 and 9202 are distinct registered conditions. the exact44 reachable factor census achieved 2,147/2,147 source/reference sites; it is bounded, not proof of all conceivable mission factors. evidence: static comparison and edf5/edf6 native scheduler reverse engineering, source facts bvm-multi-flag, bvm-multi-to-event-type, bvm-multi-census, bvm-end-event-sentinel, official-port-eventtype-deviations, bvm-factor-map.

a count in a squad call usually counts followers, not leaders several observed edf5 custom-call layouts differ from names inferred from older disassemblers. this is important for reading enemy numbers: the leader sgo, follower sgo, count, active flag, spawn point and hp scalar occupy distinct argument positions. call native source meaning (ordered arguments) 2009 area ground enemy group: shape, sgo, count, hp scale, active, extra float (6) 2011 enemy at spawn: spawn point, sgo, hp scale, active, extra float (5) 1022 / 1023 transporter: spawn point, drop route, carrier sgo, string, cargo vehicle sgo, float (6) 1013 friendly squad: id, spawn point, radius, semicolon-joined follower sgos, count, hp scale 2020 / 2021 start with object id, then spawn point, radius, sgo, count, hp scale 2030 enemy squad: spawn point, radius, leader sgo, leader hp, follower sgo, follower count, follower hp, active 2200 drop-boat crew: drop-boat object id, leader sgo, leader hp, follower sgo, follower count, follower hp, active 2200 uses the boat as its first argument and the leader's sgo as its second. for example dlc mission dm003 uses one e503_armorfrog_sg_leader and three e503_armorfrog_af followers. the first sgo does not become a spawn point. similarly m044's 2030 creates one e506_biggrey_sg_leader and three e506_biggrey_af. mistaking the follower count for a leader count would triple the leader population in that example. a repeated generator's amount has still different semantics: it can cap live instances in a wave rather than count the total enemies created over the entire mission. native generator mechanics documents that boundary. evidence: edf5 bvm argument/corpus interpretation bvm-spawn-call-layouts-2, bvm-call-2200-dropboat-squad, bvm-squad-leader-once, bvm-generator-calls-2100-2101. source static; runtime spawn scheduling also depends on event conditions.

setgenerator configures a persistent spawner, not one immediate batch the observed edf5 bvm uses 2100 setgenerator to configure repeating generation, and 2101 to release a one-time batch. in the 141 shipping source bvms, 2100 occurs 609 times across 49 scripts; 2101 occurs 270 times across 28 scripts. in the game binary their call handlers prepare a native object message 0x20100; the receiver is a generator component of a ship, hive, nest, anchor, fortress or boss. 0x20100 payload offset meaning in the examined edf5.exe build +0x00 mode: 0 repeating (2100), 1 one-shot (2101) +0x04 wave interval in frames; repeating script interval multiplied by 60 +0x08 amount: wave size / live cap for repeating mode +0x0c gap between individual spawns in frames; script parameter ×60 +0x10 enemy hp multiplier, already multiplied by mission script global factor +0x14 boolean flag +0x18 spawned sgo path +0x38 observed constant 1 +0x40 hatch/generator index for the repeating mode, the game keeps a standing setup and an active setup. each update decreases wave and per-spawn delays, checks the pool slot, spawns one unit when eligible, and reduces the remaining count. after the last position in the wave, it reuses the standing setup. a pool slot still occupied by a living enemy is skipped; the amount is not the total number created in the whole encounter. a one-shot 2101 has no such persistent pool slot reservation; when it ends, it returns control to the standing setup. eight observed component owners are generatorpoll (teleport anchors), anthill, bignest, movingfortress, humanoid_biggreyboss, ufocarrier, ufomother511, and ufomother511ringunitparts. some have generator arrays and select an element by hatch index. the source identifies additional 0x20101 signaling used as a wave gate by certain ship/ring components; it is not demonstrated to apply to all eight owner types. a frequent cataloging error is to read the 2100 wave cap as a fixed enemy count. this miscounts missions with infinite/repeated spawning. the message fields above are native edf5 executable reconstruction, not a universal offset map for edf6. evidence: static steam-5d11de53 reverse engineering bvm-generator-calls-2100-2101, bvm-setgenerator-native, generator-message-0x20100, generator-waves-repeat, generator-owner-classes; includes game rvas in the underlying research, but no new game session test.

two different hp modifiers can affect one enemy edf5 has a script-wide enemy factor and a per-object durability adjustment. treating both as a single difficulty setting obscures native behavior, particularly when waves spawned later in a mission differ in strength. cuscall0 20 takes a float and writes the current script enemy multiplier to the audited build's script field +0x414 (initialized to 1.0). later native spawn calls multiply their own hp argument by this active factor. the source survey found 28 call sites in 14 shipping missions, often in difficulty branches: in m065 the observed hard/hardest/inferno values include 0.9, 0.8, 0.75. this factor changes subsequent spawns; it does not itself establish retroactive modification of every already-created enemy. cuscall0 3019 instead takes (object handle, percent). the recovered handler multiplies an object's max hp at +0x1f8 by percent / 100 and assigns its current hp at +0x1fc the minimum of its old current hp × factor and the new maximum. this is not simply “set remaining hp percent.” the 141-script source set has 54 calls across 14 scripts, sometimes used for friendly vehicles (e.g. m041's combat frames and railguns at 10%). the final hp of an individual spawn may therefore depend on its own sgo baseline, the per-spawn argument, the active 20 factor and later 3019 operations, with float32 multiplication order affecting exact parity. the source survey found factors other than 1 in 65/141 missions; in 38 missions the same sgo receives different hp factors on the same difficulty depending on wave. m015 has ordinary black-ant groups with factor 1.0 and repeating teleport-ship waves with factor 0.7; m009's final two spider groups use factor 0.5. do not apply these offsets blindly to edf6 structures. also do not equate hp scalar and attack scalar without inspecting each native actor class; the available attribution to jp wiki discussions is narrower than a universal engine proof. evidence: native edf5 executable and source-script static census bvm-call-20-hp-factor, bvm-spawn-hp-factors, bvm-call-3019-durability, bvm-eval-call-3019, bvm-switch-form; no new live damage measurement.

enemy counts cannot be determined from simple string or call-site frequency the retained original edf5 source analysis covers 141 shipping bvm scripts. custom call 21 queries difficulty in the observed source set: its numeric cases represent easy through inferno (0–4). a mission may branch on this value and modify spawn counts, hp factors, generator parameters or event timing. across the source survey, 92/141 missions change enemy lists or counts by difficulty. the study records that 111/141 call 21; other scripts can still vary by external game difficulty logic. a source walkthrough must preserve branches, repeated event handlers and loops. for example, an edf5 switch can place case bodies before a backward dispatch ladder: a reader that follows the physical instruction order can accidentally run the last difficulty case for every mission. in m059 the correct sampled blue tadpole count across difficulties is 2 / 4 / 6 / 8, not 8 at every difficulty. the script totals were compared with historical japanese wiki tables (not all tables were expressed in the same way). exact totals across difficulties were found in 23 missions, with another 21 matching only at inferno. remaining differences are not automatically errors in the bvm interpreter. generators can spawn repeated waves; a wiki may show an infinity marker, an interval or the highest difficulty's population, rather than a raw sequential script count. concrete examples show different interpretations: m021 / offline 31: source script spawns 240 enemies in its audited path; the wiki reports 335 because it counts the outpost itself and 94 turrets inside the sgo (240 + 1 + 94 = 335). m000 / offline 1: script and wiki totals differ because one ant is created as an event object and two target-group handlers exist; the summary lists only one of the two groups. m004: the source survey gives 153/155 teleport anchors on examined paths; the source author explicitly marked the 28-anchor repeat hypothesis unverified. do not relabel its runtime explanation as proven. m008: a carrier wait loop can remain active until external event state changes; simply stopping at a repeated branch undercounts later enemies. the observations establish the importance of mission execution context. they do not establish an exact final number of enemies killed in a live game session, which also depends on death, generator ownership and player actions. evidence: bvm-getdifficulty-21, bvm-per-difficulty-eval, bvm-eval-loop-exit-fix, bvm-switch-form, bvm-wiki-gaps-explained (static), m004-anchor-event-twice (unverified). two exact mission-table cross-checks these examples compare specific source script states with external japanese mission tables, not generic difficulty scaling claims: m046_3 (offline 70 / online 69): eight waiting imperial drones consist of one 2006 area group of five plus three 2001 createenemy2 calls, all inactive at spawn and scalar 1.0. the cited sergeant's factor 1.5 is a 1010 friendly leader, and the railgun factor 2.0 comes from 1029. a later fourth drone switches to attack mode via 3022. this bvm has no 21 getdifficulty, so its authored enemy list is fixed across difficulties in the inspected script. m081 (scorched earth; offline 108 / online 107): verified static table-vs-bvm hp factors include deroy 0.65, spiders 0.8, type-2 drones 0.7, greys 0.8, queen bee 0.7 and imperial drones 0.7. the extra-large teleport anchor is 0.36 at hard and below, 0.48 at hardest/inferno. four large anchors use 0.6 / 0.8 by difficulty; the mission-wide call-20 factor is 1 / 1 / 0.9 / 0.9 / 0.8. these are two distinct multiplier layers, not a combined final native hp value. evidence: native source / external table static comparison for atwiki-matches-script-m046-3 and atwiki-matches-script-m081 in edf5/mission-vm.md, build steam-5d11de53. the game was not replayed for these checks.

disabling an outpost weapon can address a component group rather than spawn new enemies the original edf5 bvm call 2300 takes an object, a group argument, an index and a byte-like flag. the native dispatcher sends message 0x8000002b with these fields via the target object's message route. unlike enemy spawn calls it does not create a new enemy. the receiving class implementation was not conclusively identified in the source reverse engineering; therefore the precise flag meaning remains unresolved. the script supplies group values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. the outpost sgo's parts_setting contains a third integer field in the range 0–5, with six corresponding groups. a proposed mapping is group mask = 1 shifted left by that third field. it is supported by a specific mission count cross-check but remains a hypothesis, not a native binary handler proof. proposed mask observed sgo part category count in the studied outpost configuration 1 large cannons 3 2 medium cannons 9 4 smallcannon1 42 8 smallcannon2 52 16 smallcannon3 13 32 smallcannon1_g 6 for m021, the script activates masks 8 and later 4; 52 + 42 = 94 matches the japanese wiki's outpost turret tally in that mission. counting these 94 sgo components as ordinary scripted bvm enemy spawns would misrepresent the source: the whole outpost and its turrets can be one object hierarchy. this page distinguishes three facts: the actual 2300 message is statically established, the sgo parts grouping is observed, and the bitmask interpretation of that message's group field is unverified. evidence: bvm-calls-1141-2300, bvm-call-2300-native, outpost-part-group-mask (unverified), outpost-2300-calls-per-mission, bvm-wiki-gaps-explained. investigated edf5.exe build only. e510 fortress part resources: design differences rather than one interchangeable object the examined edf5 standard e510 composition and its edf5 dlc variant both contain 125 parts_setting entries. their top-level part order, numeric part configuration and embedded blobs are identical; 125 resource path references and 10 resource-list entries differ. this indicates that the edf5 dlc difference in the top-level asset is predominantly a resource-selection difference, while its child sgo components can encode substantially different durability and loot values. when comparing edf5 standard with edf6 standard, three small-cannon resource bindings switch from the green variant e510_fortress_parts_smallcannon1_g.sgo to the purple ...smallcannon1_p.sgo, at part indices 99, 105 and 111. these are not color-only aliases: the native green small cannon uses bullet_small_1_green / laserbullet02, while the purple version uses bullet_small_1_purple / pulsebullet01. the examined edf6 m055 fort composition differs again: six medium-cannon slots use mediumcannon_2, so it is not a safe stand-in for original edf5 dlc behavior. e510 child type edf5 dlc durability edf5 standard durability edf6 standard durability large cannon 2,400 3,600 3,600 medium cannon 1,200 1,800 1,200 small cannon 1 200 300 300 small cannon 1 aa/g/x 400 600 600 small cannon 2 ~266.667 400 400 small cannon 3 600 900 900 the inspected source dlc large/medium cannon drop_item_2 values differ too: 3.29 / 2.29 versus edf6 standard 0.29 / 0.29. exact sgo child references, weapon parameters, durability and resource availability must be assessed together, not guessed from an e510 basename. an observed 141-mission app:/object/*.sgo inventory contained 183 unique referenced object basenames and five missing from the edf6 native resource tree: four belonged to synthetic dm006_2 frog search-radius variants, and one was the original edf5 dlc e510_dlc_fortress.sgo resource. a source-only port must address their identities without falsely calling generated compatibility sgos native assets. this resource and script-mask comparison is binary/source evidence, not proof that the unlocated bvm 2300 message receiver implements every hypothesized bitmask rule. it also does not make edf5 dlc object data freely redistributable. sources: e510_fortress_dlc_feature_parity_audit_2026-08-27.json and r46_shipping141_object_resource_existence_audit_2026-08-27.json.

the archelus in m032_5 has an authored nonlethal exit the examined original mission m032_5 (listed as offline mission 37 / online mission 36, monster elimination plan) is the only source script in this surveyed set that spawns e504_monstera_m034_3, the scripted archelus variant. its sgo has game_object_level_adjust = 3. this is a mission-level cinematic/progression actor, not simply a boss with ordinary kill-to-clear logic. main creates erginus using 2000 createenemy at spawn point エルギヌス with source hp scale 0.9. handler func_3 fades the bgm, plays radio line ae005_034_e, and creates the variant archelus at spawn point 新型 (new type). the script uses 3020 setnodamagewhenhpremain with 10 and 3021 no-damage mode; it assigns advance route 新型進行ルート using 3101. later handlers disable invulnerability with a 30 minimum-hp protection and register an 9200 condition at 85% durability. the ending switches no-damage protection back on and sends archelus along 新型撤退ルート (new-type retreat route); after ae141_084_e the script clears the mission with missionclear. therefore the scripted archelus can take damage yet is not intended to be killed in this sequence. seeing it retreat without dying is supported by the authored source control flow, not evidence of a broken damage model. boundary: the original contributor did not completely trace which earlier registrations arm the last two event blocks. this is a source script reconstruction, not a new full in-game observation of every radio cue, branch and animation. do not infer a universal 3020 threshold abi for every edf edition from this one mission. evidence: m032-5-scripted-archelus, original disassembly lines and contributor source notes from edf5/mission-vm.md.

edf 4.1 original map geometry: 16-family mad survey and 3d surface connectivity what was measured: a bounded, read-only analysis of original edf 4.1 map geometry, using native source mac/mad data. evidence: original game asset records inspected offline; not a recovered game pathfinding graph and not a runtime playtest. results below are from the r21 sample dated 15 november 2026 and apply to that specific corpus and selection method. what the survey actually establishes all 16 inspected map families yielded parseable source geometry from a retained, root-preserving 18-family source archive; 31 static-body samples contain 284,840 triangles in total. for an hkpstorageextendedmeshshape with multiple meshstorage pools, vertices need independent pool-local index decoding and rebasing before a combined triangle list is meaningful. each trianglessubparts subpart has its own offsets, transform and index/count bounds; simply concatenating indices without the subpart mapping can corrupt the apparent geometry. the earlier two sk_crater01 road bodies that had been rejected by a single-storage assumption were successfully decoded: sk_craterroad01 2,430 triangles and sk_craterroad02 2,394 triangles. this is a native source-mesh format observation, not evidence that a particular npc can traverse the roads. 3d adjacency is not 2d footprint overlap for the sample, candidate surface triangles were filtered by an absolute normal-based 55° slope rule and joined only when their quantized three-dimensional edges matched (weld tolerance 0.001 source units). triangles overlapping in the xz plane but lying at different heights were not joined. this matters for multi-storey buildings, caves, roofs and bridges: a 2d top-down polygon graph cannot by itself tell whether two surfaces connect physically. an absolute-normal slope check is orientation-agnostic: ceiling triangles may qualify alongside floor triangles. edge-connected components are therefore diagnostic geometry components, neither guaranteed walkable areas nor independently proven havok navmesh islands. winding, obstacles, agent width, step height, stairs/doors and links between different bodies remain separate problems. per-map bounded source sample the table reports only the sampled bodies, not the full static scene, and should not be used as a map-wide triangle budget. component counts are edf5 → edf6 humanoids: standing and low postures, capsule contacts, and collision welding scope and provenance. this page reconstructs a bounded case: edf5 dlc1 dm001 imported into an edf6 build using the native cave501 map and a stock edf6 humanoid_basic-family enemy (e506, with e503/e617 controls). it connects measured map/character geometry with static binary analysis and reported modded-game runtime observations. it is not a universal rule for all enemies, map ceilings or retail builds. the underlying detailed research log predates the later practical route resolution; see the current dm001 case study. the apparent paradox: why can the enemy traverse a gap it cannot initially occupy? in the original diagnostic k spawn, the alien appeared at the specified position, was briefly visible in a pre-animation/t-pose state and then rapidly moved up through the cave ceiling. similar behavior occurred for other humanoid_basic-family comparators, arguing against an e506-mesh-only defect. a delayed route assignment did not prevent the first-frame displacement: the early failure preceded execution of the scripted walking route. the sampled native cave501 floor-to-ceiling clearance at k was approximately 15.7716 world units. two nearby successful initialization positions, o and n, had approximately 15.9973 and 16.7999. once initialized safely, a humanoid could later stoop and traverse a passage with approximately 13.8694 units of clearance. these figures do not establish a clearance threshold. moving the spawn also changes which individual triangle, edge and contact manifold the capsule intersects. at k, the vertical ceiling query hit near a triangle vertex: closest edge distance about 0.00481, ceiling normal approximately (0.0459, -0.9975, 0.0531). this near-vertical surface normal favors upward separation for a deep collision, but the exact solver response is not recovered solely from the geometry. shape dimensions and postures read-only reverse engineering reported the following nominal profile geometry in both edf5 and edf6 for the studied humanoid_basic class: profile capsule spine endpoints, local units radius overall nominal vertical extent standing (d10) (0,4.5,0) to (0,20.5,0) 4.5 about 25 low / stoop (d18) (0,4.5,0) to (0,7.5,0) 4.5 about 12 there are additional physical profiles. the same nominal standing geometry makes “edf6 simply enlarged the alien capsule” an insufficient explanation for the observed difference. initialization exposes the standing body; later locomotion can choose a smaller physical profile. the two phases must be evaluated separately. different havok contact paths edf5 uses the older hkpcharacterrigidbody path. the audited code has character-specific capsule-contact unwelding: for eligible contacts along the standing capsule, a normal originating from local triangle geometry can be redirected using the capsule's axis/shape. its depth eligibility boundary is near the negative capsule radius (-4.5 for this case). an ideal infinite roof plane intersecting the central capsule spine also yields a signed capsule-plane separation of about -r. that coincidence makes the actual edge/vertex feature and small changes of penetration depth important. edf6 uses an hknpcharacterrigidbody-based sandlot wrapper. its studied character-body quality is 10 (preset_character), which requests flag 0x80 = enable_neighbor_welding. the native cave501 static-body quality supports that bit. the character's configured capsule radius is passed into hknpcharacterrigidbodycinfo.weldingtolerance (+0x6c in the audited layout), so its runtime material uses about 4.5 rather than the constructor's nominal approximately 0.1. this is an observed active parameter path, not merely a debug string. the native cave501 world has enablepenetrationrecovery=1, collision tolerance approximately 0.05 and aabb margin approximately 0.02; the studied humanoid does not opt out of penetration recovery. the capsule also has a reported maxallowedpenetration of about 1.484375. none of these values, individually, is established as a hard ejection threshold. in particular, knowing that neighbor welding is requested does not reveal the final welded contact normal or prove it alone caused the upward movement. engine-level distinction: edf5's character-specific late normal rewrite and edf6's earlier hknp neighbor-welded manifold handling are meaningfully different contact pipelines. the exact causal sequence feature selection → welded normal → solver/recovery output at k remains an unresolved reconstruction rather than a traced, runtime-verified chain. low-stance selection versus climbing the audited edf6 humanoid_basic state logic has a useful specific distinction. a condition equivalent to eac & 0x100 or a nonzero 10f0 counter selects the low d18 profile. two environment-query sites around virtual addresses 0x1804718da and 0x180471c7b can set 10f0 = 16. while this counter remains active, the studied update bypasses a d28-related climbcollisioncheck branch and continues through the low-state path. these addresses are specific to the analyzed edf6 binary; they are not portable patch offsets. during earlier r33/r33c diagnostics, the actor could initialize from a high-clearance position but stalled while attempting to climb at the subsequent narrow passage. a source-like humanoid_climb_setting=[6.0,20.5] did not by itself resolve the initial eject or this later stalled traversal. that observation narrows the problem to stance, path and contact interplay; it does not prove that the low-state counter was the sole missing input. later accepted dm001 outcome takes precedence: the practical r33p-c repair kept a safe spawn and made a native lower-branch guide the first active route target, instead of first aiming at the problematic original wp0. the resulting route was accepted in the tested mission context, with an additional encounter-timing adjustment described in dm001 r33p-c. do not present the earlier r33c stall as the current open mission blocker, or infer that the final solution changed edf6's global collision engine. what the evidence does and does not establish observed in the reported modded-game test: k first-frame upward displacement, successful alternative spawn initialization, subsequent low traversal controls, and the eventual practical r33p-c route result. static native research: matching nominal capsule profiles in the two generations; hkp-versus-hknp character contact architecture; edf6 quality/welding settings, recovery flags and low/stoop state-selection sites. proposed mechanism, not demonstrated end-to-end: a k vertex-neighbor contact retaining an upward-looking welded normal and causing solver penetration recovery through the roof. not established: a universal minimum tunnel height, a per-map automatic route-repair algorithm, identical behavior in all edf6 executable versions, or a general fix by changing only a single character sgo field. primary research source: /edf5_edf6_research/research/knowledge/dm001_root_cause_research_live_2026-08-29.md, sections 2–15 and later r33/r33c experiments. later superseding outcome: /edf5_edf6_research/research/ledgers/dm001_current_practical_authority_2026-09-04.md, as reconciled in the existing dm001 practical case page. native/sdk-based conclusions are paraphrased; proprietary source fragments are not reproduced.
